disease_original_title: pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure, Telomere-related, 3
submitted_as_notes: Regulator of telomere elongation helicase 1 (*RTEL1*) was first reported in relation to semidominant telomere biology disorder by two independent research groups in 2013 (Ballew et al., PMID: 23329068 & Walne et al., PMID: 23453664). Disease related to variation in *RTEL1* is characterized in many cases with an early onset and severe spectrum of features including but not limited to: bone marrow failure, immunodeficiency, developmental delay, microcephaly, and cerebellar hypoplasia. For cases with a later onset, respiratorypulmonary features like pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial pneumonia and dyspnea have been observed both as part of a syndromic presentation or isolated (PMID 25607374). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in the molecular mechanism or phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, autosomal dominant dyskeratosis congenita 4/ autosomal recessive dyskeratosis congenita 5 (OMIM:615190) and telomere related pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure syndrome 3 (OMIM:616373). 18 variants (3 nonsense, 1 splice-site, 1 frameshift, and 13 missense) that have been reported in 15 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 23329068, 23959892, 23453664, 25848748, 39748130) are included in this curation. Segregation in at least one family with multiple genotype positive and consistent phenotypes has a calculated eLOD of 2.31(4 genotype positive affected and 4 genotyped but unaffected; PMID: 23959892). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function, an animal model and rescue in a patient derived cell line (PMIDs: 21097466, 40530700, 23959892). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *RTEL1* and semidominant telomere biology disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen ILD GCEP on the meeting date December 16, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *ELMOD2* gene was first reported in relation to an unknown inheritance disorder of familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 2006 (Hodgson et al., PMID: 16773575). There has not been further evidence in the literature associating this gene with a specific phenotype. There is no proband described in this paper. Currently, there are no OMIM phenotypes associated with this gene.

A gene-disease relationship in the published case report was postulated by genome wide linkage analysis combined with haplotype association. However, the families were reportedly all from within three rural municipalities where the prevalence of FPF was 50-fold higher than in the rest of the country and potentially shared a common ancestor. This evidence was not scored in the present curation due to no variant being discussed.

In summary, there is no evidence for a causal role for *ELMOD2* in an unknown inheritance disorder of familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has been reported. This classification was approved by the ClinGen ILD GCEP on the meeting date October 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

FAS was first reported in relation to semidominant autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) in 1995 (Fisher et al., PMID: 7540117). ALPS is an immune dysregulation disorder caused by defective lymphocyte homeostasis and characterized by the following: 1) non-malignant lymphoproliferation (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly with or without hypersplenism) that often improves with age; 2) Autoimmune disease, mostly directed toward blood cells; 3) lifelong increased risk for both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found distinct but complementary molecular mechanisms, haploinsufficiency and dominant negativity, in a semidominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance, where monoallelic cases consistently show less severe presentations compared to biallelic cases. Additionally, loss-of-function variants affecting the extracellular domain of FAS shown reduced penetrance (~30%), appearing to require a second somatic hit or loss-of-heterozygosity to cause clinical disease, while missense variants that disrupt the FAS-FADD interaction act in a dominant negative manner and show high penetrance (~80%). Therefore, a single disease entity has been curated: autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (OMIM: 601859).
More than 100 distinct variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site, and large deletions) have been reported in more than 200 probands in several publications (PMIDs: 21490157, 34171534, 7540117, 15459303, 9028321, 9821419, 23524443) are included in this curation. For example, Hauck et al., 2011 reports on a four generation kindred with 12 heterozygous carriers of a start loss variant (c.3G>T) that presents as ALPS in a daughter and father. The proband was shown to have a loss of heterozygosity in their double-negative T-cells (PMID: 23524443). The other heterozygous carriers are affected by milder, mostly sub-clinical phenotypes, though all show impaired apoptosis cellularly. There is a failure of peripheral tolerance in FAS-ALPS resulting in an accumulation of autoreactive T cells that become double negative T cells. Impaired apoptosis also affects B cells resulting in hypergammaglobulinemia (PMID: 31309545) and production of autoantibodies observed in the autoimmune cytopenias. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be both loss-of-function or dominant negativity depending on where the FAS variant falls in the gene. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by extensive animal modeling (PMID:1910678, 7930845, 7533326, 8700897). There is a natural partial knockout allele on the MRL murine background caused by a retrotransposon insertion in intron 2 which presents as lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly when in a homozygous state (PMID: 1910678). Complete Fas KO mice have also been engineered and exhibit more severe and earlier symptoms than the natural models [PMID: 8700897].
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between FAS and semidominant autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over three decades of research. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date October 14, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFA9* and *NDUFA9*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 18, 2024. The *NDUFA9* gene encodes the NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit A9, a non-catalytic complex I accessory protein required for complex I assembly and function within the mitochondria. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The *NDUFA9* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFA9*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2012 (PMID: 22114105). *NDUFA9* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 26 [OMIM# 618247]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFA9*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFA9* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on August 21, 2019 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Moderate. 
This current curation for the association with *NDUFA9*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique missense variants identified in three unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 22114105, 28671271, 37970307). Age of onset varies from the neonatal period to childhood, and outcomes are variable. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, hypertonia, chorea, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, motor and sensory neuropathy, hearing loss, retinopathy, metabolic acidosis, and complex I deficiency in skeletal muscle and skin fibroblasts.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and by rescue studies in both HEK293T cells (PMID: 23223238) and in patient cells (PMID: 28671271).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFA9* and autosomal recessive *NDUFA9*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 18, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: intellectual developmental disorder and retinitis pigmentosa; IDDRP
disease_original_title: intellectual developmental disorder and retinitis pigmentosa; IDDRP
submitted_as_notes:
Biallelic pathogenic variants in the *SCAPER* gene were first reported in 2017 in association with autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with retinitis pigmentosa, sometimes referred to as SCAPER-related intellectual disability–retinal dystrophy syndrome (PMID: 28041643, PMID: 28794130). Affected individuals typically present with developmental delay or intellectual disability, behavioral abnormalities, short stature, and progressive retinal degeneration leading to night blindness and visual field constriction. The retinal phenotype is a consistent and defining feature but can vary in onset and severity (PMID: 28794130, PMID: 30723319; PMID: 31192531). In contrast, intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental features, although frequently co-occurring, show greater phenotypic variability and broader tissue involvement, suggesting pleiotropic effects. Functional studies demonstrate that disease-causing *SCAPER* variants disrupt ciliary dynamics, leading to abnormal cilia elongation—an established pathogenic mechanism in inherited retinal dystrophies. Therefore, for the purposes of this gene curation, *SCAPER* has been evaluated in relation to *SCAPER*-related ciliopathy.

To date, multiple loss-of-function variants have been identified in affected individuals, including frameshift, nonsense, splice-site variants (PMID: 28794130). The spectrum of pathogenic variants and the available functional data strongly support loss of function as the primary disease mechanism for *SCAPER*-related disease. Functional studies in patient-derived fibroblasts and transfected cell lines demonstrated that mutant SCAPER proteins show abnormal localization to the primary cilium, particularly at the ciliary tip, in contrast to wild-type SCAPER, which is rarely detected along the ciliary axoneme. Cells expressing mutant SCAPER exhibited elongated cilia, suggesting impaired ciliary disassembly. These findings implicate SCAPER in ciliary dynamics and link its dysfunction to retinal degeneration and neurodevelopmental phenotypes, consistent with a ciliopathy-like mechanism (PMID: 28794130, PMID: 30723319).

This gene-disease relationship is further supported by experimental evidence that SCAPER (S-phase Cyclin A–Associated Protein in the ER) encodes a large nuclear and cytoplasmic protein involved in cell cycle regulation and ciliary dynamics. SCAPER was originally identified as a cyclin A–interacting protein, with expression peaking during late G1 and S phase, suggesting a role in S-phase progression and mitotic regulation (PMID: 28794130, PMID: 30723319). *SCAPER* is ubiquitously expressed across a wide range of human tissues, including retina and brain. SCAPER is robustly expressed in the retina, where it localizes predominantly to the cytoplasm of retina cells, and is detected across multiple retinal layers, with highest expression in the retinal pigment epithelium and in photoreceptor inner and outer segments (PMID: 28794130, PMID: 30723319).

In summary, *SCAPER* is Definitively associated with *SCAPER*-related ciliopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated across multiple studies in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time without the emergence of conflicting evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina gene Curation Expert Panel on January 15th, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

*CWC27* was first reported in relation to retinitis pigmentosa with or without skeletal anomalies in 2017 (Xu et al., PMID: 28285769). Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia-retinitis pigmentosa syndrome is characterized by retinal degeneration (average onset of night blindness of 10 years of age, followed by restriction of visual fields), brachydactyly (affects primarily the distal phalanges), craniofacial abnormalities (include frontal bossing, downslanting palpebral fissures, large columella, hypoplastic nares, micrognathia, and large low-set ears), short stature, and neurologic defects. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, no differences were found in molecular mechanism (loss-of-function) and inheritance pattern (autosomal recessive) among the reported cases with or without skeletal features. As a result, diverse cases have been curated under the lumped disease term *CWC27*-related retinopathy with or without syndromic features.

This curation includes ten variants (five nonsense, three frameshift, and two disrupting splicing) that have collectively been reported in ten probands in four publications (PMID: 28285769, PMID: 36718996, PMID: 31481716, PMID: 34828430). The variants segregated fully with disease, and were not found in the heterozygous state. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss-of-function.

This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence. CWC27 encodes a member of the cyclophilin family of peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases. However, the N-terminal peptidyl-prolyl isomerase domain lacks catalytic activity due to its lack of a conserved active-site tryptophan, and is instead predicted to be a proline-binding protein. Three mouse models have been created; *Cwc27K338fs/K338fs* and two versions of *Cwc27* knockout, where all three models recapitulated the ocular phenotypes observed in human subjects (PMID: 28285769). The *Cwc27K338fs/K338fs* mouse, which carried the equivalent of the hypomorphic C-terminally truncating human allele p.Val335Serfs13, showed late onset ocular defects with no significant embryonic lethality compared to the more severe phenotype observed in the two *Cwc27* knockout mouse models (high embryonic lethality, growth retardation, ocular defects, and craniofacial/limb defects). The decreased severity of the phenotype may be explained by incomplete loss of expression of *Cwc27* (PMID: 28285769).

In summary, *CWC27* is Definitively associated with *CWC27*-related retinopathy with or without syndromic features. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of conflicting evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 3rd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Pathogenic variants in MAN2A2 were first reported to cause a novel autosomal recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG) in 2023 [Mahajan et al., PMID:36357165]. MAN2A2 (also known as alpha-MIIx) is a protein coding gene mapped to chromosome 15q16.1. It is predicted to be involved in N-glycan processing, enabling alpha-mannosidase activity. Two recent reports describe three unique variants in humans, including a homozygous truncating variant [PMID:36357165], a missense mutation, and a premature stop codon [PMID:40628855] in association with a MAN2A2-related CDG. Common symptoms among the reported cases include dysmorphic facial features,  neurodevelopmental disturbance with mild/moderate intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, additional psychiatric issues such as bipolar disorder, social withdrawal, and emotional dysregulation [PMIDS:36357165, 40628855]. This gene-disease relationship is supported by relevant genetic evidence (case-level functional evidence and segregation data [PMIDS:40628855, 8524845]) and experimental evidence (an animal model [PMID:16754854] and expression studies [PMIDS:40628855, 8524845]). A complementation assay for MAN2A2 was recently created, allowing for future screening of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) [PMID:36357165]. Currently, the biological evidence is clear, but clinical evidence is lacking. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on December 1, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

CHST14 (OMIM: 608429) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1 (OMIM:601776) in 2009 (Dundar et al., PMID: 20004762). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. The CHST14 gene encodes the enzyme carbohydrate sulfotransferase 14 which is also known as Derman-4-O sulfotransferase. This enzyme actively transfers an active sulfate to position 4 of N-acetyl-D-galactosamine residues on dermatan sulfate. Pathogenic variants in the CHST14 gene result in a deficiency of dermatan sulfate, disrupting glycosaminoglycan constituents in fibroblasts impairing collagen fibril linkage. The disease mechanism is therefore loss-of –function. 
The major clinical features include distinctive craniofacial dysmorphism, congenital contractures including adducted thumbs and clenched fists, clubfeet, severe kyphoscoliosis, muscular hypotonia, hyperextensible thin skin that bruises easily and atrophic scarring, wrinkled palms, joint hypermobility, and ocular involvement (PMID: 34815299). Affected fetuses have been found to have the following ultrasound abnormalities: congenital contractures, adducted thumbs and hydronephrosis. 
At least 26 variants (missense, nonsense, in-frame deletion and frameshift) have been reported in humans. For the purposes of this curation, 15 variants in this gene were scored in the following 7 publications: PMIDs 20004762, 20533528, 21744491, 20842734, 25703627, 30249733, 35464846. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence and/or experimental evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. This gene-disease association is supported by biochemical and expression studies (20004762, 20533528, 25703627).
In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between CHST14 and autosomal recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Prenatal Expert Panel on the 10/01/2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFS3* and *NDUFS3*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of September 19, 2024. The *NDUFS3* gene encodes a complex I subunit from the iron-sulfur protein fraction of complex I.

The *NDUFS3* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFS3*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2004 (PMID: 14729820). *NDUFS3* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 8 [OMIM# 618230].  This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFS3*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFS3* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on June 10, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *NDUFS3*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included five unique variants (four missense, one intronic variant shown to impact splicing) identified in four unrelated cases from four publications (PMIDs: 14729820, 22499348, 30140060, 33097395). Additional cases are reported in the literature, but did not meet criteria to be included in scoring (PMIDs: 36531773, 19167255). Age of onset is childhood. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, encephalomyopathy, developmental delay and regression, ataxia, dystonia, optic atrophy, pancreatitis, respiratory insufficiency, and lactic acidosis. Complex I deficiency is seen in muscle biopsy.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in non-patient cells (PMID: 30796225), and a conditional knockout mouse model (PMID: 33148885) with subsequent studies showing rescue of the phenotype with AAV vector-based gene replacement of NDUFS3 (PMID: 39169163).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFS3* and autosomal recessive *NDUFS3*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 19, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *ATP5F1D* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 9, 2026. The *ATP5F1D* gene encodes the ATP synthase F(1) subunit delta, a subunit of oxidative phosphorylation complex V.

The first and only report of the *ATP5F1D* gene in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2018 (PMID: 29478781). *ATP5F1D* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency [OMIM# 618120]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two homozygous missense variants identified in two unrelated cases from one publication (PMID: 29478781). Clinical features in affected individuals include metabolic decompensation, dilated cardiomyopathy, myopathy, developmental delay, seizures, short stature, metabolic acidosis, and lactic acidosis. Complex V deficiency was noted in skin fibroblasts.

The mechanism of disease appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and *Drosophila melanogaster* model (PMID: 29478781).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel February 9, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *MIR140* gene is located on chromosome 16 at 16q22.1 and encodes microRNA 140, a noncoding RNA gene. *MIR140* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, Nishimura type in 2019 (Grigelioniene et al., PMID: 30804514). The Nishimura type of spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia is characterized by disproportionate short stature with short limbs, small hands and feet, and midface hypoplasia with small nose. 
Evidence supporting this gene disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. One variant that has been reported in 2 probands in 1 publication (PMID: 30804514) is included in this curation. Functional analysis demonstrated that the variant causes widespread derepression of wildtype miR-140-5p targets, and the gene appears to have a loss of function effect (PMID: 30804514). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental data, specifically by an animal model showing that mice harboring the variant identified in humans displayed phenotypic features that were highly consistent with those observed in human patients (PMID: 30804514). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date January 16, 2026 (SOP Version 11) .

The relationship between *COA6* and *COA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 22, 2024. *COA6* encodes a complex IV assembly factor which participates in the biogenesis of the CuA site for complex IV. 

The *COA6* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *COA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2012 (PMID: 22277967). *COA6* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 13 [OMIM#616501]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *COA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique variants (one nonsense, two missense) identified in three unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 22277967, 25339201, 35094435). Two of the three reported individuals had fatal infantile cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis (PMIDs: 22277967, 25339201) and the third had Leigh syndrome and cardiomyopathy (PMID: 35094435).

This gene-disease association is further supported by known protein interaction with COX subunits and assembly factors (PMID: 26160915), model systems including *S. cerevisae* (PMIDs: 22984289, 24549041) and *D. rerio* (PMID: 24549041), functional alteration studies in non-patient cells (PMID: 24549041), and rescue studies (PMID: 26160915). Additional publications were reviewed but not included in scoring as a maximum score for experimental evidence had been reached (PMIDs: 31515291, 35750769). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *COA6* and autosomal recessive *COA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 22, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: dyskeratosis congenita and related telomere biology disorder
disease_original_title: dyskeratosis congenita and related telomere biology disorder
submitted_as_notes:
*RPA1* encodes the largest subunit of the Replication Protein A (RPA) complex, a single stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding hetero-trimeric protein (PMID: 9242902).

In 2022, Sharma R et al  reported 4 un-related female probands with heterozygous missense variants in *RPA1* and features of Dyskeratosis Congenita/Telomere Biology Disorder (PMID: 34767620). The three reported variants (c.718G>A, p.E240K, c.680T>C, p.V227A and c.808A>G, p.T270A) cluster to DNA-binding domain-A of RPA1 protein and are near ssDNA-binding grooves. All RPA mutant heterotrimeric proteins showed evidence of gain of function effect illustrated by increased affinity for ssDNA forming an altered complex. RPAV227A and RPAE240K showed increased capacity to unfold human telomeric G-quadruplex DNA. Clinical features in the reported probands include mucocutaneous triad of deskeratosis congenita, pancytopenia, pulmonary fibrosis and Immunodeficiency.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism or phenotypic variability between the pulmonary fibrosis and dyskeratosis congenita phenotypes. Therefore, those entities have been lumped into one entity DC/TBD (MONDO:0800467). In a pediatric malignancy cohort, Sharma et al 2023 identified 80 cases with heterozygous variants among RPA heterotrimer genes and different types of cancer (hematologic, noncentral nervous system (CNS) solid tumors, and CNS tumors) (PMID: 37869077). Unlike the aforementioned variants, pediatric cancer-associated RPA1 variants are scattered along RPA1 domains and in the linker regions. Also, there is evidence of epistasis especially in the patients with AML who are carrying variants in the DNA-binding domain-A. Therefore, patients with pediatric malignancy are not included in this curation.

One of the scored probands exhibited stabilization of blood counts- with lack of progression of mucocutaneous leukoplakia- and telomere shortening. Serial bone marrow evaluations revealed somatic genetic rescue in hematopoietic cells due to an acquired truncating (stop-gain) *RPA1* mutation and uniparental isodisomy with loss of the mutant allele, coincident with stabilization of blood counts (PMID 34767620). It is noteworthy that somatic genetic rescue has been also reported in individuals with germline variants in other telomere-related genes (PMID: 33882640).

In another patient with MDS and pre-existing facial dysmorphism, there was a combination of a GOF *RPA1* variant (c.680T>C, p.V227A) and a de-novo NRAS variant (c.35G>A (p.Gly12Asp). The father and sister of this patient who carry the *RPA1* heterozygous variant do not have a clinical phenotype. This suggests there might be epistatic modulation of the phenotype in the patient carrying heterozygous variants in the two genes. This patient is not scored for this curation, but noted for information.

This gene-disease relationship is supported by functional and cell culture model evidence. Human RPA showed ability to bind and unfold G-quadruplex, structures that inhibit telomerase activity and have to be disrupted for telomere elongation during S phase. Additionally, quadruplex opening by hRPA was much faster than observed with the complementary DNA, indicating an essential role in telomere maintenance (PMID: 16973897). Knocking-in the RPA1E240K mutation into healthy inducible pluripotent stem cells resulted in severe telomere shortening and impaired hematopoietic differentiation (PMID 34767620).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen ILD GCEP on the meeting date November 18th, 2025 (SOP Version11).

The relationship between *SDHA* and autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 11, 2025. The *SDHA* gene encodes the flavoprotein subunit of complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), which plays an essential role in both the citric acid cycle and in the electron transport chain by catalyzing the oxidation of succinate to fumarate. 

The *SDHA* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease in 2000 (PMID: 10976639). *SDHA* has been associated with four disease entities to date; autosomal recessive cardiomyopathy, dilated, 1GG [OMIM# 613642], autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1 [OMIM# 252011], autosomal dominant neurodegeneration with ataxia and late-onset optic atrophy [OMIM# 619259], and autosomal dominant pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5 [OMIM# 614165]. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, this Expert Panel found a difference in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotypic variability among several of these entities. Therefore, the two autosomal recessive disease entities (autosomal recessive cardiomyopathy, dilated, 1GG [OMIM# 613642] and autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1 [OMIM# 252011]) have been lumped into one disease entity, renamed autosomal recessive *SDHA*-related primary mitochondrial disease, and curated separately. The autosomal dominant disease entities (autosomal dominant neurodegeneration with ataxia and late-onset optic atrophy [OMIM# 619259], and autosomal dominant pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5 [OMIM# 614165]) have been split and curated separately. The autosomal dominant neurodegeneration with ataxia and late-onset optic atrophy [OMIM# 619259] disease entity is curated here and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.  

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two unique missense variants [NM_004168.4, c.1351C>T (p.Arg451Cys) and c.1984C>T (p.Arg662Cys)] identified in three unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 10976639, 27683074, 33471299). Of note, the c.1351C>T (p.Arg451Cys) variant has been reported in two unrelated cases with overlapping phenotypes and functional validation supports a deleterious effect (PMIDs: 10976639, 27683074). Clinical features in affected individuals include myopathy, ataxia, developmental delay, optic atrophy, and cardiomyopathy.
 
This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and yeast models (PMIDs: 1511876, 28724664, 39321216). Of note, this Expert Panel elected to score experimental evidence conservatively as no other complex II genes have been associated with autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease and because *SDHA* has a Definitive association with a separate phenotypic entity, autosomal dominant hereditary paraganglioma and pheochromocytomas. The mechanism of disease is unclear however further studies are needed as it is unclear why some autosomal dominant *SDHA* variants are associated with a predisposition to hereditary cancer syndromes while others are associated with a primary mitochondrial disease.

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 11, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *MRPS7* and autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of June 17, 2024. The *MRPS7* gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal subunit S7, a component of the small subunit of the mitochondrial ribosome.

The *MRPS7* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease in 2015 (PMID: 25556185). *MRPS7* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 34 [OMIM# 617872]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique variants (two missense, one nonsense) identified in two unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 25556185, 36421788). The first reported case was a child with sensorineural hearing loss, failure to thrive, pancytopenia, liver failure and elevated lactate, as well as mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiency with rescue studies performed in fibroblasts (PMID: 25556185). There was a less severely affected sibling with elevated lactate, episodic hypoglycemia, mild learning difficulties, primary adrenal failure, elevated thyroid stimulating hormone, and primary hypogonadism. The second case was a 25-year-old female with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and premature ovarian insufficiency (PMID: 36421788).

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 17, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The *NR2E3* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in 2007 (Coppetiers et al., PMID: 17564971). Affected patients typically present with night blindness between late childhood and early adulthood, and can exhibit reduced visual acuity, progression to undetectable rod function with a relatively late decline in cone function, concentric rings of hyper-autofluorescence surrounding the fovea, vascular arcades, and far periphery, visual field constriction, cystoid macular degeneration, cataract development, photophobia, and/or mixed nummular and bone spicule intraretinal pigmentation in the later stages (PMID: 17564971). The published literature has also linked *NR2E3* to cases of autosomal recessive enhanced S-cone syndrome that have been reported since 2000 (Haider et al., PMID: 10655056). These recessive cases may alternatively be diagnosed as Goldmann-Favre syndrome (PMID: 18294254), retinitis pigmentosa (PMID: 11071390) or retinoschisis (PMID: 18294254). They typically present with night blindness in childhood or adolescence and exhibit progressive loss of visual acuity and slow concentric reduction of the visual field during the subsequent decades, with some retention of vision even in elderly individuals, increased sensitivity to blue light, decreased electroretinogram responses from rods in particular but also from cones, retinal pigment epithelium atrophy with hypopigmented pigment deposits in the peripheral retina, macular schisis, and/or optic disc pallor. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, dominant cases of retinitis pigmentosa exhibited some overlap in phenotypes with recessive cases of enhanced S-cone syndrome or autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa. However, the shared mode of inheritance and molecular mechanism (biallelic loss-of-function) among recessive cases motivated enhanced S-cone syndrome and autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa to be combined into a lumped disease entity referred to as *NR2E3*-related enhanced S-cone syndrome, which has been curated separately. Cases with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance show a unique molecular mechanism (dominant negative), and contrast with the unaffected heterozygous carriers from the recessive families. For the purposes of this curation, dominant cases have been curated as a separate disease entity, referred to as *NR2E3*-related dominant retinopathy.

Two suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation, both of them missense substitutions encoding the dominant negative variant p.Gly56Arg. The NM_014249.4(NR2E3):c.166G>A and NM_014249.4(NR2E3):c.166G>C forms of the variant have collectively been identified and scored in twelve probands in seven publications (PMID: 17564971, PMID: 26910043, ). All of the probands scored in this curation harbored the variant allele in the heterozygous state. Multiple large families with evidence of co-segregation of the genotype with affected status contributed to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship (PMID: 17564971, PMID: 24938718, PMID: 26910043, PMID: 28912962, PMID: 30718709, PMID: 32531858, PMID: 36460718). Functional studies characterizing the effects of the variant are discussed in further detail below.

This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence indicating that *NR2E3* is highly specifically expressed in retinal tissues (PMID: 30239781) and encodes a ligand-dependent transcription factor that is involved in photoreceptor differentiation and suppression of cone differentiation in rod photoreceptor cells (PMID: 19379737, PMID: 37510230). The protein product physically interacts with the photoreceptor cell transcription factors NRL and CRX (PMID: 15190009), both of which are encoded by genes that can harbor inherited retinal disease-causing variants. Functional studies characterizing the p.Gly56Arg variant indicate that it preserves interaction with CRX (PMID: 19823680) but disrupts NR2E3 localization (PMID: 33807610) and DNA binding (PMID: 19823680), resulting in aberrant activation of rod-specific genes and repression of cone-specific genes (PMID: 19823680). Antisense oligonucleotide-based or CRISPR/Cas9-based therapeutic strategies for silencing the expression of the p.Gly56Arg variant are in development (PMID: 31083481, PMID: 33807610 ), but rescue experiments have not been scored as part of this gene curation.

In summary, *NR2E3* is definitively associated with *NR2E3*-related dominant retinopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 6th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*EFNB2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant syndromic congenital heart disease in 2018 (PMID: 29508392). There is one proband included in this curation who expressed a hypoplastic left ventricle that required surgery at two months old, and was found to have a missense variant in *EFNB2* (PMID: 29508392). The gene-disease relationship is supported by two mouse models, mouse model functional alteration, and expression data (PMIDs: 11880349, 15223333, 27530629, 9630219). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship due to a lack of *EFNB2* variants found and reported in patients. More evidence is needed to either support or refute the role *EFNB2* plays in human syndromic congenital heart disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date March 3rd, 2026 (SOP Version 12)

*STT3B* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation in 2013 (Shrimal et al., PMID: 23842455). Two variants (splice, missense) that have been reported in two probands in two publications are included in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by rescue in patient cells (Shrimal et al., PMID: 23842455) and protein interaction with *STT3A* (which is definitively associated with CDG) (Wen et al., PMID: 36139350). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date April 6, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*POLR1C*, which encodes a subunit of RNA Polymerase I and III, was first reported in relation to disease in 2011, associated with autosomal recessive Treacher Collins Syndrome 3 (TCS3) (Dauwerse et al., PMID: 21131976). TCS is characterized by a combination of bilateral downward slanting of the palpebral fissures, colobomas of the lower eyelids with a paucity of eyelashes medial to the defect, hypoplasia of the facial bones, cleft palate, malformation of the external ears, atresia of the external auditory canals, and bilateral conductive hearing loss, with a high degree of phenotypic variability (PMID:21131976). Although the initial publication did not comment on brain imaging, a 2015 publication described individuals with biallelic *POLR1C* variants and hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, designated HLD11 (PMID: 26151409). Subsequent papers reported individuals with leukodystrophy and TCS features (PMIDs 33597727, 32042905, 32319256, 37197783). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern, and we found that the phenotype represents a spectrum. Therefore, TCS3 (OMIM:248390) and HLD11 (OMIM:616494) have been lumped into one disease entity, *POLR1C*-related disorder (MONDO: 0700278).

Sixteen variants (missense, nonsense, in-frame indel, frameshift, splice site) reported in 11 probands across 6 publications (PMIDs: 37197783, 32042905, 26151409, 21131976, 33597727, 32319256) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental evidence including protein interaction and an animal model (PMIDs: 26151409, 2744828). Mutations in *POLR3A *and *POLR3B*, which encode two other subunits of RNA Pol III and physically interact with *POLR1C*, are definitively associated with hypomyelinating leukodystrophies (PMID: 26151409). *POLR1C*-knockout zebrafish display TCS features including craniofacial cartilage hypoplasia, mandibular hypoplasia, microcephaly, microphthalmia (PMID 27448281). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *POLR1C* and autosomal recessive *POLR1C*-related disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date March 24, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

submitted_as_notes: *B3GALNT2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy (congenital with brain and eye anomalies), type a, 11 in 2013 (Stevens et al., PMID: 23453667). Eleven variants (nonsense, missense, frameshift) that have been reported in seven probands in three publications (PMIDs: 23453667, 24084573, 40665687) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a knockout zebrafish model (PMID: 23453667), an enzyme activity assay (PMID: 40665687), and a glycosylation assay (PMID: 40665687). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *B3GALNT2* and autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy (congenital with brain and eye anomalies), type a, 11. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date 15 December 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *PNPLA8* and *PNPLA8*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of March 24, 2025. The *PNPLA8* gene encodes the patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 8, an enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis and release of oxidized aliphatic chains from cardiolipin.

The *PNPLA8* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *PNPLA8*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2015 (PMID: 25512002). *PNPLA8* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis [OMIM# 251950]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *PNPLA8*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included nine variants (two missense, three nonsense, four frameshift) identified in seven unrelated cases from five publications (PMIDs: 25512002, 29681094, 34177434, 37057294l, 37671596). The maximum score was reached for case level evidence, however additional cases have been reported (PMID: 39082157).  Clinical features in affected individuals include myopathy, dystonia, ataxia, spasticity, developmental regression, seizures, microcephaly, and elevated lactate.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 39082157), a cell culture model (PMID: 39082157), and a mouse model (PMID: 25512002).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *PNPLA8* and autosomal recessive *PNPLA8*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 24, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *UQCC2* and *UQCC2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of September 30, 2024. The *UQCC2* gene encodes a complex III assembly factor that cooperates with *UQCC1* to mediate cytochrome b protein expression and subsequent complex III assembly.

The *UQCC2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *UQCC2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2013 (PMID: 24385928). *UQCC2* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 7 [OMIM# 615824]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *UQCC2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two homozygous variants (one splice region variant, one complex missense variant) identified in two unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 24385928, 28804536). The two reported probands had similar presentations including intrauterine growth restriction, neonatal lactic acidosis, and complex III deficiency. One proband was alive at age 9 years and also had renal tubular dysfunction, seizures, global developmental delay, sensorineural hearing loss, and autism spectrum disorder (PMID: 24385928). The other proband died at age 33 days after experiencing respiratory distress and seizures (PMID: 28804536).

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support the relationship between *UQCC2* and autosomal recessive *UQCC2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. However, given the consistent clinical and biochemical phenotype seen in the two reported cases, this Expert Panel elected to upgrade the classification to moderate. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 30, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*ANTXR1* is located on chromosome 2 at 2p13.3 and encodes the Anthrax toxin receptor 1. This gene functions as a receptor for the protective antigen of anthrax toxin, facilitating the entry of the toxin into cells. Additionally, it plays a role in cell adhesion, extracellular matrix interactions, and angiogenesis, particularly in tumor vascularization. *ANTXR1* was first reported in relation with autosomal recessive GAPO syndrome in 2013 (Stránecký et al., 2013 PMID: 23602711). This is a rare syndrome with multiple congenital anomalies characterized by growth retardation, alopecia, pseudoanodontia and ocular manifestations (GAPO). The main facial features of the syndrome include frontal bossing, puffy eyelids, a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted wide nostrils, a thick upper lip, low-set ears, a very small jaw, and a premature aging appearance due to wrinkling of the skin.

Nine unique variants (2 nonsense, 2 duplications, 2 canonical splice-site, 1 deletion, 1 missense, 1 intronic) reported in 10 families have been included in this curation (PMIDs: 23602711, 27587992, 30575274). Biallelic variants in *ANTXR1* most likely result in loss-of-function alleles. The maximum score for genetic evidence (12pts) has been reached; however, additional case reports exist in the literature (PMIDs: 25045128, 28870703, 38577561, 36094357, 38691016, 38423276, 29436111). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including two mouse models, expression data, and evidence from biochemical function and functional alternation(PMIDs: 32244499, 19622764, 38653789). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *ANTXR1* and autosomal recessive GAPO syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the Syndromic Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 18th, 2025 (SOP Version 11)

The *FOXE3* gene was first reported in relation to ocular disease in 2001, in affected members of a family who inherited anterior segment dysgenesis and cataracts in an autosomal dominant fashion (PMID: 11159941). The known spectrum of disease continued to expand with the 2006 identification of *FOXE3* variants in cases of congenital primary aphakia, with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance (PMID: 16826526). *FOXE3* variants have since been identified as the basis for both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant cases of congenital cataract (PMID: 17893665, PMID: 20806047), indicating the potential for a broad range of phenotypic presentations. Cases diagnosed with anterior segment dysgenesis 2 generally exhibit features such as congenital aphakia, aplasia or hypoplasia of the iris, microphthalmia, Peters anomaly, anterior chamber synechiae, corneal opacity, cataract, coloboma, reduced visual acuity, and/or developmental glaucoma. Cases diagnosed as cataract 34 generally present with congenital cataract either in isolation or accompanied by additional ocular features such as microphthalmia and/or corneal opacity. Cases with autosomal recessive inheritance generally have more severe presentation than those with autosomal dominant inheritance. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the phenotypic variability between cases of anterior segment dysgenesis 2 (MIM# 610256, MONDO:0014508) and cataract 34 (MIM# 612968) appears to represent a spectrum of disease rather than separate disease entities. Despite variability in the mode of inheritance across published cases, the molecular mechanism appears to be *FOXE3* loss of function, either by two null or hypomorphic alleles or one dominant negative allele. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *FOXE3* variants have been lumped into a single disease entity, referred to as FOXE3-related anterior segment dysgenesis, with a semidominant mode of inheritance.

Eleven suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (one nonsense, two frameshift, four missense, and four stop-loss), which have been collectively reported in eleven probands in nine publications (PMID: 11159941, PMID: 16826526, PMID: 17893665, PMID: 19708017, PMID: 20140963, PMID: 20806047, PMID: 21150893, PMID: 25504734, PMID: 27218149). Four of the probands scored in this curation harbored a heterozygous stop-loss variant near the 3’ end of the *FOXE3* coding region, while the other seven probands harbored biallelic nonsense, frameshift, or missense *FOXE3* variants. Missense variants were generally located within the forkhead domain responsible for DNA binding. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of *FOXE3* function conferred by either monoallelic dominant negative variants or biallelic null and/or hypomorphic variants. Null or hypmorphic variants do not appear to cause disease in the heterozygous state, as the carriers from families with autosomal recessive inheritance are all reportedly unaffected. Two families with segregation evidence contributed to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship (PMID: 17893665). Additional probands and family segregation evidence were available but not necessary to include, as the maximum scoring for these evidence types had already been reached.

This gene-disease association is also supported by biochemical evidence that *FOXE3* encodes a transcription factor that coordinates lens development through control of gene expression (PMID: 27218149). Consistent with this finding, *in situ* hybridization studies in mouse embryos have shown that *Foxe3* is specifically expressed in the developing lens (PMID: 10652278). Spontaneous and targeted mouse models of homozygous *Foxe3* disruption recapitulate human patient features such as microphakia, microcoria, microphthalmia, cataract, corneal opacity, corneolenticular adhesions (PMID: 10652278, PMID: 16199865). These models also provide additional insight into disease processes at the histological level, including reduced proliferation and enhanced apoptosis of lens epithelial cells (PMID: 10652278) and disrupted expression of key markers of eye development (PMID: 16199865).

In summary, *FOXE3* reached a definitive association with FOXE3-related anterior segment dysgenesis. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glaucoma / Neuro-Opthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 20th, 2023 (SOP Version 9).

The relationship between *NAXE* and *NAXE*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 22, 2024. The *NAXE* gene encodes NAD(P)HX epimerase that catalyzes the conversion of R-NAD(P)HX to S-NAD(P)HX, which are toxic cellular metabolites, so that S-NAD(P)HX can be reconverted to S-NAD(P)H by the dehydratase NAXD, thus preventing the accumulation of toxic metabolites. Toxic metabolites cannot act as electron carriers and inhibit other key dehydrogenases. 

The *NAXE* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NAXE*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2016 (PMIDs: 27616477, 27122014). *NAXE* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; encephalopathy, progressive, early-onset, with brain edema and/or leukoencephalopathy [OMIM# 617186]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NAXE*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NAXE* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on March 24, 2021 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *NAXE*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 17 unique variants (10 missense, three nonsense, one frameshift, one in-frame deletion, and two splice site variants) identified in 15 unrelated cases from eight publications (PMIDs: 27616477, 27122014, 30022751, 31745726, 32020600, 34786481, 35819538, 36773198), although there have been at least 26 affected individuals from 18 families reported to date (additional case reports included in PMIDs: 34120322, 31758406, 34678889). Age of onset ranges from early in life to adulthood and the outcome is variable as some affected individuals die shortly after presenting and others alive at the time of report (oldest age 21 years). Disease progression is similarly variable. Clinical features in affected individuals include typically acute onset of neurologic deterioration/leukoencephalopathy, sometimes after febrile illness, as well as ataxia, seizures, and skin lesions. Brain imaging is consistent with leukoencephalopathy and/or LSS, and labs show elevated blood lactate levels.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 27616477), and a yeast model system (PMID: 30098110). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *NAXE* and autosomal recessive *NAXE*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 22, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

CLDN9 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNB116) in 2019 (Sineni et al., PMID:31175426). 3 variants (c.86delT, p.Leu29ArgfsTer4; c.475G>A, p.Glu159Lys; c.370_372dupATC, p.Ile124dup) that have been reported in 3 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs:31175426, 34265170) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, as downregulation of CLDN9 can regulate inner hair cell differentiation (PMID:37873357). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by data showing that CLDN9 is expressed in the outer and the inner hair cells, the supporting cells, the stria vascularis, and in the Reissner’s membrane during embryonic development and in adult mice (PMID:34265170). Additionally, ENU-induced mutant mice with a missense variant in CLDN9 showed no reaction to loud sound bursts and had elevated ABR thresholds compared to wildtype mice (PMID:19696885). A transgenic mouse model also showed that embryonic regulation of CLDN9 levels induces functional ectopic inner hair cells, and that postnatal downregulation of CLDN9 levels coordinates stem cell differentiation into inner hair cells (PMID:37873357). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.

Variants in the *TULP1* gene were first asserted in relation to autosomal recessive retinal dystrophies in 1998 (Hagstrom et al., PMID: 9462750). While the first cases were described as retinitis pigmentosa (RP 14, MIM#: 600132), subsequent publications expanded the spectrum of disease to include cases diagnosed as Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA 15, MIM#: 613843, PMID: 15024725). LCA patients present with severe visual impairment from infancy, nystagmus, and extinguished electroretinogram responses, while RP cases show later-onset night blindness and progressive peripheral vision loss. Both groups of TULP1-related retinopathies consistently show early and severe photoreceptor degeneration, consistent with a single spectrum of disease (PMID: 10440267, PMID: 17962469, PMID: 30950243). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the molecular mechanism (biallelic loss of function in the TULP1 gene product) and mode of inheritance (autosomal recessive) were also found to be consistent among the two groups of patients. Therefore, these cases have been lumped for the purposes of gene curation into a single disease entity, referred to as *TULP1*-related retinopathy.

Identified disease-causing *TULP1* variants include missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice-site variants. This curation has included genetic evidence from 4 probands and 3 families with co-segregation of the variant with affected status (PMID: 10440267, PMID: 17962469, PMID: 30950243, PMID: 38450199). The disease mechanism appears to be biallelic loss-of-function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence that *TULP1* encodes TUB-Like protein 1, a member of the tubby-like protein (TULP) family that is highly specifically expressed in the retina and essential for the trafficking of rhodopsin from the inner segments through the connecting cilium to the outer segments (PMID: 17620573). TULP1 protein localizes to the periciliary region and synaptic terminals, interacting with cytoskeletal elements and vesicular transport components, such as microtubules and clathrin-associated complexes (PMID: 9462750, PMID: 36396940). Disease-causing *TULP1* variants disrupt these processes, resulting in mislocalization of phototransduction proteins and photoreceptor degeneration. *Tulp1*-knockout mice exhibit early-onset retinal degeneration with histological studies showing rapid photoreceptor loss, disrupted outer segment structure, and mislocalization of rhodopsin and cone opsins. Electroretinograms show severely diminished or absent responses (PMID: 9462750, PMID: 36396940). Zebrafish with knockout of the two orthologous genes similarly show opsin mislocalization in photoreceptor cells and severe degeneration at an early age (PMID: 36396940).

In summary, *TULP1* is definitively associated with *TULP1*-related retinopathy. This association has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time wtihout the emergence of conflicting evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retinal Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 5th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *UQCRFS1* and *UQCRFS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 4, 2024. The *UQCRFS1* gene encodes the ubiquinol-cytochrome *c* reductase (mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III) subunit 5, which is also known as the Rieske iron-sulfur protein.
 
The *UQCRFS1* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *UQCRFS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2020 (PMID: 31883641). *UQCRFS1* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 10 [OMIM# 618775]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *UQCRFS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three variants (one splice variant resulting in an in-frame deletion, one missense variant, and one nonsense variant) identified in three unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 31883641, 39421685). Disease onset in all three cases was very early life. Clinical features in affected individuals include fetal bradycardia, intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, feeding difficulties, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pericardial effusion, hypotonia, muscle weakness, developmental delay, thrombocytopenia, blood coagulation abnormalities, alopecia, sparse body hair, cholelithiasis, cataracts, hearing impairment, lactic acidosis, and elevated creatine kinase. Complex III activity and assembly were reduced.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), mouse (PMID: 22028811) and yeast (PMID: 2538628) model systems, and rescue in patient cells (PMID: 31883641).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *UQCRFS1* and autosomal recessive *UQCRFS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 4, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: immunodeficiency 78 with autoimmunity and developmental delay
disease_original_title: immunodeficiency 78 with autoimmunity and developmental delay
submitted_as_notes:
*TPP2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive immunodeficiency 78 with autoimmunity and developmental delay in 2014 (Wei Lu, et al., PMID 25525876). The condition is characterized by recurrent bacterial, viral and fungal infections since early childhood, autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, as well as developmental delay, cerebral vascular accident and bronchiectasis. T (mainly CD8+) and B-cell lymphopenia may be present, as well as decreased naïve lymphocytes, increased levels of differentiated T and B lymphocytes, hypergammaglobulinemia (with increased IgE and decreased IgM) and autoantibodies. At least 7 variants (3 missense, 1 nonsense, 1 frameshift, 1 splice site, 1 large deletions) have been reported in 12 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 25525876, 25414442, 33682069, 33586135, 30968598) are included in this curation. A score of 8.2 for genetic evidence has been reached with all reported cases included. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, biochemical function studies, and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 18362329, 25525876, 25414442). Studies show that TPPII controls the balance between intracellular amino acid availability, lysosome number, and glycolysis, essential to produce effector cytokines (including IFNg and IL-1b), which is vital for adaptive and innate immunity and neurodevelopmental health.
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *TPP2* and autosomal recessive immunodeficiency 78 with autoimmunity and developmental delay. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 12/16/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*HCN2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2011 (DiFrancesco JC et al., PMID: 22131395). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotype for *HCN2*-related disorders. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple curations: autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder (this curation), autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder, and autosomal dominant epilepsy. The split curations for the two autosomal dominant *HCN2*-related disorders are presented separately.

Six variants, including missense and frameshift substitutions, reported in six homozygous probands from three publications are included in this curation (PMID: 22131395, 30237576, 40468825). Clinical features associated with biallelic variants in the *HCN2* gene include mild to severe intellectual disability, sometimes associated with epilepsy, movement disorders, hypotonia, or nystagmus. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function; functional studies in select missense variants demonstrated complete loss of function (PMID: 40468825). This gene-disease relationship is supported by mouse models. *HCN2*-deficient mice are smaller, ataxic, and have spontaneous seizures (PMIDs: 12514127, 19150498). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *HCN2* and autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date February 3, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

*TMEM165* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation in 2012 (Foulquier et al., PMID: 22683087). Eight unique variants (splice, missense, and nonsense) that have been reported in seven probands in four publications are included in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a yeast complementation model (Rosnoblet et al, PMID: 23575229) showing that certain *TMEM165* variants are unable to complement a naturally occurring *TMEM165*-negative strain, and two HEK293 knockout cell models (Foulquier et al., PMID: 22683087 and Morelle et al, PMID: 28323990) showing that lack of *TMEM165* results in glycosylation defects. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date April 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The relationship between *MRPS14* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of June 17, 2024. The *MRPS14* gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal subunit S14, a component of the small subunit of the mitochondrial ribosome.

The first and only report of *MRPS14* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2019 (PMID: 30358850). *MRPS14* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 38 [OMIM#618378]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 30358850). Clinical features in this case included hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Wolff-Parkinson-White arrhythmia, growth restriction, and intellectual disability. It was noted that the clinical phenotype stabilized at age two years, and development and cardiomyopathy improved. Serum lactate was elevated. Complex IV deficiency was noted in skeletal muscle and skin fibroblasts.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416). 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 17, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*GRHL3* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant GRHL3-related orofacial clefting in 2014 (Peyrard-Janvid et al., PMID: 24360809). GRHL3-related orofacial clefting is characterized by lower lip pits; cleft lip; cleft palate; and uvular anomaly. 9 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splicing) that have been reported in at least 9 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 24360809, 27018475, 28886269, 34459660, 36901693) are included in this curation. The maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse model, zebrafish model; PMID: 24360809). The mouse and zebrafish models demonstrate that mutants have disrupted periderm development, atypical oral periderm, lack of epistasis, and, occasionally, cleft palate. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *GRHL3* and autosomal dominant GRHL3-related orofacial clefting. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 1/18/2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *OGDH* and *OGDH*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 19, 2026. The *OGDH* gene encodes oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, the E1 component of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (α-KGDH) complex. α-KGDH catalyzes the conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-coenzyme A (succinyl-CoA) in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle.

The *OGDH* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *OGDH*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2021 (PMID: 32383294), however the biochemical etiology was reported in several papers between 1982-2000 (PMIDs: 1640293, 10774994, 8295396, 7075624). *OGDH* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; oxoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency [OMIM# 203740]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *OGDH*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included four missense variants identified in five unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 32383294, 36520152). The age of onset ranges from the neonatal period to early childhood and the reported outcomes range from death at 12 months old to living at 6 years old. Clinical features in affected individuals include global developmental delay, hypotonia, dystonia, dysmetria, ataxia, seizures, microcephaly, decompensation with illness, and dysmorphic features (bitemporal narrowing, full cheeks, nasal bridge abnormalities (broad, depressed), and micrognathia). Of note, there are reports of sudden deteriorations after events such as head trauma (PMID: 32383294) or anesthesia (reported in a case where only the biochemical phenotype was known, PMID: 8295396). Brain imaging shows ventriculomegaly, brain atrophy, agenesis of the corpus callosum, hypoplasia of the pons, delayed myelination, deep gray matter signal abnormalities (dentate nuclei, globi pallidi, subthalamic nuclei) and MRS showing lactate peak. Elevated lactate, elevated ammonia, and elevated urine α-ketoglutarate are also noted.
