The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and *Drosophila melanogaster* model (PMID: 32383294).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *OGDH* and autosomal recessive *OGDH*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 19, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

*CFTR* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive cystic fibrosis (CF) in 1989 (Riordan et al., PMID: 2475911). CF is a disease generally characterized by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and elevated sodium and chloride concentration in sweat. Infertility is common among male patients (due to congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens) and decreased longevity is common in all patients, although recent therapies have enhanced patient outcomes and increased longevity. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in phenotypic variability. Therefore, this curation is only concerning *CFTR * and cystic fibrosis. The other disease entities associated with *CFTR* including sweat chloride elevation, aquagenic palmoplantar keratoderma (Orphanet:498359), and hereditary pancreatitis (OMIM:167800) are not evaluated in this curation. Eleven variants (missense, in-frame indel, nonsense, and frameshift) that have been reported in 6 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 1682496, 1757966, 7477025, 15614862, 18306312, 31187952, 32454915) are included in this curation. Of note, the ∆F508 variant, c.1521_1523del (p.Phe508del), is reported to be present in ~70% of CF cases (Kerem et al., PMID: 2570460). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be LOF. This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence (animal models, in vitro functional assays, and biochemical function) (PMIDs: 7540133, 7545494, 7685652, 10330420, 24727426). Loss of function in *CFTR* causes Cl- channel dysfunction in the apical membrane of epithelial tissues across the body, leading to the disruption of fluid and electrolyte transport, the quantity and composition of epithelial fluids, and healthy organ function (Wang et al., PMID: 24727426). This is supported by altered protein trafficking, processing, and/or function as demonstrated by the ΔF508, c.1679G>C (p.R560T), and c.14C>T (p.P5L) variants as well as a *CFTR*-null mouse model (Ratcliff et al., PMID: 7685652) and a homozygous ΔF508 mouse model (Colledge et al., PMID: 7545494). In summary, *CFTR* is definitively associated with autosomal recessive cystic fibrosis. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.

CLDN11: Hypomyelinating Leukodystrophy 22, autosomal dominant

CLDN11 was first associated with autosomal dominant hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 22 (HLD22) in 2021 (OMIM 619328, PMID 33313762). HLD22 is characterized by early-onset spastic movement disorders, expressive speech disorders, and eye abnormalities, as well as hypomyelination in the brain.  Affected individuals have borderline intellectual disability, dysarthria, drooling, lower limb hyperreflexia, lower and upper limb hypertonia. Additional features often include delayed milestones including speech and language development and ability to sit and/or walk, as well as eye findings including astigmatism, hypermetropia, nystagmus, and strabismus.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found a consistent phenotype and no difference in molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern; therefore, the single disease entity of HLD22 has been maintained. 

The CLDN11 gene encodes claudin 11, also known as oligodendrocyte transmembrane protein (OTM) or oligodendrocyte specific protein (OSP). Claudin 11 is a member of the claudin tight junction family, which plays a structural role in the radial component of the myelin sheath, acting as a diffusion barrier. 

Two stop-loss variants have been reported in 3 probands across 1 publication (PMID 33313762). All variants occurred de novo in the affected individuals. The mechanism of pathogenicity is not well understood; at the protein level, the de novo stop-loss variants occur in the last exon (exon 3) and are predicted to lead to an extension of 39 amino acids to the cytoplasmic C-terminus of claudin-11 (PMID 33313762). 

The gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. CLDN11 is highly expressed specifically in oligodendrocytes and early oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (PMID 10797530). Claudin-11 knockout mice exhibit hindlimb weakness and absent tight junction strands in optic nerves, which mirror the neurologic and visual phenotype in affected patients (PMID: 10612400). Cultured cells with mutated CLDN11 demonstrated decreased morphological differentiation and decreased expression of oligodendroglial differentiation marker proteins PLP1 and MBP (PMID 41752091). 

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between CLDN11 and autosomal dominant hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 22, also known as CLDN11-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date of March 5, 2025 (SOP Version 12).

Variants in the *OPN1LW* gene were first reported in 1993 in relation to X-linked cases of blue cone monochromacy caused by combined disruption of the *OPN1LW* and *OPN1MW* genes (Nathans et al., PMID: 8213841). Affected individuals exhibit color deficiency with absence of L- and M-cone function and reduced cone electroretinogram (ERG) responses with preservation of the short-wave S-cone ERG, accompanied by reduced visual acuity, myopia, nystagmus and/or photoaversion. Subsequent publications starting in 2002 have revealed a more limited phenotype associated with monogenic disruption of *OPN1LW* alone, which generally consists of protan color deficiency with absence of L-cone function, mildly to moderately reduced cone ERG responses, childhood-onset high myopia, and subnormal visual acuity (PMID: 12051694). The spectrum of disease has been asserted to include cases of early-onset high myopia in the absence of protan vision defects (PMID: 37097228). However, this emerging assertion may require support from additional research due to the high frequency of myopia in general, so has not been considered in this curation. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, this curation has focused on cases in which the cause of disease is monogenic *OPN1LW* loss-of-function, with the disease entity referred to as *OPN1LW*-related cone dysfunction. However, it is important to note the higher frequency and clinical importance of blue cone monochromacy resulting from digenic *OPN1LW* and *OPN1MW* loss-of-function.

Eight suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (three nonsense, four frameshift, and one missense), which have been collectively reported in eight probands from five different sources (PMID: 12051694, PMID: 26114493, PMID: 37097228, PMID: 40227176). One of the probands scored in this curation is unpublished but comes from a detailed ClinVar submission (SCV004176720.2). All of the probands scored in this curation were males who harbored the variant allele in the hemizygous state. Large families with co-segregation of the genotype with affected status were not found, so segregation evidence did not contribute to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship. 

This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence indicating that *OPN1LW* encodes a long-wave-sensitive opsin that enables photoperception of red wavelengths (PMID: 9579484, PMID: 10191338), consistent with patients’ lack of spectral sensitivity for red light (PMID: 15148406). The neighboring gene *OPN1MW* shares a similar function (encoding a medium-wave-sensitive opsin that enables photoperception of green-range wavelengths), and its disruption similarly results in color vision defects (PMID: 1302020). *OPN1LW* is highly specifically expressed in the human retina and found in the retinal pigment epithelium (PMID: 30239781), and some disease-associated *OPN1LW* variants exhibit reduced abundance at the mRNA level when exogenously expressed (PMID: 30996587). While *OPN1LW* is a primate-specific gene, subretinal injection of virally packaged human *OPN1LW* into young *Opn1mw−/−/Opn1sw−/−* mice has the ability to promote cone outer segment regeneration and rescue cone functions such as the b-wave amplitude of the long wavelength-mediated ERG response and visually guided behavior (PMID: 35272502). Similarly, male squirrel monkeys lacking an intact *OPN1LW* locus gained red wavelength sensitivity following *OPN1LW* gene therapy and acquired the ability to access color vision-based food rewards (PMID: 19759534).

In summary, *OPN1LW* is definitively associated with *OPN1LW*-related cone dysfunction. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 4th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *YARS2* and *YARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 29, 2024. The *YARS2* gene encodes mitochondrial tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase 2, one of the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which function in mitochondrial translation by catalyzing the attachment of amino acids to their cognate tRNAs. Defects in tRNA charging can result in impaired synthesis of oxidative phosphorylation complex protein subunits.

The *YARS2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *YARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2010 (PMID: 20598274). YARS2 has been associated with a single disease entity to date; myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia 2 [OMIM#613561]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *YARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included eight unique variants (six missense, one in-frame duplication, one nonsense) identified in seven unrelated cases from five publications (PMIDs: 20598274, 24344687, 22504945, 25638461, 28395030). Onset is typically in childhood and clinical features in affected individuals are variable and include sideroblastic anemia, lethargy, exercise intolerance, muscle weakness, respiratory insufficiency, dysphagia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, failure to thrive, and lactic acidemia. Muscle biopsies have shown ragged red fibers, decreased COX staining, and variable respiratory chain complex enzyme deficiencies.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), rescue in patient cells (PMID: 22504945), and rescue in a cell culture model (PMID: 33610547).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *YARS2* and autosomal recessive *YARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

Spectrin repeat-containing nuclear envelop protein 1 (*SYNE1*) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia 8 (SCAR8) in 2006 (Gros-Louis et al., PMID 17159980). The age of onset and phenotypic spectrum vary widely but can include adult onset pure ataxia, and a syndromic ataxia which can include but is not limited to, motor neuron dysfunction and scoliosis. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found a difference in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive 8 (OMIM: 610743) and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita 3, myogenic type (OMIM: 618484). There are assertions in the literature of an autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy 4 (OMIM: 612998) associated with missense variation in *SYNE1* but will be curated seperately. 6 variants (3 nonsense, 1 frame-shift, and 2 canonical splice site) that have been reported in 6 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs 17159980, 27086870) are included in this curation. Genetic case evidence includes segregation from a family with a published LOD score of 3 for a 500 kb linkage region where *SYNE1* is the only gene. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by an animal model and expression study (PMIDs 19008300, 22768332). Expression in the brain is strong but there is also evidence of multple spliceforms with varying expression in other tissues. In a mouse model with the terminal KASH domain removed, mice homozygous for the change experienced high rates of death near birth from respiratory failure with surviving adults showed signs of abnormal gait, muscle pathology, kyphoscoliosis, hind limb weakness and cardiac conduction defects. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *SYNE1* and autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataixa GCEP on the meeting date December 10, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

GLDN encodes gliomedin, a Schwann cell–secreted adhesion protein required for the initiation and stabilization of nodes of Ranvier through interactions with axonal Neurofascin-186 (NF186) and Schwann cell NrCAM. This process is essential for clustering sodium channels and establishing normal peripheral nerve conduction.
The gene–disease association was first established by Maluenda et al., (PMID: 27616481) who identified biallelic GLDN variants in individuals with fetal akinesia and congenital contractures. Since the initial description, multiple unrelated families have been reported with nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice, and missense variants segregating with disease in an autosomal recessive pattern. Many pathogenic variants localize to the conserved extracellular olfactomedin domain critical for NF186 binding (PMIDs: 28726266, 35806855, 39713852). Multiple recurrent and non-recurrent variants comprising missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice variants have been reported in affected individuals, some of which segregated with disease in multiple affected individuals within families. Variants from more than 10 independent publications have been scored as part of this curation and the maximum score for genetic evidence (+12pts) has been reached.
 The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function, and in vitro studies demonstrate that pathogenic GLDN variants impair gliomedin trafficking to the cell surface and abolish NF186 binding (PMID: 27616481). Mouse models lacking gliomedin show disrupted Schwann cell microvilli organization and failure of early sodium channel clustering at heminodes without defects in myelination (PMID: 20188654). Double knockout mice lacking both gliomedin and NrCAM show nodal defects and motor abnormalities closely mirroring the human phenotype (PMID: 24719088).
Prenatal ultrasound findings commonly include polyhydramnios, decreased or absent fetal movements, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, fixed limb joints, short long bones, hydrops fetalis, and pulmonary hypoplasia, with detection often late in gestation (mean 30-32 weeks) (PMID: 35806855). Outcomes include neonatal death, elective termination, or survival with significant respiratory and neuromuscular morbidity.
Although initially described as uniformly lethal, later reports demonstrate phenotypic variability, with survival beyond infancy and into adolescence documented in a subset of individuals receiving intensive supportive care (PMIDs: 35806855, 39713852). These observations support a continuous phenotypic spectrum rather than distinct disease entities.
In summary, the Prenatal Gene Curation Expert Panel concludes that GLDN has DEFINITIVE evidence for autosomal recessive Lethal Congenital Contracture Syndrome 11. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.  This classification was approved by the ClinGen Prenatal GCEP on the meeting date 11/18/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*TNNI1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive congenital myopathy in 2024 (Donkervoort *et al.* PMID: 38569017). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in inheritance pattern, molecular mechanism, and phenotypic variability for *TNNI1* variant carriers. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split and curated separately: 1) autosomal recessive congenital myopathy expressed as a hypocontractile phenotype with early-onset; and 2) autosomal dominant congenital myopathy expressed as a hypercontractile phenotype with childhood and adult onset. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship include case-level, experimental, and expression data. The initial cohort study by Donkervoort *et al.* identified one splice-site and two missense variants in three probands with childhood onset myopathy with clinical presentations of mainly proximal muscle weakness with varying severity and progression, ptosis, scoliosis, contractures of elbows and hips, severe generalized hypotonia, and presence of nemaline bodies in patient muscle tissue (PMID: 38569017). These probands came from three families, however, disease segregation within each family was limited to one generation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. The gene-disease association is supported by expression data (Uhlen *et al.* PMID: 25613900, Li *et al.* PMID: 36520026) and functional alteration in patient myofiber biopsy (Donkervoort *et al.* PMID: 38569017) which supports a hypocontractile phenotype consistent with a potential loss-of-function mechanism. 

In summary, there is LIMITED evidence to support the association between *TNNI1* and autosomal recessive congenital myopathy. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease association. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Myopathy Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date November 24, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

**KCNJ8- Brugada syndrome- autosomal dominant**
KCNJ8 encodes the inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir6.1, a subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channel complex with SUR2. It is primarily expressed in cardiac and adipose tissue, with lower expression observed across various other tissues [PMID: 11984590, 9573340, 24339868]. Given its role in regulating potassium influx, variants in KCNJ8 have been proposed to contribute to arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death (SCD) [PMID: 22056721]. 

Evidence linking KCNJ8 to Brugada syndrome was initially published in 2009 from a case report of a patient with J-point elevation and frequent (>100) unresponsive ventricular fibrillation, who was found to carry a heterozygous p.Ser422Leu variant [PMID: 19120683]. Subsequent studies reported the same p.Ser422Leu variant in additional Brugada or early repolarization cases. A 2010 study identified one Brugada syndrome case and one early repolarization case with the identical missense variant p.Ser422Leu [PMID:20558321]. In 2012, the KCNJ8 p.Ser422Leu variant was found in three patients with Brugada syndrome and one patient with early repolarization syndrome [PMID: 22056721]. 

Crotti et al. also identified a patient with the same p.Ser422Leu in a cohort of 129 unrelated patients with possible/probable Brugada syndrome [PMID:22840528]. The p.Ser422Leu variant has a population allele frequency of 1.08 x10-3, including an allele frequency of 0.03121 in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. These data suggest that the allele is too common for a condition with complex genetics and reduced penetrance. Previous literature has also similarly raised concerns that the KCNJ8 p.Ser422Leu variant may be too common to be considered causative of Brugada Syndrome, and its inclusion in associated gene lists has been cautioned against [PMID: 29959160, 30821013].

The same p.Ser422Leu variant was also reported in four probands diagnosed with early repolarisation syndrome [PMID: 22056721, 22562657. 19120683, 20558321].  Additional studies have also reported KCNJ8 variants in the context of sudden death, however the allele frequencies are either too high or the variants display comparable functional effects to variants that are common [PMID 21836131]. There is also a case report of a homozygous carrier of the  p.Ser422Leu variant who displayed no cardiac phenotype [PMID: 23632791]. 

The relationship between KCNJ8 and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome was originally evaluated by the ClinGen Brugada Syndrome Gene Curation Expert Panel in 2017 and was classified as disputed. This gene-disease pair was re-evaluated by the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on April 8, 2025. Following re-evaluation and the consideration of new evidence, the gene-disease classification remains classified as disputed. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on Dec 10, 2025 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

*B3GLCT* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Peters plus syndrome in 2006 (Lesnik Oberstein et al. PMID:16909395). Twelve variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splicing) that have been reported in 7 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 16909395, 23889335) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached. Peters plus syndrome is characterized by ocular features, systemic malformations, developmental delay, growth retardation, short stature, and brachydactyly. The disease mechanism appears to be biallelic loss of function. Heterozygous carriers are reportedly unaffected. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by the biochemical function of B3GLCT, which is involved in the synthesis of Glcβ1,3Fucα1-O-linked disaccharide found on the thrombospondin type-1 repeats (TSRs) of many biologically important proteins (PMID: 17032646). Additional experimental evidence includes in vitro and in vivo assays showing a defect in glycosylation (PMIDs 34058199, 18199743) as well as animal models (PMIDs 31600785, 28926587).  In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *B3GLCT *and autosomal recessive Peters plus syndrome.This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date January 5, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

*AKT2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD) in 2004 (George et al., PMID: 15166380). George et al. described a rare, highly penetrant *AKT2* mutation (NM_001626:6:c.821G>A, p.Arg274His) in a single kindred, co-segregating with insulin resistance in four individuals across three generations. Three of these also had diabetes, and the proband assessed in more detail showed reduced body fat compared to that predicted for height and weight. Two affected family members assessed later showed increased TG-enriched VLDL, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL cholesterol levels, low leptin and adiponectin concentrations, while one assessed further also showed increased de novo lipogenesis and liver fat content (Semple et al., PMID: 19164855). No other penetrant disease-associated *AKT2* alleles have been described in the literature, but at the population level, a rare coding variant (c.148C>A, p.Pro50Thr, rs184042322, gnomAD v4.1 Grpmax FAF = 0.000038) has been reported at higher frequency in the Finnish population (MAF = 0.012) than other populations. This variant is not associated with classic Mendelian disease but has measurable associations with metabolic traits and type 2 diabetes risk at the population level and demonstrated a mild deleterious impact on function in vitro (PMIDs: 28341696, 29141982, 36409629). Genetic evidence score: 0.5 points. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function, evidenced by in vitro functional assays showed that the *AKT2* Arg274His allele has little or no kinase activity. Limited evidence from reporter assays also raises the possibility of a dominant negative activity of the mutant allele (PMID: 15166380). AKT2  signaling is also important for adipocyte differentiation (PMID: 15166380). Akt2 knockout mice developed severe diabetes with age dependent partial lipoatrophy (PMIDs:12843127, 11387480). Also, Adipo-AKT-KO mice (PMID: 27408773) recapitulate many of the features observed in FPLD caused by the LoF variant p.Arg274His, including insulin resistance and hepatomegaly. Summary of experimental data: 5.5 points. Total score for genetic evidence and experimental evidence: 6 points.
A single variant in *AKT2* (c.49G>A, p.Gly17Lys) has been reported in individuals with hypoinsulinemic hypoglycemia, some with mild hemihypertrophy (PMIDs: 21979934, 24285683, 26003998, 35602880, 38344362, 34673243). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanisms and phenotypic variability underlying *AKT2*-related disease entities. Therefore, the curation of *AKT2* has been split into: i) AKT2-related FPLD (MONDO:0019192), included in this curation and ii) hypoinsulinemic hypoglycemia and body hemihypertrophy (HIHGHH, MONDO:0009416). 

In summary, while the mechanistic link between AKT2 dysfunction and lipodystrophic insulin resistance is highly plausible and well evidenced, current genetic evidence supporting the human gene-disease relationship is limited.  

This classification was approved by the MDGCEP on January 14, 2026. Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) - SOP11.

*RBM10* was first reported in relation to X-linked recessive TARP syndrome in 2010 (Johnston et al., PMID: 20451169). Nine variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice site, and missense) that have been reported in 9 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 20451169, 24259342, 28577551, 30189253, 25186178, 21910224) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a study in mouse embryos that demonstrated an expression pattern that correlates well with the human malformations observed in TARP syndrome (PMID: 20451169). Additionally, a functional alteration study in a mouse embryonic mandibular cell line demonstrated a role for *RBM10* in the regulation of alternative splicing in mouse early development (PMID: 27763814). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *RBM10* and X-linked recessive TARP syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date October 7, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Variants in *VCL* have been reported in association with cardiomyopathy phenotypes, particularly dilated cardiomyopathy. Congenital cardiac anomalies have been reported in individuals from families with cardiomyopathy. A family with dilated cardiomyopathy carrying a *VCL* variant was reported to have relatives with bicuspid aortic valve (PMID: 24062880). However, these observations occurred in a cardiomyopathy pedigree and in the presence of additional variants in another gene, and therefore do not establish a causal relationship between *VCL* and congenital heart disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date July 8th, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *BCS1L* and *BCS1L*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of September 19, 2024. The *BCS1L* gene encodes a complex III assembly factor presumed to facilitate insertion of Rieske Fe/S proteins.

The *BCS1L* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *BCS1L*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2002 (PMID: 12215968). *BCS1L* has been associated with three disease entities to date; Bjornstad syndrome (characterized by sensorineural hearing loss, pili torti, and hypotrichosis) [OMIM# 262000]; growth restriction, aminoaciduria, cholestasis, iron overload, lactic acidosis, and early death (GRACILE) syndrome [OMIM# 603358]; and mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 1 [OMIM# 124000]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *BCS1L*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *BCS1L* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on September 9, 2019 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *BCS1L*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 17 unique variants (12 missense, four premature truncation, one synonymous variant shown to impact splicing) identified in nine unrelated cases from eight publications (PMIDs: 17403714, 20472482, 25895478, 31435670, 35960161, 34650211, 28105683, 34662929), although more affected individuals have been reported to date (PMID: 34662929). While some reported individuals have features consistent with one of the three clinical syndromes reported to be associated with *BCS1L*, it is now known that these features occur on a spectrum and include LSS, developmental regression, seizures, exercise intolerance, growth restriction, short stature, failure to thrive, decreased liver function, cholestasis, optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing loss, pili torti, hypotrichosis, renal tubulopathy, and metabolic acidosis. Cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and thalamic and basal ganglia involvement can be seen on brain imaging. Ragged red fibers and complex III deficiency are seen in skeletal muscle.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by the known protein interaction with complex III subunits and assembly factors (PMIDs: 17314340, 30030361, 24466228), functional alteration studies in patient cells showing evidence of complex III deficiency (PMIDs: 17314340, 28427446), and model systems including fruit fly, mouse, and yeast (PMIDs: 34274978, 22829922, 21274865, 17314340). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *BCS1L* and autosomal recessive *BCS1L*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 19, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *COXFA4* and *COXFA4*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of March 24, 2025. The *COXFA4* gene encodes cytochrome *c* oxidase subunit FA4. This gene was known as *NDUFA4* in the past as it was initially thought to encode a subunit of complex I. It has since been demonstrated to be a subunit of complex IV and not complex I. Defects of this protein lead to complex IV deficiency.

The *COXFA4* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *COXFA4*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2013 (PMID: 23746447). *COXFA4* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 21 [OMIM# 619065]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *COXFA4*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *COXFA4* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on June 8, 2020 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *COXFA4*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included four unique variants (two splice site, two deletions) identified in four unrelated cases from four publications (PMIDs: 23746447, 36344503, 38674434, 39967265). Disease onset is early in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, developmental delay, spastic diplegia, seizures, feeding difficulty, ataxia, dystonia, and lactic acidosis. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration in non-patient cells (PMID: 22902835), rescue in non-patient cells (PMID: 22902835), and a frog model (PMID: 39967265).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *COXFA4* and autosomal recessive *COXFA4*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 24, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *LIG3* and *LIG3*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 11, 2025. The *LIG3* gene encodes DNA ligase 3, an enzyme with several functions. This enzyme is involved in the crucial joining of the 5’ and 3’ termini of the nascent strands as a conclusive event of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) replication and base-excision repair. It is the only ligase responsible for mtDNA replication and maintenance, working alongside DNA polymerase gamma and other mtDNA replisome factors. DNA ligase 3 also interacts with X-ray repair cross-complementing protein 1 (XRCC1) for DNA maintenance by base excision repair, however other nuclear ligases can compensate for defects in this enzyme.

The *LIG3* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *LIG3*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2021 (PMIDs: 3385532, 34165507). *LIG3* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mtDNA depletion syndrome 20 (MNGIE type) [OMIM# 619780]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *LIG3*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included eight unique variants (four missense including one predicted to alter splice-site recognition, three nonsense, one intronic resulting in aberrant splicing) identified in four unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 3385532, 34165507). Clinical features in affected individuals resembled mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalomyopathy (MNGIE) and included gastrointestinal dysmotility, epilepsy, stroke-like episodes, migraines, developmental delay, myopathy, leukoencephalopathy, and progressive cortical and/or cerebellar atrophy. Muscle biopsy showed ragged red fibers and reduced COX staining, as well as variable respiratory chain enzyme deficiencies and mtDNA depletion.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 33855352), a zebrafish model (PMID: 33855352), and a mouse model (PMID: 21390131).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *LIG3* and autosomal recessive *LIG3*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 11, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*CHST6* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive macular corneal dystrophy (MCD) in 2000 (Hasegawa et al., PMID: 11053262). MCD is an ocular disease characterized by bilateral, progressive corneal opacification, and reduced corneal sensitivity. The age of onset occurs in the first decade of life. Characteristics of MCD can include painful attacks with photophobia, foreign body sensations, and recurrent erosions. MCD is divided into the clinically indistinguishable types I, IA, and II based on analysis of the normally sulfated, or antigenic, keratan sulfate levels in serum and immunohistochemical evaluation of the cornea. Patients with types I and IA macular corneal dystrophy have undetectable serum levels of antigenic keratan sulfate, whereas those with type II macular corneal dystrophy have normal or low levels, depending on the population examined.


Seventeen variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in fifteen
probands and one non-human model organism in four publications (PMIDs: 26585178, 20539220, 19365571, 27829782) are included in this curation. MCD is due to deposition of an unsulfated keratan sulfate both within the intracellular space (within the keratocytes and endothelial cells) and in the extracellular corneal stroma. *CHST6* coding variants only occur within the third exon of three, meaning that there is no predicted nonsense mediated decay. However, several variants scored showed a reduction between 20% and 50% of the predicted protein sequence. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models (PMIDs: 39642091, 11053262). *CHST6* results in the protein GlcNAc6ST being made. Paper chromatography and High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) show a relationship between the activity of GlcNAc6ST and MCD, in where GlcNAc6ST may be decreased or disappear in cornea with MCD (PMID:11053262). The decrease in GlcNAc6ST activity in the cornea with MCD might result in the occurrence of low- or nonsulfated keratan sulfate and thereby cause corneal opacity. Zebrafish models show that disrupted *CHST6* results in opaque accumulations formed in the eye, loss of cKS in the corneal stroma, and a decrease in corneal thickness which are consistent with human MCD. Pont Labrador Retrievers models show that the inheritance of a homozygous variant (c.814C>A, p.R272S) results in MCD the same way it presents in humans, with corneal clouding being a prominent feature. 


In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CHST6* and autosomal recessive macular corneal dystrophy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen CDG GCEP on the meeting date February 2, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: short-rib thoracic dysplasia 17 with or without polydactyly
disease_original_title: short-rib thoracic dysplasia 17 with or without polydactyly
submitted_as_notes: *DYNLT2B* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive inheritance of Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dysplasia (now known as Short rib thoracic dysplasia 17 with or without polydactyly) in 2015 (Schmidts et al, PMID:26044572). A total of 5 variants (nonsense, frameshift, and intronic variants) that have been reported in 4 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 26044572, 27894351, 32860008) are included in this curation. [Additional essential genetic evidence description]. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be a loss of function, but more evidence is needed. This gene-disease relationship is also not supported by experimental evidence as a mouse model with a knockout of the gene demonstrating effects in the male testes (PMID:39827215). This knockout mouse study demonstrated it causes male infertility with no skeletal phenotypes. Other experimental evidence reported (IP assays) don't fully support the skeletal phenotype reported in patients. In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *DYNLT2B* and autosomal recessive short rib thoracic dysplasia 17 with or without polydactyly. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Skeletal Disorders GCEP on the meeting date Jan 7th, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, brain anomalies, distinctive facies, and absent language
disease_original_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, brain anomalies, distinctive facies, and absent language
submitted_as_notes: The *RNU4-2* gene is located on chromosome 12 at 12q24.23 and encodes the U4 small nuclear RNA, a component of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP complex of the major spliceosome that mediates RNA splicing. The U4/U6 snRNA duplex is important for correctly positioning the U6 ACAGAGA sequence to receive the 5’ splice site during spliceosome activation. *RNU4-2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant *RNU4-2*-related ReNU syndrome in 2024 (Chen et al., 2024 PMID: 38991538 and Greene et al., 2024 PMID: 38821540). This multi-system disorder is characterized by moderate to severe global developmental delay/intellectual disability, speech anomalies (mostly non-verbal), hypotonia, abnormal brain MRI (reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and delayed myelination), dysmorphic facial features, short stature, microcephaly, behavioral issues, seizures and feeding difficulties, as well as variable vision, gastrointestinal, endocrine, skeletal, genitourinary, cardiac, and cutaneous anomalies. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. Twenty-one unique pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants (12 single nucleotide variants, 9 single base-pair deletion/insertion variants) have been reported in over 200 unrelated probands across two publications (PMID: 38991538, Nava et al., 2025 PMID: 40379786) and are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The gene disease association is supported by high expression of *RNU4-2* in the developing human brain (PMID: 38991538). Functional studies of RNA-sequencing data from individuals with *RNU4-2*-related ReNU syndrome are consistent with systematic disruption of 5′ splice-site usage (PMID: 38991538, PMID: 40379786). In summary, there is strong evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. No convincing contradictory evidence has emerged to date. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date September 3rd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*EVC2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis (WAD) in 2006 (Ye et al. 2006, PMID: 16404586). Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis is characterized by postaxial polydactyly of hands and/or feet, dysplastic nails, dental abnormalities, but no cardiac involvement.  Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome is associated with reduced stature, shortened limbs, post-axial polydactyly of hands and/or feet, dysplastic nails and teeth, and cardiac defects. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome (OMIM:225500) and Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis (OMIM: 193530). The split curation for autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome has been curated separately. 

Five variants (nonsense, frameshift), that have been reported in 27 probands in five publications (PMIDs: 16404586, 18182642, 19810119, 23220543, 38531627) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be dominant negative, as premature termination codons generated in exon 22 of *EVC2* do not undergo nonsense mediated decay potentially resulting in interference of normal protein function. This gene-disease relationship has minimal direct experimental evidence, as all animal models of *EVC2* are full gene knockouts or targeted to non-exon 22 regions. *EVC2* is a transducer of extracellular signals and positively regulates Hedgehog (Hh) which is associated with bone formation and limb development and is required for ciliogenesis, and loss of the last 43 residues in *EVC2*, encoded by exon 22, can modify and disturb the Hedgehog signaling (PMID: 19810119).  The extended pedigree of Ye et al. 2006 (PMID: 16404586) provides an estimated LOD of 3 and candidate gene sequence contributing one point of support. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *EVC2* and autosomal dominant Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Skeletal Disorders GCEP on the meeting date February 2, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *RP1L1* gene was first reported in relation to ocular disease in 2010, in affected members from four families with autosomal dominant inheritance who were diagnosed with occult macular dystrophy (PMID: 20826268). *RP1L1* variants were subsequently identified in 2013 as the basis for autosomal recessive inheritance of retinitis pigmentosa (PMID: 23281133). Cases diagnosed with occult macular dystrophy generally present with a decline in visual acuity and exhibit variable age of onset ranging from the first decade to the seventh decade of life, with incomplete penetrance. Other features include progressive loss of macular function with normal ophthalmoscopic appearance, subnormal pattern electroretinogram, decreased cone electroretinogram responses, photophobia, dyschromatopsia, hypermetropia, optic disc pallor, and/or optical coherence tomography showing disruption or blurring of the inner segment ellipsoid line in the foveola or interdigitation zone absence. Cases diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa often present with night blindness and exhibit complete penetrance among family members, with unaffected heterozygous carriers. Other phenotypes include slowly progressing loss of visual acuity and visual fields, electroretinogram responses showing a rod-cone pattern, retinal blood vessel attenuation, optic disc pallor, subtle granulation of the retinal pigment epithelium, and/or optical coherence tomography showing thinning of the photoreceptor layer toward the periphery. Thus, the cases diagnosed as occult macular dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa overlap phenotypically yet are clinically distinguishable (PMID: 39486507). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the molecular mechanism (monoallelic dominant negative vs. biallelic *RP1L1* loss of function) and mode of inheritance (autosomal dominant vs. autosomal recessive) appear to be distinct between patients with occult macular dystrophy or retinitis pigmentosa 88. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *RP1L1* variants have been split into two separate disease entities. The present curation has focused on autosomal dominant cases referred to as *RP1L1*-related dominant macular dystrophy.

Fourteen suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (all of them missense). These variants have been collectively reported in twenty probands in five publications (PMID: 20826268, PMID: 23281133, PMID: 30025130, PMID: 27623337, PMID: 40172514). Functional studies of disease-causing variants have not been sufficient to determine the mechanism of pathogenicity. The variant encoding the p.Arg45Trp substitution was identified in multiple apparently unrelated probands from diverse geographic origins, as were several missense substitutions between codons 1198 and 1201. Other probands with missense variants at codons 958 and 1258 were included in the curation but received minimal scoring due to the need for additional evidence of functional impact. Two families with co-segregation of the variant with affected status contributed to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship (PMID: 20826268). Additional genetic evidence was available but was not necessary to include in this curation, as the maximum for this category of evidence had already been reached.

This gene-disease association is also supported by biochemical evidence that *RP1L1* encodes a paralog of the RP1 protein that localizes to the photoreceptor outer segment and may play a role in maintaining outer segment organization and structure and preventing photoreceptor degeneration (PMID: 19657028). RP1L1 protein also physically interacts with RP1 (PMID: 19657028), which itself is encoded by a gene that harbors variants causing both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive retinopathies (PMID: 10391211, PMID: 10391212). *RP1L1* mRNA is highly specifically expressed in human retinal tissue and to a lesser extent in the retinal pigment epithelium (PMID: 30239781).

In summary, *RP1L1* has a Definitive association with *RP1L1*-related dominant macular dystrophy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 15th, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: short stature, amelogenesis imperfecta, and skeletal dysplasia with scoliosis
disease_original_title: short stature, amelogenesis imperfecta, and skeletal dysplasia with scoliosis
submitted_as_notes:
*SLC10A7*, the gene encoding solute carrier family 10 (sodium/bile acid cotransporter family), member 7, also called Na(+)/bile acid cotransporter 7, SBF-domain containing protein, has been reported in individuals with skeletal dysplasia with amelogenesis imperfecta, also described as short stature, *amelogenesis imperfecta* and skeletal dysplasia with scoliosis (SSASKS, OMIM #618363; Ashikov et al. 2018. PMID: 29878199; Dubail et al. 2018. PMID: 30082715; Laugel-Haushalter et al. 2019. PMID: 31191616). The SLC10 family (Solute Carrier Family 10), known as bile acid and steroid transport family containing the signature SBF (Sodium Bile transporter Family - Pfam PF017) domain, is composed of seven members. The initially identified family members function as Na+ and bile acid cotransporters while the biological functions of the other members are still unclear. SLC10A7, the last member of SLC10 protein family, does not exhibit any transport activity for the typical SLC10 substrates, and is an orphan carrier (Durin et al. 2022. PMID: 34999954). SLC10A7 is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues and localizes to different cellular compartments of the secretory pathway, especially the Golgi complex, and is hypothesized to be a negative regulator of intracellular calcium signaling (Karakus et al. 2020. PMID: 32350310). SLC10A7-CDG patients have overrepresented high-mannose N-glycans, only composed of N-acetylglucosamine and mannose residues, and decreased sialylation degree of complex (mature) N-glycans (Ashikov et al. 2018. PMID: 29878199) and decreased heparan-sulfate (HS) and accumulation of chondroitin sulfate (CS) at proximity of chondrocytes in KO mice (Dubail et al. 2018. PMID: 30082715). SLC10A7 is suggested to be a key Golgi transmembrane protein maintaining the tight regulation of calcium homeostasis in the ER and Golgi compartments, both essential for glycosylation (Durin et al. 2025. PubMed ID: 39779512).

To date, 11 variants in *SLC10A7* (OMIM: 611459) including four missense, four nonsense, three splicing variants, and one entire gene deletion variant have been reported or submitted to ClinVar as pathogenic or likely pathogenic as causative for SSASKS. This curation includes nine variants (including four missense, two nonsense, and three splicing variants) from nine probands in four publications (Ashikov et al. 2018. PMID: 29878199; Dubail et al. 2018. PMID: 30082715; Laugel-Haushalter et al. 2019. PMID: 31191616; Zhang et al. 2023. PMID: 38037133). The score for genetic evidence has reached the maximum of 12 pts. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. This includes the non-human animal models of zebrafish and mouse with *SLC10A7* deficiency, which recapitulate the clinical and histopathological features of the disease in humans (Ashikov et al. 2018. PMID: 29878199; Dubail et al. 2018. PMID: 30082715). In addition, biochemical functional studies in isogenic *SLC10A7* KO HAP1 cells and SLC10A7-CDG patient fibroblasts have shown loss of SLC10A7 leads to severe Golgi O‑GalNAc glycosylation defects and increased ER and Golgi calcium contents (Durin et al. 2025. PubMed ID: 39779512). (Experimental evidence – 4.5 points).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *SLC10A7* and autosomal recessive SSASKS/SLC10A7-CDG. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on November 17, 2025 (SOP Version v11).

FAM20C was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Raine syndrome in 2007 (Simpson et al., PMID 27862258). Raine syndrome is also known as osteosclerotic bone dysplasia, lethal, and as osteomalacia, sclerosing, with cerebral calcification. Prenatal features  have been identified as early as the first trimester, including FGR, cerebral alterations (large choroid plexuses, echogenic appearance of brain, intracerebral calcifications), brain structural defects (cortical dysplasia, cerebellar hypoplasia, gliosis, ocular defects, corpus callosum and hypophysis dysgenesis), bone sclerosis (usually long bones and skull), and a distinctive craniofacial phenotype (ocular proptosis and nasal hypoplasia with choanal atresia/stenosis and a flat facial profile).  

Raine syndrome was initially associated with death shortly after birth or in early infancy; the perinatal lethal phenotype includes severe craniofacial anomalies, respiratory distress, and severe choanal atresia. A non-lethal FAM20C-associated Raine syndrome phenotype was identified in 2009 (19250384), presenting with a variable neonatal phenotype, attenuated craniofacial anomalies, and age-related features including hypophosphatemic rickets, amelogenesis imperfecta, deformative brain defects, and functional neurological defects. 

The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function of the FAM20C protein kinase activity. FAM20C is a protein kinase that phosphorylates secreted phosphoproteins and acts on substrates with known roles in regulating biomineralization. It has ubiquitous expression, especially in mineralized tissues. Lethality is associated with absence or significant impairment of kinase activity, while non-lethality is associated with nonsense or truncated proteins with missense variants that maintain the kinase domain. Pathogenic variants have been identified in all exons. All splicing variants are lethal, and pathogenic variants associated with lethal versus non-lethal Raine are situated close to functional protein regions such as catalytic, dimerization and glycosylation sites. Family variants are common; this curation includes affected probands with four different homozygous variants (24039075,  32833257) and two distinct compound heterozygous variants (32093234). 

This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental evidence (mouse model, rescue in non-human model organisms, expression data, functional expression in non-patient cells, biochemical function evidence, protein interaction evidence, expression-level data; PMIDs: 22732358, 22615579, 22900076, 28926103, 32093234, 24982027). The protein sequence of FAM20C is well conserved across species, including mice. FAM20C null mice exhibit perinatal lethality, severe hypophosphatemia, stunted growth, neurological abnormalities, reduced bone density, amelogenesis imperfecta, and craniofacial anomalies including flat facial profile. Global deletions of FAM20C in mice resulted in skeletal defects and progressive development of intracerebral brain calcifications. Expression of the Fam20c transgene fully rescued skeletal defects in conditional knockout mice. 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support this gene-disease relationship, with substantial replication over time. Only FAM20C has been associated with Raine syndrome. No convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Prenatal GCEP on the meeting date 6/25/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*STEEP1* is located on the X chromosome at Xq24 and encodes the STING1 ER exit protein 1. The encoded protein is thought to be essential in transport of the STING protein from the golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum. *STEEP1* was first reported in relation to X-linked intellectual disability in 2018 (Verkerk et al., PMID: 29374277). This condition is characterized by intellectual disability, global developmental delay (including in speech and motor development), characteristic facial features (such as elongated face and large/prominent ears), ADHD, tremors, and gait difficulties. 5 variants (small in-frame deletion, large deletion, 2 x frameshift, nonsense) that have been reported in at least 5 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 29374277, 31822863, 37495270) and ClinVar (SCV004099241, Greenwood Genetic Center) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (expression-level data) . The gene is shown to be expressed in hippocampal neurons (PMID: 29374277). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 10/28/2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *COX11* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 26, 2024. The *COX11* gene encodes cytochrome c oxidase assembly factor 11, a mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV assembly factor. 

The *COX11* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease in 2022 (PMID: 36030551). *COX11* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 23 [OMIM#620275]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included four unique variants (two missense, two frameshift) identified in three unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 36030551, 38068960). Age of onset ranges from congenital to early infancy. Clinical features in affected individuals are variable and include intrauterine growth restriction, sensorineural hearing loss, poor feeding and failure to thrive, seizures, global developmental delay, and cerebellar and pyramidal signs. Lactate is elevated in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Brain imaging showed progressive brain atrophy, dentate nucleus lesions, bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensities, and diffuse white matter disease.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 26, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *UQCRH* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of September 30, 2024. The *UQCRH* gene encodes a structural subunit of complex III of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. 

The first and only report of *UQCRH* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2021 (PMID: 34750991). *UQCRH* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 11 [OMIM# 620137]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous in-frame deletion identified in one proband and a similarly affected first cousin from one publication (PMID: 34750991). The two affected individuals had recurrent episodic vomiting and metabolic acidosis in the setting of a viral trigger.
The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies and rescue in patient cells (PMID: 34750991), and a *Uqcrh-/-* mouse model (PMID: 34750991).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 30, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *ATP5PO* and *ATP5PO*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 26, 2024. The *ATP5PO* gene encodes the oligomycin sensitivity-conferring protein (OSCP) of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation complex V. Defects of this protein lead to complex V deficiency. 

The *ATP5PO* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *ATP5PO*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2022 (PMID: 34954817). *ATP5PO* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency, nuclear type 7 [OMIM#620359]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *ATP5PO*-related primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique variants (one nonsense, two variants resulting in altered splicing) identified in three unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 34954817, 35621276). The age of onset was neonatal in all three cases and clinical features in affected individuals included intrauterine growth restriction, neonatal respiratory distress, seizures that developed into refractory status epilepticus, microcephaly, global developmental delay, dystonia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and hydronephrosis and renal insufficiency. Cerebrospinal fluid lactate was elevated. Brain imaging showed progressive brain atrophy, periventricular cysts with mild ventriculomegaly, arachnoid cysts in the posterior fossa and left anterior-inferior temporal lobe, white matter hypersignal around the ventricles, and thin corpus callosum.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 21874297), yeast model (PMID: 35621276), and zebrafish model (PMID: 38128843).

In summary, there is strong evidence to support the relationship between ATP5PO and autosomal recessive *ATP5PO*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 26, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*TRA2B* encodes a splicing regulator. *TRA2B* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2023 (Ramond et al., PMID: 36549593). Affected individuals present with developmental delay and intellectual disability, frequently associated with hypotonia, infantile spasms, microcephaly, brain abnormalities (including brain atrophy, ventricle enlargement, and corpus callosum hypoplasia), behavioral abnormalities (including autism spectrum disorder), feeding difficulties, and short stature.

Eleven *de novo* variants (2 nonsense, 3 splice, and 6 start loss) that have been reported in 11 probands in two publications (PMIDs: 36549593, 37958557) are included in this curation. In addition, a splice variant inherited from a similarly affected parent has been reported (PMID: 36549593). All variants clustered in the 5′ region of *TRA2B*, upstream of an alternative start codon in exon 3. The mechanism of pathogenicity is suggested to be dominant negative, whereby pathogenic variants reduce expression of the canonical Tra2β-1 isoform while increasing expression of the shorter Tra2β-3 isoform, which interferes with the normal function of the canonical protein (PMID: 36549593). However, the possibility of a gain-of-function mechanism — caused by increased expression of the Tra2β-3 protein isoform and leading to changes independent of Tra2β-1 — cannot be ruled out (PMID: 36549593).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence showing splicing defects in a *TRA2B* target gene in patient and non-patient cells carrying a pathogenic variant (PMID: 36549593).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *TRA2B* and autosomal dominant syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 6, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The relationship between *SDHA* and autosomal recessive *SDHA*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 17, 2024. The *SDHA* gene encodes the flavoprotein subunit of complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), which plays an essential role in both the citric acid cycle and in the electron transport chain by catalyzing the oxidation of succinate to fumarate. 

The *SDHA* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *SDHA*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 1995 (PMID: 7550341). *SDHA* has been associated with four disease entities to date; autosomal recessive cardiomyopathy, dilated, 1GG [OMIM# 613642], autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1 [OMIM# 252011], autosomal dominant neurodegeneration with ataxia and late-onset optic atrophy [OMIM# 619259], and autosomal dominant pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5 [OMIM# 614165]. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, this Expert Panel found a difference in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotypic variability among several of these entities. Therefore, the two autosomal recessive disease entities (autosomal recessive cardiomyopathy, dilated, 1GG [OMIM# 613642] and autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1 [OMIM# 252011]) have been lumped into one disease entity and renamed autosomal recessive *SDHA*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *SDHA* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with autosomal recessive Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on May 13, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with autosomal recessive *SDHA*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS. The autosomal dominant disease entities (autosomal dominant neurodegeneration with ataxia and late-onset optic atrophy [OMIM# 619259], and autosomal dominant pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5 [OMIM# 614165]) have been split and curated separately. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 10 unique variants (six missense, two nonsense, one in-frame deletion, one intronic) identified in nine unrelated cases from seven publications (PMIDs: 7550341, 12794685, 16798039, 20551992, 16361598, 24781757, PMID: 33960148), although more affected individuals have been reported in the medical literature. Disease onset is typically early in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, developmental delay and regression, myopathy, seizures, ataxia, tremor, dystonia, spasticity, cardiac arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, anemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, metabolic acidosis, and Complex II deficiency. Brain imaging can be normal, consistent with LSS, or show a leukodystrophy.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration in patient cells (PMID: 10746566), yeast studies (PMIDs:9730279, 1511876), and an embryonic lethal mouse knockout (PMID: 27626380).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *SDHA* and autosomal recessive *SDHA*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 17, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *UQCC3* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 26, 2024. The *UQCC3* gene encodes ubiquinol-cytochrome-c reductase complex assembly factor 3, which is required for the assembly of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase complex (mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III).

The first and only report of *UQCC3* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2014 (PMID: 25008109). *UQCC3* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 9 [OMIM#616111]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one missense variant identified in the homozygous state in one case from one publication (PMID: 25008109). Clinical features in the single reported case included lactic acidosis, feeding difficulty, hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, developmental delay, and growth delay. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416). 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 26, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

SLC25A24 is located in chromosome 1 at 1p13.3 and encodes the solute carrier family 25 (Mitochondrial Carrier, Phosphate Carrier), member 24. Multiple disease entities have been reported in association with this gene. According to criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was no evidence of differences in their molecular mechanism and phenotypic spectrum. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity (MONDO:0012853): Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss syndrome, Fontaine–Farriaux syndrome (FFS), and Fontaine progeroid syndrome. Petty–Laxova–Wiedemann syndrome was not included in this entity due to lack of molecular diagnosis (PMIDs: 2309786,19725131, 20583180). SLC25A24 was first reported in connection with SLC25A24-related Fontaine Progeroid syndrome in 2017 (PMID: 29100093; Ehmke et al. 2017). Fifteen probands across seven publications have been included in this curation (PMIDs: 38980211; 32732226; 31231135; 31775791; 30329211; 29100094; 29100093). Pathogenic SLC25A24 variants are missense and de novo, consisting of p.Arg217His (more frequent) or p.Arg217Cys. The mechanism of disease is gain-of-function where both p.Arg217Cys and p.Arg217His narrow the substrate cavity of the protein and disrupt transporter dynamics, leading to impaired mitochondrial ATP synthesis, increased mitochondrial membrane potential (hyperpolarization), and increased proton leak (PMID: 38980211). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by functional alteration assays, biochemical evidence, and a mouse model (PMIDs: 28350015; 25599384; 29100094; 29100093). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between SLC25A24 and autosomal dominant SLC25A24-related Fontaine Progeroid syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the Craniofacial Malformations Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date 09/18/2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between TMEM168 and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome was suggested by Shimizu et al. in 2020, following the identification of the TMEM168 c.1616G>A, p.Arg539Gln variant in a family with Brugada syndrome (PMID: 32175648). Functional evidence from mouse and cell models suggested a mechanism involving decreased cardiomyocyte cell surface Nav1.5 expression in cells with the p.Arg539Gln variant. In a follow-up publication, Nguyen et al. suggested that the TMEM168 p.Arg539Gln variant was involved in sequestering αB-crystallin, thereby promoting Nav1.5 degradation (PMID: 34086898). However, with an allele frequency of 9.88 x 10-5 in the South Asian population (and 1.24 x 10-5 overall in gnomAD v4.1) this variant is too common to be a monogenic driver of autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome. As of the date of this classification, there are no further reports of TMEM168 variants causing cardiac disease in the literature.

This gene-disease relationship was evaluated on January 13, 2026, by the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP. Given the absence of compelling clinical genetic data, this gene-disease classification was disputed. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on January 13, 2026 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

DHODH was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive postaxial acrofacial dysostosis (also known as Miller Syndrome) in 2010 (Ng et al., PMID: 19915526). This condition includes features of high-severity micrognathia, orofacial cleft, underdeveloped/lack of post axial components of the limbs, short forearms, digit anomalies, ocular coloboma, and supernumerary nipples. 21 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splicing, and a large deletion) that have been reported in at least 12 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 19915526, 21851494, 22692683, 27370710, 33262786, 37120754) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (functional alteration evidence in patient and non-patient cells; PMIDs: 22967083, 27370710). Functional alteration evidence in both patient cells and HeLa cells shows altered enzyme activity, reduced protein stability, and increased levels of DHO in plasma and urine in mutants. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between DHODH and autosomal recessive postaxial acrofacial dysostosis. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 6/15/2023 (SOP Version 9).

The *FTL* gene codes for the ferritin light chain. Synthesis of both heavy H- type and light L- type ferritin subunits is controlled by a common cytosolic protein known as iron regulatory protein (IRP), which binds to the iron-responsive element (IRE) in the 5′-UTR of the H- and L-ferritin mRNAs (PMID:11389486). The L-ferritin subunit helps with electron transport in and out of the ferritin core protein and plays a role in iron release, as Fe+2, from ferritin and storage of iron in a soluble, non-toxic, readily available form. Variants in *FTL* have been reported in individuals with  Hereditary Hyperferritinemia cataract syndrome (HHCS) (MIM#600886). The disease displays autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and can occur with isolated hyperferritinemia.
