Summary of case-based evidence: 23 variants, with 20 substitutions and 3 deletions have been documented with variants affecting upper stem, lower stem, C-bulge, hexanucleotide loop *FTL* mRNA IRE hair pin which disrupt its specific interaction and optimal binding with the cytoplasmic iron regulatory protein (IRP) leading to failure of suppression of L-ferritin translation. (PMIDs: 16518306, 22881709, 24983587,18710380, 9414313, 9292547, 21410535, ,24766965, 28636169, 26849797, 15690351, 21569394, 15234655, 29269865, 10366804, 15861269, 41300832, 24936091, 19887780, 21410535, 15223007, 23421845, 10759702, 7493028, 11923255). Haplotype analysis was conducted in three publications (PMID: 16518306, 27096259, 23592921) and published LOD scores included in the scoring. Summary of experimental evidence: This gene-disease association is supported by experimental evidence from the study on apoferritin when subjected to high iron increments, heteropolymers of ferritin with L:H ratios are highly efficient in incorporating iron (PMID: 8182740) . Further, it was observed that on using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to delete the endogenous eIF3 interaction site in FTL (human eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 (eIF3) acts as a distinct repressor of FTL mRNA translation) disruption of eIF3 interactions with FTL mRNA due to specific variants in the *FTL* 5’- UTR likely contributes to a subset of hyperferritinemia cases (PMID:31414986). Another study on plasmid constructs with the IRE region of L-Ferritin, computer modelling and nuclease mapping experiments have indicated IRE forms the central part of a large stem-and-loop structure near the 5’-end of ferritin mRNAs. Mutations that disrupt the base-pairing in the upper stem, alter the IRE-BP binding by causing a kink in the RNA helix (PMID: 1644834). Experimental studies measuring the ability of the mutant IREs to compete with radiolabelled wild-type L-ferritin IRE *in vitro* using band-shift competition assays were used to study correlation between binding affinity with clinical severity (PMID:10473603). Expression studies of human *FTL* and its mouse counterpart  in the lens, detected RT–PCR amplicons containing full-length protein-coding regions and strong *in situ* localization of FTL1 transcripts to the lens equatorial epithelium and peripheral cortex (PMID: 23592921). In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between variants in the *FTL* gene and Hereditary Hyperferritinemia cataract syndrome. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP on January 23, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

FAM111A was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Kenney-Caffey syndrome type 2 [MIM: 127000, ORPHA: 93325, MONDO: 0007478] and autosomal dominant Gracile Bone Dysplasia/Osteocraniostenosis [MIM 602361, ORPHA:2763, MONDO:0011215] in 2013 (Unger et al, PMID 23684011). At least 16 unique variants (missense, in-frame indel, frameshift, and splicing) have been reported in humans. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there is insufficient evidence of a difference in molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern despite a few genotype:phenotype correlations that may explain the phenotypic spectrum observed from FAM111A variation. There is one case of bi-allelic variants causing disease in each entity, with no appreciable phenotype reported in either heterozygous parent. There is also a heterozygous variant (P527T) that has been reported in both disease entities. Therefore Kenney-Caffey Syndrome type 2 and Gracile Bone Dysplasia/Osteocraniostenosis have been lumped into one disease entity, “FAM111A-related skeletal dysplasia” with autosomal dominant/autosomal recessive inheritance. 

This disease is characterized by skeletal, ocular, endocrine, neurologic, splenic, renal, and growth anomalies, as well as facial dysmorphism, with the most frequent features being short stature, cortical thickening of the tubular bones with stenosis or obliteration of the medullary cavity and hypoparathyroidism. The reported prenatal phenotype by ultrasound examination for milder presentations includes fetal growth restriction, and for more severe presentations includes short thin tubular bones with flared metaphyses, thin ribs, small thorax, undermineralized skull, cloverleaf skull or frontal bossing, fractures, and perinatal edema (increased nuchal translucency, ascites, pleural effusion) in more severe presentations. Features detected on fetal postmortem external physical examination and Xray in severe presentations additionally include hypoplastic or absent spleen, micropenis, ventricular septal defect, and micropthalmia. As all cases in the literature were either liveborn or terminated pregnancies, the risk of fetal demise or stillbirth is unknown.

This curation scored 17 variants across the following 8 publications: PMIDs 23684011, 28138333, 33263187, 33750016, 35205306, 38679371, 36916904, and 39501122. More evidence is available in the literature but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached. A recurrent variant, R569H, was reported in a total of 19 probands across 18 unrelated families. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and variant-level experimental data in both engineered cells and patient cells. Experiments with patient variants in engineered cells has shown primarily gain-of-function of FAM111A (PMIDs 32165630, 33369867), with an additional case demonstrating a homozygous hypomorphic splice variant in patient cells (PMID 39501122). The ultimate pathogenesis of disease in patients is not currently understood.

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between FAM111A and AD/AR FAM111A-related skeletal dysplasia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Prenatal Expert Panel on the meeting date April 2, 2025 (SOP version #10)

*THOC2* was first reported in relation to X-linked complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2015 (Kumar et al., PMID: 26166480). *THOC2* encodes a member of the THO sub-complex, which is an essential component of the large TREX complex involved in mRNA export, chromosome alignment, mitotic progression, and genomic stability in humans. The reported *THOC2* variants, except one, were detected in affected males and are associated with an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance. Affected males present with speech delay, intellectual disability (borderline to profound), hypotonia, short stature, gait disturbances, variable brain MRI anomalies, and behavior problems (PMIDs: 26166480, 29851191, 32116545). Additional features in a subset of individuals can include microcephaly, seizures, movement disorders, overweight, respiratory abnormalities, and congenital defects.

Twenty variants (17 missense, 1 splice, 1 splice region, and 1 intragenic deletion) reported in 20 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 26166480, 29851191, 32116545, 35183220) are included in this curation. Variants can be inherited from unaffected carrier mothers or arise *de novo*. Asymptomatic female carriers have highly skewed X-chromosome inactivation. The only reported female patient — a severely affected girl with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and a *de novo* *THOC2* missense variant (PMID: 29851191) — was not included in this curation; her X-chromosome inactivation status is unknown. Large families have been reported with evidence of strong segregation in multiple affected males, including one family with 11 affected males (PMID: 26166480). The mechanism of disease is suggested to be altered gene product structure leading to partial loss of function (PMID: 32116545). Missense variants lead to decreased protein stability of THOC2 and its TREX-complex partners, while the splicing-defective variants and the intragenic deletion result in C-terminally truncated proteins with partial loss of the RNA binding domain (PMIDs: 29851191, 32116545). *THOC2* is highly constrained for both missense (Z = 5.53, gnomAD v2.1.1) and loss-of-function variants (pLI = 1).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including biochemical function, and cell culture, mouse, and yeast models (PMIDs: 22314234, 23222130, 23749989, 38331934). Another THO complex gene, *THOC6*, is also implicated in a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID: 15998806). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *THOC2* and X-linked complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 6, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 1
disease_original_title: Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 1
submitted_as_notes:
The *DNAJC30* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy in 2021 (Stenton et al., PMID: 33465056), with the spectrum of disease also including patients diagnosed with Leigh syndrome (PMID: 35148383) or Kjer-type optic atrophy (PMID: 35091433). Affected individuals are generally reported with visual impairment, optic atrophy, central retinal vessel tortuosity / circumpapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy, abnormal retinal nerve fiber layer morphology, and/or retinal nerve fiber layer pseudoedema. Some patients exhibited additional clinical features including abnormal brain morphology affecting the putamen, caudate nucleus, and/or thalamus, gait ataxia, limb dystonia, and/or increased serum lactic acid. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the molecular mechanism (biallelic loss of function) and mode of inheritance (autosomal recessive) were found to be consistent among patients regardless of diagnosis, while the phenotypic variability between them appeared to represent a spectrum of disease rather than separate disease entities. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *DNAJC30* variants have been lumped for curation as a single disease entity, referred to as "*DNAJC30*-related Leber-like optic neuropathy".

This curation has scored nine suspected disease-causing variants (two nonsense, one frameshift, five missense, and a short in-frame deletion), which have collectively been reported in fourteen probands from five publications (PMID: 21397065, PMID: 21532570, PMID: 21850159, PMID: 23127749, PMID: 31992737). Three of the variants are truncating, consistent with a biallelic loss-of-function mechanism of pathogenicity. Co-segregation of the homozygous genotype with affected status in the proband’s family was only observed in smaller families and was not incorporated into the genetic evidence component of this curation (PMID: 33465056).

This gene-disease association is also supported by evidence that DNAJC30 is expressed in the relevant tissues, with highest levels in the trabecular meshwork, as well as in the testis (PMID: 30239781). Biochemical studies indicate that *DNAJC30* encodes a chaperone that can be detected in mitochondria isolated from the human superior temporal cortex and that interacts with various subunits of ATP synthase (PMID: 30318146). The DNAJC30 protein participates in mitochondrial complex I repair by facilitating the efficient exchange of complex I subunits exposed to reactive oxygen species, and *DNAJC30* defects lead to impaired exchange of assembled respiratory chain subunits (PMID: 33465056). *DNAJC30* knockout in HEK293 cells results in a complex I–dependent respiration defect, impaired exchange of complex I respiratory chain subunits, and a subtle increase in complex I levels (PMID: 33465056), while fibroblast cells from an affected patient exhibit similar respiratory complex defects and can be rescued by exogenous expression of *DNAJC30*. *Dnajc30-/-* mice show defects in pyramidal neuron morphology, as well as hypofunctional and dysmorphic mitochondria in the neocortex that show reduced oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis (PMID: 30318146).

In summary, *DNAJC30* has Definitive evidence of association with *DNAJC30*-related Leber-like optic neuropathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glaucoma and Neuro-Ophthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 16th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *COX7B* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of September 30, 2024. The *COX7B* gene encodes the cytochrome *c* oxidase (complex IV) subunit 7B.

The first and only report of the *COX7B* gene in relation to X-linked primary mitochondrial disease was in 2012 (PMID: 23122588). *COX7B* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; linear skin defects with multiple congenital anomalies 2 [OMIM# 300887]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three variants (one nonsense, one frameshift, one splice acceptor) identified in three unrelated female probands from one publication (PMIDs: 23122588). All three probands had microcephaly, linear skin lesions on the face and neck, and poor growth. The mother of one proband also had the variant and presented at birth with linear skin defects. Additional features seen in the probands include intellectual disability, learning disability, and short stature. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional studies in HeLa cells (PMID: 23122588), and a medaka fish model (PMID: 23122588).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *COX7B* and X-linked primary mitochondrial disease. However, this Expert Panel elected to downgrade the classification to limited as biochemistry was not performed in the probands, and because almost all of the evidence comes from one publication. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 30, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*BBIP1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive ciliopathy-*BBIP1* (MONDO:0005308) in 2013 (Scheidecker et al., PMID: 24026985). Individuals with ciliopathy-*BBIP1* presented with Bardet-Biedl syndrome, including retinitis pigmentosa, obesity, kidney failure, intellectual disability, hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, polydactyly and brachydactyly. At the time of curation, four individuals with ciliopathy-*BBIP1* were described in the literature or in ClinVar. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no differences in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern and no significant phenotypic variability. *BBIP1* has previously been associated with only one disease entity: autosomal recessive Bardet-Biedl syndrome 18 (MIM #615995). Four variants (3 nonsense and 1 splice-affecting variant, all homozygous) that have been reported in four probands in three publications and one ClinVar entry (PMIDs: 24026985, 32055034, 37239474 and VCV000626905.3) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, showing *BBIP1* expression in the primary cilium, its physical interaction and functional role within the BBsome, a functional role for ciliogenesis and microtubule acetylation and ciliopathy phenotypes in knockdown zebrafish embryos (PMIDs: 19081074, 25964651, 24026985). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *BBIP1* and autosomal recessive ciliopathy-*BBIP1*. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on the 8th of September 2025 (SOP version 11).

disease_title: optic atrophy 10 with or without ataxia, intellectual disability, and seizures
disease_original_title: optic atrophy 10 with or without ataxia, intellectual disability, and seizures
submitted_as_notes:
*RTN4IP1* was first reported in 2015 in relation to isolated and syndromic optic neuropathies in families with early-onset recessive optic neuropathy (Angebault, *et al*., PMID: 26593267). Whole exome sequencing detected a variant encoding p.Arg103His in the homozygous state in four affected individuals from three consanguineous families. Two affected compound heterozygous individuals were identified in a family of unrelated parents harboring the p.Arg103His and p.Lys201Ter variants. All parents and five unaffected siblings were heterozygous for their family variant(s) and four unaffected siblings were homozygous for the wildtype alleles. Subsequent studies investigating the causative variants for optic neuropathy identified disease-associated variants in *RTN4IP1* in patients with autosomal recessive isolated and syndromic optic neuropathies. The disease entity associated with *RTN4IP1* has been described as optic atrophy 10 with or without ataxia, impaired intellectual development and seizures (MIM# 616732), associated with autosomal recessive inheritance. This disease entity is referred to as *RTN4IP1*-related optic atrophy with or without neurological features for the purposes of this gene curation.

This curation includes eighteen suspected disease-causing variants, including missense, nonsense, frameshift, splicing defect, and deletion variants, which have been reported in 25 probands in 9 publications (PMID: 26593267, PMID: 28638143, PMID: 29181510, PMID: 31077085, PMID: 33037779, PMID: 33136666, PMID: 33315831, PMID: 36231115, PMID: 35439212). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, which is supported by expression studies and *in vitro* functional studies with patient-derived cells and by studies with non-human model organisms (PMIDs: 26593267, 29181510, 31077085, 37884807).

*RTN4IP1* (OMIM #610502) is a nuclear gene encoding mitochondrial matrix protein RT4I1, which is a potent inhibitor of regeneration following spinal cord injury. RT4I1 protein plays a role in the regulation of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) neurite outgrowth and in the development of the inner retina and optic nerve. RT4I1 also has NAD(P)H oxidoreductase activity and required for CoQ biosynthesis.

In summary, *RTN4IP1* is Definitively associated with *RTN4IP1*-related optic atrophy with or without neurological features. This has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glaucoma and Neuro-Ophthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 20th, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: progressive retinal dystrophy due to retinol transport defect
disease_original_title: progressive retinal dystrophy due to retinol transport defect
submitted_as_notes:
The *RBP4* gene was first reported in relation to ocular disease in 1999, in affected members from a family with autosomal recessive inheritance who were diagnosed with retinal dystrophy and showed iris coloboma and comedogenic acne (Seeliger et al., PMID: 9888420). Affected individuals generally exhibit retinal features including night blindness, progressive loss of visual acuity, peripheral visual field constriction, reduced or absent rod and reduced cone electroretinogram responses, white dots in the fundus, retinal pigment epithelium atrophy, and/or retinal blood vessel attenuation. These are accompanied in some cases by the presence of colobomas and/or comedonal acne that may be severe or extend into later adulthood. Some cases have been reported with rheumatoid arthritis (PMID: 36317196) or osteoarthritis (PMID: 23189188), which could potentially be part of the spectrum of disease. Circulating retinol and retinol binding protein are generally reduced or undetectable. Families were subsequently identified with microphthalmia, clinical anophthalmia, and/or coloboma in the absence of retinal involvement, showing autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and a parent of origin effect in which maternal genotype and dietary vitamin A during pregnancy influenced the expressivity of the phenotype (PMID: 25910211). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the biallelic and monoallelic cases were distinguishable not only by their mode of inheritance, but by the presence or absence of retinal features, and by the underlying molecular mechanism (loss-of-function vs. dominant negative variants). Therefore, cases caused by inherited *RBP4* variants have been split into two separate disease entities, with the present curation focusing on autosomal recessive cases referred to as *RBP4*-related recessive retinopathy with or without ocular malformation and acne vulgaris.

Seven suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (two missense, two nonsense, and three disrupting canonical splice sites). These variants have been collectively reported in six probands in six publications (PMID: 9888420, PMID: 23189188, PMID: 28041643, PMID: 32323592, PMID: 36317196, and PMID: 35743034). The variant types and functional studies of disease-causing missense variants (PMID: 9888420) indicate that the mechanism of pathogenicity is biallelic loss-of-function. The reported families had relatively small numbers of affected individuals, so segregation evidence did not contribute to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship.

This gene-disease association is also supported by biochemical evidence that *RBP4* encodes a retinol binding protein that is secreted from hepatocytes into the bloodstream in a complex with transthyretin to deliver retinol to target cells (PMID: 35334893), including photoreceptor cells in the retina. *RBP4* shows high expression in the liver as well as in adipose tissue, breast, and retinal pigment epithelium (PMID: 30239781). Mice with homozygous knockout of *Rbp4* exons 1 and 2 show impaired dark-adapted electroretinogram responses and reduced retinol levels (PMID: 10469643), recapitulating the molecular features and impaired retinal function of the human patients. These defects could be rescued by transgenic overexpression of human *RBP4* (PMID: 10469643).

In summary, *RBP4* has a Definitive association with *RBP4*-related recessive retinopathy with or without ocular malformation and acne vulgaris. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 5th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: combined immunodeficiency due to GINS1 deficiency
disease_original_title: combined immunodeficiency due to GINS1 deficiency
submitted_as_notes:
*GINS1* (also known as *PSF1*), along with *GINS2-4*, belongs to the Go-Ichi-Ni-San (GINS) complex. The GINS complex is required for initiation and elongation of DNA replication by unwinding DNA and binding to single-stranded DNA. 

Overall, 5 patients with unaffected carrier parents from 4 unrelated families were found to be compound heterozygous for 4 rare variants, including two missense (p.R83C and p.C152Y) and two 5′ UTR nucleotide substitutions (c.–48C>G and c.–60A>G). These individuals show pre- and post-natal growth restriction, susceptibility to viral infections thought to be caused by NK cell deficiency, low or normal numbers of circulating T and B lymphocytes, and chronic neutropenia without adrenal insufficiency (PMID: 28414293).

This gene-disease relationship is supported by biochemical function, expression studies, functional studies, a zebrafish model, and a mouse model.

Cottineau et al further investigated the role that *GINS1* plays in NK deficiency. GINS1 patients had low proportions of both CD56bright and CD56dim subsets, which did not respond to stimulation with IL-2 or IL-15. Cells from patients had lower *GINS1* protein levels than control, suggesting that both 5′ UTR and missense mutations affected protein levels. *GINS3 *and *GINS4* protein expression levels are also decreased in patient derived cells, indicating that GINS complex stability and function are affected by loss of *GINS1* protein expression.

Additionally, fibroblasts from patients exhibited abnormal nuclear morphology, indicating a failure to maintain genome integrity and signify mis-segregation of chromosomes. DNA fiber analysis determined that patient cells had a decreased amount of replication clusters and bidirectional forks as well as an increase in stalled replication forks. Patient fibroblasts proliferate slower than controls and have a senescent phenotype. It is likely that these phenotypes contribute to natural killer deficiency, although the basis for neutropenia found in *GINS1* is not understood. 

There is evidence that in zebrafish, the absence of GINS function causes DNA replication to be cell impaired. Also, *gins1* mutants exhibit elevated levels of apoptosis restricted to actively proliferating regions of the central nervous system (PMID: 32548116). 

Mice homozygous for a nonfunctional mutant of *PSF1* died in utero. *PSF1-/-* blastocysts failed to show outgrowth in culture and exhibited a cell proliferation defect (PMID: 16287864). 
Possibly explaining the lack of homozygous human patients studied.

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Whilst more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.

The *RNU2-2* gene is located on chromosome 11 at 11q12.3 and encodes the U2-2 small nuclear RNA, a component of the of the major spliceosome complex that directs accurate removal of intronic sequences from pre-mRNAs. *RNU2-2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant *RNU2-2* developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in 2025 (Greene et al., 2025 PMID: 40210679 and Jackson et al., 2025 PMID: 40442284). This disorder is characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, impaired intellectual development, microcephaly, autistic behavior, and seizures. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. Six unique noncoding variants (5 single nucleotide variants, 1 single bp insertion) that have been reported in 28 unrelated probands across two publications (PMID: 40210679, 40442284) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is altered intermolecular interactions in the spliceosome altering spliceosome function, a type of gain-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function and protein interaction studies as a part of the major spliceosome complex and a mouse model showing neurodegeneration and alternative splicing defects. In summary, there is strong evidence to support the relationship between *RNU2-2* and autosomal dominant *RNU2-2* developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date September 19th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

SCN3B encodes the sodium channel β-subunit 3 (Navβ3). SCN3B variants were first reported in atrial fibrillation cohorts in 2010 (Wang et al. PMID: 20558140; Olesen et al. PMID: 21051419). Navβ3 variants have been suggested to cause cardiac disease by modulating the trafficking of Nav1.5 to the cell membrane or by affecting the function of the Nav1.5 channel (PMID: 20031595, 23257389, 38450374, 20042427, 39761910).

Homozygous knockout mouse models implicate SCN3B in cardiac disease, with reports of electrophysiological abnormalities including shorter ventricular effective refractory periods and increased susceptibility to ventricular tachycardia following programmed electrical stimulation (PMID: 19351516). Evidence of perturbed atrial function with increased susceptibility to atrial tachycardia and fibrillation following atrial burst pacing has been reported (PMID: 19796257). Immunoprecipitation experiments also show that Navβ3 interacts with Nav1.5 (PMID: 20042427, 39761910).

There are a handful of publications reporting SCN3B variants in cases of atrial fibrillation (PMIDs: 20558140, PMID: 21051419, PMID: 36362949). However, there is also significant evidence suggesting that SCN3B variants are not a monogenic cause of autosomal dominant atrial fibrillation. Notably, SCN3B has very low mRNA expression in the heart (left ventricle TPM = ~0.5, GTEx), with SCN5A exhibiting much higher expression (left ventricle TPM = ~36, GTEx). Further, most of the functional work performed to assess SCN3B variants as having an impact on sodium current has been performed by co-expressing Navβ3 variants with Nav1.5 in cell models (PMIDs: 20031595, 23257389, 26179811, 39761910, 38450374, 21051419, 34867379). Since SCN3B has low mRNA abundance in cardiac tissue, these models may overestimate the effects of SCN3B variants on Nav1.5 function in vivo. SCN3B homozygous loss-of-function has also been reported in two consanguineous families with a neurodevelopmental disorder with no cardiovascular phenotype being reported in either heterozygous or homozygous carriers of truncating variants (PMID: 40879121). While homozygous knockout mouse models report evidence of perturbed electrophysiological function (PMIDs: 19351516, 19796257), these animal studies model a more severe genetic defect than the heterozygous missense variants reported in the literature.

This gene-disease relationship was evaluated on 25 November 2025,  by the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP. For the reasons highlighted above, this gene-disease classification is disputed. This classification was approved by the ClinGen HCVD GCEP on 25 November 2025 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

*PIGY* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Hyperphosphatasia with impaired intellectual development syndrome 6 (MONDO:0014780) in 2015 (Ilkovski B et al., 2015, PMID: 26293662). This condition is caused by variants in the *PIGY* gene, which encodes the smallest subunit of GPI-GnT, which is directly associated with the catalytic subunit *PIG-A*.(PMID:16162815)

45 unique variants (e.g., synonymous, missense, in-frame indel, nonsense, frameshift) have been reported in humans by ClinVar; 27 of these variants are classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic in ClinVar. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. Two variants that have been reported in 2 probands in 1 publication (Ilkovski B et al., 2015, PMID: 26293662), are included in this curation. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by protein interaction; *PIGY* directly interacts with *PIG‑A *through co‑immunoprecipitation (co‑IP) and GST pull‑down experiments. In these assays, when *PIG‑A* (the catalytic subunit) is pulled down, *PIG‑Y* is co‑precipitated, indicating a physical binding between the two proteins. (Murakami Y et al., 2005, PMID: 16162815. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date October 20, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Saul Wilson syndrome (SWS) was first reported by Saul and Wilson in 1990 (PMID:2309787). Later, Ferreira et al. found that Saul Wilson syndrome is caused by a *COG4* heterozygous de novo variant p.Gly516Arg (c.1546G>A or c.1546G>C, PMID:30290151). Saul Wilson syndrome is a rare skeletal dysplasia characterized by a unique set of phenotypes including but not limited to short stature, progeroid facial appearance, prominent eyes, cataracts, micrognathia, platyspondyly, irregular end plates of vertebral bodies, speech and motor delays, coxa valga, blue sclerae, narrow nasal bridge with a convex nasal ridge, brachydactyly, and early developmental delay. Molecularly, patient fibroblasts demonstrate impaired Golgi to ER vesicle trafficking including an increase in retrograde trafficking and an apparent decrease in anterograde trafficking from Brefeldin A trafficking assays. Additionally, many SWS patients show abnormal Golgi architecture and collapsed Golgi stacks. In total, 15 individuals have been identified with Saul Wilson syndrome and the *COG4* p.Gly516Arg variant from two publications (PMIDs: 30290151, 35455576). Importantly, a decision to split this curation from autosomal recessive *COG4*-CDG (moderate classification) was made based upon significant differences in molecular mechanism, clinical phenotypes, and mode of inheritance by the CDG GCEP. 

This gene disease relationship is supported by experimental evidence including the biochemical function of *COG4*, a subunit of the octameric COG complex, which is a specific tethering complex that is important to orchestrating retrograde and anterograde vesicle trafficking by interacting with several proteins including SNARES, Rab GTPases, and COPI coat protiens (PMID:30290151). Additionally, the p.Gly516Arg variant has been expressed into Zebrafish embryos and a chrondocyte-like cell line. In Zebrafish embryos, the p.Gly516Arg variant recapitulated molecular phenotypes observed in SWS fibroblasts including an increase in glypicans and elevated wnt4 transcripts, while showing additional phenotypes such as shortened embryonic anterior–posterior body axis and embryonic defects in chondrocyte morphogenesis (PMID: 34595172). Meanwhile, in a chrondocyte-like cell line, expression of p.Gly516Arg recapitulated phenotypes observed in SWS fibroblasts such as accelerated Brefeldin A (BFA)-induced retrograde transport and increased apoptosis in a 3D pellet culture, while also showing impaired chondrogenic differentiation and an inability to form spheroids in the presence of BMP2 (PMID:36393834). In summary *COG4* is definitively associated with autosomal dominant Saul Wilson Syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Skeletal Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 06/05/2023 (SOP Version 9).

*TDP2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia 23 (MONDO:0014846) in 2014 (Gómez-Herreros *et al.*, PMID:24658003) in which siblings  presented with progressive ataxia, seizures refractory to antiepileptic drugs, and intellectual disability were found to have null biallelic variants in the *TDP2* gene. Subsequent reports of individuals with pathogenic biallelic *TDP2* variants noted cerebellar ataxia, drug-resistant epilepsy, and moderate to severe intellectual disability as core clinical features with majority of the patients also presenting with craniofacial dysmorphism (PMID: 41457191). 

Ten variants (one missense, five nonsense, one frameshift, two splice site variants) that have been reported in eight probands in eight publications (PMIDs: 24658003, 30109272, 31410782, 32651480, 34606976, 37558815, 38433132, 41457191) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression studies and in vitro functional assays (PMID: 24658003). mRNA analyses of fetal and adult human tissue samples by Gómez-Herreros *et al.*, demonstrated that *TDP2* is highly expressed in various regions of the brain (PMID: 24658003). Moreover, neural tissue and cells of Tdp2 conditional knockout mice showed absence of 5’-TDP activity and reduced capacity for the repair of TOP2-induced double strand breaks after treatment with etoposide (PMID: 24658003). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *TDP2* and autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia 23. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Ataxia GCEP on the meeting date January 14th, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

CASP8 was FIRST reported in relation to autosomal recessive Caspase 8-related immune disorder in 2002
(Chun HJ et al. PMID:12353035). A review of the literature shows three main phenotypes in affected individuals: a lymphoproliferative pheontype, a immunodeficiency phenotype (characterized by sinuopulmonary bacterial infections and EBV/HSV/molluscum viruses, and an autommunune/autoinflammatory phenotype most notably very early onset IBD. At least two missense variants have been reported in humans. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes genetic data, segregtion data, and extensive experimental data. 

Variants in this gene have been reported in at least 6 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 12353035, 25814141, 30267714, 41026346).

The landmark study (PMID: 12353035) identified 2 siblings with a homozygous missense variant (R248W).

A second report (PMID: 25814141) described 2 adult siblings with a homozygous variant (G445C) presenting with late-onset lymphocytic infiltration.

There are reports of at veo-IBD documented in the literature (PMID: 30267714). 

Variants in this gene segregated with disease in additional family members across these consanguineous pedigrees.

Summary of Case-Control Data
This gene-disease relationship has been studied in at least 1 case-control study (PMID: 12353035) at the single variant level, primarily exploring the contribution of CASP8 polymorphisms to the susceptibility of the CEDS phenotype. Aggregate variant level case-control studies for this specific ultra-rare immunodeficiency are limited due to the small global patient population.

Comment on statistics: Monogenic disease (CEDS) is driven strictly by rare, biallelic loss-of-function or damaging missense variants with clear segregation.

The mechanism is homozygous loss of function. While Caspase-8 is pro-apoptotic, its deficiency in humans results in a paradox of both lymphoproliferation (failure to die) and immunodeficiency (failure of T/B/NK cell activation via the NF-κB pathway). 

Final Gene-Disease Validity Classification
● DEFINITIVE: In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between CASP8 and Autosomal Recessive Caspase-8 Deficiency State (CEDS). This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time through the identification of distinct biallelic variants in multiple unrelated families.

This classification was approved by the ClinGen Immune Dysregulation Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date April 21, 2026 (SOP Version [12]).

*HCN2* was first reported to have a potential link to autosomal dominant epilepsy in 2008 (Tang B et al., PMID: 17931874). Some case-level data exists to suggest a possible gene-disease relationship. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotype for *HCN2*-related disorders. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple curations: autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder, autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder, and autosomal dominant epilepsy (this curation). The split curations for autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder are presented separately.

Four missense variants reported in five probands from three publications are included in this curation (PMID: 24324597, 29064616, 40468825). The phenotype consisted of febrile, generalized, and/or focal seizures, sometimes noted to be photosensitive. Seizures were isolated or associated with borderline/mild intellectual disability. Though these probands have overlapping features with those described in the AD complex neurodevelopmental disorder curation, co-expression of these variants with wild type *HCN2* in Xenopus oocytes indicates these variants exhibit a depolarizing shift in activation, a greater slope, and faster activation kinetics compared to controls, consistent with a gain-of-function effect (PMID: 24324597, 29064616, 40468825) (as opposed to a dominant-negative effect observed in the AD complex neurodevelopmental disorder curation). Additionally, most variants in the autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder curation were do novo, while most variants in this curation were inherited from affected parents. Other missense variants were given zero points due to a lack of detailed clinical information, lack of segregation in affected family members, higher than expected population frequency in gnomAD v4.1.0, and/or functional studies showing no significant difference in channel properties compared to wild-type (PMIDs: 17931874, 21615589, 29064616, 20437590, 28807990). 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.  This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date February 3, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The first report indicating a relationship of the FADD gene with autosomal recessive FADD-related autoimmune lymphoproliferative immune disorder (also called immunodeficiency 90 with encephalopathy, functional hyposplenia, and hepatic dysfunction) was made by Bolze et al., 2010 (PMID 21109225). This report featured a single consanguineous Pakistani family with several affected family members who carried the same homozygous variant in the FADD gene, with each affected individual displaying a heterogeneous number of symptoms including increased infections, recurrent liver inflammation, febrile seizures with encephalopathy, variable cardiac malformations and variable autoimmune features. Since that publication, there have been five other publications that were discovered in these curation efforts, featuring a total of five different ITCH variants. The proposed mechanism for the gene-disease relationship is protein loss of function leading to impaired FADD-mediated apoptosis in affected cells.
In summary, FADD is MODERATELY associated with autosomal recessive FADD-related autoimmune lymphoproliferative immune disorder. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, functional data and model organisms. This classification was presented to the ClinGen Primary Immunodeficiencies Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 17, 2026, and approved thereafter.

TMEM106B Hypomyelinating Leukodystrophy 16, autosomal dominant
Preferred name: TMEM106B-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy

The TMEM106B gene encodes for a glycoprotein that is located in the membrane of late endosomes and lysosomes (PMID: 37563705). This protein is thought to be involved in endolysosome sorting and fusion, retrograde transport of lysosomes, lysosome acidification and protein degradation (PMID: 37563705). A heterozygous variant in TMEM106B was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 16 (HLD16) in 2017 (Simons et al., PMID: 29186371). Affected individuals present with nystagmus, saccadic pursuit, poor feeding, hypotonia, hypertonia, delayed development (primarily motor), intellectual disability, learning differences, gait ataxia, intention tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, dysmetria, hyperreflexia, pyramidal signs, hypomyelination, and thin corpus callosum. Onset occurs in infancy. 

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found a consistent phenotype and no difference in molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern; therefore, the single disease entity of HLD16 has been maintained. A single recurrent missense variant has been reported in 10 probands across 7 publications (PMIDs: 29186371, 29444210, 32595021, 36046422, 36950148, 37077564, 38008000). All variants occurred de novo in the affected individual, except one case in which the variant was inherited from a mosaic parent. The mechanism of pathogenicity is unknown although gain-of-function or dominant-negative mechanisms have been suggested (PMID: 30643851). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. A knockout mouse demonstrated mild motor coordination issues as well as myelination defects (PMID: 32572497). Protein interaction studies show that the protein encoded by the VPS11 gene, which has been implicated in a different hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, interacts with TMEM106B cytoplasmic domain (PMID: 25066864). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between TMEM106B and autosomal dominant hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 16, also known as TMEM106B-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date June 23, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: neuropathy, hereditary sensory and autonomic, type 1A
disease_original_title: neuropathy, hereditary sensory and autonomic, type 1A
submitted_as_notes:
SPTLC1: autosomal dominant HSAN (HSAN1A).
In context with an autosomal dominant, axonal Hereditary Sensory Neuropathy phenotype, SPTLC1 was first identified by linkage analysis, co-segregating in 11 families, the largest of which displaying 51 affected individuals (LOD score 6.08) (Dawkins et al., PMID: 11242114; Nicholson et al., PMID: 8673084). The same, recurrent variants located in hot-spot region  p.Cys133 have been replicated in several other publications (PMIDs: 15546589, 31742231), with functional evidence showing elevated 1-deoxy sphingoid bases as a shared biomarker (PMID: 20097765) for specific gain-of-function mutations causing a shift in substrate specificity of the serine-palmitoylCoA transferase complex, the first catalytic subunit of which is encoded by SPTLC1. Interestingly, according missense variants in SPTLC2 lead to the same phenotype, underlining its pathophysiological relevance. Other than HSAN1-related variants, missense mutations affecting the transmembrane regions of SPTL1 and SPTLC2 can disrupt interaction with its main inhibitor, ORMDL3, which leads to generalized sphingolipid overproduction not selective to the 1-deoxy-sphingoid bases. This mechanism is associated with juvenile-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a different disease entity with a separate curation (split). However, missense variants in the hot-spot region around position p.Ser331 can cause a complex phenotype with sensory impairment, wound healing disturbances, and foot ulcerations (all typical for HSAN1) and additional features like generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness as well as cataracts (PMIDs: 21618344, 24247255, 19651702, 23454272). We included these variants in the present curation due to phenotype overlap and elevated plasma 1-deoxy-sphingolipids as a shared mechanism-specific disease marker. With several unrelated reports, including both large ancestries and de-novo cases, all supported by variant-specific functional evidence, the genetic evidence alone is sufficient to establish a definitive gene-disease relationship.
Additionally, data on biochemical function and functional alteration (PMID: 20097765), variant-specific mouse models (e.g. PMID: 16210380) and several demonstrations of successful rescue by L-serine (PMID: 2204557) and allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides (PMID: 41124364) have provided extensive experimental evidence to the gene curation. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial on oral L-serine supplementation in 16 HSAN1 patients with pathogenic variants in SPTLC1 (PMID: 30626650) has shown some clinically meaningful improvements (not significant in this pilot cohort), underscoring the treatment relevance of mechanistic disease understanding.
In summary, strong clinical evidence, including a specific phenotype, variant recurrency, high LOD scores, and de-novo occurrence, is supported by experimental data on gene and variant level and has been replicated over time. We therefore classify the gene-disease relationship of SPTLC1 and autosomal dominant HSAN1 as definitive.

The *RUSC2* gene (RUN And SH3 Domain Containing 2) is located on chromosome 9 at 9p13.3. The encoded protein was originally characterized as an interacting partner of Rab1b and Rab1-binding protein GM130 (Bayer et al, 2005, PMID: 15796781). Later studies showed that the protein facilitates the transport of AP-4-derived, ATG9A-positive vesicles from the trans-Golgi network to the cell periphery (Davies et al, 2018, PMID: 30262884). Features reported among these affected individuals include intellectual disability, developmental delay, seizures, dysmorphic features, microcephaly, and limb spasticity. 

*RUSC2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder in 2016 (Alwadei et al, 2016, PMID: 27612186). Four unique variants (frameshift, nonsense, missense and splice variant) that have been reported in 3 probands in 3 publications are included in this curation (Alwadei et al., 2016, PMID:  27612186; Jauss et al., 2022, PMID: 36553572; SCV002970374.3; SCV004389982.2). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.This gene-disease relationship is also supported by protein interaction data (PMID: 27612186, PMID: 30262884, PMID: 36553572). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date October 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *DNA2* and *DNA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 9, 2026. The *DNA2* gene encodes DNA replication helicase/nuclease 2, a conserved helicase / nuclease involved in the maintenance of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA stability. DNA2 is critical for long-patch base-excision repair, the predominant pathway for repairing small DNA lesions induced by oxidation, alkylation, and spontaneous hydrolysis. It likely plays a role in the repair of oxidative lesions in mitochondrial DNA.

The *DNA2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant *DNA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2013 (PMID: 23352259). *DNA2* has been associated with three disease entities to date; progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal dominant 6 [OMIM# 615156], Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, type 4 [OMIM# 620819], and Seckel syndrome 8 [OMIM# 615807]. Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, type 4 and Seckel syndrome 8 are distinct disease entities from progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal dominant 6. Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal dominant 6 [OMIM# 615156] is a distinct disease entity and is curated here, however has been renamed as *DNA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, several cases have been reported to have a phenotype consistent with primary mitochondrial disease (PMIDs: 25635128, 28554558, 36064591, P1 in 31636600) but were excluded from this curation as the variants were purported to cause loss of function whereas the suspected disease mechanism for autosomal dominant *DNA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease is a dominant negative.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included eight missense variants identified in eight unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 23352259, 31478350, 31636600). Affected individuals had predominantly adult-onset myopathy, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and cataracts with multiple mtDNA deletions detected in muscle.

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be dominant negative as single variants are associated with impaired nuclease, helicase, and ATPase activities (PMID: 23352259). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *DNA2* and autosomal dominant *DNA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 9, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

LMNB1 was first associated with primary autosomal dominant microcephaly 26 in 2020 (MCPH26: OMIM #150340) (PMID: 32910914). MCPH26 is characterized by congenital or early-onset progressive microcephaly with global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Affected individuals often present with hypotonia, motor delay, speech impairment, and variable behavioral abnormalities. Additional features may include seizures, feeding difficulties, and growth restriction. Prior to this disease description, LMNB1 was associated with disease in 2006 in autosomal dominant leukodystrophy with autonomic disease (ADLD), which is caused primarily by genomic duplications of a region within chromosome 5q23.2 that includes the entire LMNB1 gene (Padiath et al., PMID: 16951681). ADLD is an adult onset leukodystrophy characterized by progressive motor and cognitive impairment with autonomic symptoms. 
The LMNB1 gene encodes lamin B1, a major structural component of the nuclear lamina that maintains nuclear shape and integrity, regulates chromatin organization, and supports essential cellular processes including transcription, DNA replication, and nuclear assembly. Heterozygous variants in LMNB1 act in a dominant-negative manner to disrupt lamin B1 function and nuclear lamina stability, leading to abnormal nuclear morphology and altered chromatin organization during brain development.
Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we identified significant differences in phenotype and molecular mechanism between ADLD and MCPH26 (PMID: 32910914). Therefore, MCPH26 is curated as a distinct disease entity from ADLD. ADLD has been curated by the ClinGen Dosage Sensitivity Working Group. 
This curation of autosomal dominant MCHP26  included six missense variants and two in-frame deletions reported in 13 probands across three publications (PMIDs: 32910914, 33033404, 33584783). In total we found 8.7 points for genetic evidence. This gene–disease relationship is further supported by 4 points of experimental evidence, including two unique mouse models demonstrating the essential role of lamin B1 in brain development and nuclear structure (PMIDs: 21976703, 15232008). 
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between LMNB1 and autosomal dominant microcephaly 26, also known as LMNB1-related microcephaly,  with rigorous and reproducible evidence in research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date: December 10, 2025 SOP Version #11.

The relationship between *NDUFA13* and *NDUFA13*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 18, 2024. This gene is also known as *GRIM19*. The *NDUFA13* gene encodes NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit A13, which plays a role in complex I assembly and function within the mitochondria.  Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The *NDUFA13* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFA13*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2015 (PMID: 25901006). *NDUFA13* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 28 [OMIM# 618249]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFA13*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFA13* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on October 12, 2020 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *NDUFA13*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique variants (two missense, one frameshift leading to a premature truncation) identified in two unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 25901006, 32722639). Disease onset was early in life.  Clinical features in the two reported individuals include LSS, developmental delay, chorea, seizures, spasticity, optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing loss, cardiomyopathy, failure to thrive, and cerebellar atrophy with basal ganglia lesions.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in non-patient cells (PMID: 27626371), and by an embryonic lethal mouse knockout model with evidence of complex I deficiency in blastocysts (PMID: 15367666).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFA13* and autosomal recessive *NDUFA13*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 18, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The *CRB1* gene was first reported in relation to ocular disease in 1999, in affected members from a family with autosomal recessive inheritance who were diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa 12 (den Hollander et al., PMID: 10373321). The spectrum of disease subsequently expanded to include cases diagnosed as Leber congenital amaurosis 8 or RP with Coats-like exudative vasculopathy (PMID: 11389483), or isolated macular disease (PMID: 29391521). Affected individuals generally exhibit retinal features including night blindness, progressive loss of visual acuity, peripheral visual field constriction, photophobia, pigmentary retinopathy with para-arteriolar preservation, central thinning of the outer nuclear layer, hypermetropia, drusen, vascular sheathing, and/or cystoid macular edema. A family was subsequently identified with pigmented paravenous chorioretinal atrophy showing autosomal dominant inheritance (PMID: 15623792). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the cases diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa 12 or Leber congenital amaurosis 8 shared a recessive mode of inheritance and biallelic loss-of-function mechanism, with overlapping phenotypes that were consistent with a single spectrum of disease. The autosomal dominant cases were distinguishable by their mode of inheritance, the scarcity of additional affected families following the initial report, and the absence of evidence of affected status among heterozygous carriers from the autosomal recessive pedigrees. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *CRB1* variants have been split into two separate disease entities, with the present curation focusing on autosomal recessive cases referred to as *CRB1*-related retinopathy.

Fifteen suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (seven missense, one in-frame deletion, three frameshift, three nonsense, and one predicted to disrupt splicing). These variants have been collectively reported in ten probands in three publications (PMID: 10373321, PMID: 11231775, PMID: 22065545). The variant types indicate that the mechanism of pathogenicity is biallelic loss-of-function. At least one reported family had a large number of affected individuals who were homozygous for the suspected disease-causing variant, contributing to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship through segregation evidence.

This gene-disease association is also supported by evidence that *CRB1* is highly specifically expressed in the human retina and to a lesser extent in the retinal pigment epithelium, the optic nerve, and the brain (PMID: 30239781). CRB1 protein localizes to the subapical cell surfaces of rod, cone, and Müller glial cells in order to maintain adherens junctions, regulate apical-basal polarity, and modulate apical membrane size in collaboration with the cadherin-catenin complex (PMID: 760678,7 PMID: 28424578, PMID: 32817065). Mutations in the *Drosophila* ortholog *crumbs* result in embryonic lethality associated with morphological abnormalities, cell death of epithelial tissues, and overactivation of autophagy in the eye leading to neurodegeneration (PMID: 28306104, PMID: 39965731). *Crb1* loss-of-function in zebrafish results in retinal dystrophy with enhanced rod sensitivity to damage by white light and loss of cone sensitivity to bright white light (PMID: 32817065). Homozygous *Crb1* loss-of-function in mice causes congenitally short photoreceptor inner and outer segments, as well as retinal folds associated with retinal spotting and regions of photoreceptor degeneration (PMID: 12915475).

In summary, CRB1 has a Definitive association with *CRB1*-related retinopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 5th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

GATM was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant in Fanconi renotubular syndrome in 2018 (Reichold et al., PMID: 29654216). This condition is characterized by chronic kidney disease (which often progresses to end-stage renal disease); hypokalemia; hypophosphatemia; metabolic acidosis; urine anomalies (glycosuria; aminoaciduria; and proteinuria); osteomalacia; and other skeletal anomalies (such as osteoporosis). Eight variants (all missense) that have been reported in at least ten probands in six publications (PMIDs: 29654216, 36148635, 37286521, 38310177, 38876250, 39544690) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain-of-function (PMIDs: 29654216). Heterozygous GATM variants in a specific region of the protein, approximately residues 290-350, result in the production of a de novo surface for interaction, leading to aggregates of multimers within mitochondria (PMID: 29654216). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (expression, functional alteration, biochemical function, and rescue evidence; PMID: 29654216). GATM is expressed in proximal renal tubule cells. Rescue evidence revealed that creatine supplementation decreased expression of the gene in mice. Other experimental evidence showed that GATM is key in creatine biosynthesis, and that GATM mutants lead to protein aggregates in mitochondria. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Tubulopathy GCEP on the meeting date 2/18/2026 (SOP Version 12).

The phosphodiesterase 6d (PDE6D) gene is located on chromosome 2 at 2q37.1 and encodes the retinal rod rhodopsin-sensitive cGMP 3',5'-cyclic phosphodiesterase subunit delta, consisting of 150 amino acids. This protein is a key enzyme in the phototransduction cascade and also has an additional role in the PDE complex, in which the protein is thought to bind to prenyl groups of proteins to target them to subcellular organelles called cilia. Multiple disease entities have been reported in association with this gene. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was no evidence of differences in their molecular mechanism and/or inheritance pattern and/or phenotypic spectrum. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: AR Ciliopathy: MONDO:0005308.

*PDE6D* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Joubert syndrome 22 in 2014 (Thomas et al., PMID: 24166846). The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. Patients with *PDE6D* gene mutation present with the constellation of symptoms found in Joubert syndrome (JS): congenital cerebellar ataxia,  congenital malformation of the brainstem, agenesis/hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis leading to an abnormal respiratory pattern, nystagmus, hypotonia, ataxia, and delay in achieving motor milestones. Other features sometimes include retinal dystrophy, hepatopathy, nephronophthisis, and polydactyly. 

A total of 3 variants, (deletion, insertion and single nucleotide variant) have been reported in over 3 probands in over 5 publications from 2014 to 2023 (PMIDs: 24166846, 30293248, 30423442, 32055034 and 37644014). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by the following studies. Thomas et al.(PMID: 24166846) identified *PDE6D* as a novel disease gene in ciliopathies through comprehensive genetic, structural, and functional analyses. Using exome sequencing in a consanguineous family with Joubert syndrome–like features, they discovered a homozygous splice-site mutation in *PDE6D*, a gene encoding a prenyl-binding protein crucial for ciliary trafficking. Functional experiments in zebrafish demonstrated that loss of *PDE6D* leads to retinal and renal developmental defects that are rescued by wild-type but not mutant *PDE6D*, confirming the mutation’s pathogenicity. Structural modeling showed that the gene encodes key hydrophobic residues forming part of *PDE6D’s* nonpolar binding pocket; its deletion disrupts the protein’s conformation and ability to bind prenylated cargo. Proteomic analysis revealed that INPP5E, a farnesylated ciliary protein previously linked to JS, is a major *PDE6D* interactor. Mutant *PDE6D* fails to bind or deliver INPP5E to cilia and also loses interaction with ARL3, which mediates cargo release. Expression profiling found high *PDE6D* levels in the brain, kidney, and respiratory epithelia, which are tissues typically affected in ciliopathies. Overall, the article provides the first evidence that prenyl-binding–dependent trafficking defects underlie certain ciliopathies. A previous study in 2007 by Zhang et al. (PMID: 17496142) investigated the physiological role of *PDE6D* by generating a *PDE6D* knockout mouse. Despite being viable and fertile, knockout mice exhibited 20–30% lower body weight and progressive retinal dysfunction and degeneration. Immunoblotting and immunocytochemistry confirmed loss of *PDE6D* and reduced levels of prenylated phototransduction proteins such as GRK1 and cone PDE6α′, while non-prenylated proteins (rhodopsin, rod transducin) remained unaffected. GRK1 and cone *PDE6D* were mislocalized and largely absent from outer segments in both rods and cones, indicating defective trafficking of prenylated proteins. Functional testing showed increased single-photon sensitivity, delayed photoresponse recovery, and markedly reduced photopic b-wave amplitudes (−70%), consistent with impaired light adaptation. Histologically, the retina developed normally but displayed gradual rod/cone dystrophy, with outer segment shortening by 4 weeks and loss of photoreceptor nuclei by 20 months. Overall, the study demonstrated that *PDE6D* is essential for the proper transport of prenylated proteins to photoreceptor outer segments, and its absence leads to disrupted visual signaling and slowly progressive retinal degeneration.

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *PDE6D* and AR ciliopathy. This has been demonstrated in both clinical diagnostic and research settings. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on the meeting date August, 27th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFA12* and *NDUFA12*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 18, 2024. The *NDUFA12* gene encodes NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit A12, a non-catalytic complex I accessory protein which plays a role in complex I assembly and function.

The *NDUFA12* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFA12*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2011 (PMID: 21617257). *NDUFA12* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 23 [OMIM# 618244]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFA12*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFA12* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on August 21, 2019 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *NDUFA12*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included six unique variants (one missense, two frameshift, three nonsense) identified in six unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 21617257, 29093663, 33715266). Of note, the maximum case level data score was reached, but there are an additional nine cases from six kindreds that have been reported (PMID: 35141356). Age of onset varied from early in life to childhood and most reported individuals were living at the time of report. Clinical features in affected individuals include Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder and optic atrophy. Muscle biopsies showed complex I deficiency when performed. Elevated blood lactate was seen.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and by functional alteration studies in non-patient cells (PMIDs: 27626371, 24717771). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFA12* and autosomal recessive *NDUFA12*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 18, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

WD repeat-containing protein antisense to TP53 (WRAP53) was first reported in relation to a form of dyskeratosis congenita in 2011 (Zhong et al., PMID: 21205863). Individuals with *WRAP53* variants presented with features of the classic dyskeratosis congenita mucocutaneous triad (oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, abnormal skin pigmentation) in addition to more severe phenotypes that include but are not limited to, bone marrow failure, aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome. Short telomeres have been observed in all cases where telomere length was measured, and the age of onset ranges from very early childhood to adulthood. While interstitial lung disease (ILD) is associated with many telomere biology related diseases (PMID: 30540921), no cases with ILD were found in a literature search. There was however, one case reported to have a hepatopulmonary syndrome along with respiratory insufficiency (PMID: 37149759).

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanisms or phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entity has been curated as a single autosomal recessive disease entity. A single report was found that asserts a single case of aplastic anemia with short telomeres in a heterozygous WRAP53 variant carrier however further data are required to clarify that monoallelic *WRAP53* variant carriers can present with disease (PMID: 30523342 ). Cases have been reported in the literature with the severe form of telomere biology disorder referred to as Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson (PMID: 37149759). Other assertions have been made in the literature for Ewing sarcoma (PMID: 28125078), pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 31470354), primary immunodeficiency (PMID: 32888943), craniometadiaphyseal dysplasia (PMID: 34484289), gastric cancer (PMID: 28875981), and breast cancer (PMID: 17683073); however, these additional assertions were split due to sequencing errors (PMID:36116037), presence of variants in other genes, and high allele frequencies.

Ten missense variants that have been reported in 7 probands across 6 publications (PMIDs: 21205863, 29514627, 32303682, 34599657, 30552426, 37149759) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be a loss of function that results in shortened telomeres (PMID: 21205863).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including biochemical function data that is consistent with the phenotype (PMID: 19179534), protein interactions with other genes known to cause dyskeratosis congenita (PMID: 32303682), functional alteration in iPSCs that demonstrate the human disease process (PMID: 21602826), and a cell culture model that displayed telomere shortening and the necessity of *WRAP53* for Cajal body formation (PMIDs: 19179534, 21072240).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Interstitial Lung Disease GCEP on the meeting date March, 17 2026 (SOP Version 12).

This gene-disease pair was originally evaluated by the General GCEP on January 25, 2017. It was reevaluated on March 17, 2026. As a result of this reevaluation, the classification did not change.

*TNIK* encodes the TRAF2 and NCK-interacting protein kinase involved in dendrite development and synaptic transmission. *TNIK* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive non-syndromic intellectual disability in 2016 (Anazi et al., PMID: 27106596). A homozygous nonsense variant (p.Arg180*) was reported in two multiplex, consanguineous Saudi Arabian families with five affected males, and was determined to be a founder variant. Affected individuals exhibit intellectual disability, speech delay, and hyperactivity. Western blot analysis of patient cells showed absence of the TNIK protein. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including functional alterations in human cells, and a mouse model. TNIK functions as a postsynaptic density (PSD) signaling hub, and *TNIK* mutations in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons have been shown to disrupt immature synapse function and impair MAPK-dependent phosphorylation of core PSD proteins (PMID: 38638602). *Tnik* knock-out mice show impairments in dentate gyrus neurogenesis, cognitive deficits, and hyperlocomotor behavior (PMID: 23035106).

In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *TNIK* and autosomal recessive non-syndromic intellectual disability. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. The classification was downgraded from moderate to limited because only two families with the same founder variant have been reported since 2016. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 6, 2025 (SOP Version 12).

*DMRT1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant spermatogenic failure in 2013 (Lopes et al., PMID: 2355527). *DMRT1* encodes a highly conserved transcription factor essential for postnatal testicular differentiation, maintenance of male germ cell identity, and progression of spermatogenesis (PMID: 26005864). Disruption of *DMRT1* function is thought to impair germ cell survival and meiotic progression, leading to progressive germ cell depletion and spermatogenic failure (PMID: 20951351, PMID: 27583450). *DMRT1*-related spermatogenic failure is characterized by impaired or absent sperm production in otherwise phenotypically normal 46,XY males. Affected individuals most commonly present with non-obstructive azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia due to primary testicular failure (PMID: 23555275). Histological findings frequently include Sertoli cell–only syndrome, maturation arrest (often at the spermatogonial or spermatocyte stage), or markedly reduced germ cell numbers (PMID: 24934491). External genitalia, pubertal development, and secondary sexual characteristics are typically normal, distinguishing this condition from disorders of sex development (DSD), also caused by variants in *DMRT1* (PMID: 22573722). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, while there is no clear molecular distinction between the variants causing spermatogenic failure and DSD, these are clinically distinct disorders with significant phenotypic differences. Therefore, the following have been curated separately: spermatogenic failure (MONDO:0004983) and autosomal dominant 46,XY differences of sex development (MONDO:0020040). 

Seventeen variants (including missense and large deletions) that have been reported in sixteen probands in six publications (PMIDs: 36572623, 38614076, 35366911, 39777458, 26139570, 24934491) are included in this curation. Multiple missense and predicted loss-of-function variants, as well as gene-spanning deletions, have been reported in *DMRT1* in males with spermatogenic failure. Variants cluster in the critical DM domain and the proximal coding region, suggesting a key role in testicular function.
