Both point mutations and CNVs support haploinsufficiency and/or dominant-negative effects as mechanisms. The enrichment of rare, damaging variants in affected cohorts compared to population databases (e.g. gnomAD v4.1) strongly supports the relationships.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. *DMRT1* is robustly expressed in human testis, specifically in spermatogenic cells, indicating its relevance for spermatogenesis (PMID: 16617334). Functionally, *DMRT1* acts as a pioneer factor that opens chromatin and enables SOX9 binding to reprogram sexual cell fate, functioning cooperatively with SOX9 and SOX8 (PMID: 34096593). Missense variants in the DNA-binding DM domain, such as c.221C>T (p.Pro74Leu) and c.344T>A (p.Met115Lys), reduce DNA binding and disrupt transcriptional regulation of genes critical for spermatogenesis and Sertoli cell function, leading to tubular atrophy, loss of germ and Sertoli cells, and male infertility (PMID: 39777458, PMID: 36572623). Animal models support *DMRT1’*s essential roles in both germ cells and Sertoli cells. Dmrt1⁻/⁻ mice show absent spermatogenesis, incomplete Sertoli cell maturation, and reduced testis size. Transgenic expression of *DMRT1* in Sertoli cells partially improves tubule structure and sperm parameters but cannot fully rescue fertility, which requires expression in both germ and somatic cells (PMID: 23255335). Dmrt1-deficient spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) lose expression of SSC markers (PLZF, ID4-GFP, GFRα1), fail to self-renew, and cannot regenerate after cytotoxic depletion, resulting in stem cell pool collapse and spermatogenesis failure. Human *DMRT1* variants are associated with Sertoli-only or severely impaired spermatogenesis, supporting a conserved role in SSC maintenance (PMID: 27583450). Loss of *DMRT1* in Sertoli cells leads to partial transdifferentiation toward granulosa-like cells, activation of female gene programs (Foxl2), repression of male pathway genes (Sox9), disruption of seminiferous tubule structure, and infertility (PMID: 21775990). Heterozygous *DMRT1* knockout in rabbits (DMRT1+/−) causes progressive male infertility, Oligo-/Azoospermia, Sertoli-cell-only tubules, and disrupted spermatogonial differentiation, supporting haploinsufficiency as a mechanism for male spermatogenic failure (PMID: 40169148). Together, these data demonstrate that *DMRT1* is required for SSC maintenance, proper Sertoli cell function, and normal spermatogenesis. Loss-of-function or hypomorphic variants impair both germline and somatic components of the testis, leading to male infertility.
More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for experimental evidence (6 pts.) has been reached. 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *DMRT1* and autosomal dominant spermatogenic failure. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on the meeting date February 18, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The relationship between *SCO2* and *SCO2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 7, 2024. The *SCO2* gene encodes a copper metallochaperone essential for the synthesis and maturation of cytochrome *c* oxidase subunit II (MT-CO2/COX2), and is involved in transporting copper to the Cu(A) site on MT-CO2/COX2.

The *SCO2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *SCO2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 1999 (PMID: 10545952). *SCO2* has been associated with two disease entities to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 2 [OMIM# 604377] and myopia 6 [OMIM# 608908]. The myopia 6 phenotype is a distinct disease entity and is outside the scope of this curation. The mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 2 phenotype is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *SCO2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *SCO2* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on March 25, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Definitive. This current curation for the association with *SCO2*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 12 unique variants (eight missense, three nonsense, one frameshift) identified in 18 unrelated cases from 13 publications (PMIDs: 10545952, 11673586, 18924171, 20159436, 19879173, 33098801, 32668698, 27290639, 25058219, 29351582, 31844624, 35112411, 10749987). Disease onset is typically early in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dystonia, myopathy, and neuropathy. Complex IV deficiency was noted in several tissues in affected individuals when assessed.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 15229189), functional alteration in patient cells (PMID: 16083427), and a mouse model (PMID: 19837698).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *SCO2* and autosomal recessive *SCO2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 7, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations
disease_original_title: retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations
submitted_as_notes:
Heterozygous variants in TREX1 were first associated with retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations (RVCLS) in 2007 (Richards et al., PMID: 17660820). RVCLS is an adult-onset disorder involving the microvessels of the brain and resulting in central nervous system degeneration with progressive loss of vision, stroke, motor impairment, and cognitive decline. TREX1 was first associated with disease in 2006 in autosomal recessive Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) (Crow et al., PMID: 16845398). In 2007, heterozygous TREX1 variants were shown to cause an autosomal dominant form of AGS (PMID: 17660818). Additional heterozygous TREX1 variants have since been associated with other autosomal dominant autoimmune phenotypes, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Kirsch et al., PMID: 17660816) and familial chilblain lupus (FCL) (Rice et al., PMID: 25703219). RVCLS has been classified to be a distinct manifestation of TREX1 variants due to its unique molecular mechanism.
The TREX1 gene encodes for the major mammalian three prime repair exonuclease 1, a cytosolic 3’→5’ DNA exonuclease that degrades aberrant endogenous DNA derived from replication. TREX1 plays a critical role in preventing accumulation of intracellular DNA and inappropriate activation of the innate immune response. Frameshift variants in TREX1 at the C terminus of the TREX1 gene are associated with RVCLS, causing protein truncation. Expression studies indicate the truncated proteins retained exonuclease activity but lost normal perinuclear localization.
Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, TREX1 disorders demonstrate differences in inheritance pattern, molecular mechanism, and phenotypic variability. TREX1 can cause disease through either biallelic or monoallelic variants, necessitating a separate curation of autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant entities. We elected to split retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations (RVCLS) due to its distinct molecular mechanism and phenotype. Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, familial chilblain lupus, and systemic lupus erythematosus are lumped as TREX1-related type I interferonopathies. 
This curation of retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations (RVCLS) included six frameshift variants reported in six probands across four publications (PMIDs: 27604306, 27604306, 39119967, 26691497). 11 points of genetic evidence was reached. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model that accurately represented human RVCLS (PMID: 38834133) giving a total of 13 pts for genetic and experimental evidence.
In summary, definitive evidence supports the relationship between TREX1 and autosomal dominant retinal Vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations, with rigorous and reproducible evidence in research and clinical diagnostic settings. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date: November 5, 2025 SOP Version #11. The Syndromic Disease GCEP contributed to this curation.

*FAN1* (OMIM: 613534), encodes FANCD2/FANCI-associated nuclease 1, a structure-specific endonuclease in the DNA damage response required for the repair of DNA interstrand cross-links (ICLs) (PMID: 20603016). The curated disease entity is autosomal recessive *FAN1*-related karyomegalic interstitial nephritis (KIN; OMIM: 614817; MONDO:0013898), characterized by chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular karyomegaly and progressive CKD that frequently progresses to kidney failure. The molecular mechanism is biallelic loss of function, with some pathogenic missense variants also reported (PMID: 22772369). At least 38 distinct likely pathogenic/pathogenic *FAN1* variants have been identified, the majority being protein-truncating (nonsense, frameshift, and canonical splice-site) variants (PMID: 41565023).

The gene–disease relationship is supported by genetic evidence (12/12 points; maximum score reached). The initial discovery study identified biallelic *FAN1* variants across 9 families with KIN, establishing *FAN1* as the causal gene (PMID: 22772369). Subsequent independent reports expanded the allelic and phenotypic spectrum across diverse ancestries, including a recurrent founder variant p.Trp707Ter in French Polynesian families (PMID: 34386670), c.1673dup (p.Met558IlefsTer4) in a large Hungarian family (PMID: 38892095), and a homozygous nonsense allele c.2260C>T (p.Arg754Ter) in a biopsy-confirmed multisystem case (PMID: 39294548). A comprehensive natural-history study identified 86 affected families (122 individuals) from 22 countries, with 56 genetically confirmed KIN-*FAN1* families carrying 38 distinct variants, a median age at kidney failure of 45 years, and frequent extra-renal involvement including liver test abnormalities (46%) and pulmonary complications (39%) (PMID: 41565023).

The relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (6/6 points). Biochemical and expression studies confirm FAN1's role in ICL repair and its high expression in kidney tissue relative to other organs (PMID: 22772369). Functional alteration studies in patient-derived fibroblasts demonstrate hypersensitivity to the ICL-inducing agent mitomycin C, and truncating variants abolish FAN1 protein expression on Western blot (PMID: 22772369). Non-human model organism data from *Fan1* nuclease-defective knock-in mice and knockout models recapitulate KIN-like renal pathology with tubular karyomegaly, polyploidy, and DNA damage sensitivity (PMIDs: 26980188, 26980189, 27026368).

In summary, there is Definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *FAN1* and autosomal recessive karyomegalic interstitial nephritis, with a total score of 18/18 points (genetic evidence 12/12; experimental evidence 6/6). This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on March 11, 2026 (SOP version 12).

The *WNT3* gene is located on chromosome 17 at 17q32.32 and encodes Wnt family member 3 (*WNT3*), a signalling protein within the Wnt/b-catenin signalling pathways. *WNT3* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive tetra-amelia syndrome 1 in 2004 (PMID: 14872406). Tetra-amelia syndrome is characterized by the complete absence of all four limbs with additional multisystem malformations. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. To date, the disorder has been reported in a single consanguineous family of Aramaic descent. The disorder was diagnosed prenatally in four affected fetuses which were terminated between weeks 13 and 20 of gestation. Positional cloning identified a homozygous stop-gain variant c.247C>T p.(Gln83Ter) in the affected fetuses. The mechanism of pathogenicity is presumed to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (expression and mouse model evidence). The gene disease association is supported by a spatial and temporal expression pattern in the developing mouse embryo which is consistent with the clinical phenotype (PMID: 12569130). Both targeted and conditional knockout mouse models support a crucial role for *WNT3* during embryogenesis and limb formation, recapitulating aspects of the phenotype spectrum associated with tetra-amelia syndrome 1 (PMID: 12569130, 10431240).
In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic disorders GCEP on the meeting date 16th May 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *HOXA13* gene (OMIM:142959) is located on chromosome 7 at 7p15.2 and encodes a sequence-specific, AT-rich binding transcription factor. *HOXA13* is part of a developmental regulatory system that provides cells with specific positional identities on the anterior-posterior axis. Two disease entities have been reported in association with this gene: hand-foot-genital syndrome (MONDO:0007698) and Guttmacher syndrome (MONDO:0008301). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was no evidence of differences in phenotypic variability and inheritance pattern between hand-foot-genital syndrome and Guttmacher syndrome. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: hand-foot-genital syndrome (MONDO:0007698). The *HOXA13* gene was first reported in relation to  autosomal dominant hand-foot-genital syndrome in 1997 (Mortlock & Innis 1997, PMID: 9020844). Hand-foot-genital syndrome (MONDO:0007698) is characterized by the following symptoms: distal limb malformations (Bilateral thumb and great-toe hypoplasia) and urogenital defects (abnormality of the uterus, bicornuate uterus, hypospadias). Distal limb malformations appear at 100% penetrance, while urogenital defects are 50% penetrant. 
Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. There are at least 50 individuals with hand-foot-genital syndrome reported in literature, 14 of which were scored in this curation (Goodman et al., 2000, PMID: 10839976; Debeer et al., 2002, PMID: 12414828; Frisen et al., 2003, PMID: 12676922; Innis et al., 2004 , PMID: 15385446; Utsch et al., 2007, PMID: 17935235; Jorgensen et al. 2010, PMID: 19591980; Owens et al., 2013, PMID: 23532960). Most of the pathogenic variants are polyalanine expansions. The length of the expansion appears to correlate with the severity of the symptoms (PMID: 17935235). The curation also includes heterozygous missense and nonsense variants. Supporting experimental evidence includes biochemical function (Chip-Seq in mouse knockouts; Sheth et al., 2016, PMID: 27974206), functional alteration (COS-T cell transfection with mutant *HOXA13*, PMID: 17935235), as well as newt and mouse models. Both models showed an absence of digit formation - a limb phenotype consistent with human cases (PMID: 15385446; Takeuchi et al., 2022, PMID: 35274676). Polyalanine expansion knock-in in the mouse showed normal levels of Hoxa13 RNA, but reduced protein levels, which is suggestive of protein instability. In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *HOXA13* and hand-foot-genital syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date July 22nd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*EVC2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome (EvC) in 2002 (Galdzicka et al. 2002, PMID: 12468274). Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome is associated with reduced stature, shortened limbs, post-axial polydactyly of hands and/or feet, dysplastic nails and teeth, and cardiac defects. Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis is characterized by postaxial polydactyly of hands and/or feet, dysplastic nails, dental abnormalities, but no cardiac involvement. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome (OMIM:225500) and Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis (OMIM: 193530). The split curation for autosomal dominant Weyer’s acrofacial dysostosis has been curated separately. 

Nine variants (missense, indel, nonsense, frameshift), that have been reported in sixteen probands in five publications (PMIDs: 12468274, 12571802, 19810119, 23220543, 38531627) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function due to nonsense mediated decay. This gene-disease relationship is also supported knockout animal models, expression studies, biochemical function, and protein interaction (PMIDs: 19810119, 23026747, 26219237, 27164562, 38531627). *EVC2* is a transducer of extracellular signals and positively regulates Hedgehog (Hh) which is associated with bone formation and limb development and is required for cilliogenesis (PMID: 19810119). Disruption of *EVC2* in animal models with conventional and conditional knockouts resulted in skeletal defects of limbs and crania, as well as reduced growth and reduction or no expression of *EVC2* in cilia (PMIDs: 23026747, 26219237, 27164562). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *EVC2* and autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld Syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Skeletal Disorders GCEP on the meeting date February 2, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

FGF12 encodes the fibroblast growth factor 12, a sodium channel binding protein that binds to Nav1.5 (PMID: 12401812). Hennessey et al. first suggested a relationship between FGF12 and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome in 2013 (PMID: 24096171). Following screening of a cohort of 102 patients with Brugada syndrome, the authors identified one rare missense variant in the gene (c.20A>G, p.Gln7Arg). The recombinant p.Gln7Arg protein was shown to have a decreased binding affinity for Nav1.5 and resulted in decreased sodium current density in a transfected FGF13 KO rat cardiomyocyte model. This variant is also absent from gnomAD v4.1. 

However, since this initial publication, there has been no further compelling genetic evidence corroborating this gene-disease relationship. Indeed, two separate studies have specifically considered the prevalence of FGF12 variants in Brugada syndrome cohorts and have not found any rare variants within the coding exons of the gene (PMID: 25650408, 26220970). Additionally, no cardiac features have been reported in FGF12 homozygous knockout models (PMIDs: 30065296, 17678857). Li et al. have also reported several FGF12 variants in a cohort of patients with idiopathic ventricular tachycardia however more evidence is required to substantiate this relationship (PMID: 28775062).

This gene-disease relationship was evaluated on December 9 2025, by the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP. Given the absence of compelling clinical genetic data, this gene-disease classification was disputed. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on December 9, 2025 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *COX16* and *COX16*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 11, 2025. The *COX16* gene encodes a complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX) assembly factor. Defects of this protein lead to complex IV deficiency.

The first and only reports of *COX16* in relation to autosomal recessive *COX16*-related primary mitochondrial disease was in 2020 (PMID: 33169484). *COX16* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 22 [OMIM# 619355]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *COX16*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous nonsense variant predicted to escape nonsense mediated decay seen in two unrelated cases from one publication (PMID: 33169484). Both cases had neonatal lactic acidosis. Additional clinical features seen in these cases include hypotonia, areflexia, failure to thrive, liver failure, coagulopathy, cardiomyopathy, and sensorineural hearing loss. Muscle and skin fibroblasts showed complex IV deficiency.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies and rescue in patient cells (PMID: 33169484), functional alternation in non-patient cells (PMID: 29355485), and *C. elegans* model system (PMID: 29355485).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *COX16* and autosomal recessive *COX16*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Although the gene curation point total is in the Definitive range, there have not yet been two independent scored publications documenting human genetic evidence over at least 3 years. Therefore, the classification comes to Moderate. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 11, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: growth hormone insensitivity with immune dysregulation 1, autosomal recessive
disease_original_title: growth hormone insensitivity with immune dysregulation 1, autosomal recessive
submitted_as_notes:
*STAT5B* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 1 in 1998 (Iida K et al. PMID:9467570). GHISID1 is an autosomal recessive form of growth hormone insensitivity syndrome, a congenital disease characterized by short stature, growth hormone deficiency in the presence of normal to elevated circulating concentrations of growth hormone, resistance to exogeneous growth hormone therapy, and recurrent infections. Patients often have features of immune dysregulation.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, GHISID-2 (OMIM:618985), GHISID-1 (OMIM:245590). The split curation for autosomal dominant growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 2 has been curated separately.

Six variants (missense, in-frame indel, nonsense) that have been reported in six probands in six publications (PMIDs: 13679528, 15827093, 17389811, 16787985, 17030597, 39037394) are included in this curation. Several functional studies of proband variants show non-stable expression and/or limited immunodetection. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and expression studies (PMIDs: 17158201, 22912632, 37162340). Zebrafish and mouse models highlight growth defects (including cyclopia and pericardial edema), deficiency of IFG-I transcription in the liver, and defective postnatal skeletal muscle development (including bent spine). Biochemical function studies indicate that *STAT5B* is essential for IL-2–driven transcription of *IL2RA* (*CD25*) and *FOXP3*, crucial for Treg lineage specification. *STAT5B* deficiency leads to decreased Treg numbers and impaired function, promoting autoimmunity (e.g., eczema, autoimmune thyroiditis).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *STAT5B* and autosomal recessive growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 1. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen PIRD GCEP on the meeting date December 16, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *FARS2* and *FARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of December 16, 2024. The *FARS2* gene encodes mitochondrial phenylalanine-tRNA synthetase 2, one of the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which function in mitochondrial translation by catalyzing the attachment of amino acids to their cognate tRNAs. Defects in tRNA charging can result in impaired synthesis of protein subunits of oxidative phosphorylation complexes I, III, IV, and V. 

The *FARS2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *FARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2012 (PMID: 22499341). *FARS2* has been associated with two disease entities to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 14 [OMIM# 614946] and spastic paraplegia 77, autosomal recessive [OMIM# 617046]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *FARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *FARS2* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on October 14, 2019 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *FARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 10 unique variants (nine missense, one deletion) identified in 10 unrelated cases from six publications (PMIDs: 22499341, 27549011, 29126765, 22833457, 27095821, 30177229), although more than 40 affected individuals have been reported to date. Age of onset varies from neonatal period to childhood and outcomes are variable. There are two predominant phenotypes (early onset encephalopathy and later onset spastic paraplegia) however there is overlap in some cases. Several cases have features consistent with Alpers syndrome and/or Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder. Additional medical concerns include seizures, infantile spasms, epilepsia partialis continua (EPC), microcephaly, developmental delay and regression, hypotonia, spasticity, muscle weakness, myoclonus, neuropathy, tremor, dystonic movements, poor growth, vomiting, constipation, cortical blindness, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and lactic acidosis. Muscle biopsies were variable and some showed mitochondrial respiratory chain complex enzyme deficiencies. Brain imaging is similarly variable and includes cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and abnormal signal intensities in the deep cerebellar white matter and basal ganglia.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 33168986), and a *Drosophila melanogaster* model (PMID: 36205831).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *FARS2* and autosomal recessive *FARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 16, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia
disease_original_title: X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia
submitted_as_notes:
*MAGT1* was first reported in relation to X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia (i.e., XMEN) in 2011 (Li FY, et al., PMID: 21796205). XMEN is a congenital disorder of glycosylation presenting as combined immunodeficiency. This is a heterogeneous disorder typically characterized by increased susceptibility to Epstein-Barr virus and associated lymphomas (e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma), increased susceptibility to otitis media and sinopulmonary infections, an increased naïve B cell population, a decreased CD4+:CD8+ T cell ratio, decreased NKG2D expression on CD8+ T and natural killer cells, and defective N-linked glycosylation (PMID: 21796205, 23846901, 30470981, 31815737, 31865525, 32451662, 35145548, 35182234, 35264785, 38041964). Phenotypic features of patients with XMEN may also overlap with autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome including autoimmune cytopenias and an increased population of TCR alpha-beta double-negative T cells (PMID: 24550228, 25956530).

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia (OMIM: 300853) and X-linked intellectual disability (OMIM: 301031). The split curation for X-linked intellectual disability has been curated separately. 

Seven variants (frameshift, nonsense, missense) that have been reported in 7 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 21796205, 30470981, 31865525, 35145548, 35264785) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, expression studies, and ex vivo and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 19717468, 23846901, 29051561, 29581357, 33051095, 34086870). 

Bone marrow transplant and hematopoietic stem cell transplant appear to be curative options for patients with XMEN (PMIDs: 30470981, 38143450, 38578340). In addition, promise is shown for CAR T-cell therapy based on treatment of patients, gene-editing of *MAGT1* with CRISPR based on experiments in patient cells, and expression of TUSC3 based on in vitro studies (PMID: 34086870, 37086924, 38578340). Notably, magnesium supplementation does not appear to have significant therapeutic effects (PMID: 34655400).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *MAGT1* and X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders on the meeting date November 28, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *TAMM41* and *TAMM41*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 27, 2025. The *TAMM41* gene encodes mitochondrial translocator assembly and maintenance homolog 41, a phosphatidate cytidylyltransferase that is the first mitochondrial enzyme of the cardiolipin biosynthesis pathway, catalyzing the conversion of phosphatidic acid (PA) to CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DAG).

The first and only report of the *TAMM41* gene in relation to autosomal recessive *TAMM41*-related primary mitochondrial disease was in 2022 (PMID: 35321494). *TAMM41* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 56 [OMIM# 620139]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *TAMM41*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included six variants identified in three unrelated cases from one publication (PMIDs: 35321494). Clinical features in affected individuals included failure to thrive, global developmental delay, myopathy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, respiratory failure, elevated creatine kinase, and decreased activities of the respiratory chain in skeletal muscle.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration in non-patient cells (PMID: 29253589), and a yeast model (PMID: 35321494).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *TAMM41* and autosomal recessive *TAMM41*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 1
disease_original_title: cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 1
submitted_as_notes:
CTC1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Coats Plus syndrome in 2012 (Anderson et al., PMID: 22267198). Characteristic features of Coats Plus include retinal telangiectasia and exudates (Coats disease), leukodystrophy and brain cysts, osteopenia with a tendency to fractures and poor bone healing, and a high risk of life-limiting gastrointestinal bleeding caused by vasculature ectasias in the stomach, small intestine and liver (PMID: 22267198). In the same year, another group published a cohort of patients with cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 1 (CRMCC1; PMID 22387016). This cohort presented with very similar features to those in the Coats Plus cohort. Bilallelic variants in CTC1 have also been published in two individuals described as having Dyskeratosis congenita, which is a bone marrow failure syndrome with elevated cancer risk (PMIDs 22532422, 32543263); one proband also had intracranial calcifications (PMID 32543263). 

The CTC1 gene encodes CST telomere replication complex component 1, which functions in a telomere-associated complex with STN1 and TEN1. The CST complex protects telomeres by inhibiting telomerase activity (PMID 22763445). Patients presenting with these phenotypes have been found to have short telomeres (PMID 30891747). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern across the three aforementioned disease entities; furthermore we found that the spectrum of phenotypic variability could exist between the described disease entities. Therefore, these disease entities have been lumped into a single disease entity CRMCC1 (MONDO:0024564), also known as CTC1-related telomere biology disorder . 

This curation includes ten variants (missense, in-frame indel, frameshift) that have been reported in eight probands in four publications (PMIDs: 22387016, 22267198, 22532422, 30891747). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is supported by a mouse model (PMID: 22531781). In this study, CTC1 knockout mice demonstrated complete bone marrow failure that likely led to their premature death. This phenotype was observed in some patients described with bone marrow failure and CTC1 biallelic variants.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CTC1 and autosomal recessive CRMCC1, with the preferred name of CTC1-related telomere biology disorder. Two other GCEPs contributed to this curation: The Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer (CAYA) GCEP and the Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD) GCEP. The CAYA GCEP found that although there were no reported cases of leukemia or other malignancies in patients with CTC1 variants, telomere-biology disorders generally imply elevated cancer risk. The ILD GCEP noted cases of pulmonary involvement, but insufficient evidence to split out an isolated pulmonary disease from the curated disease entity from the lumped group of disease entities. 

This gene-disease relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date November 12, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*CFAP410* (a.k.a. C21orf2) was first reported in relation to CFAP410-related ciliopathy, an autosomal recessive condition, in 2013 (Abu-Safieh et al, PMID: 23105016). In OMIM, *CFAP410 *is associated with two conditions, retinal dystrophy with macular staphyloma (MIM# 617547) and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, axial (MIM# 602271). The gene has also been associated with Jeune Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (McInerney-Leo et al, 2017, PMID: 28422394). These three conditions are characterized by variable retinal findings and skeletal features, and autosomal recessive inheritance. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in the molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern or phenotypic variability between these conditions. Therefore, these disease entities have been lumped together as *CFAP410*-related ciliopathy. *CFAP410 *has also been reported as a risk factor for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in case-control studies (van Rheenen et al, 2016, PMID: 27455348; Scaber et al, 2022, PMID: 37159497) and further studies have indicated that ciliary defects may be involved in the pathogenesis of ALS. Two adult siblings have been reported to have ALS and retinopathy (Kurashige et al, 2020, PMID: 31431468). However, given that this is the only case of phenotypic overlap, ALS has been split from *CFAP410*-related ciliopathy at the current time. The split curation for ALS has been performed by the ClinGen ALS GCEP.

Over 50 probands with *CFAP410*-related ciliopathy have been reported in the literature (Shinbashi et al, 2023, PMID: 36950666; Schmidt et al, 2025, PMID: 40246852). Twelve variants (five missense, three splice site/intronic, three frameshift, and one deletion resulting in loss of the start codon) that have been reported in nine probands in three publications (Abu-Safieh et al, PMID: 23105016; Wang et al, 2016; Schmidt et al, 2025, PMID: 40246852) are included in this curation. Variants reported in more than one proband include c.218G>C (p.Arg73Pro) and c.319T>C (p.Tyr107His). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. *CFAP410* encodes Cilia- and Flagella-Associated Protein 410. Results of multiple experimental types indicate that this gene is important in ciliogenesis. siRNA knockdown of the gene in various cell types, including mIMCD3), hTERT-RPE1, and SH-SY5Y, results in fewer and shorter cilia ((Wheway et al, 2015, PMID: 26167768). CFAP410 localizes to cilia, mainly the basal body, and the photoreceptor connecting cilium, where it has been shown to physically interact with NEK1 and SPATA7 (Wheway et al, 2015, PMID: 26167768).  Variants in these genes cause retinopathy and "short-rib thoracic dysplasia with or without polydactyly" respectively. The functional interaction between CFAP410 and NEK1 was shown by the partial rescue of phenotype in zebrafish in which Nek1 had been knocked down (De Decker et al, 2025, PMID: 39703094). The ClinGen Retina GCEP classified the relationship between SPATA7 and retinopathy as definitive. The relationship between NEK1 and retinopathy has not yet been assessed by any ClinGen GCEP; but in OMIM this gene is associated with "short-rib thoracic dysplasia 6 with or without polydactyly" which includes skeletal features and retinopathy in rare cases. Drosophila with knockdown of the CFAP410 orthologue have symptoms consistent with ciliary dysfunction (De Decker et al, 2025, PMID: 39703094) Multiple genes that localize to and function in cilia have been found to have a definitive gene-disease clinical validity by the ClinGen Retina GCEP (experimental evidence 2.5 points).

In summary, there is Definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CFAP410* and autosomal recessive *CFAP410*-related cliliopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time without the emergence of conflicting evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina gene Curation Expert Panel on January 15, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

*POFUT1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation in 2018 (Takeuchi et al., PMID: 29452367). The proband presented with a syndromic condition characterized by recessive microcephaly, global developmental delay, and cardiac and vascular features. Variants in *POFUT1* have also been reported in individuals with Dowling-Degos disease 2 (OMIM: 615327). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities. The split curation for autosomal dominant Dowling-Degos disease 2 has been curated separately. One missense variant that has been reported in humans is included in this curation. The mechanism for disease is unknown. This gene-disease relationship is supported by two animal models (PMID: 19161597, 12697902) and a cell culture rescue study (PMID: 29452367). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date December 15, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *MRPL12* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 27, 2025. The *MRPL1*2 gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal protein L12.

The first and only report of *MRPL12* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2013 (PMID: 23603806). *MRPL12* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 45 [OMIM# 618951]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 23603806). This child had Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder (psychomotor delay, changes on brain MRI noted in the white matter and basal ganglia, elevated blood lactate, reduced activities of complexes I and IV in fibroblasts).

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel October 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFA1* and *NDUFA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 18, 2024. The *NDUFA1* gene encodes NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit A1. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The *NDUFA1* gene was first reported in relation to X-linked *NDUFA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2007 (PMID: 17262856). *NDUFA1* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 12 [OMIM# 301020]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFA1* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on March 25, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *NDUFA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique missense variants identified in four unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 17262856, 25356405, 29506883; additional details provided in PMIDs: 20153825, 28429146). Age of onset was the first year of life for all reported cases. Outcomes were variable and ranged from death at age 14 months to alive at age 10 years. All four cases had LSS. Complex I deficiency was noted on muscle biopsy and blood lactate levels were normal to elevated. Additional cases have been reported but were excluded from this curation given lack of clinical and variant details (PMID: 25356970), or high variant allele frequency (PMIDs: 21596602, 29353736, 29272804, 19185523, 35131137).

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in HEK293T cells, and model systems including Chinese hamster cell line (PMIDs: 10200266, 14722084, 15576048) and mouse model (PMIDs: 15293270, 12557286, 28506826).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFA1* and X-linked *NDUFA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 18, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The *PLD4* gene encodes a 5’->3’ exonuclease that localizes in endolysosomes and cleaves single-stranded RNA and DNA, restricting overactivation of TLR7 and TLR9 and their inflammatory signaling pathways. *PLD4* was first reported in relation to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in 2019 by Akizuki et al. (PMID: 30679154), who performed a GWAS meta-analysis for SLE which identified significance in a region containing *PLD4*. 

Genetic evidence was reported in 2025 by Wang et al. (PMID: 40931063). One frameshift and six missense variants in *PLD4* were identified; the variants were present in either homozygous or proven/suspected compound heterozygous states in five affected individuals. Exonuclease activity assays were performed for the six unique missense variants identified in this study as well as on a patient sample, all of which showed impaired exonuclease activity compared to controls.

Additional experimental evidence includes two mouse models. Akizuki et al. (PMID: 30679154) showed that mice homozygous for a *PLD4* nonsense variant had notably increased anti-dsDNA production, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Wang et al. (PMID: 40931063) showed that homozygous *PLD4* knockout mice had autoimmune phenotypes, including significantly elevated dsDNA antibodies, as well as severe nephritic phenotypes.

In summary, there is **moderate** evidence supporting the relationship between *PLD4* and autosomal recessive Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Systemic and Incomplete Lupus Erythematosus GCEP on the meeting date November 12, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *NR2E3* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive enhanced S-cone syndrome in 2000 (Haider et al., PMID: 10655056). Subsequent publications expanded the phenotypic spectrum associated with homozygous or compound heterozygous *NR2E3* variants to include related diagnoses such as Goldmann-Favre syndrome (PMID: 18294254), retinitis pigmentosa (PMID: 11071390) and retinoschisis (PMID: 18294254). These cases typically present with night blindness in childhood or adolescence and exhibit progressive loss of visual acuity and slow concentric reduction of the visual field during the subsequent decades, with some retention of vision even in elderly individuals, increased sensitivity to blue light, decreased electroretinogram responses from rods in particular but also from cones, retinal pigment epithelium atrophy with hypopigmented pigment deposits in the peripheral retina, macular schisis, and/or optic disc pallor. The published literature also includes cases of retinitis pigmentosa with a heterozygous *NR2E3* variant, particularly the dominant negative variant p.Gly56Arg. Affected patients typically present with night blindness in late childhood or adolescence, and can exhibit photophobia, progression to undetectable rod function with a relatively late decline in cone function, concentric rings of hyper-autofluorescence surrounding the fovea, vascular arcades, and far periphery, and mixed nummular and bone spicule intraretinal pigmentation in the later stages (PMID: 17564971). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, recessive cases of enhanced S-cone syndrome or autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa were compared with dominant cases of retinitis pigmentosa. The shared mode of inheritance, molecular mechanism (biallelic loss-of-function) and phenotypic overlap among recessive cases motivated enhanced S-cone syndrome and autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa to be combined for the purposes of this gene curation, with the lumped disease entity referred to as NR2E3-related enhanced S-cone syndrome. On the other hand, cases with overlapping phenotypes but a dominant mode of inheritance differed in their molecular mechanism (dominant negative), in contrast with the unaffected heterozygous carriers from the recessive families. Therefore, dominant cases have been lumped into a separate disease entity, referred to as NR2E3-related dominant retinopathy.

Ten suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (three frameshift, one canonical splice site variant, five missense variants in the DNA-binding domain, and one short in-frame deletion in the DNA-binding domain), which have been collectively reported in eleven probands in four publications (PMID: 10655056, PMID: 18294254, PMID: 22605927, PMID: 33138239). Ten of the probands scored in this curation harbored the variant allele in the homozygous state, with three reported as consanguineous, while one other proband harbored variants in compound heterozygosity. One large family with evidence of co-segregation of the genotype with affected status contributed to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship (PMID: 11071390).

This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence indicating that *NR2E3* is highly specifically expressed in retinal tissues (PMID: 30239781) and encodes a ligand-dependent transcription factor that is involved in photoreceptor differentiation and suppression of cone differentiation in rod photoreceptor cells (PMID: 19379737, PMID: 37510230). The protein product physically interacts with the photoreceptor cell transcription factors NRL and CRX (PMID: 15190009), both of which are encoded by genes that can harbor inherited retinal disease-causing variants. Homozygous loss-of-function of the mouse ortholog *Nr3e2* in the *rd7* model results in enhanced blue cone sensitivity, over-proliferation of ectopic retinal progenitors, increase in blue opsin expressing cone cells, increased expression of cone-associated genes, disrupted outer nuclear layer histology, retinal spotting throughout fundus, late-onset rod and cone cell death, and reduction of outer nuclear layer thickness (PMID: 19379737, PMID: 11487564, PMID: 34561487, PMID: 17266784). These defects can be rescued in young mice by subretinal injection of adeno-associated virus packaged *Nr2e3* (PMID: 32123325).

In summary, *NR2E3* is definitively associated with NR2E3-related enhanced S-cone syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 2nd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *GPKOW* gene is located on chromosome X at Xp11.23 and encodes the G-Patch Domain And KOW Motifs protein, a putative RNA-binding protein. *GPKOW* was first reported in relation to X-linked holoprosencephaly-hypokinesia-congenital contractures syndrome in 2017 (Carroll et al., PMID: 28612833). The syndrome is characterised by holoprosencephaly / microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction, hypokinesia, and congenital contractures. Additional phenotypes include dysmorphic features, skeletal dysplasia, microphthalmia, macroglossia. Female carriers usually present with short stature and small head circumference. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. Six variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift and splice variants ) that have been reported in six probands in three publications and 2 ClinVar entries are included in this curation (PMIDs: 28612833, 32426895, 40221893, SCV006060217.1, SCV006060182.1). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including model organism and biochemical function. A fruit fly animal model supports that this gene contributes to microphthalmia and reduced brain size (PMIDs: 40221893). Limited biochemical evidence of direct interaction with DHX16/hPRP2 and RNA supports *GPKOW*’s role in pre-mRNA splicing (PMID: 25296192). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date December 3, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFB7* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of April 29, 2024. The *NDUFB7* gene encodes the NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit B7, an accessory subunit of complex I. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The first and only report of *NDUFB7* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2021 (PMID: 33502047). *NDUFB7* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 39 [OMIM# 620135]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous intronic variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 33502047). The proband presented in the prenatal period at gestational week 25 with intrauterine growth restriction, intrauterine anemia, and cardiomegaly. Clinical features present after birth included lactic acidosis, pulmonary hypertension, cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and cystic and dysplastic corpus callosum. The child died at 55 days old from cardiopulmonary respiratory failure. There was evidence of complex I dysfunction in fibroblasts. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and by knockout studies in HEK293T cells showing severe reduction in complex I assembly (PMID: 27626371).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

EDN1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive auriculocondylar syndrome 3 in 2013 (Gordon et al., PMID: 24268655). 3 missense variants that have been reported in 3 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 24268655, 35170830) are included in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression and protein interaction studies supporting a genetic interaction between EDN1 and PLCB3, and demonstrating expression of EDN1 in the arch epithelium, paraxial mesoderm-derived arch core, and arch vessel endothelium (PMIDs: 17239364, 9449664). Additionally, two mouse models indicate that mice deficient in the endothelin receptor ETA mimic human conditions including severe craniofacial malformations, and that mice deficient in EDN1 also demonstrate craniofacial anomalies (PMIDs: 9449664, 8152482). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date November 20, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

CSF1R was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids (HDLS) in 2011 (Rademakers et al., PMID: 22197934). HDLS (also known as adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia; ALSP) is a rare adult-onset disorder with onset typically in the fourth or fifth decade of life (mean age of onset: 40±10 years in females and 47±11 years in males). Symptoms and disease course are variable and can include behavioral, cognitive, and personality changes, progressive motor impairment (pyramidal and/or extrapyramidal), sometimes with ataxia or seizures. Most individuals show a rapid progression of disability and typically lose their ability to speak, perform voluntary movements, and eventually become unaware of their surroundings. At the late stage of disease, symptoms progress to a vegetative state with presence of primitive reflexes. AD CSF1R-related disorder is considered a primary gliopathy, and pathology is also notable for demyelination, axonal spheroids and reactive astrocytes. Of note, biallelic variants in CSF1R have been implicated in the autosomal recessive disorder BANDDOS which is characterized by brain abnormalities, progressive neurologic deterioration, and sclerotic bone dysplasia akin to dysosterosclerosis. 

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern, phenotypic variability, and, potentially, molecular mechanism for the gene CSF1R. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities, autosomal recessive CSF1R-related disorder (aka BANDDOS, OMIM: 164770) and autosomal dominant CSF1R-related disorders (aka HDLS/ALSP, OMIM: 221820). The split curation for autosomal recessive CSF1R-related disorder has been curated separately. This curation includes 15 probands with 15 distinct variants (missense, splicing, and multi-exonic deletion) reported across two publications (PMIDs: 22197934, 39031193). Additional segregation analyses from a family from Rademakers et al., 2011 (PMID 22197934) was also included in the curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The disease mechanism has not been clearly delineated, but variant distribution and functional studies suggest altered tyrosine kinase activity and defective autophosphorylation of CSF1R as the potential mechanism (PMID 22197934, 24336230). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by an animal model (PMID: 25497733) involving a Csf1r heterozygous knock-out mouse, which recapitulates the neurological, behavioral, and pathological phenotype seen in humans. Additional experimental evidence exists, but was not included in this curation as definitive status had been reached. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CSF1R and autosomal dominant CSF1R-related disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. 

This classification was approved by the Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy Working Group on October 27, 2025 (SOP Version #11).

*AP3B2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in 2016 (Assoum, et.al. PMID: 27889060).  This condition is characterized by early-onset seizures, global developmental delays, hypotonia, microcephaly, visual impairment, motor delays, and abnormal MRI.  Fourteen total variants (6 frameshift variants, 4 nonsense variants, 2 canonical splice site variants, 1 silent variant, and 1 large deletion) that have been reported in fourteen probands in five publications (PMIDs: 27889060, 27431290, 36356440, 36493596, 34540776) are included in this curation. RNA studies indicated that a canonical splice site variant and a silent variant led to aberrant transcripts that would lead to a non-functional protein (PMID: 27889060). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a null mouse model that recapitulates the human phenotype by displaying behavioral abnormalities and seizures  (PMID: 15537701; more detailed information can be found at (https://www.informatics.jax.org/reference/J:205908)). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *AP3B2* and autosomal recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date September 16, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*CACNA1G* is located on chromosome 17 at 17q21.33 and encodes the calcium voltage-gated channel subunit alpha 1G protein, the pore-forming subunit of the low-voltage-activated (T-type) Cav3.1 channel. Variants in *CACNA1G* have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: spinocerebellar ataxia 42 (OMIM:616795) and spinocerebellar ataxia 42, early-onset, severe, with neurodevelopmental deficits (OMIM: 618087). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found insufficient functional evidence to distinguish the molecular mechanism of disease. Therefore, these twodisease entities have been lumped into one disease entity spinocerebellar ataxia 42 (OMIM:616795).
*CACNA1G* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia 42 in 2015 (Morino et al., PMID 26715324). It is characterized by slowly progressive gait instability,  dysarthria, pyramidal signs, nystagmus, and cerebellar atrophy. The age at onset and severity of the disorder is highly variable. Additionally, some individuals present with spinocerebellar ataxia 42, early-onset, severe, with neurodevelopmental deficits (SCA42ND) which is characterized by severe hypotonia, delayed psychomotor development with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, variable spasticity, dysmorphic features, and epileptic encephalopathy. SCA42ND is typically caused by de novo variants.
Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. At least seven unique missense variants have been reported in 25 individuals/families from 10 publications (PMIDs: 26715324, 31229688, 28490766, 29629410, 30200108, 34248568, 33098379, 32736238, 29878067, 3287833). Variants in this gene segregated with disease in nine families presenting with spinocerebellar ataxia 42 without neurodevelopmental deficits. This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental data including expression studies, in vitro functional assays, and an animal model. *CACNA1G* is expressed in subsets of neurons (PMID: 18853439). Both heterozygous and homozygous knock-in mice show motor impairments due to ataxia and degenerative change of Purkinje cells (PMID 31229688). The mechanism of disease remains unclear with variants demonstrating either gain-of-function, loss-of-function, or mixed effects due to the opposing shifts of the activation and inactivation curves of Ca2+ currents conducted on patient variants in in vitro functional assays (PMID: 32878331). In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *CACNA1G* and autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia 42. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date December 4th, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

PLS1 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNA76) in 2019 (Schrauwen et al., PMID: 30872814). Such hearing loss is typically moderate-to-profound in severity. 5 variants (missense, splicing) that have been reported in at least 6 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 30872814, 31397523, 31432506, 36537221) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse model, zebrafish model, expression-level data; PMIDs: 25124451, 36537221). A mouse model shows hearing loss and disorganized hair cells in mutant mice. A zebrafish model shows that mutants have inner ear structural anomalies and altered behavior in a swimming test. Evidence in mice and gEAR database expression in humans shows that PLS1 is expressed in the hair cells, cochlear duct, and endothelial cells of the ear. In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting this gene disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.

disease_title: FDXR-related optic atrophy mitochondrial dysfunction syndrome
disease_original_title: FDXR-related optic atrophy mitochondrial dysfunction syndrome
submitted_as_notes:
*FDXR* was first reported in relation to optic atrophy in 2017, in patients with optic atrophy and auditory neuropathy (PMID: 28965846), and in 2018 in patients with optic atrophy and mitochondriopathy (PMID: 29040572). Whole exome sequencing revealed biallelic variants in *FDXR* in probands and affected siblings and heterozygous variants in unaffected parents and siblings in the families. Subsequently, over 50 disease-associated *FDXR* variants have been reported in more than 50 probands with optic atrophy with or without extraocular phenotypes. A few recurrent variants have been reported in cases with primarily optic atrophy as well as cases with optic atrophy and variable extraocular presentations, which can include cerebral atrophy, hearing loss, myopathy, and developmental delay. The phenotypic variability between affected individuals appears to represent a spectrum of disease rather than separate disease entities. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, this curation has included cases reported as auditory neuropathy and optic atrophy (OMIM # 617717) as well as cases reported as multiple mitochondrial dysfunction syndrome 9B (OMIM # 620887), with the lumped disease entity referred to as *FDXR*-related optic atrophy mitochondrial dysfunction syndrome, with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

This curation has included and scored twenty-nine unique *FDXR* variants identified in twenty-one probands and reported in six publications (PMID: 28965846, PMID: 29040572, PMID: 33348459, PMID: 33938912, PMID: 38885337, PMID: 39669623). Among the reported variants (missense, nonsense, splice site mutations, frameshift and small deletions), approximately 90% are missense variants. Notably, approximately 25% of cases from 3 publications (PMID: 29040572, PMID: 33348459, PMID: 39669623) were homozygous or compound heterozygous for the p.Arg386Trp variant, with the vast majority of these affected individuals being of Hispanic origin, suggesting a founder effect. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence that *FDXR* encodes ferredoxin reductase, a mitochondrial flavoprotein that serves as an electron transfer protein in the mitochondrial P450 system and is involved in steroid and cholesterol metabolism (PMID: 2845396). Further experimental support is provided by studies showing altered FDXR function in patient-derived cells and recapitulation of clinical features from affected patients in non-human model organisms with successful rescue (PMID: 28965846, PMID: 29040572, PMID: 38885337).

In summary, *FDXR* is Definitively associated with FDXR-related optic atrophy mitochondrial dysfunction syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both clinical and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glaucoma and Neuro-Ophthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 17th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: combined immunodeficiency and megaloblastic anemia with or without hyperhomocysteinemia
disease_original_title: combined immunodeficiency and megaloblastic anemia with or without hyperhomocysteinemia
submitted_as_notes: *MTHFD1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive combined immunodeficiency and megaloblastic anemia with or without hyperhomocysteinemia in 2011 (Watkins et al., PMID: 21813566). Combined immunodeficiency and megaloblastic anemia with or without hyperhomocysteinemia (CIMAH) is an inborn error of folate metabolism due to deficiency of methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase-1. Manifestations may include hemolytic uremic syndrome, macrocytosis, epilepsy, hearing loss, retinopathy, mildly impaired intellectual development, lymphopenia involving all subsets, and low T-cell receptor excision circles. Seven variants (including missense and nonsense) that have been reported in four probands in four publications (PMIDs: 32414565, 23296427, 25633902, 21813566) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be partial loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (e.g. animal models, expression studies, biochemical function, functional alteration) (PMIDs: 32414565, 25633902, 19033438). Experimental evidence from an animal model study using mice demonstrates that the *MTHFD1* gene is essential in mice as all *MTHFD1*-null mice were shown to be not viable in the study (MacFarlane et al., PMID: 19033438). Skin fibroblasts taken from patients with biallelic *MTHFD1* variants were shown to have decreased Mthfd1 protein activity compared to heterozygote relatives as well as controls (Bidla et al., PMID: 32414565). While heterozygous carriers present with no clinical symptoms of *MTHFD1* deficiency, in vitro enzyme testing suggests that heterozygous carriers have enzyme activity levels that are approximately half that of non-carriers. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between the *MTHFD1* gene and autosomal recessive combined immunodeficiency and megaloblastic anemia with or without hyperhomocysteinemia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP on the meeting date April 16, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

Inactivating variants in *ABCC8*, encoding the SUR1 (Sulfonylurea Receptor 1) regulatory subunit of the pancreatic beta-cell KATP channel, were first reported in relation to autosomal recessive congenital hyperinsulinism, in 1995 (Thomas et al., PMID: 7716548). Subsequently, autosomal dominant (Huopio et al., PMID:11018078; Thornton et al., PMID: 12941782) inheritance patterns have been reported for *ABCC8* -related hyperinsulinism. 
Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern as well as mechanism and phenotypic variability among variants associated with recessive and dominant *ABCC8*-related hyperinsulinism, and monogenic diabetes. Therefore, the curation of *ABCC8 *has been split into (1) autosomal recessive and (2) autosomal dominant forms of hyperinsulinism (MONDO:0002177), and (3) monogenic diabetes (MONDO:0015967).  

*ABCC8*-related hyperinsulinism can be classified according to the pancreatic histopathology which is determined in part by the source of inheritance of the *ABCC8* variant. Diffuse pancreatic disease, characterized by increased numbers of islet cells with nucleomegaly throughout the pancreas, is caused by bi-allelic recessive loss-of-function or dominant missense/in-frame deletion *ABCC8* variants. Recessive variants, including stop gain, splice site, frame shift, missense and copy number variants, lead to absent, nonfunctional or less functional KATP channels. This results in persistent beta-cell membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and inappropriate insulin release, regardless of blood glucose levels. A range in disease-severity and treatment response is observed among children with recessive biallelic variants with those at the mildest end of the clinical spectrum having transient hyperinsulinism which responds well to treatment while others may have treatment-refractory disease that may require subtotal pancreatectomy to manage hypoglycemia. 

At least 300 different variants in the *ABCC8* gene including nonsense, splice site, frameshift, and missense variants have been reported in association with autosomal recessive hyperinsulinism in humans. Variants in this gene have been curated in at least 8 probands in 7 publications (PMIDs: 35621279, 23266803, 17466004, 24661758, 36034573, 26162674, 29739729), with clinical presentations consistent with *ABCC8*-related hyperinsulinism. More evidence is available to support the gene-disease association in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached this has not been curated exhaustively.

Focal hyperinsulinism, typically characterized by a small lesion of endocrine cells, within an otherwise histologically unremarkable pancreas, is caused by a single paternally-inherited recessive inactivating variant followed by a somatic loss of the maternal chromosome 11p.15 region because of paternal uniparental isodisomy. The focal lesion develops because the chromosome 11p15.5 region contains several imprinted genes including the maternally-expressed H19 (a candidate tumor suppressor gene) and CDKN1C (a negative regulator of cell proliferation) and paternally-expressed growth factor genes such as IGF2. When paternal uniparental isodisomy occurs within a pancreatic beta-cell during fetal development, the imbalance between imprinted genes (increased IGF2 and diminished H19 and CDKN1C) gives rise to the increase in proliferation of a population of beta-cells resulting in the focal lesion. As this cell contains a heterozygous ABCC8 recessive variant on the paternal allele, the uniparental disomy unmasks the variant causing it to be homozygous which results in dysregulated insulin secretion from the focal lesion. 

Rapid parental testing should be performed for all individuals with a single heterozygous recessive *ABCC8* variant as paternal inheritance offers a positive predictive value up to 94% for focal HI (pubmed: 23275527 and 24401662). For these individuals pancreatic imaging using 18F-DOPA PET scan is recommended to confirm focal disease and localize the lesion prior to lesionectomy which is curative in >97% of cases.  For these cases consultation with an HI expert is recommended.

This gene–disease relationship is supported by functional assays, expression studies, and animal models. Homozygous K499X zebrafish (SUR1⁻/⁻) displayed a loss of KATP channel activity (PMID: 36455737). Furthermore, an in vitro human stem cell model with biallelic *ABCC8* knockout (*ABCC8*⁻/⁻) effectively recapitulated the phenotype of congenital hyperinsulinism, further supporting the pathogenicity of biallelic *ABCC8* loss-of-function variants (PMID: 28600547). Total points for the experimental evidence are 5.5. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 17.5.
In summary, *ABCC8* is definitively associated with autosomal recessive hyperinsulinism, with most cases presenting in early infancy.  This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on the meeting date January 7, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

COQ7: autosomal recessive distal hereditary motor neuropathy (dHMN)
