Evidence Summary: Coenzyme Q7 (COQ7) encodes a mitochondrial hydroxylase that catalyzes the penultimate step in the biosynthesis of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), an essential electron carrier of the mitochondrial respiratory chain required for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production (Jacquier et al., PMID: 36454683). Pathogenic variants in COQ7 have been associated with primary CoQ10 deficiency (Freyer et al., PMID: 26084283) and distal hereditary motor neuropathy (dHMN) (Jacquier et al., PMID: 36454683; Rebelo et al., PMID: 37170631). Both primary CoQ10 deficiency and dHMN due to COQ7 biallelic variants were lumped into a single disease entity, as both phenotypes share the same autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, overlapping neurological features including motor neuropathy and upper motor neuron signs, and a common loss-of-function mechanism resulting in CoQ10 deficiency, with at least 3 shared gene variants (R54Q, R107W, I200WfsTer56). Affected individuals with dHMN and biallelic COQ7 variants present with distal motor neuropathy with pes cavus, often accompanied by upper motor neuron signs like brisk reflexes and/or Babinski sign. Evidence supporting this gene–disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data from multiple independent cohorts, with multiple missense or null variants reported (Jacquier et al.; Rebelo et al.; Liu et al., PMID: 36758993; Smith et al., PMID: 37077559; Zhang et al., PMID: 37077559). Functional studies demonstrated decreased COQ7 mRNA and protein expression, impairing CoQ10 biosynthesis and mitochondrial respiration in vitro. Patient-derived iPSC motor neurons also showed reduced protein levels of COQ7 and increased levels of neurofilament light protein leakage, indicating axonal damage (Rebelo et al.). In summary, there is STRONG evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Charcot-Marie-Tooth Expert Panel on the March 13 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *IARS2* and *IARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of December 16, 2024. The *IARS2* gene encodes mitochondrial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase 2, one of the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which function in mitochondrial translation by catalyzing the attachment of amino acids to their cognate tRNAs. Defects in tRNA charging can result in impaired synthesis of oxidative phosphorylation complex protein subunits.

The *IARS2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *IARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2014 (PMID: 25130867). *IARS2* has been associated with one disease entity to date; cataracts, growth hormone deficiency, sensory neuropathy, sensorineural hearing loss, and skeletal dysplasia, or CAGSSS [OMIM# 616007]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *IARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *IARS2* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on November 20, 2019 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *IARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 17 unique variants (11 missense, three nonsense, two frameshift, and one deletion spanning exons 1 and 2) identified in 10 unrelated cases from eight publications (PMIDs: 25130867, 30419932, 28328135, 33327715, 35228874, 36704128, 39169373, 30041933). Disease onset is early in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, developmental delay and regression, seizures including infantile spasms, dystonia, peripheral neuropathy, cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss, short stature, growth hormone deficiency, adrenal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism, skeletal dysplasia, sideroblastic anemia, exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, Wolff-Parkinson-White arrhythmia, and elevated lactate.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration in non-patient cells (PMID: 39169373), an embryonic lethal knockout mouse model (PMID: 36305825), and a study performing shRNA knockdown in HEK293T cells with rescue (PMID: 39169373).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *IARS2* and autosomal recessive *IARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 16, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*PPP3CA* (protein phosphatase 3 catalytic subunit alpha) encodes the catalytic A-subunit of calcineurin (CaN), a calcium/calmodulin-regulated serine–threonine phosphatase that plays a critical role in neuronal signalling, synaptic plasticity, and brain development. The gene comprises 14 exons and encodes a protein with five functional regions: the catalytic domain (CD), calcineurin regulatory subunit–binding domain (CnBB), calmodulin-binding domain (CaMB), regulatory domain (RD), and autoinhibitory domain (AID).  

Published data support distinct *PPP3CA*-associated phenotypic groups, driven by variant mechanisms and affecting different protein domains: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE91), most often associated with loss-of-function missense or truncating variants clustering in the regulatory domain, and ACCIID (arthrogryposis, cleft palate, craniosynostosis, impaired intellectual development), most often associated with gain-of-function variants affecting the autoinhibitory domain. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split: AD developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 91 (OMIM: 617711) and Arthrogryposis, cleft palate, craniosynostosis, and impaired intellectual development (OMIM: 618265). The gain of function variants will be assessed separately. 

Pathogenic variants in *PPP3CA* were first reported in 2017 in individuals with severe neurodevelopmental disorders associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) (PMID: 28942967). Individuals with DEE typically present with early-onset epilepsy, most commonly infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS/West syndrome), which often evolves into multiple seizure types and shows marked pharmacoresistance. Neurological features include global developmental delay, frequently severe to profound intellectual disability, hypotonia, and characteristic EEG abnormalities such as hypsarrhythmia or multifocal/generalised epileptiform discharges. Across 10 independent publications and cohorts reported between 2017 and 2025, a total of 24 unique variants have been described, including missense, nonsense, frameshift, and structural rearrangements in unrelated individuals (PMIDs: 28942967, 29432562, 30455226, 30951195, 32593294, 33963760, 36158964, 39305655, 39707491, 40548073). Most variants were de novo, with at least 10 variants observed in more than one unrelated individual. Truncating variants appear to cluster within a narrow region of the regulatory domain, between the calmodulin-binding domain and the autoinhibitory domain, which is consistently associated with particularly severe DEE phenotypes.
 
This gene-disease relationship is supported by functional and expression studies, reported alongside case-level data, further supporting domain-dependent pathogenic mechanisms, providing strong biological plausibility for the observed clinical phenotypes .

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *PPP3CA* and autosomal dominant developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence and/or experimental evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date December 16, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Variants in the *ABCC8* gene, which encodes the SUR1(Sulfonylurea Receptor 1) regulatory subunit of the pancreatic beta- cell KATP channel, were first reported in relation to congenital hyperinsulinism in 1995 (Thomas et al., PMID: 7716548), with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.  Heterozygous variants causing autosomal dominant hyperinsulinism presenting in infancy or early childhood, followed by later development of impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes, were first described in in 2000 (Huopio et al., PMID: 11018078). 

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern as well as mechanism and phenotypic variability among variants associated with dominant and recessive *ABCC8*-related hyperinsulinism, and monogenic diabetes. Therefore, the curation of *ABCC8* has been split into (1) autosomal dominant and (2) autosomal recessive forms of hyperinsulinism (MONDO:0002177), and (3) monogenic diabetes (MONDO:0015967). We note here that included in the autosomal recessive curation are paternally inherited monoallelic loss of function variants that result in focal hyperinsulinsm due to somatic loss of the maternal chromosome 11p15 region due to somatic uniparental disomy, because ultimately they are recessively acting.     
The clinical presentation among individuals with dominant heterozygous variants is variable, often presenting as a milder form of congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) in infancy than the recessive form, with subtle or intermittent hypoglycemia that responds well to medical therapy. Others experience severe, treatment-refractory hypoglycemia that may require subtotal pancreatectomy.    In some cases, the hypoglycemia is not severe enough to be detected during infancy, and thus may go unrecognized or misdiagnosed until adolescence or adulthood when they may develop mild hypoglycemia or, paradoxically, impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes. 

Heterozygous dominant *ABCC8* variants cause diffuse pancreatic histology. In rare cases, atypical histological findings, characterized by features consistent with diffuse disease confined to localized regions of the pancreas, have been linked to somatic mosaicism for a dominant *ABCC8* variant. All reported dominant *ABCC8* variants have been missense changes or in-frame deletion variants associated with this broad spectrum of clinical severity in hyperinsulinism (PMIDs: 20573158, 11018078, 31218401, 22106158, 18596924, 31464105).  The mechanism for many dominantly acting variants appears to be the generation of a SUR1 subunit that can participate in the formation of a KATP channel heterooctamer (which normally consists of four SUR1 subunits and four Kir6.2 [encoded by *KCNJ11*] subunits) that can localize to the cell membrane but has a diminished response to MgADP  (PMID: 18596924).  Because of the existence of some normal or partially normal KATP channels, individuals with dominant variants are more likely to respond to treatment with diazoxide (PMIDs: 18596924, 31464105) than those with the recessive form (PMID: 23275527).      

Dominantly acting variants in this gene have been curated in at least 16 probands in 9 publications (PMIDs: 39441403, 20573158, 11018078, 31218401, 20042013, 22106158, 18596924, 21536946, 31464105) with clinical presentations consistent with ABCC8-related hyperinsulinism. More evidence is available to support the gene-disease association in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached this has not been curated exhaustively.  

This gene–disease relationship is strongly supported by functional studies, expression data, and animal models. Total points for the experimental evidence are 3. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 15.  

In summary,  *ABCC8* is definitively associated with autosomal dominant hyperinsulinism, with most cases presenting in early infancy or childhood.  Some cases have a mild presentation that is missed in infancy but may be noticed in later childhood or adulthood manifesting as mild hypoglycemia or impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes.    This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on the meeting date January 7, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

ITPR3: autosomal dominant demyelinating CMT (CMT1J)
In the context of an autosomal dominant, demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT1J) phenotype, ITPR3 was first described co-segregating in three affected individuals of one family by Schabhüttl et al. in 2014 (PMID:24627108). The same, recurrent variant has been replicated in another 9 families from different ancestries and one additional de-novo case by now (PMIDs: 39287469, 38938188). There are two more variants likewise co-segregating with a demyelinating CMT phenotype (PMID: 32949214). Within affected families, the authors observed a striking range in phenotype severity and disease onset. ITPR3 is a metabotropic calcium channel expressed in Schwann cells (PMIDs: 36444295, 38938188). Besides CMT, heterozygous missense variants in ITPR3 have been observed in a dominant immune disease with tooth infections (PMIDs: 39560673, 39270020), with neuropathy reported in some, but not extensively assessed in all patients.
In transfected HEK293 cells, all CMT-associated variants resulted in elevated basal cytosolic Ca2+ levels, decreased endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ store content, and constitutive store-operated Ca2+ entry in the absence of any stimuli, consistent with a leaky IP3R channel pore (PMID: 36444295). In Lancashire Heeler dogs, a spontaneous homozygous stop mutation led to a likewise demyelinating neuropathy phenotype associated with reduced IP3R-mediated Ca2+ flux upon stimulation of G-protein-coupled-receptors in the affected dogs’ fibroblasts (PMID: 39804930). In summary, strong clinical evidence, including a specific phenotype, variant recurrency, an overall LOD score of 5.71, and de-novo occurrence, is supported by experimental data on gene and variant level and has been replicated over time. We therefore classify the gene-disease relationship of ITPR3 and autosomal dominant, demyelinating CMT as definitive.

ALG10B (historically KCR1) encodes alpha-1,2-glucosyltransferase B, a glucosyltransferase that has been shown to co-precipitate with Kv11.1. Early biochemical investigations suggested that ALG10B might modulate Kv11.1 sensitivity to proarrhythmic drugs, thus playing a role in acquired (or drug induced) long QT syndrome (PMID: 14525949). An initial publication from 2010 by Hayashi et al. reported the p.Glu33Asp variant in a 70-year-old man with acquired long QT and ventricular fibrillation (PMID: 20950623). This variant is now known to have an allele frequency of 1.34 x10-4 in the East Asian population, which is inconsistent with the variant being a driver of severe Mendelian disease.

In 2023, Zhou et al. suggested that ALG10B variants were a rare novel cause of autosomal dominant long QT syndrome, reporting a multigenerational pedigree with an autosomal dominant LQT2-like phenotype. A rare c.16G>A, p.Gly6Ser ALG10B variant was observed in six affected family members, although incomplete penetrance was observed, with several unaffected genotype-positive carriers being reported (PMID: 37071726). iPSC-cardiomyocyte models suggested that the p.Gly6Ser variant decreased ALG10B protein expression, with increased Kv11.1 retention in the endoplasmic reticulum and prolonged action potential duration relative to isogenic controls, prompting the authors to speculate that the variant might affect Kv11.1 trafficking (PMID: 37071726).

There are no further reported rare ALG10B variants currently implicated in familial long QT syndrome. Further, ALG10B has relatively low expression in cardiac tissue (left ventricle TPM ~0.8, GTEx). Based on recent insights from gnomAD v4.1, ALG10B is not highly constrained against missense (o/e =0.96) or nonsense variation (pLI=0, LOEUF = 1.02). These constraint metrics are inconsistent with haploinsufficiency being a cause of severe Mendelian disease as suggested by Zhou et al.
Overall, there is limited evidence to support a relationship between ALG10B and autosomal dominant long QT syndrome. This limited classification is based on the current absence of clinical genetic evidence, the lack of constraint against nonsense variation as well as the low ALG10B mRNA expression in cardiac tissue. This classification was approved by the ClinGen HCVD GCEP on January 13, 2026 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

disease_title: sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency type B2
disease_original_title: sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency type B2
submitted_as_notes:
*MOCS3 *was first reported in relation to “sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency type B2”, an autosomal recessive disorder of molybdenum cofactor (moco) biosynthesis, in 2017 (Huijmans et al, PMID: 28544736). This is the only known disease entity asserted to be caused by variants in *MOCS3*. Moco deficiency has been shown to be caused by variants in genes involved in moco biosynthesis, including *MOCS1*, *MOCS2*, and *GEPH*. There is a spectrum of clinical severity. The most severe cases present shortly after birth with neonatal-onset severe encephalopathy, refractory seizures, opisthotonos, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and apnea. Brain MRI changes MRI changes like hypoxic–ischemic lesions. Most patients die in infancy. Individuals with milder, late-onset condition often present with acute neurologic decompensation during illness, with altered mental state, dystonia, choreoathetosis, ataxia, nystagmus, and fluctuating hypotonia and hypertonia (Misko et al, 2021, PMID: 34870926; Johannes et al, 2022, PMID: 36296488). The clinical features are believed to be related to loss of sulfite oxidase (SOX) activity, one of four human proteins that require moco to function. Reduction of SOX activity results in accumulation of sulfite and secondary metabolites, S-sulfocysteine and thiosulfate, that are toxic, as well as a decrease in cysteine and cystine. 

Three variants (two missense, one nonsense) that have been reported in 2 probands in 2 publications were scored in this curation. The first reported patient was noted to have a mild phenotype with normal or low normal uric acid levels in plasma and urine, normal urine sulfite level, and normal sulfite oxidase activity, unlike patients with severe moco deficiency (Huijmans et al, 2017, PMID: 28544736). The second patient reported had a severe neonatal onset; sulfite oxidase activity was not reported (Tian et al, 2021, PMID: 33897766). In addition to these two cases, molecular analysis of a pregnancy loss with non-immune hydrops fetalis identified homozygosity for a nonsense variant (Shamseldin et al, 2018, PMID: 28749478; SCV001870500.1). A subsequent report indicated that the variant had been found in homozygosity in an individual with “no phenotype”; details of the age of the homozygous individual and evaluation were not provided (Aladbi et al, 2025, PMID: 3950496).

This gene-disease relationship supported by experimental evidence including the biochemical function of the gene product and its interaction with MOCS2A, one of the two proteins encoded by *MOCS2*, a gene previously classified as having a definitive relationship with “sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency type B1”. MOCS3 activates MOCS2A by ATP-dependent adenylation and formation of a thiocarboxylate group, required for molybdopterin (MPT) synthesis (Matthies et al, 2004, PMID: 15073332; Chowdhury, 2012, PMID: 22453920; Johannes et al, 2022, PMID: 36296488).

In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *MOCS3* and autosomal recessive “sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency type B2”. This classification was approved by the ClinGen General Inborn Errors of Metabolism Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 24, 2026 (SOP v12).

*AKT2* was first reported in relation to hypoinsulinemic hypoglycemia with body hemihypertrophy in 2011 by Hussain et al. (PMID: 21979934). This report described three unrelated children with unexplained, recurrent and severe fasting hypoglycemia and asymmetrical overgrowth. All patients carried the same de novo variant in *AKT2* (NM_001626.6; c.49G>A; (p.Glu17Lys)), in two cases as heterozygotes and, in one case, in mosaic form (20% variant allele frequency). The mild left hemihypertrophy became less evident with age. Two of them developed obesity, likely from overfeeding, while one avoided it. Two of the originally reported patients were re-studied at 17 years old. At this age both were independent of percutaneous feeding overnight, one showed evidence of resolution of fasting hypoglycemia, while the other showed persisting hypoglycemic tendency (PMID: 28541532). Since then, the same variant (p.Glu17Lys) has been reported in at least 6 additional patients with hypoinsulinemic hypoglycemia and hemihypertrophy (PMIDs: 24285683, 26003998,  35602880, 38344362). Genetic evidence score: 8 points. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain of function, evidenced by in vitro functional assays showing that the *AKT*2 Glu17Lys disrupts the interaction between the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain and the kinase domain of *AKT2*. This causes the kinase to be constitutively recruited to the plasma membrane and activated without the need for insulin binding to its receptor (PMIDs: Arya et al., 24285683; Hussain et al., 21979934; Siklar et al. 32157856). This leads to continuous, low level activation of downstream insulin signaling, mimicking the effects of insulin even when insulin is absent or undetectable in the blood (PMIDs: Arya et al., 24285683; Hussain et al., 21979934; Siklar et al. 32157856). As a result, lipolysis and ketogenesis are inhibited, and hepatic gluconeogenesis is suppressed, with effects on glucose uptake into muscle and adipose tissue not yet determined —the net effect is to produce a biochemical profile identical to that of hyperinsulinism (hypoketotic, hypo-fatty-acidemic hypoglycemia), but with lower requirement for glucose infusion to maintain euglycemia, and, importantly, without elevated insulin or C-peptide levels (PMIDs: Arya et al., 24285683; Hussain et al., 21979934; Siklar et al. 32157856). Summary of experimental data: 3.5 points. Total score for genetic evidence and experimental evidence: 11.5 points. 

A single variant in *AKT2* (NM_001626:6: c.821G>A, p.Arg274His)) has been reported in only one family with FPLD (PMID: 15166380). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanisms and phenotypic variability underlying *AKT2*-related disease entities. Therefore, the curation of *AKT2* has been split into: i) *AKT2*-related FPLD (MONDO:0019192), included in this curation and ii) hypoinsulinemic hypoglycemia and body hemihypertrophy (HHBH, MONDO:0009416).

In summary, current genetic and functional evidence supporting the human gene-disease relationship between *AKT2* (currently p.Glu17Lys variant only) and HHBH are definitive.  Although this gene/variant causes hypo- rather than hyperinsulinism, similarities in phenotype warrant inclusion on a testing panel for hyperinsulinism.  The possibility of mosaicism for this variant should be considered.  An apparent negative result in the presence of strong clinical suspicion of HHBH warrants more targeted interrogation of the variant.

This classification was approved by the MDGCEP on March 4, 2026. Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) - SOP12.

The *MYRF* gene is located on chromosome 11 at 11q12.2 and encodes the Myelin Regulatory Factor, a transcription factor. *MYRF* was first reported in association with Cardiac-urogenital syndrome (CUGS) in 2018 (Pinz et al., PMID: 29446546). CUGS is characterized postnatally by congenital diaphragmatic hernia, primary pulmonary hypoplasia, congenital heart defects, anomalies of the internal and external genitalia, ocular anomalies, developmental delay, and intellectual disability. Prenatal presentations include hypoplastic left heart syndrome, disorders of sex development in 46,XY fetuses, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and pulmonary hypoplasia (PMID: 39542847). Nanophthalmos and high hyperopia are common features within the CUGS phenotypic spectrum (PMID: 36375006). Per the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, no differences were identified in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, or phenotypic variability. Therefore, Cardiac-urogenital syndrome (CUGS; MIM: 618280) and Nanophthalmos 1 (MIM: 600165) have been lumped into a single disease entity. The autosomal dominant Encephalitis/encephalopathy, mild, with reversible myelin vacuolization (MIM: 618113) phenotype has been curated separately.
At least 59 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, including frameshift, nonsense, missense, and splice-altering variants, have been reported in more than 60 affected individuals across 13 publications (PMIDs: 30070761, 29446546, 30532227, 31048900, 31266062, 30985895, 31069960, 31700225, 31172260, 35432193, 35365939, 39542847, 39868768). Six de novo variants are included in this curation. Additional genetic evidence exists in the literature; however, the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be domain-specific. Variants affecting the intramolecular chaperone auto-processing domain result in loss of function, variants within the DNA-binding domain exert a dominant-negative effect, and C-terminal truncating variants have an unclear mechanism but are likely hypomorphic (PMIDs: 31964908, 28160598). This gene–disease relationship is further supported by experimental evidence, including animal models (mouse, zebrafish, and C. elegans), expression analyses, and in vivo and in vitro functional studies (PMIDs: 31048900, 38901241, 33646289, 36129575, 40313921, 33798553, 37584388, 31964908, 36013096, 22956843, 28441531, 28160598, 33950834, 38488284).
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *MYRF* and autosomal dominant Cardiac-urogenital syndrome. This relationship has been consistently demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on July 2, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

NEIL3 encodes Nei endonuclease VIII-like 3, a DNA glycosylase involved in the base excision repair pathway, with proposed roles in the repair of oxidative DNA damage, particularly in proliferating cells, including immune cells. Evidence involving NEIL3 is limited to a single published report describing 3 siblings with combined LRBA deficiency and NEIL3 variants, as well as one individual with isolated NEIL3 deficiency (Massaad et al., 2016). In this study, three siblings with biallelic LRBA deficiency and NEIL3 variants exhibited severe autoimmunity, while a female individual with NEIL3 deficiency alone demonstrated a mild phenotype characterized by the presence of autoantibodies without overt clinical autoimmunity. Functional studies in the report demonstrated that LRBA deficiency was associated with absent protein expression and was sufficient to explain the primary immune dysregulation phenotype, suggesting that NEIL3 functioned as a modifier enzyme, rather than acting as a primary disease-causing gene. This interpretation has been confirmed with Dr. Michel Massaad, first author of the JCI study, who stated that autoimmunity in the reported patients was primarily attributable to LRBA deficiency, with NEIL3 acting as a modifier. Consistent with this role, NEIL3 was not included as a gene implicated in immune dysregulation in the IUIS classification.
To date, there are no additional independent reports establishing NEIL3 as a cause of a monogenic immune disorder, and there is no functional evidence demonstrating that NEIL3 deficiency alone results in a fully penetrant immune regulatory phenotype. While NEIL3 variants can modulate autoimmunity, particularly in the presence of other pathogenic variants, the available evidence does not support a definitive or limited gene–disease relationship.
Based on the limited published data, NEIL3 is interpreted as a modifier gene that may modulate autoimmunity in the context of other disease-causing variants, rather than as a gene associated with an independent monogenic primary immune regulatory disorder. Therefore, the relationship between NEIL3 and immune dysregulation is classified as Disputed at this time.

disease_title: KCND2-related neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures
disease_original_title: KCND2-related neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures
submitted_as_notes:
*KCND2* encodes Kv4.2, a voltage-dependent potassium channel that produces an A-type potassium current in neurons. This fast-activating channel is crucial for repolarization of the membrane during action potentials. *KCND2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant KCND2-related neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures in 2014 (Lee et al., PMID: 24501278). This disorder is characterized by significant early-onset global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and, in some cases, epilepsy (including developmental and epileptic encephalopathy), autism, neuroimaging abnormalities, and mild dysmorphic features. 

Five missense variants that have been reported in 8 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 24501278, 34245260, 35510384) are included in this curation. Variants occurred de novo in all instances in which parental DNA was available. The variants affect sites critical for channel gating, and four cluster at residues 402–404, including recurrent variants affecting p.Pro403 and p.Val404. The variants were shown to result in gain-of-function and/or partial loss-of-function effects (PMIDs: 24501278, 29581270, 34245260, 35510384), but more evidence is needed to clarify the mechanism of pathogenicity. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function, animal models and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 11102480, 32822706, 41188451, 41554648). Electrophysiological studies of patient-associated missense variants demonstrate altered Kv4.2 channel gating, including slowed inactivation and changes in activation kinetics (PMID: 24501278, 29581270, 34245260, 35510384). Knock-in mice with the patient variant *Kcnd2* V404M exhibit epileptiform activity and impaired learning and memory (PMID: 41554648). Multiple voltage-dependent potassium channel genes have been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. Another member of the Kv4 family, *KCND3*, which encodes the closely related Kv4.3 channel, is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders with epilepsy. 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 4, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*FBN2*, which encodes fibrillin-2, was first reported in association to autosomal dominant Congenital Contractural Arachnodactyly (CCA) in 1995 (PMID: 7773290). CCA is a connective tissue disorder characterized by the following: congenital joint contractures, arachnodactyly, crumpled ears, kyphoscoliosis, Marfanoid habitus, dolichostenomelia, micrognathia, highly arched palate, sternal deformities, and muscle hypoplasia (OMIM: 121050; PMID: 31316167). *FBN2* variants have also been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (TAAD) and early-onset macular degeneration. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Guidelines, CCA and TAAD have been lumped into a single disease entity, as no differences in molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern were identified, and both interfamilial and intrafamilial variability were observed. Given no evidence of overlap between early-onset macular degeneration and CCA and an unclear molecular mechanism, early-onset macular degeneration has been split and may be curated as a separate disease entity by the ClinGen Retinal GCEP in the future.

Evidence supporting the gene-disease relationship between *FBN2* and CCA includes case-level, family segregation, functional, and experimental data. The majority of reported pathogenic variants cluster within exons 24–35, a region critical for microfibril assembly (PMID: 18767143). Notably, *FBN2* variants leading to premature termination are underrepresented, with only six nonsense variants reported as likely pathogenic or pathogenic in ClinVar to date. In contrast, there is an overrepresentation of pathogenic in-frame variants, including missense and splice-site, likely resulting in in-frame exon skipping. While the primary mechanism of disease is not yet well-established, a dominant negative effect is considered most likely. This curation describes 27 unique variants (16 missense, 10 splice site, and 1 nonsense) and 3 families with a combined LOD of 6.3 (PMIDs:7493032, 11754102, 17345643 19006240, 25975422, 35360850, 38326314, 31143044, 27912749, 33638605, 36936417). 

This gene-disease relationship is further supported by experimental data in the form of expression studies and mice models. FBN2 expression is highly specific to early embryonic development (PMID: 23715323, Accession phs000424.v10.p2). Fbn2 null mice models exhibit phenotypes consistent with CCA, including multiple joint contractures, supporting pathogenic equivalency between dominant-negative and loss-of-function variants (PMIDs:11470817, 20855508). Graded deficiency of Fbn1 and Fbn2 demonstrates that elastic tissue formation may be driven by the total amount of extracellular microfibrils and that fibrillin-2 containing microfibrils may play a functionally distinct role in organizing the embryonic matrix (PMID: 16407178). 

Aortic disease has been documented in individuals with pathogenic *FBN2* variants and clinically diagnosed CCA (PMIDs: 11754102, 25975422, 19006240). Perhaps most notable, is an adult male in a family of at least four affected individuals, with a splice site variant (*FBN2*:c.4222+5G>A), who passed at age 61yo due to an acute type A aortic dissection (PMID: 25975422). The risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm is approximately 10-15% among this population (GeneReviews, Callewaert, 2022). However, without routine screening for cardiovascular disease, the prevalence may be underreported. Given the potential risks, screening for TAAD should be considered. Currently, there is no evidence for gene-specific surgical management guidelines.

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support this gene-disease relationship with replication over time. Although additional functional studies could further elucidate the molecular mechanism(s), no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the above evidence regarding *FBN2*-related CCA. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Heritable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection subgroup of the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disease GCEP on 11/7/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*HCN2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2023 (DiFrancesco JC et al., PMID: 37746765). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotype for *HCN2*-related disorders. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple curations: autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder, autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder (this curation), and autosomal dominant epilepsy. The split curations for autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder and autosomal dominant epilepsy are presented separately.

Six variants, including missense and in-frame substitutions, reported in eleven probands from three publications are included in this curation (PMID: 37746765, 37853563, 40468825). Clinical features associated with heterozygous variants in the *HCN2* gene causing complex neurodevelopmental disorder include mild to severe intellectual disability, sometimes associated with epilepsy, movement disorders, hypotonia, or nystagmus. Several recurrent variants have been reported in unrelated probands, including c.1432_1434del (p.(E478del)), c.1088 C>T (p.(A363V)), and c.1379G>A (p.(G460D)). The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be dominant negative (PMID: 40468825) and the variants are typically de novo. Co-expression of several of these variants with wild type *HCN2* in Xenopus oocytes indicates they exhibit lower conductance, faster kinetics, and open at more hyperpolarizing potential than wild type *HCN2*, consistent with partial loss-of-function and a dominant negative effect of the variant on channel function (PMID: 40468825). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *HCN2* and autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in the clinical diagnostic setting and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date February 3, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *PRSS56* gene was first reported in relation to microphthalmia in 2011, with the identification of homozygous or compound heterozygous *PRSS56* variants in a number of affected individuals including multiple large families (Gal et al., PMID: 21397065, Nair et al., PMID: 21532570, and Orr et al., PMID: 21850159). Affected individuals are generally reported with a diagnosis of posterior microphthalmia or nanophthalmia and exhibit clinical features including short axial length, high hypermetropia, reduced visual acuity, high intraocular pressure, angle closure glaucoma, crowded optic discs, and/or papillomacular fold. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the molecular mechanism (biallelic loss of function) and mode of inheritance (autosomal recessive) were found to be consistent among patients regardless of diagnosis, while the phenotypic variability between them appeared to represent a spectrum of disease rather than separate disease entities. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *PRSS56* variants have been lumped for curation as a single disease entity, referred to as PRSS56-related nanophthalmos.

This curation has scored eight suspected disease-causing variants (three frameshift, four missense, and one canonical splice site disruption), which have collectively been reported in eight probands from six publications (PMID: 21397065, PMID: 21532570, PMID: 21850159, PMID: 23127749, PMID: 31992737, PMID: 33203948). Two of the variants are predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay, consistent with a biallelic loss-of-function mechanism of pathogenicity. Co-segregation of the homozygous genotype with affected status in the proband’s family was also incorporated into the genetic evidence component of this curation (PMID: 23127749). Additional genetic evidence was available but not included in this curation.

This gene-disease association is also supported by evidence that *PRSS56* is highly expressed in retina, as well as in the testis, muscle and brain (PMID: 30239781). The specific areas of the retina with highest expression are the inner nuclear layer and the ganglion cell layer (PMID: 21532570). Biochemical studies indicate that *PRSS56* encodes a secreted serine protease (PMID: 21532570, PMID: 37400936). This is consistent with electron microscopy results from mice indicating that homozygous *Prss56* loss-of-function results in focal hypoplasia of the trabecular meshwork, reduced collagen fibrils in the trabecular beams, increased occurrence of open spaces lacking extracellular matrix, and foci of collagen fibril crowding in the sclera (PMID: 21532570). Mouse models additionally show short axial eye length, reduced vitreous chamber depth and equatorial diameter, and reduced distance between the retina and Schlemm's canal leading to angle closure, as well as choroidal expansion, anterior chamber enlargement, hyperopia, high intraocular pressure with reduced outflow facility, and glaucomatous nerve damage with optic nerve excavation and nerve fiber layer thinning (PMID: 21532570, PMID: 32152063).

In summary, *PRSS56* has definitive evidence of association with PRSS56-related nanophthalmos. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glaucoma and Neuro-Ophthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 15th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*IRX5* was first reported in relation to *IRX5*-related craniofacial dysostosis with osteopenia, intellectual disability and dental anomalies in 2012 by Bonnard et al. (PMID: 22581230). This condition, first described by Hamamy et al., 2007 (PMID: 17230486), includes features such as cranial anomalies (like brachycephaly); facial anomalies (including abnormal philtrum, bulging midface, broad nasal bridge; and extreme ocular hypertelorism); cleft palate/dental anomalies; hearing loss; vision issues (like progressive myopia); cardiac features (such as patent ductus arteriosus and intraventricular conduction delay); skeletal/digital features (like syndactyly, clinodactyly, hip dysplasia, and long bone fractures); genital features (gonadal issues, hydrocele, cryptorchidism); and developmental delay. 3 variants (missense) that have been reported in at least 4 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 22581230, 30729910, 34899143) are included in this curation. Additional genetic evidence (PMIDs: 28940097, 38318288) has been evaluated but not scored due to high allele frequencies, a different inheritance pattern, and/or variants in other associated genes. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse and xenopus models, rescue evidence, biochemical functional data, and interaction evidence; PMIDs: 22581230, 32662900). Biochemical functional evidence shows that IRX5 is key in bone development. Model organism evidence shows genital anomalies, bone issues (like reduced bone density), and deficient cranial neural crest cell migration in mutants. Deficient cranial neural crest migration in IRX5 morphants could be rescued with wild-type IRX5. Interaction evidence shows that IRX5 and TRPS1 exhibit co-immunoprecipitation amid craniofacial development. The maximum score for experimental evidence (6 pts.) has been reached. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting data 7/21/2025 (SOP Version 11).

RARS1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 9 in 2014 (Wolf et al, 2014 PMID:24777941). Reported phenotypes include spasticity, nystagmus, delayed development, intellectual disability (mild to severe), hypertonicity, ataxia, dysmetria, dysarthria, tremoring, and hypomyelination on brain MRI (Wolf et al, 2014 PMID:24777941).

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern. Therefore, there is one disease entity, hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 9 (OMIM: 616140).

29 variants (12 putative null (4 start codon, 4 fs, 4 splice), 16 missense, 1 in-frame deletion) that have been reported in 40 patients in 11 publications (PMID:24777941, 30791064, 28905880, 31814314, 40594583, 33190326, 38618971, 30500859, 39762984, 37186453, 29451896). 9 probands and 5 publications are included in the genetic evidence of this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, and a maximum score of 12 for genetic evidence has been reached (max 12).

The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function (Li 2021, PMID33515434). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a knockout zebrafish model (Kim 2025 PMID: 39762984).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between RARS1 and autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 9, also known as RARS1-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.

This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date December 22, 2025 (SOP Version 11). Curation scoring was updated to reflect SOP Version 12 changes.

The *YWHAZ* gene is located on chromosome 8 at 8q22.3 and encodes the tyrosine 3-monooxygenase/tryptophan 5-monooxygenase activation protein zeta protein, which mediates signal transduction by binding to phosphoserine-containing proteins. *YWHAZ* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2019 (Popov et al., PMID:31024343). Seven variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) that have been reported in 7 probands in 3 publications are included in this curation (PMIDs: 31024343, 23999528, 36001342, 35143101). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including animal models that suggest that this gene contributes to neurobehavioral deficits, and plays a role in establishing neuronal connectivity and modulating neurotransmission (PMIDs: 35501409, 22124272, 26207352). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date August 15, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

TWNK was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Perrault Syndrome in 2005 (Nikali et al., PMID: 16135556). This condition is characterized by childhood-onset, progressive, and moderate-to-profound hearing loss, as well as ocular anomalies (such as nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia); ataxia; hypotonia; neuropathy; seizures; brain structural anomalies (including cerebellar atrophy); demyelination; and, in females, amenorrhea/gonadal dysgenesis. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, Perrault Syndrome (OMIM: 616138) and Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome (OMIM: 271245). However, due to a different inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability the following disease assertion was split from the other two assertions: Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (OMIM: 606075). The split curation for autosomal dominant Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia will be curated separately. 25 variants (missense, frameshift, nonsense, and splicing) that have been reported in over 20 probands in 11 publications (PMIDs: 16135556, 24102492, 24816431, 25355836, 26920903, 26970254, 27551684, 28178980, 31455392, 32281099, 39780253) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse models; gEAR database expression; PMID: 16301523). Mouse models of TWNK missense and duplication mutants indicate that mutants have altered TWNK expression, mitochondrial degradation, and run longer distances in the cage wheel study, compared to the wild-type. Expression level evidence shows strong cochlear expression. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between TWNK and autosomal recessive Perrault Syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.

*CEP41* is located on chromosome 7 (7q32.2) at chr7: 130,393,771-130,442,433 and comprises 11 exons that make up a 373 amino acid protein (PMID: 22246503). The gene product is *CEP41*, a centrosomal protein that facilitates axonemal glutamylation.  This protein is predicted to contain two coiled-coils and a rhodanese-like domain which is structurally related to the catalytic subunit of Cdc25 class of phosphatases (but lacks activity). The cellular role of *CEP41* is an area of active investigation currently and has been shown to aid microtubule assembly and cell proliferation (PMID: 38841887). Bi-allelic alterations in *CEP41* have only been reported to cause autosomal recessive Joubert Syndrome and related disorders. Therefore, per criteria outlined by the Clingen Lumping and Splitting Workgroup, this disease entity has been lumped into one group with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. The preferred disease name suggested for this disorder is ciliopathy-*CEP41*. 

*CEP41* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Joubert Syndrome in 2012 by Lee JE et al., (PMID: 22246503). In this study, the authors utilized an initial linkage analysis mapping and direct *CEP41* sequencing to identify bi-allelic loss of function mutations in *CEP41* in three individuals from unrelated families with reported consanguinity. These probands demonstrated phenotypes including polydactyly, nephronophthisis, hypotonia, developmental delay, liver abnormalities and the characteristic molar tooth sign (MTS), culminating in a clinical diagnosis of Joubert Syndrome for all of the affected individuals. Since the first report of *CEP41*’s in relation to Joubert Syndrome, other studies have reported other bi-allelic variants in this gene (identified via trio exome sequencing) to cause similar phenotypes in other affected individuals who share features of Joubert Syndrome (PMIDs: 22246503). So far, all reported *CEP41* variants are loss of function. The majority of the variants were found in the compound heterozygous state, while one study reported disease-causing homozygous variants (PMID: 22246503). A total of 8 points for genetic evidence has been reached. 

This gene disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence that demonstrates a functional alteration upon the loss of *CEP41* in patient cells. Patient fibroblasts lacking *CEP41* demonstrate ciliogenesis defects as well as reduced glutamylation of the ciliary axoneme, which is rescued by the introduction of human *CEP41*(PMID: 22246503). Additionally, knockdown of cep41 in zebrafish results in similar ciliary phenotypes and heart asymmetry, some of which are partly rescued by reintroducing human *CEP41*. A total of 4 points for experimental evidence was curated. 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CEP41* and ciliopathy. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cystic and Ciliopathy Expert Panel on the meeting date 12/03/2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *MRPL24* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 27, 2025. The *MRPL24* gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal protein L24.

The first and only report of the *MRPL24* gene in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2020 (PMID: 32344152), in a girl with cerebellar atrophy, choreoathetosis, intellectual disability and combined complex I and IV deficiency. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 32344152). This girl had normal development until age 8 months when she experienced developmental regression (lost ability to sit and vocalize). By age 3 years, she had spasticity, dystonic posturing of distal upper and lower limbs, and dyskinetic facial grimacing. By age 8 years, she was sitting with support. She also had intellectual disability with lack of interaction with the environment and behavioral disturbance. Her course was stable at 14 years. Brain imaging at age three years showed bilateral alterations at the level of the putamen and cerebellar atrophy. She had elevated plasma lactate and decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain activities (combined defect of complexes I and IV) in skeletal muscle and cultured skin fibroblasts. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and a zebrafish model (PMID: 32344152).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel January 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

PCK1 encodes the cytosolic phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK-C) that is the rate-limiting enzyme in gluconeogenesis and crucial for cataplerosis. This isoform is highly expressed in the liver and accounts for approximately 50% of total PEPCK activity. PCK1 variants were first reported in association with autosomal recessive PEPCK-C deficiency in 2014 (Adam et al., PMID: 24863970). The primary features include fasting or illness associated episodic hypoglycemia, lactic and/or metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates, and, in some cases, liver involvement such as steatosis and hepatic inflammation. Clinical presentation and disease severity are highly variable.
Eight PCK1 variants (including missense, in-frame deletion, frameshift, and splicing variants) have been reported in eight probands across five publications (PMIDs: 24863970, 26971250, 35868242, 37924129, 40092582) and are included in this curation. In addition, a homozygous missense variant, c.925G>A (p.Gly309Arg), reported as a founder mutation in the Finnish population, has been identified in 16 unrelated probands (PMIDs: 28216384, 34622459). The proposed mechanism of pathogenicity is biallelic loss of function.
This gene–disease relationship is further supported by experimental evidence. Whole-body PCK1 knockout (KO) mice exhibit hypoglycemia, elevated malate and lactate levels, hepatic lipid accumulation, and early death (PMID: 16300682). Both hypoglycemia and lifespan were partially rescued by adenovirus mediated PCK1 delivery in the liver of KO mice (PMID: 27785616). Studies of patient liver tissue and transfected cell models demonstrate reduced PEPCK-C protein levels and enzymatic activity, likely due to increased protein instability, as evidenced by time-dependent protein degradation (PMIDs: 24863970, 28216384, 26971250).
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between PCK1 and autosomal recessive PEPCK-C deficiency. This relationship has demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and remains consistent over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP on April 24, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

TRPM4 encodes a homotetrameric calcium-activated nonselective cation channel. The TRPM4 channel is only permeable to monovalent ions and has been proposed to facilitate the influx of Na+ during depolarisation and the efflux of K+ during repolarisation (PMIDs: 24721656, 25441424).
 
The relationship between TRPM4 and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome was initially suggested by Liu et al. in 2013 following the identification of 11 unique variants in a cohort of patients with SCN5A-negative Brugada syndrome (PMID:23382873). Two further publications have reported TRPM4 variants in two patients with Brugada syndrome, including a carrier of compound heterozygous null TRPM4 variants (PMIDs: 28494446, 30142439). This collective clinical genetic evidence is insufficient for establishing a causal relationship between TRPM4 and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome:

 1. While some rare variants have been reported, many of the variants have population frequencies that are too high for a severe autosomal dominant condition such as Brugada syndrome.

2. The suggested mechanism of disease appears to be haploinsufficiency, yet TRPM4 is tolerant to nonsense variation (pLi=0, LOEUF=1.084, gnomAD v 4.1). Consistent with this tolerance to nonsense variation, the relatively common p.Lys914Ter variant (AF= 1.02x10-3) reported by Liu et al. results in a greater decrease in current density in transfected cell models than the rare p.Pro779Arg variant.

3. Burden testing has failed to identify any statistically significant enrichment of TRPM4 variants in patients with Brugada syndrome relative to controls (PMID: 25650408). 

The relationship between TRPM4 and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome was originally evaluated by the ClinGen Brugada Syndrome Gene Curation Expert Panel in 2017 and was classified as disputed. This gene-disease pair was re-evaluated by the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on 11 November, 2025. Following re-evaluation and the consideration of new evidence, the gene-disease classification was changed to refuted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on 11 November, 2025 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *SPG7* and autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 19, 2026. The *SPG7* gene encodes paraplegin, a mitochondrial inner membrane metalloproteinase that is a component of the m-AAA protease along with *AFG3L2*. The m-AAA protease is an ATP-dependent proteolytic complex of the mitochondrial inner membrane that degrades misfolded proteins and regulates ribosome assembly.

*SPG7* has been associated with one disease entity to date; spastic paraplegia 7, autosomal recessive [OMIM# 607259], however there have also been reports of an autosomal dominant *SPG7*-related disorder characterized by spasticity, ataxia, and/or optic atrophy (PMIDs: 11222789, 22571692, 39978794, 37983191).  Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, this Expert Panel found a difference in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability among these entities. Therefore, the autosomal recessive disease entity has been split, is curated separately, and has been renamed as autosomal recessive *SPG7*-related primary mitochondrial disease. The autosomal dominant disease entity is curated here.
 
As described above, there have been reports of an autosomal dominant *SPG7*-related disorder characterized by spasticity, ataxia, and/or optic atrophy (PMIDs: 11222789, 22571692, 39978794, 37983191, 32548275). However, there is minimal functional evidence to support the deleterious nature of these variants in the heterozygous state, and many variants are now recognized to be too common in the general population to be associated with the reported phenotypes.

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *SPG7* and autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role this gene plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 19, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

CYP27B1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive vitamin D-dependent rickets in 1997 (Fu et al., PMID: 9415400). This condition is characterized by features including rickets, increased susceptibility to bone fractures, other skeletal features (such as enlargement of the wrists and ankles), hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, hypotonia, seizures, and aminoaciduria. 14 variants (missense, frameshift, splicing, nonsense) that have been reported in 10 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 9415400, 9486994, 12050193, 31261480, 35663328, 39452491) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature (PMID: 39778955), but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (biochemical functional evidence, mouse models; PMIDs: 9295274, 30031146). Biochemical function evidence revealed that this gene is essential in calcium homeostasis. In a mouse model, knockout mice had skeletal anomalies, rickets, hypocalcemia, and growth delay. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CYP27B1 and autosomal recessive vitamin D-dependent rickets. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Tublopathy GCEP on the meeting date 6/04/2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *LIAS* and *LIAS*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 29, 2024. The *LIAS* gene encodes lipoic acid synthase, an enzyme important for the synthesis of lipoic acid, which is a cofactor of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) and other mitochondrial enzyme complexes [α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (KGDH), branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (BCDH), 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase, and the glycine cleavage system (GCS)]. PDC catalyzes conversion of pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, thus is the link between glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. PDC deficiency leads to impaired energy metabolism. 

The *LIAS* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *LIAS*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2011 (PMID: 22152680). *LIAS* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; hyperglycinemia, lactic acidosis, and seizures [OMIM# 614462]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *LIAS*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *LIAS* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on September 21, 2020 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *LIAS*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included nine unique variants (seven missense, one nonsense, one intronic variant impacting splicing) identified in six unrelated cases from five publications (PMIDs: 22152680, 24334290, 26108146, 28817111, 36680912).  Onset is typically early in life and clinical features include LSS, seizures, myoclonic movements, cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and non-ketotic hyperglycinemia.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), rescue studies in patient cells (PMID: 24334290), and an embryonic lethal mouse knockout model (PMID: 16135825).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *LIAS* and autosomal recessive *LIAS*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: CAMK2D-related neurodevelopmental disorder and dilated cardiomyopathy
disease_original_title: CAMK2D-related neurodevelopmental disorder and dilated cardiomyopathy
submitted_as_notes:
*CAMK2D* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant *CAMK2D*-related neurodevelopmental disorder and dilated cardiomyopathy in 2024 (Rigter et al., PMID: 38272033). *CAMK2D* encodes a member of the family of type II multifunctional calcium- and calmodulin-dependent protein kinases, which play a central role in synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. *CAMK2D* is the major CAMK2 isozyme present in the heart and plays an important role in cardiac function. Affected individuals present with speech and motor delays, intellectual disability (mild to profound), dysmorphic facial features, behavioral abnormalities (including autism spectrum disorder), skeletal abnormalities, brain MRI anomalies, and dilated cardiomyopathy often requiring cardiac transplantation (PMIDs: 37372357, 38272033). Additional features in a subset of individuals can include seizures, visual abnormalities, digestive problems (including tube feeding), and kidney abnormalities. 

Six missense variants reported in 8 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 27479843, 37372357, 38272033) are included in this curation, with most variants arising *de novo*. One recurrent variant, p.Arg275His, has been reported in at least 3 families, 2 of which are scored in this curation (PMIDs: 27479843, 37372357, 38272033). The third family includes a set of 3 siblings with dilated cardiomyopathy; 2 of these siblings also have neurodevelopmental disorders and a 16p11.2 microdeletion (PMID: 38272033). Their father, deceased at the time of the report (and therefore unavailable for testing), also had a history of dilated cardiomyopathy. While not scored due to the compounding 16p11.2 microdeletion, the presence of dilated cardiomyopathy within this family lends additional support to the assertion that variation in this gene causes cardiac phenotypes in addition to neurodevelopmental disorders.  Functional assays assessing protein levels, kinase activity, and impact on neuronal migration of these patient-specific *CAMK2D* missense variants demonstrated both gain-of-function and loss-of-function effects, with only gain-of-function variants proposed to be associated with the cardiac phenotype (PMID: 38272033). However, more evidence is needed to determine a specific phenotype correlation with disease mechanism. *CAMK2D* is constrained for missense (Z = 3.41, gnomAD v4.1.1) but not loss-of-function variants (pLI = 0.02, LOEUF = 0.58). One individual with a *de novo* splice variant predicted to lead to a frameshift was not scored for this reason.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including biochemical function, protein interactions, and mouse knockdown, overexpression and rescue models (PMID: 38272033). The 3 other members of the CAMK2 family, *CAMK2A*, *CAMK2B*, and *CAMK2G*, are also involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (PMID: 39631163), and form homo- and hetero-oligomeric complexes with CAMK2D.

In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between *CAMK2D* and autosomal dominant *CAMK2D*-related neurodevelopmental disorder and dilated cardiomyopathy. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 15, 2025 (SOP Version 12).

PPIP5K2 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss in 2018 (Yousaf et al., PMID: 29590114). One missense variant (c.2510G>A, p.Arg837His) that has been reported in 12 affected individuals across two families in one publication (PMID: 29590114) is included in this curation. The affected individuals presented with prelingual bilateral severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression data indicating that PPIP5K2 is expressed in the cochlear and vestibular sensory hair cells, supporting cells, and ganglion neurons. A mouse model also showed that PPIP5K2 with a truncated phosphatase domain resulted in a statistically significantly elevated hearing threshold compared to wild-type mice which emphasized the role of the phosphatase domain in PPIP5K2 (PMID: 29590114), however this mechanism was not reflective of the missense variant reported in patients. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hearing Loss GCEP on the meeting date September 17, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

TREX1 was first associated with disease in 2006 in autosomal recessive Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) (Crow et al., PMID: 16845398), a neuroinflammatory disorder characterized by early-onset encephalopathy, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, and elevated interferon signaling. In 2007, heterozygous TREX1 variants were shown to cause an autosomal dominant form of AGS (PMID: 17660818). Additional heterozygous TREX1 variants have since been associated with other autosomal dominant autoimmune phenotypes, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Kirsch et al., PMID: 17660816), familial chilblain lupus (FCL) (Rice et al., PMID: 25703219), and retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations (RVCLS) (Richards et al., PMID: 17660820).
The TREX1 gene encodes for the major mammalian three prime repair exonuclease 1, a cytosolic 3’→5’ DNA exonuclease that degrades aberrant endogenous DNA derived from replication. TREX1 plays a critical role in preventing accumulation of intracellular DNA and inappropriate activation of the innate immune response. Loss or alteration of TREX1 function results in chronic activation of type I interferon signaling, leading to autoimmune and neuroinflammatory disease.
TREX1-related autosomal dominant type I interferonopathy is characterized by immune-mediated neurological and systemic disease driven by chronic activation of interferon signaling. Clinical features vary depending on phenotype but commonly include neuroinflammation, vasculopathy, autoimmune manifestations, and variable neurologic impairment. Individuals with autosomal dominant TREX1 variants may present with chilblain skin lesions, lupus-like autoimmunity, cognitive decline, stroke-like episodes, retinal vasculopathy, and progressive leukoencephalopathy. Unlike classic AGS, autosomal dominant disease often has later onset and prominent vascular and autoimmune features.
Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, TREX1 disorders demonstrate differences in inheritance pattern, molecular mechanism, and phenotypic variability. TREX1 can cause disease through either biallelic or monoallelic variants, necessitating a separate curation of autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant entities. We elected to split retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations (RVCLS) due to its distinct molecular mechanism and phenotype. Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, familial chilblain lupus, and systemic lupus erythematosus are lumped as TREX1-related type I interferonopathies. In this curation, autosomal dominant TREX1-related type I interferonopathy is treated as a distinct disease entity due to its inheritance pattern and overlapping autoimmune-neuroinflammatory features, separately curated from the autosomal recessive TREX1-related type I  interferonapathies.
This curation of autosomal dominant TREX1-related type 1 interferonopathy included seven missense and two frameshift variants reported in eight probands across four publications (PMIDs: 21270825, 24300241, 32293470, 17660818). 10.5 points of genetic evidence was reached. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model (PMID: 30872080) and biochemical function (PMID: 19442247) for a total of 1.5 points. The mouse model capitulates human disease but was downgraded due to the use of homozygous mice.
In summary, definitive evidence supports the relationship between TREX1 and autosomal dominant TREX1-related type 1 interferonopathy, with rigorous and reproducible evidence in research and clinical diagnostic settings. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date: November 5, 2025 SOP Version #11. The Syndromic Disease GCEP contributed to this curation.

*MINPP1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive pontocerebellar hypoplasia in 2020 (Appelhof et al., PMID: 33168985). This condition is characterized by severe global developmental delay, microcephaly, brain structural anomalies (such as cerebellar, cerebral cortical, pontine, and thalamic hypoplasia), intellectual disability, motor complications, lack of/unclear speech, epilepsy, axial hypotonia, stereotypies, and facial dysmorphism. Sixteen variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in at least 16 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 33168985, 33257696, 35568357, 40508022, 41025723) are included in this curation. The maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse, HEK293 cell, and patient fibroblast models; PMIDs: 10938126, 33257696). Experimental data shows that the gene is key in maintaining cell growth and phosphate homeostasis. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between MINPP1 and autosomal recessive pontocerebellar hypoplasia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebral Palsy GCEP on the meeting date March 16th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

Autosomal recessive D-glyceric aciduria was first reported in 1974 (Brandt NJ et al., PMID: 4434100); however, the causative gene and variant were not identified until 2010 (Sass JO et al., PMID: 20949629). Several patients have been described in the literature, the majority based primarily on biochemical findings without accompanying genomic data. The reported clinical spectrum is highly variable, ranging from severe, progressive infantile encephalopathy to a nearly asymptomatic condition.

Subsequent investigations have provided additional insights into the etiology of symptoms described in earlier reports. For example, Swanson MA et al. (PMID: 28462797) demonstrated that the nonketotic hyperglycinemia phenotype reported by Brandt NJ et al. (PMID: 4434100) and Sass JO et al. (PMID: 20949629) was attributable to a homozygous missense variant in *AMT* (c.350C>T; p.Ser117Leu). Similarly, Kingma SDK et al. (PMID: 39619776) reported a patient whose hearing loss was attributed to a homozygous pathogenic variant in *STRC* (c.4837G>T; p.Glu1613*). These findings make it unclear whether the clinical features described across reports represent a consistent phenotype attributable to *GLYCTK*, or whether they were influenced by additional genomic findings that were not assessed in earlier studies.

The most consistent phenotypic feature curated for this disease entity is the accumulation of D-glycerate in urine, and in some cases serum and cerebrospinal fluid, detected by urine organic acid analysis.

To date, four variants (all frameshift) have been reported across three publications (PMID: 4434100; PMID: 20949629; PMID: 39619776) and are included in this curation. The proposed disease mechanism is loss of function, supported by in vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells demonstrating that mutant proteins were not expressed and lacked enzymatic activity (Sass JO et al., PMID: 20949629). In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting a gene–disease relationship between *GLYCTK* and autosomal recessive D-glyceric aciduria. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP at the meeting on December 12, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

EXTL3 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive immunoskeletal dysplasia with neurodevelopmental abnormalities in 2017 (Oud et al., PMID: 28132690). This condition is characterized by variable expression of T cell lymphopenia, skeletal abnormalities, neurodevelopmental delays, and in some cases, liver and kidney cysts. Heterozygous carriers are reported to be unaffected. 11 missense variants that have been reported in 14 probands in 9 publications (PMIDs: 28132690, 28148688, 28331220, 38010033, 39215781, 35114981, 35080095, 38010729, 34089299) are included in this curation. Variants in this gene segregated with disease in five additional family members. EXTL3 deficiency causes defective thymopoiesis and specifically defective differentiation of thymic epithelial progenitors. The mechanism of pathogenicity is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by zebrafish model systems and rescue studies, functional alteration studies in patient cells, and expression studies in T cell and B cell lymphocytes (PMIDs: 28148688, 28132690). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP on the meeting date February 19, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*KPNA7* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive epilepsy in 2014 (Paciorkowski et al. PMID: 24045845). *KPNA7* has also been reported in association with oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest (Wang et al. 2012 PMID: 22281085). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in phenotypic variability and have split out the disease entity oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest (OMIM:620319), which will be assessed separately. At this time, only two probands have been reported in relation to epilepsy, with compound heterozygous missense variants in proband one (p.Pro339Ala and p.Glu344Gln) and a nonsense variant in proband two (p.Arg25Ter) (PMIDs: 24045845, 29302074). At this time, the mechanism of pathogenicity is unknown and no functional evidence is available for this gene-disease relationship.
