In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date 10/7/2025 (SOP version 11).

disease_title: FLNB-associated autosomal dominant filamin related bone disorder
disease_original_title: FLNB-associated autosomal dominant filamin related bone disorder
submitted_as_notes:
Filamin B (FLNB; MIM#603381) is a large dimeric actin binding protein and multi-functional signaling scaffold with roles in crosslinking actin cytoskeleton filaments, and signaling through interactions with a variety of receptors, signaling molecules, and transcription factors.  FLNB is associated with both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive disease entities with opposing mechanisms of disease.  Given the difference in inheritance pattern and disease mechanism, the Prenatal Gene Curation Expert Panel has split these two disease entities into FLNB-associated autosomal dominant filamin related bone disorder(MONDO:1060173) and Spondylocarpotarsal Synostosis Syndrome (MONDO:0010094), inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.  These have been curated separately. 

Heterozygous variants in the FLNB gene were first reported in relation to a skeletal dysplasia in Krakow, et.al. 2004 [PMID:14991055] and since have been reported in many affected individuals with a wide phenotypic spectrum ranging from pre- or perinatal lethal skeletal dysplasia historically referred to as Boomerang Dysplasia to a milder form with survival to adulthood often referred to as Larsen syndrome, as well as intermediate phenotypes Atelosteogenesis Type I and Atelosteogenesis Type III.  The Prenatal Gene Curation Expert Panel has found no evidence of different inheritance patterns or disease mechanism between these entities, with several recurrent variants or variants at the same amino acid associated with variable phenotypic presentations and severity (p.Met202, p.Gly1691Ser, p.Trp189Arg).  Given this, the Prenatal Gene Curation Expert Panel has lumped these into a single disease entity, FLNB-associated autosomal dominant filamin related bone disorder (MONDO:1060173).  Prenatal phenotypes are highly variable and include prenatal or perinatal lethality, hydrops or cystic hygroma, phocomelia, micromelia or absent bones of the limbs in the severe form of disease; and short limb dwarfism, club feet, polyhydramnios, congenital joint dislocations, fetal growth restriction, and dysmorphic features including micrognathia, cleft palate, hypertelorism and hypoplastic vertebrae in more mild presentations.  Maximum genetic evidence was reached with both recurrent and non-recurrent variants, often identified de novo in affected individuals or inherited from variably affected parents [PMID:16752402, 2219045, 16801345, 19085972, 14991055, 22354125, others].  Genetic evidence is supported by functional evidence including protein-protein interactions, expression studies, and functional alterations demonstrating focal accumulations of FLNB with actin [PMID:11807098, 28175289, 17360453, 17635842, 17510210, 14991055, 22190451].   
The mechanism of disease is proposed to be gain-of-function or dominant negative, and while missense and in-frame indel variants associated with milder phenotypic manifestations are found throughout the protein, variants found in the CH2 domain are more commonly associated with phenotypes on the more severe end of the spectrum [PMID:22190451].  In summary the Prenatal Gene Curation Expert Panel has found sufficient genetic and functional evidence to classify FLNB as DEFINITIVE for FLNB-associated autosomal dominant filamin related bone disorder (Gene-Disease Validity SOPv11).

The relationship between *COA5* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of June 17, 2024. The *COA5* gene encodes cytochrome c oxidase assembly factor 5, a mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV assembly factor.

The first and only report of *COA5* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2011 (PMID: 21457908). *COA5* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 9 [OMIM#616500]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 21457908). This case had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and died at eight days old. Cultured fibroblasts showed severe complex IV deficiency. Postmortem microscopic investigations showed accumulation of lipid droplets in cardiomyocytes and mitochondrial proliferation. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416). 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 17, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *UQCRB* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 7, 2024. The *UQCRB* gene encodes the ubiquinol-cytochrome *c* reductase binding protein, a component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome *c* oxidoreductase (complex III) that binds ubiquinone and participates in the transfer of electrons when ubiquinone is bound.

The *UQCRB* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease in 2003 (PMID: 12709789). *UQCRB* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 3 [OMIM# 615158]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous frameshift variant identified in two unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 12709789, 35221877). Features in the two reported individuals include metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and elevated lactate.

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 7, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *NDUFAF7* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of May 20, 2024. The *NDUFAF7* gene encodes NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) assembly factor 7 which transiently interacts with and dimethylates NDUFS2, a core subunit of mitochondrial complex I.

This gene has been reported in association several phenotypes in the medical literature including high myopia (PMIDs: 28837730, 32215939, 36964802), dilated cardiomyopathy (PMID: 35414514), and leukodystrophy (PMID: 32488467). The cases with isolated high myopia were excluded from this curation as this phenotype is not concerning for a primary mitochondrial disease. The cases with dilated cardiomyopathy and leukodystrophy were excluded from this curation as there was no functional evidence to support any deleterious effect of the variants reported.

Experimental evidence supporting the gene-disease relationship include biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), siRNA knockdown studies in non-patient human fibroblasts (PMID: 24838397), and morpholino knockdown studies in a zebrafish model (PMID: 24838397).

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *NDUFAF7* and primary mitochondrial disease has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role this gene plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 20, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *GOT2* and *GOT2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 27, 2025. The *GOT2* gene encodes the mitochondrial glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase, also known as aspartate aminotransferase. *GOT2* is a pyridoxal 5’-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme that is part of the malate-aspartate shuttle (MAS) which plays an important role in intracellular NAD(H) redox homeostasis.

The *GOT2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *GOT2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2019 (PMID: 31422819). *GOT2* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 82 [OMIM# 618721]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *GOT2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 10 variants (eight missense, one in-frame deletion, one exon 1 duplication) identified in 10 unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 31422819, 37977948, 41001736). Clinical features in affected individuals include global developmental delay, spastic quadriplegia, absent speech or very limited verbal communication, severe to profound intellectual disability, acquired microcephaly, infantile onset seizures, feeding difficulties, and frequent infection. Variable brain MRI abnormalities have been reported in all affected individuals to date including cerebral atrophy and corpus callosum hypoplasia. Consistent metabolic abnormalities include elevated serum lactate and ammonia levels. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration in patient cells (PMID: 31422819), and mouse and zebrafish models (PMID: 31422819).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *GOT2* and autosomal recessive *GOT2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features
disease_original_title: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features
submitted_as_notes:
*RAB11A* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features in 2017 (McRae et al., PMID:28135719, Hamden et al., PMID:29100083). This disease is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder that involves more than one phenotype associated with the central nervous system, including but not limited to intellectual disability, developmental delay. Other variable features include seizures, gait disturbances, motor disability, hypotonia, magnetic resonance imaging abnormalities, visual anomalies, dysmorphisms, early adrenarche, and obesity. At least 15 unique missense variants that have been reported in 19 probands in six publications (PMIDs: 28135719, 29100083, 33875846, 39181022, 40225156, 40959816) are included in this curation. 

Most of the variants are reported to be *de novo* occurrences. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be gain-of-function (PMID: 40959816). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including the biochemical function of *RAB11A* as a part of the family of small GTPases, Rab, that regulates intercellular trafficking. Evidence also demonstrates distinct expression patterns of RAB11A in the developing cortex, and a zebrafish model shows reduced central nervous system area in mutants (PMIDs: 39883192, 40959816). Of note, an individual with intellectual disability, seizures, and motor disorders was found to have a homozygous nonsense variant in *RAB11A* along with a homozygous pathogenic LAMA2 variant. Variants in LAMA2 have been associated with autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy. This individual was not scored. 

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between RAB11A and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebral Palsy GCEP on the meeting date December 15, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Bi-allelic pathogenic variants in *INSR*, which encodes the insulin receptor protein, were first reported in association with severe and moderate insulin resistance syndromes, including Donohue syndrome (OMIM:246200) described in 1948 by Donohue, and Rabson–Mendenhall syndrome (OMIM:262190) described in 1956 by Rabson and Mendenhall. We have curated the inheritance pattern for *INSR*-related severe insulin resistance syndrome as autosomal recessive; however, autosomal dominant monoallelic cases causing type A insulin resistance have also been reported and will be curated separately.

INSR protein is a heterotetrameric glycoprotein composed of two extracellular α-subunits and two transmembrane β-subunits (α₂β₂), linked by disulfide bonds. The α-subunits are responsible for binding insulin, while the β-subunits span the membrane and contain an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain. When insulin binds to the receptor, it induces a conformational change that activates the kinase domain, leading to autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues and initiation of downstream signaling pathways such as the PI3K–AKT pathway and MAPK pathway. These signaling cascades mediate key biological effects of insulin, including glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipid metabolism, protein synthesis, and cell growth (Taylor et al, 1986, 1992: PMIDs: 1327927, 3009519).

Individuals with autosomal recessive (biallelic) *INSR* variants present with a spectrum of severe insulin resistance syndromes that reflect the underlying functional severity of the receptor defect. When two pathogenic alleles are present, the phenotype may range from Donohue syndrome (formerly sometimes known as “leprechaunism”), the most severe form characterized by profound insulin resistance, extreme growth failure, dysmorphic features, and early infant mortality, to a form of type A insulin resistance that tends to be more severe than the monoallelic form. An intermediate form of bi-allelic disease in which affected individuals survive beyond infancy but exhibit marked insulin resistance along with short stature, dental abnormalities, characteristic facial features, and other developmental abnormalities, is historically known as Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome. These disorders arise from diverse molecular mechanisms affecting receptor function, including impaired biosynthesis, defective intracellular processing or trafficking, reduced insulin binding, diminished tyrosine kinase signaling, or increased receptor degradation, all of which ultimately compromise insulin receptor activity and lead to severe metabolic dysregulation (PMID’s:3009519,1327927,1730618).

Per the criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we identified differences in inheritance patterns and phenotypic variability among variants associated with biallelic and monoallelic *INSR*-related insulin resistance syndromes. Therefore, the curation of INSR has been split into (1) the spectrum of autosomal recessive disease that includes Donohue and Rabson–Mendenhall syndromes as well as severe type A insulin resistance and (2) autosomal dominant type A insulin resistance syndrome due to functionally significant variants in the kinase domain.

Evidence supporting the relationship of this gene with autosomal recessive severe insulin resistance includes case-level data and experimental data. The *INSR* gene including nonsense, splice site, deletions and missense variants have been reported in association with autosomal recessive insulin resistance syndrome in humans. Variants in this gene have been curated in at least 8 probands in 7 publications (PMIDs; 26974131, 22399506, 81101305, 8270132,17201797,2834824,26160152), with clinical and phenotypic features consistent with Donohue and Mendenhall syndrome. More evidence is available to support the gene-disease association in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached this has not been curated exhaustively.

This gene–disease relationship is supported by functional assays, expression studies, and animal models. The Insr⁻/⁻ mouse model exhibits severe growth retardation, and profound metabolic dysregulation due to complete loss of insulin receptor function (PMID: 8528241). In mice, neonatal death is caused by ketoacidosis.  Human patients with biallelic loss-of-function INSR variants, such as those with Donohue syndrome, present with severe intrauterine and postnatal growth failure, extreme insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, hyperglycemia, and early mortality, often within the first year of life, due to a variety of causes, usually infection. Together, these findings demonstrate that complete loss of insulin receptor signaling leads to a severe and lethal phenotype in both mice and humans, providing further functional evidence supporting the pathogenicity of null *INSR* variants. Total points for the experimental evidence are 5.5. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 17.5.

In summary, *INSR* is definitively associated with autosomal recessive severe insulin resistance syndrome, with most cases presenting prenatally or in early infancy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. 

This classification was approved by the MDGCEP on April 8, 2026.  Gene-Disease Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) – SOP12.

disease_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment, autism, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder
disease_original_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment, autism, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder
submitted_as_notes:
*CAPRIN1* encodes an mRNA-binding protein that regulates mRNA transport, translation and stability, and plays a role in neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity in neurons, and in cell proliferation and migration in multiple cell types. *CAPRIN1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment, autism, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder in 2023 (Pavinato et al., PMID: 35979925) in ten unrelated individuals with protein truncating variants (PTVs). Phenotypic features in individuals with *CAPRIN1* haploinsufficiency include language delay and/or speech impairment, intellectual disability (usually mild) or learning disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder. Less common findings include mild limb and/or skeletal anomalies, seizures, and respiratory problems at birth.

Of note, a separate clinical entity defined by early onset ataxia and cognitive decline has been described in individuals with a recurrent *de novo* missense variant (p.Pro512Leu) in *CAPRIN1* leading to a gain of function (PMIDs: 36136249, 39878554). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability between Neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment, autism, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (OMIM: 620782), and Neurodegeneration, childhood-onset, with cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline (OMIM: 620636). The split curation for autosomal dominant Neurodegeneration, childhood-onset, with cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline is presented separately. 

Twenty-two PTVs that have been reported in 22 probands in six publications (PMIDs: 28135719, 31398340, 31981491, 33057194, 35979925, 35982160) are included in this curation. Except for the PTVs reported by Pavinato et al., the other variants were identified in large-scale sequencing studies of neurodevelopmental disorders, with no detailed phenotype information. Twelve PTVs occurred *de novo*, nine were inherited (including one inherited from an affected father), and one was of unknown inheritance. Of note, a sequencing study in over 20,000 ASD individuals identified ten PTVs in *CAPRIN1*; three were *de novo* and seven were inherited from reportedly unaffected parents, including two also present in unaffected siblings (PMID: 35982160). No information was available regarding the phenotype of the transmitting parents. In one family, the paternally inherited variant was present in two siblings with ASD but not in their sister, who was also diagnosed with ASD (PMID: 35982160). *CAPRIN1* PTVs have also been reported in three individuals with schizophrenia and seven controls (PMID: 35396579). Taken together, these findings indicate that *CAPRIN1* haploinsufficiency is associated with incomplete penetrance and/or variable expressivity and additional studies are needed to better understand the phenotypic spectrum. *De novo* missense variants in *CAPRIN1* have been observed in a small number of individuals with developmental disorders (PMID: 33057194) or ASD (PMID: 35982160), but they were not scored due to the lack of supportive functional evidence. *CAPRIN1* is highly constrained for PTVs (pLI 1, LOEUF 0.37, gnomAD v4.1.0), but not for missense variants. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function (PMID: 35979925).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including protein interaction, and cell culture and mouse models (PMIDs: 22737234, 26865403, 29157358, 35979925).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. The classification was downgraded from strong to moderate due to multiple instances of PTVs inherited from unaffected parents or present in unaffected siblings and controls. More evidence is needed to determine the  penetrance and phenotypic spectrum of *CAPRIN1* haploinsufficiency. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 2, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *PET100* and *PET100*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 17, 2024. The *PET100* gene encodes a protein with essential roles in complex IV assembly and maturation. 

The *PET100* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *PET100*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2014 (PMID: 24462369). *PET100* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 12 [OMIM# 619055]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *PET100*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *PET100* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on May 13, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *PET100*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two unique variants (Lebanese founder start loss variant and a nonsense variant) identified in eight unrelated cases from four publications (PMIDs: 24462369, 31406627, 25293719, 32313153). Onset is in the first few months of life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, seizures, dystonia, microcephaly, spasticity, feeding difficulty, short stature, respiratory failure, cardiomyopathy, and lactic acidosis. Complex IV deficiency is seen in skeletal muscle and skin fibroblasts.  

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 25293719), rescue in patient cells (PMID: 24462369), and a yeast model (PMID: 8702496).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *PET100* and autosomal recessive *PET100*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 17, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*KCNJ11*, which encodes a subunit of the β‐cell ATP‐sensitive potassium channel, was first reported in relation to familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia 2 (OMIM: 601820) in 1997 (Nestorowicz et al., PMID: 9356020). We have curated the inheritance pattern for *KCNJ11*-related hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia as autosomal recessive, although there have been autosomal dominant cases reported which will be curated separately. A subset of cases are caused by paternally inherited heterozygous mutations that lead to focal disease due to somatic loss of heterozygosity. Loss of heterozygosity results in expression of this AR condition in a histologically focal manner. 

Individuals with pathogenic, inactivating *KCNJ11* variants typically present with hypoglycemia due to unregulated insulin secretion. Cases may present as diffuse, with all β-cells impacted, or focal, with the abnormality confined to a region of the pancreas. Recessive bi-allelic variants, including truncating, missense, and small indel variants (PMID 32027066), lead to an absent, nonfunctional or less functional KATP channel, resulting in persistent beta-cell membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and dysregulated insulin release. Focal hyperinsulinism, typically characterized by a small lesion of endocrine cells, within an otherwise histologically unremarkable pancreas, is caused by a single paternally-inherited recessive inactivating variant followed by a somatic loss of the maternal chromosome 11p.15 region because of paternal uniparental isodisomy. The focal lesion develops because the chromosome 11p15.5 region contains several imprinted genes including the maternally-expressed *H19* (a candidate tumor suppressor gene) and *CDKN1C* (a negative regulator of cell proliferation) and paternally-expressed growth factor genes such as *IGF2*. When paternal uniparental isodisomy occurs within a pancreatic beta-cell during fetal development, the imbalance between imprinted genes (increased IGF2 and diminished *H19* and *CDKN1C*) gives rise to the increase in proliferation of a population of beta-cells resulting in the focal lesion. As this cell contains a heterozygous *KCNJ11* recessive variant on the paternal allele, the uniparental unmasks the variant causing it to be homozygous which results in dysregulated insulin secretion from the focal lesion. 

Rapid parental testing should be performed for all individuals with a single heterozygous recessive *KCNJ11* variant as paternal inheritance offers a positive predictive value up to 94% for focal HI (PMIDs: 23275527, 24401662). For these individuals pancreatic imaging using 18F-DOPA PET scan is recommended to assess for focal disease and localize the lesion prior to lesionectomy which is curative in >97% of cases.  For these cases consultation with an HI expert is recommended.

Evidence supporting the relationship of this gene with autosomal recessive hyperinsulinism includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. A large number of variants have been reported in *KCNJ11* in individuals with congenital hyperinsulinism (PMID: 32027066).  For the purpose of this curation, 10 probands from 7 publications are included (PMIDs: 9356020, 18250167, 20589481, 20980454, 20686794, 28442472, 15998776). More evidence is available to support the gene-disease relationship in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached; this has not been curated exhaustively. Variants in this gene have also been shown to segregate with disease in at least five family members (PMID: 24421282). The aggregated score for case and segregation-level data is 12 points.

This gene-disease relationship is supported by functional assays, mouse models, expression studies, and protein interactions (PMIDS: 9488482, 9724715, 20694718, 14699091, 8549751, 854975, 11310506). Of note, we have reduced the points allotted to the mouse models, as they do not fully recapitulate the human phenotype. The mouse models described do not have sustained neonatal hypoglycemia, but rather stabilize blood glucose within a few days of birth, and develop glucose intolerance later in life (PMIDs: 9724715, 20694718, 11310506). Total points for experimental evidence are 5. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 17. 

In summary, *KCNJ11* is definitively associated with autosomal recessive hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on February 4, 2026. Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) - SOP11.

*IRF9* was first reported in relation to Autosomal Recessive susceptibility to viral infection in 2018 (PMID:30143481). At least 2 unique variants (missense, frameshift) have been reported in humans. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. Experimental evidence incldues evidence of functional alteration (PMID 35182547, 30143481 and 30826365), rescue model (PMID 30143481 and 30826365), cell culture model (PMID 30826365), and mouse model (PMID 22496215). Variants in this gene have been reported in at least 2  probands in 2 publications (PMID 30143481 and 30826365). Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 1 additional family member. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.

disease_title: progressive essential tremor-speech impairment-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability-abnormal behavior syndrome
disease_original_title: progressive essential tremor-speech impairment-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability-abnormal behavior syndrome
submitted_as_notes:
Th*e SLC6A17 g*ene was first reported in association with autosomal recessive intellectual disability type 48 in 2015 (Iqbal Z et al., PMID: 25704603). To date, at least five affected individuals from two unrelated families have been described in the literature (family 1 with two probands and family 2 with three probands). Across two publications, three missense variants have been reported; however, detailed functional characterization has been performed for only two variants, which were included in this curation (Iqbal Z et al., PMID: 25704603).
Overall, functional data support a loss-of-function disease mechanism. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models where studies demonstrate that loss of SLC6A17 impairs glutamine transport into presynaptic compartments. Furthermore, both Slc6a17 knockout mice and mice homozygous for the P633R patient variant show significantly reduced glutamine levels in synaptic vesicles (Jiao X et al., PMID: 37440432). Additionally, NTT4 (SLC6A17) knockout mice exhibit impaired retention of conditioned memory associations when conditioned and unconditioned stimuli are separated by a longer temporal gap which recapitulates the phenotypes described in the literature (Nicoli AL et al., PMID: 40436200). In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting a gene–disease relationship between SLC6A17 and intellectual disability type 48. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP at the meeting on February 13th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*UBR1* (Ubiquitin-Protein Ligase E3 Component N-Recognin 1) is located on chromosome 15q15.2 and codes for ubiquitin protein ligase E3 component n-recognin 1 protein, the recognition component of the N-end rule proteolytic pathway of the ubiquitin system, helping form a substrate-associated multiubiquitin chain. *UBR1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Johanson-Blizzard Syndrome (JBS) in 2005 (Zenker et al., PMID: 16311597). This condition is characterized by pancreatic insufficiency, nasal anomalies, oligodontia, hearing impairment, cognitive impairment, and short stature. 15 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, & splicing) that have been reported in over 20 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 16311597, 18553553, 19006206, 24599544) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (a mouse model, biochemical functional evidence and functional alteration in non-patient cells; PMIDs: 16311597, 33554225, 21931868). Homozygous mutant mice show growth delay, reduced body weight, pancreatic issues, and reductions in muscle and adipose tissue. Biochemical functional and functional alteration evidence in yeast supports that the protein is necessary in protein quality regulation, and by extension, indicates that JBS may be fully or partially due to deficiency of protein quality control triggered by *UBR1* loss-of-function. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *UBR1* and autosomal recessive JBS. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 7/22/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*LHX2* encodes a LIM-homeodomain transcription factor that plays an important role in cortical development. *LHX2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2023 (Schmid et al., PMID: 37057675). Affected individuals present with global developmental delay, variable intellectual disability, behavioral anomalies including autism spectrum disorder, and microcephaly. Magnetic resonance imaging anomalies include dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, and white matter lesions. Patients may present additional features such as ophthalmologic abnormalities (including macular degeneration and optic neuropathy), congenital heart defects, or subtle facial dysmorphisms.

Ten variants (2 nonsense, 4 frameshift, and 4 missense) that have been reported in 10 probands in 1 publication (PMID: 37057675) are included in this curation. Functional studies showed nucleolar accumulation for 2 missense variants located within the DNA-binding HOX domain, impaired interaction with co-factor LDB1 for a missense variant located in the protein-protein interaction-mediating LIM domain, and impaired transcriptional activation by luciferase assay for 4 missense variants (PMID: 37057675). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function (PMID: 37057675). 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by studies of mouse models (PMIDs: 23454273, 24781987, 26371318). The deletion of *Lhx2* in mouse cortical progenitors by Nestin-cre leads to a dramatically smaller cortex, while inactivation of *Lhx2* in mouse cortical radial glia leads to complete absence of the corpus callosum.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *LHX2* and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This gene-disease pair was originally evaluated by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 2, 2025. It was reevaluated on October 14, 2026 (SOP Version 12). As a result of this reevaluation, no new cases were found but the classification increased from Strong to Definitive because no contradictory evidence has emerged in the three years since the first publication.

The relationship between *PDHA1* and X-linked *PDHA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of July 29, 2024. The *PDHA1* gene encodes the E1 alpha subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex which provides the primary link between glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle by catalyzing the conversion of pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. 

The *PDHA1* gene was first reported in relation to X-linked *PDHA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 1989 (PMID: 2537010). *PDHA1* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; pyruvate dehydrogenase E1-alpha deficiency [OMIM# 312170]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *PDHA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *PDHA1* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on March 25, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Definitive. This current curation for the association with *PDHA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included nine unique variants (eight missense, one frameshift) identified in nine unrelated cases from eight publications (PMIDs: 29756269, 34247546, 33592356, 38497591, 9187674, 8664900, 20002461, 21914562) although there have been many additional cases reported in the literature. Disease onset varies from the prenatal period to adulthood. Clinical features in affected individuals are variable and include neonatal lactic acidosis, LSS, developmental delay and regression, episodic or paroxysmal ataxia, hemiplegia, dystonia,  microcephaly, exercise intolerance, and myopathy.  Brain imaging is also variable and can show findings consistent with LSS as well as cerebral atrophy, dysgenesis or agenesis of corpus callosum, and periventricular cysts. Common biochemical findings include lactic acidosis and elevated pyruvate with a low or normal lactate/pyruvate ratio. Both affected males and females have been reported in the literature. While often de novo, familial inheritance with variable expressivity has also been reported, as has mosaicism (PMIDs: 21914562, 38497591). 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), a mouse model (PMID: 23840713), and functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 28918066).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *PDHA1* and X-linked *PDHA1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: RNU5B-1 related neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and joint laxity
disease_original_title: RNU5B-1 related neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and joint laxity
submitted_as_notes:
*RNU5B-1* is located in chromosome 15 at 15q22.31 and encodes the U5B small nuclear 1 RNA, a key component of the major spliceosome composed of five snRNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6). The U5 snRNA is involved in forming the U4/U6 x U5 tri-snRNP complex, which is a critical intermediate in the assembly of the major spliceosome. This tri-snRNP complex facilitates ​​the correct positioning of the U4, U5, and U6 snRNAs, allowing them to interact with the pre-mRNA and carry out the splicing reaction. *RNU5B-1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant *RNU5B-1* related neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and joint laxity in 2025 (Nava et al. 2025 PMID: 40379786 and Jackson et al. 2025 PMID: 40442284). This disease is characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, macrocephaly, and failure to thrive. 
Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. Five unique pathogenic/likely pathogenic non-coding variants (2 single nucleotides, 2 single base-pair insertion, 1 transversion) have been reported in fifteen probands across 2 publications and are include in this curation ( PMIDs:40379786, 40442284). Pathogenic variants are clustered within a small region, corresponding to the highly conserved U5 5′ loop I, which is depleted in variants in gnomAD v4.1.0 and the UK Biobank (PMIDs:40379786, 40442284). Two patients reported with variants of uncertain significance (n.24G>C, n.74T>C) which are located beyond the constrained region were not counted towards genetic evidence points (PMID: 40379786). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical, protein interaction, functional alteration and expression evidence. U5 snRNA interacts with other snRNAs and plays a direct role in achieving splicing precision by actively recognizing and binding exons (PMID: 34276781). Splicing analysis in patients with *RNU5B-1* variants demonstrate significant alternative 5′SS and 3′SS events by *RNU5B-1* n.39C>G and *RNU5B-1* n.44A>G compared to controls (PMID: 40379786). Additionally, *RNU5B-1* is expressed in multiple brain regions (PMID: 40379786). In summary, there is strong evidence to support the relationship between *RNU5B-1* and autosomal dominant *RNU5B-1* related neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and joint laxity. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date September 19th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFB8* and *NDUFB8*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 18, 2024. The *NDUFB8* gene encodes mitochondrial NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit B8, which is essential for complex I activity and assembly. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency. 

The *NDUFB8* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFB8*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2018 (PMID: 29429571). *NDUFB8* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 32 [OMIM# 618252]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFB8*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFB8* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on November 23, 2020 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *NDUFB8*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included five unique variants (four missense, one frameshift) identified in three unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 29429571, 30770271). All three probands presented in the first year of life. There are limited details on the outcome of one case, one case died at age 15 months, and one case was alive but severely affected at age 5 years. Two cases had LSS and the third had cavitating leukoencephalopathy. Additional features include developmental delay, seizures, left ventricular hypertrophy, and respiratory failure. Complex I deficiency was noted in muscle biopsies and blood lactate was elevated.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), and functional alteration studies in HEK293T cells (PMID: 27626371).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFB8* and autosomal recessive *NDUFB8*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 18, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*SLC35A1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive SLC35A1-congenital disorder of glycosylation (originally called Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type IIf) in 2005 (Martinez-Duncker I et al., PMID:15576474). *SLC35A1*  functions by transporting CMP-sialic acid from the cytosol into the Golgi apparatus, functioning as an antiporter that exchanges CMP-sialic acid for CMP. Moving nucleotide sugars across the membrane is essential for glycosylation reactions that take place within the Golgi apparatus. Patient with disrupted *SLC35A1* show characteristics of macrothrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, global developmental delay, seizures, and cognitive  impairment. 

Seven variants that have been reported in five probands in five publications (PMIDs: 28856833, 30115659, 23873973, 15576474, 40613041) are included in this curation. Probands presented with considerable decrease in the amount of N- and O-glycans terminating in sialic acid as evidence by primary fibroblasts and serum levels. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model (PMID: 32303557) in a knockout mouse line. Lectin-based flow cytometry showed the mouse had thrombocytopenia, seen in humans as well. Functional alteration studies (PMID: 25552652) using flow cytometry showed Ac5SiaNPoc was completely absent in the knockout cell lines (Fig. 2D). In knockout cells complemented with a wild-type *SLC35A1* construct, Ac5SiaNPoc incorporation was completely restored, whereas complementation with mutant *SLC35A1* restored Ac5SiaNPoc incorporation for only ∼20%. While the other study confirmed the loss of terminal sialic acids showing show that *SLC35A1* is essential for synthesis of the functional O-mannose glycan on α-DG, by a mechanism that is independent from sialylation.

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *SLC35A1* autosomal recessive SLC35A1-congenital disorder of glycosylation. This classification was approved by the ClinGen CDG GCEP on the meeting date November 17, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*COG8* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive COG8-congenital disorder of glycosylation in 2007 (Foulquier, F. et al., PMID: 17220172). These multisystem disorders present with a wide variety of clinical features, such as disorders of the nervous system development, psychomotor retardation, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, coagulation disorders, and immunodeficiency. The broad spectrum of features reflects the critical role of glycosylation during embryonic development, differentiation, and maintenance of cell functions. Clinical characteristics for autosomal recessive COG8-congenital disorder of glycosylation include but are not limited to encephalopathy, hypotonia, pseudoptosis, decreased reflexes, intubation and ventilation. 

Eleven variants (missense, in-frame indel, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in nine probands in four publications (PMIDs: 30690882, 28619360, 17331980, 17220172) and five ClinVar records (SCV006081080.1, SCV005880064.2, SCV002767931.1, SCV001525055.1, SCV001150962.37) are included in this curation. CDGs are a family of inherited diseases caused by a defect in protein glycosylation pathways, some sharing the COG8-enabled trafficking pathway. They are often characterized by mis-glycosylated serum proteins, ranging from missing entire chains to terminal sugars. *COG8* specifically is missing terminal sugars.

The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression studies and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 23865579, 16051600, 17904886). Functional alterations in non-patient cells showed depletion of Cog8 markedly affected the compact organization of the Golgi apparatus in HeLa cells. Electron microscopy analysis further exposed a dilation of Golgi cisternae and accumulation of vesicles in the vicinity of the Golgi, which possibly represent vesicles that failed to fuse with the Golgi membranes. These results are consistent with previous studies in which vesiculated Golgi membranes and swollen Golgi cisternae were observed in CDG-derived Cog8-deficient fibroblasts from patient cells. Protein interactions showed Cog8 associates stably with both Cog5–7 and Cog1– 4 subcomplexes. Cog8 helps assemble the Cog1– 4 and Cog5–7 subcomplexes into the complete COG complex. Acute and short-term deficiency of Cog8 may lead to tethering defects.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *COG8* and autosomal recessive COG8-congenital disorder of glycosylation. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen CDG GCEP on the meeting date March 2, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The *SLITRK2* gene encodes a transmembrane protein expressed at postsynaptic neurons that regulates neurite outgrowth and excitatory synapse formation. *SLITRK2* was first reported in relation to X‑linked complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2022 (El Chehadeh et al., PMID: 35840571). Affected individuals present with global developmental delay, intellectual disability of variable severity, neuropsychiatric and behavioral problems (including anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and aggressive behavior), and motor abnormalities such as unsteady gait, spasticity, or dystonia. Additional findings in a subset of individuals include seizures, feeding difficulties, kyphoscoliosis, short stature, and nonspecific structural brain abnormalities.

Eight variants (6 missense and 2 nonsense) that have been reported in seven males and one female in two publications (PMIDs: 35840571, 38283150) are included in this curation. *SLITRK2* has a single protein-coding exon, which is its last exon, and is not predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay. The variants were either *de novo* (in two probands) or inherited from an unaffected mother, suggestive of an X‑linked recessive pattern of inheritance. Functional studies showed that four missense variants and a nonsense variant resulting in a truncated protein had impaired membrane trafficking and/or impaired excitatory synapse-promoting effects (PMID: 35840571). Two missense variants with no evidence of altered function, a missense variant in a male proband with a likely pathogenic variant in *ARX*, and a *de novo* missense variant in a female reported three times in gnomAD, were scored 0 points. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. *SLITRK2* is not strongly constrained for loss‑of‑function variation (pLI = 0.75, LOEUF = 0.58, gnomAD 4.1.1) or missense variants (Z = 2.76).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model. *Slitrk2* conditional knockout mice exhibit memory deficits and abnormal gait, while hippocampal CA1-specific conditional knockout of Slitrk2 impaired excitatory synapse maintenance and caused abnormalities in spatial reference memory (PMID: 35840571).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support the relationship between *SLITRK2* and X-linked complex neurodevelopmental disorder. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 2, 2025 (SOP Version 12).

The relationship between *NARS2* and *NARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of December 16, 2024. The *NARS2* gene encodes mitochondrial asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase 2, one of the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which function in mitochondrial translation by catalyzing the attachment of amino acids to their cognate tRNAs. Defects in tRNA charging can result in impaired synthesis of oxidative phosphorylation complex protein subunits.

The *NARS2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2015 (PMID: 25629079). *NARS2* has been associated with two disease entities to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 24 [OMIM# 616239] and deafness, autosomal recessive 94 [OMIM# 618434]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NARS2* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on December 9, 2019 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *NARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 21 unique variants (18 missense, one intronic, one frameshift, one nonsense) identified in 12 unrelated cases from 10 publications (PMIDs: 25629079, 25385316, 25807530, 28077841, 30327238, 32020600, 34374940, 35558980, 33596490, 35703918). Disease onset is typically early in life. Some affected individuals have clinical features consistent with LSS and/or Alpers syndrome, others have an infantile onset of severe epilepsy, and there have been reports of isolated hearing loss. Additional clinical features include myopathy, developmental delay and regression, myoclonic movements, spasticity, ataxia, dysarthria, muscle weakness, seizures include epilepsia partialias continua (EPC), microcephaly, short stature, diabetes, failure to thrive, optic atrophy, ptosis, and sensorineural hearing loss. Elevated lactate and creatine kinase levels have been reported.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in patient muscle tissue (PMIDs: 25807530, 34415467), an embryonic lethal knockout mouse model (PMID: 36305825), and a yeast model (PMID: 39230874).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *NARS2* and autosomal recessive *NARS*2-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 16, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*LRAT* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive early-onset retinal dystrophy (often described clinically as Leber congenital amaurosis / early-onset severe retinal dystrophy, with overlap into juvenile retinitis pigmentosa phenotypes) in 2001 (Thompson et al., PMID: 11381255). Per ClinGen disease-entity principles, reported LRAT-associated phenotypes fall on an early-onset retinal dystrophy spectrum (e.g., LCA/early-onset severe retinal dystrophy, autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa, and related entities such as retinitis punctata albescens). In this summary, these are considered part of a shared biallelic LRAT-related retinopathy spectrum given a consistent underlying pathway (visual-cycle deficiency) and overlapping core features (early-onset night blindness/visual impairment with progressive retinal degeneration).

Human genetic evidence includes multiple unrelated affected individuals/families with biallelic LRAT variants reported across multiple publications since the original 2001 report, as well as subsequent case reports/series expanding the phenotype and variant spectrum (e.g., homozygous frameshift reported with retinitis punctata albescens; PMID: 22559933; and an intronic splice-altering variant supported by minigene assays in a consanguineous family with early-onset RP; PMID: 29973277). Reported pathogenic variant types include missense, frameshift, and splice-altering changes (PMIDs: 11381255, 17011878, 24265693, 28418496, 24625443, 30054919, 22570351, 22559933, 29973277).
The mechanism of disease is most consistent with loss of function due to disruption of LRAT enzymatic activity in the visual cycle (supported by the nature of reported variant types and functional pathway relevance; PMIDs: 11381255, 22559933).

Evidence supporting the gene–disease relationship includes biochemical studies showing that *LRAT* encodes lecithin retinol acyltransferase, a key enzyme in the retinoid (visual) cycle in the retinal pigment epithelium, required for generation/regeneration of visual chromophore. Disruption of this pathway is consistent with severe early-onset photoreceptor dysfunction and progressive retinal degeneration (PMID: 11381255). Disease-relevant model systems demonstrate that LRAT deficiency causes retinal dysfunction/degeneration and that restoring/bypassing LRAT function can improve retinal physiology. For example, *Lrat−/−* mouse studies show a phenotype consistent with human congenital/early-onset blindness and demonstrate rescue of retinal function via AAV-mediated gene therapy and pharmacologic bypass retinoids (PMID: 16250670). Additional animal model development and phenotyping (e.g., *Lrat−/−* rat) further support a consistent retinal degeneration phenotype (PMID: 34281288).

In summary, there is Definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *LRAT* and *LRAT*-related retinopathy, based on multiple human case reports across time since 2001 and supportive experimental model/rescue data (PMIDs: 11381255, 17438524, 22559933, 29973277, 16250670, 34281288). This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 5th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*FLVCR2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Fowler syndrome in 2010 (Meyer et al. 2010 PMID: 20206334). Fowler syndrome, usually a prenatally lethal disorder, is characterized by hydranencephaly, a distinctive glomerular vasculopathy in the central nervous system and retina, and diffuse ischemic lesions of the brain stem, basal ganglia, and spinal cord with calcifications. Additional features include microcephaly, hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, joint contractures, and fetal akinesia deformation sequence. Rarely, affected individuals may survive, but are severely impaired (PMID: 25677735). 

At least 31 unique variants including missense, in-frame indels, nonsense, frameshift, splicing and exonic deletion variants have been reported in humans (PMID: 20518025, 20690116, 38302740, and 30712878). Loss of function is the proposed molecular mechanism for *FLVCR2* dysfunction with variants associated with complete or partial loss of choline transport activity (PMID: 38302740). The *FLVCR2* gene encodes a transmembrane protein that belongs to the major facilitator superfamily of secondary carriers that transport small solutes in response to chemiosmotic ion gradients (PMID: 20206334). Homozygous knockout of the gene in mice recapitulates phenotypes seen in humans with Fowler syndrome (PMID: 32369449, 38302740). 

In summary, *FLVCR2* is definitively associated with autosomal recessive Fowler syndrome. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, mouse models, and experimental data. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was reviewed and approved by the ClinGen Prenatal GCEP on October 22, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

*PAN2* is located on chromosome 12 at 12q13.3 and encodes the Pabp-dependent poly(a) nuclease 2, a subunit of a deadenylation complex with important functions in mRNA stability and post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression. *PAN2* was first reported in connection with autosomal recessive syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2018 (Maddirevula et al., 2018 PMID: 29620724). This disease is characterized by mild-moderate intellectual disability, hypotonia, sensorineural hearing loss, EEG abnormalities, congenital heart defects (e.g., tetralogy of Fallot, septal defects, dilated aortic root), urinary tract malformations, ophthalmological anomalies, short stature with other skeletal anomalies, and craniofacial features including flat occiput, ptosis, long philtrum, and short neck (PMID: 35304602).

Five variants (1 nonsense, 1 duplication, 1 canonical splice-site, 1 frameshift, 1 missense) reported in 5 families have been included in this curation (PMIDs: 35304602, 29620724, 40491293). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. The patient identified with the homozygous missense variant presented with a less severe clinical condition compared to those reported with truncating mutations. Additionally, one patient reported with a dual diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type IB and syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder was excluded from the final genetic evidence score (PMID: 35304602). This gene-disease relationship is supported by relevant experimental evidence, specifically biochemical evidence demonstrating *PAN2*’s function in deadenylation, mRNA stability, and exoribonuclease activity (PMID: 24872509).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the gene-disease relationship between *PAN2* and autosomal recessive syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the Syndromic Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 6th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: frontonasal dysplasia with alopecia and genital anomaly
disease_original_title: frontonasal dysplasia with alopecia and genital anomaly
submitted_as_notes:
ALX4 has been repeatedly described in association with autosomal recessive frontonasal dysplasia with alopecia and genital anomaly. Frontonasal dysplasia 1 is characterized by having a distinctive facial appearance with hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, short nasal ridge, splayed nasal bones with bifid nasal tip, broad columella that attaches to the lip above the alae, widely separated slit-like nares, long philtrum with prominent bilateral swellings, and midline notch in the upper lip and alveolus. 

At least 1 missense, 2 nonsense, 1 splice acceptor, and 1 deletion  mutations have been reported in at least 5 probands from 4 publications (PMIDs: 19409524, 22106187, 29215096, 34098755) This gene disease association is also supported by experimental evidence including expression data and an animal model (PMID: 20534379). In summary, ALX4 is definitively associated with autosomal recessive Frontonasal dysplasia 1. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.

HDAC9 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant auriculocondylar syndrome in 2022 (Romanelli Tavares et al., PMID: 34750192). This condition is characterized by malformation of the ears, rounding of the race, puffy cheeks, micrognathia, microstomia, dental malocclusion, and atypical mandibular condyles with temporomandibular joint anomalies. Probands can additionally have conductive hearing loss. However, the expert panel also evaluated individuals with craniosynostosis since that phenotype falls within the expertise of the GCEP. 7 variants (large deletion, large duplication, translocation, frameshift) that have been reported in 7 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 34750192, 35710300, 38318288) are included in this curation. None of the cases were scored due to impacting genomic regions/genes beyond HDAC9; implicating the locus HDAC9 is at, namely TWIST1, rather than HDAC9 itself; or lack of phenotype specificity. One type of experimental evidence, a mouse model (PMID: 35710300) was evaluated, but it was not scored due to implicating the locus the gene is at, specifically TWIST1, rather than HDAC9 itself. In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between HDAC9 and auriculocondylar syndrome has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role HDAC9 plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 11/20/2025 (SOP Version 11).

No convincing evidence for a causal role for SLC14A1 in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus has been reported. Although this gene-disease association is supported by a mouse model demonstrating urinary anomalies such as polydipsia and reduced urea permeability (PMID: 11792714), no reports have directly implicated the gene in humans. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Tubulopathy GCEP on the meeting date 03/05/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*FERMT1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Kindler syndrome in 2003 (Siegel et
al., PMID:12789646). However, Kindler syndrome was first described by Kindler T (PMID: 13149722) in 1954. Kindler syndrome is an autosomal recessive skin disorder characterized by blistering, photosensitivity, progressive poikiloderma, and extensive atrophy. Additional clinical features can include gingival erosions, ocular, esophageal, gastrointestinal and urogenital involvement, and milder disease phenotypes later onset. 

Thirteen variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) that have been reported in twelve probands in six publication (PMIDs: 12668616, 21936020, 24635080, 32973952, 17178989, 27862150) are included in this curation. Less than 150 cases of Kindler syndrome have been reported world wide, many within consanguineous families. More evidence is available in the literature, but many of the compound heterozygote probands do not meet the genetic testing guidelines of the ClinGen Genetic Evidence scoring matrix, therefore they do not contribute to the overall score. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and expression studies (PMIDs: 12789646, 19057668, 30248333). Mice with disrupted Fermt1 gene, leading to complete loss of Kindlin-1 mRNA and protein (Kindlin-1-/-) have been shown to develop skin atrophy, thin epidermis, and postnatal lethality with complete penetrance. Also, experimental evidence indicating that *KIND1* (an alias form of *FERMT1*) is highly expressed in keratinocytes. *FERMT1* is directly involved with the biochemical process of keratinocyte migration via its connection to *EGFR*. When keratinocyte migration is impaired, it can cause impaired skin barriers (including dry, irritated skin (xerosis) and chronic, inflammatory rashes); while keratinocytes that fail to multiply properly can cause thinning of the epidermis (atrophy). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *FERMT1* and autosomal recessive Kindler syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time This classification was approved by the ClinGen PIRD GCEP on April 8th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ZFHX4* encodes a transcription factor involved in neural cell maturation and region-specific brain differentiation. *ZFHX4* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2025 (Pérez Baca et al., PMID: 40367947). Affected individuals exhibit variable global developmental delay and intellectual disability, dysmorphic facial features, ophthalmological abnormalities, hypotonia, and behavioral abnormalities including autism (PMID: 40367947). Other less frequent features may include cleft lip and/or palate, short stature, structural brain abnormalities, digit abnormalities, genital abnormalities, and congenital heart defects.

Nine variants (6 protein truncating and 3 exon deletions) that have been reported in 9 probands in two publications (PMIDs: 21802062, 40367947) are included in this curation. Most reported variants occur *de novo*. Two of the curated truncating variants were inherited from parents with mild intellectual disability (PMID: 40367947), while an exonic *ZFHX4* deletion was described in a 4-generation family with 5 affected members (PMID: 21802062). Of note, *ZFHX4* loss-of-function variants have been identified in individuals with orofacial cleft, occurring as an apparently isolated finding in some cases (PMIDs: 32574564, 37434517, 39702590). The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function. *ZFHX4* haploinsufficiency is considered the major contributor to the clinical manifestations of 8q21.11 microdeletion syndrome (PMIDs: 21802062, 40367947).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including mouse and zebrafish models, and protein interactions. In neural progenitor cells, ZFHX4 interacts with proteins encoded by genes associated with neurodevelopmental disorders such as *ZMIZ1*, *WDR81*, *KMT2D*, *ZMYND8*, *NACC1*, and *WASHC4* (PMID: 40367947). 

In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between *ZFHX4* and autosomal dominant syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 3, 2025 (SOP Version 12).

The relationship between *NDUFA6* and *NDUFA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of April 29, 2024. The *NDUFA6* gene encodes the NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit A6, a complex I accessory protein required for complex I assembly and function within the mitochondria. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The first and only report of *NDUFA6* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2018 (PMID: 30245030). *NDUFA6* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 33 [OMIM# 618253]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease.
 
Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included six unique variants (one missense variant, one start loss variant, three frameshift variants, and one nonsense variant predicted to escape nonsense mediated decay) identified in four unrelated cases from one publication (PMIDs: 30245030). Age of onset ranges from the prenatal period to early childhood.  Clinical features in affected individuals include small for gestational age, intrauterine growth restriction, oligohydramnios, developmental regression, seizures, dystonia, spasticity, feeding difficulty, optic atrophy, lactic acidosis, and hypoglycemia. White matter abnormalities and/or basal ganglia lesions have been seen on brain imaging.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), NDUFA6 knock out in HEK293T cells (PMID: 27626371), and a *C.elegans* model (PMID: 38215760).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFA6* and autosomal recessive *NDUFA6*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *MRPS2* and *MRPS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 27, 2025. The *MRPS2* gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal protein S2.

The *MRPS2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *MRPS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2018 (PMID: 29576219). *MRPS2* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 36 [OMIM# 617950]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *MRPS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included four missense variants identified in four unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 29576219, 34991560, 38029925). Affected individuals had developmental delay, sensorineural hearing loss, feeding difficulty, hypoglycemia, failure to thrive, muscle weakness, elevated blood lactate, metabolic acidosis, and increased excretion of Krebs cycle intermediates. Brain imaging was normal. There were variable respiratory chain enzyme deficiencies in skeletal muscle, skin fibroblasts, and liver.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and rescue in patient cells (PMID: 29576219).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support the relationship between *MRPS2* and autosomal recessive *MRPS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. However, given the consistent clinical and biochemical phenotype seen in the four reported cases, and since it is likely homozygous or compound heterozygous nonsense variants are not compatible with life, this Expert Panel elected to upgrade the classification to moderate. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFV1* and *NDUFV1*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of May 20, 2024. The *NDUFV1* gene encodes the NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) flavoprotein 1, a core subunit of mitochondrial complex I. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The *NDUFV1* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFV1*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2011 (PMID: 11349233). *NDUFV1* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4 [OMIM# 618225]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFV1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFV1* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on November 20, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Definitive. This current curation for the association with *NDUFV1*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 13 unique variants (10 missense, one nonsense, one frameshift, and one splice site) identified in 12 unrelated cases from 10 publications (PMIDs: 11349233, 2169386, 23266820, 23334465, 27344648, 29976978, 30090137, 10080174, 15576045, 256154419). Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, myoclonic epilepsy, leukodystrophy, and optic atrophy. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 27509854), functional alteration in patient cells (PMID: 11349233), and studies in *Drosophila melanogaster* (PMID: 30972103), and *Caenorhabditis elegans* (PMID: 19672299).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFV1* and autosomal recessive *NDUFV1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 20, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *MIEF2* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 11, 2025. The *MIEF2* gene encodes mitochondrial elongation factor 2, an outer mitochondrial membrane protein that regulates membrane dynamics and mitochondrial organization. 

The first and only report of *MIEF2* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2018 (PMID: 29361167). *MIEF2* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 49 [OMIM# 619024]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data.
