This curation included one homozygous nonsense variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 29361167). This proband had progressive muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, and intermittent muscle pain.  Creatine kinase was elevated. Skeletal muscle showed ragged red fibers, COX-negative fibers, and deficiency of complexes I, II+III, and IV.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and functional alteration studies and rescue in patient cells (PMID: 29361167).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although the gene curation point total is in the Moderate range, only one case has been reported. Therefore, the classification comes to Limited. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 11, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *CRLS1* and *CRLS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 27, 2025. The *CRLS1* gene encodes cardiolipin synthase 1, an enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of cardiolipin (CL) by specifically transferring a phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol to phosphatidylglycerol.

The *CRLS1* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *CRLS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2022 (PMID: 35147173). *CRLS1* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 57 [OMIM# 620167]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *CRLS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three missense variants identified in four unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 35147173, 39417332). At least two cases were more severely affected and had non-immune hydrops fetalis and bilateral pleural effusions at birth, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, epileptic encephalopathy, and progressive neurologic deterioration with death in the first year of life. Additional features seen in reported cases include global developmental delay, slowly progressive encephalopathy, sensorineural hearing loss, seizures, and bull’s eye maculopathy.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alterations in non-patient cells (PMID: 35147173), and mouse models (PMIDs: 38556544, 31914590).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *CRLS1* and autosomal recessive *CRLS1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies
disease_original_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies
submitted_as_notes:
*SPOP* is located on chromosome 17q21.33 and encodes Speckle-type BTB/POZ protein which forms homodimers and is involved in the ubiquitin proteasome pathway (Nabais Sa et al., 2020, PMID: 32109420). *SPOP* was first reported in relation to neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies, MONDO:0032942 and neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies, MONDO:0032943 in 2020 (PMID: 32109420) and has a previously well-established role in cancer. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working group, while there was no difference in inheritance patterns, there were differences in molecular mechanisms and slightly differing clinical presentations for each disorder. Variants resulting in neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies were found to cause disease through a gain of function mechanism and those that cause neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies (MONDO:0032943) cause disease through a dominant negative mechanism (PMID: 32109420). Therefore, the disease entities have been split into two. The curation for neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies (MONDO:0032943) has been curated separately. 

Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies, MONDO:0032942 is characterised by microcephaly, intellectual disability of variable severity and consistent dysmorphic features including small forehead, full nasal tip, highly arched eyebrows and a pointed chin (PMID: 32109420).  5 variants (4 missense, 1 truncating) have been reported in 5 cases across 4 publications (PMIDs: 32109420, 35892095, 36063898, 39918173) and are included in this curation.  The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain of function (PMID: 32109420). 

This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental evidence (biochemical function, protein interaction and functional alteration in patient cells and cell lines) (PMID: 19818702, 32109420). Other genes involved in the ubiquitin proteasome pathway (*CUL3*, *CUL7*, *CUL4B*, *UBR1*, *UBE3B*) are strongly or definitively associated with neurodevelopmental or syndromic disorders. *SPOP* interacts on a protein level with *CUL3*. *SPOP* has a MATH domain which binds substrate to be tagged for degradation and binds *CUL3* via a BTB domain (PMID: 19818708, 14528312). Cellular models in patient cells demonstrated variants acted through a gain of function mechanism with increased degradation of substrate resulting in reduced substrate amount in cells (PMID: 32109420, 28805821). 

In summary there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship.. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date November 11th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*ZMYM2* was first reported in association with syndromic urinary tract malformations in 2020 (Connaughton et al. PMID: 32891193). Phenotypic features include congenital malformations of the kidney and urinary tract, cardiac defects, dysmorphic features, global developmental delay, variable intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder. Less common findings include hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures. All individuals reported with renal malformations also had neurologic features. Some individuals have isolated neurodevelopmental features without congenital malformations.

This curation includes 10 heterozygous loss of function variants (6 nonsense, 3 frameshift, 1 splice site) that are reported in 10 individuals with phenotypic similarity (PMIDs: 32891193, 37383123). Of these 10 variants, 2 have functional data to support a loss of function effect. All distinct variants available in the literature in association with congenital malformations of the kidney and urinary tract with neurodevelopmental delays are scored. Additional probands are reported in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has already been reached, those individuals were not included in this curation. There are also additional probands reported in the literature harboring heterozygous putative loss of function variants in association with cerebral palsy and schizophrenia. These were not scored.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ZMYM2* and autosomal dominant syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in the clinical diagnostic setting, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date May 22, 2025 (SOP Version 10).

IRF6 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant IRF6-related condition in 2002 (Kondo et al., PMID: 12219090). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no differences in molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern. Also, the phenotype appears to be a spectrum, with potential features of cleft lip/palate, lip pits, webbing of the skin, other skin anomalies, and genital anomalies. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: Popliteal pterygium syndrome (OMIM: 119500); Van der Woude syndrome (OMIM: 119300), and Orofacial cleft (OMIM: 608864). 19 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in at least 19 probands in 9 publications (PMIDs: 12219090, 12920575, 14618417, 14757865, 18478600, 19842205, 20184620, 20803643, 33906476) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature (PMIDs: 25691407, 27252970), but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse model, expression-level evidence, functional alteration data; PMIDs: 12219090, 17041601, 25784454). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between IRF6 and IRF6-related condition. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 1/18/2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *MRPS23* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 4, 2024. The *MRPS23* gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal protein S23.

The *MRPS23* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease in 2016 (PMID: 26741492). *MRPS23* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 46 [OMIM# 618952]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.  

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two homozygous missense variants identified in six unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 26741492, 38086984). The NM_016070:c.119C>T (p.Pro40Leu) variant was seen in affected individuals from five families from the Hmong hill tribe in Thailand (PMID: 38086984). Clinical features in affected individuals included hypoglycemia, liver disease, altered consciousness, vomiting, delayed growth, developmental delay, hearing loss, and lactic acidosis.

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 4, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

*RSRC1* encodes a serine and arginine rich-related protein that functions in spliceosome assembly and is involved in pre-mRNA splicing and transcription regulation. *RSRC1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2018 (Maddirevula et al., PMID: 28640246). Since then multiple affected individuals, all from consanguineous families, have been described. The disorder is characterized by global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, behavioral abnormalities (including autism spectrum disorder and ADHD), and non-specific dysmorphic facial features. Other variable features can include febrile seizures, gait ataxia, and abnormalities on brain MRI. 

Six variants (nonsense, frameshift, exonic deletion, splice site, and start-loss) that have been reported in six probands in three publications (PMIDs: 28640246, 29522154, 32227164) are included in this curation. Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 11 additional family members. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including biochemical function and protein interaction with proteins important in splicing and implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders.  

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *RSRC1* and autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 18, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

Lim domain-binding 3 (*LDB3*) was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) in 2006 (Theis et al., PMID 17097056). At least 5 variants (all missense) have been reported in humans. Variants in *LDB3* have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), left ventricular noncompaction (also known as hypertrabeculation) and myofibrillar myopathy. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found a difference in phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entity has been split, hyertrophic cardiomyopathy 24 OMIM:601493. A single family has been reported in the literature with an HCM phenotype and compound heterozygous LBD3 variation but there is insufficient evidence to alter the curated mode of inheritance (PMID 36452351). The split curation for autosomal dominant DCM OMIM:601493, and autosomal recessive DCM OMIM:621237 have been curated separately. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case evidence (PMIDs 14662268, 17097056, 24730657) and experimental data (PMID 10427098). All but one case in this curation have population frequencies incompatible with pathogenicity (>0.0001) according to the ClinGen HCVD GCEP. Experimental evidence includes expression data showing almost equal expression in cardiac and skeletal muscle in addition to protein interaction data with ACTN2 which is curated for a syndromic form of skeletal and cardiac myopathy. Case-control data contradicts the gene-disease relationship however with no excess found of HCM cases with rare variation in *LDB3* compared to the ExAC control database (PMID 28082330). In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *LDB3* and autosomal dominant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role *LBD3* plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disease GCEP on the meeting date January 27, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *TIMM22* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of July 29, 2024. The *TIMM22* gene encodes translocase of inner mitochondrial membrane 22, an essential component of the TIM22 complex. This complex acts as the voltage-activated and signal-gated twin pore and mediates the import and insertion of multipass proteins into the inner mitochondrial membrane.

The first and only report of *TIMM22* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2018 (PMID: 30452684). *TIMM22* has been associated with a single disease entity to date, combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 43 [OMIM# 618851]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two unique variants (one stop gain variant although nonsense mediated decay is not expected as the premature stop occurs within first 100 base pairs; one missense variant) identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 30452684). Of note, the missense variant is present in population databases including in the homozygous state, so it is hypothesized this is a hypomorphic allele given the extensive functional validation performed in fibroblasts from the single case report. The single reported case had intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight and length, reduced spontaneous movements, feeding difficulty, gastroesophageal reflux with vomiting, delayed myelination, and elevated blood lactate and creatine kinase. 

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416). 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: leukodystrophy, adult-onset, autosomal dominant, without amyloid angiopathy
disease_original_title: leukodystrophy, adult-onset, autosomal dominant, without amyloid angiopathy
submitted_as_notes:
*CST3* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant adult-onset leukodystrophy in 2024 (Bergner CG et al., PMID:38489591). The disease is characterized by adult onset of variable neurologic symptoms, including recurrent hemiplegic migraine, progressive motor abnormalities, and cognitive decline. Brain MRIs show changes involving the deep cerebral white matter, posterior limb of the internal capsule, middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebral peduncles, and globus pallidus. Neuropathologic studies do not show cerebral amyloid angiopathy or amyloid deposition. Cystatin C levels in serum and cerebral spinal fluid are decreased as compared to controls.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found distinct differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability between the disease assertions for *CST3*. One single missense variant is reported in Acys amyloidosis and only truncating variants are reported with adult-onset leukodystrophy. Neuropathologic studies do not show cerebral amyloid angiopathy or amyloid deposition in the adult-onset leukodystrophy cases. This is a defining feature of the Acys amyloidosis. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split: leukodystrophy, adult-onset, autosomal dominant, without amyloid angiopathy (MONDO:0979226) and Acys amyloidosis (MONDO:0005620). The split curation for autosomal dominant Acys amyloidosis (MONDO:0005620) has been curated separately. 

Six truncating variants (nonsense, frameshift deletion) that have been reported in nine probands in five publications (PMIDs:38489591, 38729262, 41033143, 39292282, 38965776) are included in this curation. There are pedigrees of affected families in the literature, but they do not have enough segregations to be scored, per the ClinGen Gene Curation SOP. There are more probands reported in the literature than scored here, but they carry variants that were already awarded points. All probands were downscored due to the end-truncating variants existing in either the last exon for the last 50bp of the penultimate exon. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression studies (PMID:24309898) that demonstrate that *CST3* is highly expressed in the brain, a relevant organ to this disease.

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.This classification was approved by the ClinGen Neurovascular GCEP on the meeting date April 22, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The relationship between *UQCRC1* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 27, 2025. The *UQCRC1* gene encodes ubiquinol-cytochrome *c* reductase core protein 1, a subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III, and enables ubiquitin protein ligase binding activity.

*UQCRC1* has been associated with one disease entity to date; autosomal dominant parkinsonism with polyneuropathy [OMIM# 619279]. This gene-disease association was described in 2020 (PMID: 33141179), in three individuals with parkinsonism with polyneuropathy who had single variants in *UQCRC1* suspected to be causing an autosomal dominant disorder. These cases were not included in this curation as the phenotype (parkinsonism with polyneuropathy) is not commonly associated with primary mitochondrial disorders when occurring in isolation. Furthermore, the mechanism by which these reported autosomal dominant variants could cause these medical concerns is unclear. Several additional single variants were found in a cohort of individuals with parkinsonism in subsequent publications (PMIDs: 337796942, 37984314), however no functional evidence supporting a deleterious effect of these variants is available.

Experimental evidence supporting the gene-disease relationship includes biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and a knock-in *Drosophila melanogaster* model showing age-dependent locomotor deficits, loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons, and presynaptic neuromuscular junction defects (PMID: 33141179).

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *UQCRC1* and autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role this gene plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*NANS* was first reported in relation to the autosomal recessive disorder spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Genevieve type, in 2016 (van Karnebeek et al, PMID: 27213289). *NANS* encodes N-acetylneuraminic acid phosphate synthase, also known as sialic acid synthase, an enzyme that is essential for *de novo* sialic acid synthesis. Sialic acids are a family of 9-carbon sugars; over 50 forms have been identified. The predominant sialic acid in mammals, N-acetylneuraminic acid (NANA, Neu5Ac, NeuNAc) is typically the terminal sugar in cell surface glycans, glycoconjugates, oligosaccharides, lipo-oligosaccharides, and polysaccharides, and has important numerous physiological functions such as cell-cell interactions and immune function. One condition, NANS-related CDG (spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Genevieve type) has been asserted to be caused by biallelic variants in *NANS*. This condition is characterized by skeletal dysplasia, moderate to severe intellectual disability, and facial dysmorphism, including prominent forehead, depressed nasal bridge, and full lips.
This curation includes 23 variants (12 missense, 1 initiator codon, 1 in-frame duplication,  2 nonsense, 4 frameshift, 3 intronic/splice site) that have been reported in 15 probands in 4 publications (van Karnebeek et al, 2016, PMID: 27213289; den Hollander et al, 2021, PMID: 34163424; Masunaga et al, 2022, PMID: 36224347; Yoo and Cheon, 2024, PMID: 38822623). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.
This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including the biochemical function of NANS in the synthesis of sialic acids, which is consistent with the finding of elevated precursor, N-acetylmannosamine, in urine from patients with biallelic variants in the gene. In addition, zebrafish treated with morpholinos to knock down the zebrafish orthologue of *NANS*, nansa, have features that recapitulate the human phenotype, including developmental anomalies of the skeleton; these features were ameliorated by sialic acid treatment. Of note, the features of a human infant, who was treated pre- and postnatally with sialic acid appear to be milder than those of two individuals with the same genotype (one treated postnatally, one untreated) (den Hollander et al, 2023, PMID: 37340906).
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *NANS* and the autosomal recessive disorder spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Genevieve type. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time, This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation Gene Curation Expert Panel on January 5, 2026 (SOP v11).

The relationship between *MRPL38* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of January 27, 2025. The *MRPL38* gene encodes the mitochondrial ribosomal protein L38.

The first and only report of the *MRPL38* gene in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2022 (PMID: 35379322) in a girl with Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two variants identified (one missense, one deletion) in one case from one publication (PMID: 35379322). This girl had Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder based on basal ganglia changes on brain imaging and neurodevelopmental delay, and also had intellectual disability, seizures, encephalopathy, and complex I and IV defects.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416). Additional functional evidence is provided in a pre-print (DOI:10.1101/2021.03.09.21253187) however this work has not yet been published.

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel January 27, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*PRKAB2* was first reported in relation to congenital heart disease in 2004 (Christiansen J et al, PMID: 15117819). Individuals with structural heart defects and copy number variants involving *PRKAB2* have been reported. These CNVs have been reported in individuals with congenital cardiac malformations including Tetralogy of Fallot, aortic arch obstruction, and other structural cardiac defects (PMIDs: 15117819, 31340305). No convincing reports of single-gene pathogenic variants in *PRKAB2* have been demonstrated to cause isolated congenital heart disease, and the contribution of *PRKAB2* to the cardiac phenotypes observed in CNVs remains uncertain. Additionally, experimental evidence directly linking *PRKAB2* to structural cardiac defects is limited. In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *PRKAB2* and congenital heart disease has been disputed, and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role *PRKAB2* plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date December 9th, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

The *SAG* gene, which encodes the photoreceptor protein arrestin-1, was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive retinal disease in 1995 (Fuchs et al. 1995; PMID 7670478). SAG-related recessive retinopathy, including Oguchi disease and retinitis pigmentosa, is a rare retinal disease; Oguchi disease characterized by classic presentation of night blindness and a distinctive fundus appearance termed the Mizuo-Nakamura Phenomenon, thought to be pathognomonic for the disease (PMID: 31014762), whereas retinitis pigmentosa is characterized by constriction of visual fields. There have been reports of Oguchi disease progressing to retinitis pigmentosa (PMID: 31864474). We found *SAG*-related disease is primarily inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, with biallelic disease-causing *SAG* variants resulting in a spectrum of phenotypes including Oguchi disease and retinitis pigmentosa. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, we found the molecular mechanism (biallelic loss of function in the *SAG* gene product) and mode of inheritance (autosomal recessive) to be consistent among unrelated patients diagnosed with either Oguchi disease or retinitis pigmentosa, while the phenotypic variability between them appeared to represent a spectrum of disease rather than separate disease entities. Because the cases different diagnoses all exhibit a recessive mode of inheritance and share overlapping phenotypes consistent with a single spectrum of disease, and consistent with criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, these cases have been lumped into a single disease entity, *SAG*-related recessive retinopathy. An additional disease entity has been asserted in relation to a monoallelic variant in *SAG*, specifically a substitution at codon 147 that encodes phenylalanine rather than cysteine (PMID: 28549094, 29305604). While this disease entity is characterized by similar retinal dystrophy, its different mode of inheritance and unique variant suggested a different mechanism of pathogenesis. Thus, *SAG* was separately curated for its relationship to this disease entity, referred to as *SAG*-related dominant retinopathy. 

This curation includes eight suspected disease-causing variants (four nonsense, one frameshift, and three canonical splicing variants) that have been reported in seven probands in five publications (PMID: 9452120, PMID: 15234147, PMID: 22665972, PMID: 35549688, PMID: 38219857). Homozygous variants in families from multiple countries were included in the curation (PMID: 20537394, PMID: 21069908, PMID: 18836446) from both consanguineous and non-consanguineous families. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, as multiple nonsense or frameshift mutations resulting in SAG-related disease are described in the literature (PMID: 20537394, PMID: 21069908, PMID: 18836446). To date, most reported variants are nonsense, frameshift and splicing variants.

This gene-disease association is supported by multiple model systems, including murine and canine models, that demonstrates phenotypes consistent with retinal degeneration (PMID: 18985007, PMID: 24019744). Expression of *SAG* has also been validated in human retinal tissue (PMID: 229466423). Biochemical studies have demonstrated that the SAG-encoded arrestin-1 impacts the activity of the retinal protein rhodopsin (PMID: 24921014, PMID: 39704710).

In summary, *SAG* is Definitively associated with *SAG*-related recessive retinopathy. This association has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of conflicting evidence. This classification has been approved by the ClinGen Retina GCEP on January 15th, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

CEP250 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive cone-rod dystrophy and hearing loss 2 in 2014 (Khateb et al., PMID: 24780881). Affected individuals are reported with retinal dystrophy, including cone-rod dystrophy, and hearing loss. Both features present with varying severity and age of onset. At least 10 nonsense and frameshift variants that have been reported in 6 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 24780881, 29718797, 30459346, 39610034) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence was reached (12 pts.). The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by two knockout mouse models and expression data. One knockout mouse model showed decreasing ERGs with age, increased ABR hearing thresholds, and decreased outer nuclear layer on retinal histology (PMID: 36857066). Another model showed increased ABR threshold at one frequency and OHC degeneration that was more robust in the high frequency region of the basal turn of the cochlea (PMID: 37759551). CEP250 was shown to be expressed in the inner hair cells, outer hair cells, pillar cells, supporting cells and spiral ganglion, and knockout mice showed lack of expression in these structures (PMID: 37759551). Of note, this curation also included one publication reporting autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss; however, it was determined that features of retinal dystrophy could not be fully ruled out and that the association with purely nonsyndromic hearing loss was limited (PMID: 37759551). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CEP250 and autosomal recessive cone-rod dystrophy and hearing loss 2. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hearing Loss GCEP on the meeting date July 16th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *OXCT1* and *OXCT1*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of July 15, 2024. *OXCT1*, also known as *SCOT* (succinyl CoA: 3-oxoacid-CoA transferase), catalyzes the reversible transfer of CoA from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate, the first step of ketone body utilization.  

The *OXCT1* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *OXCT1*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 1996 (PMID: 8751852). *OXCT1* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; Succinyl CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase deficiency [OMIM#245050]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *OXCT1*-related primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included five unique variants (two nonsense, two missense, one splicing) identified in five unrelated cases from five publications (PMIDs: 8751852, 21296660, 34765403, 23281106,  37091464), although there have been at least 44 cases from 39 families reported to date (PMID: 33596448). Affected individuals have episodes of ketoacidosis, often triggered by metabolic stressors, with persistent ketonuria.

This gene-disease association is supported by functional alteration in patient cells (PMID: 11757586, 15669687, 10964512), and by rescue studies performed in patient fibroblasts (PMID: 21296660). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *OXCT1* and autosomal recessive *OXCT1*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 15, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The *MN1* gene is located on chromosome 22 at 22q12.1 and encodes a transcription cofactor, *MN1* proto-oncogene, transcriptional regulator, which is required during later stages of palate development for growth and medial fusion of the palatal shelves. Two disease entities have been reported in association with this gene: craniofacial defects-dysmorphic ears-brain abnormalities-language delay-intellectual disability (CEBALID) and meningioma. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found  distinct differences in phenotype and  in molecular mechanism. Therefore, the two disease entities have been split into two disease entities for curation. This curation addresses *MN1* in association with CEBALID syndrome. 
The *MN1* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant CEBALID syndrome in 2020 (Miyake et al. 2020, PMID: 31839203; Mak et al. 2020, PMID: 31834374). CEBALID syndrome, previously known as *MN1* C-terminal truncation syndrome, is a complex developmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, variably impaired intellectual development, and craniofacial and structural brain abnormalities. Common features include abnormal skull shape, characteristic facial features with midface hypoplasia, hypertelorism, and high-arched palate, and low-set, posteriorly rotated dysplastic ears often associated with conductive or sensorineural deafness. Brain imaging typically shows rhombencephalosynapsis, perisylvian polymicrogyria and cerebellar hypoplasia/dysplasia. 

At least 10 individuals with CEBALID syndrome were identified with 10 unique variants (nonsense, frameshift, whole gene deletion) in the *MN1* gene were scored in this curation (PMIDs: 31839203, 31834374, 33351141, 33351070, 37575653). More evidence is available in the literature, however the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached (PMIDs: 31834374, 34708882, 36124717). Most of the variants occurred de novo and are located in the C-terminal region of the gene that is predicted to escape NMD. Several loss-of-function variants in the N-terminal region that are expected to undergo NMD were also reported with milder phenotypic presentations. The mechanism of pathogenicity is unclear; however, it is suggested that deletion of the C-terminal region enhances *MN1* protein aggregation which leads to disruption of *MN1* target genes. Supporting experimental evidence includes biochemical function, expression data, as well as a mouse model. Mn1 knockout null mice die at or soon after birth with a cleft palate, severe bone abnormalities, with several bones completely absent or hypoplastic (PMID: 15870292). Heterozygous mice had mild defects (hypoplastic membranous bone and incomplete penetrance of the cleft palate) and a normal lifespan. In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *MN1* and CEBALID syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 2nd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *RNU7-1* gene is located on chromosome 12 at 12p13.31 and encodes RNA, U7 small nuclear 1, a noncoding RNA gene. This gene has been shown to have a role in post-transcriptional modification of replication dependent histone pre-mRNA. Binding of *RNU7-1* to the 3 prime UTR of histone pre mRNA prevents polyadenylation and allows careful regulation of histone translation.
*RNU7-1* was first reported in association with Aicardi Goutieres syndrome 9 in 2020 (Uggenti et al., PMID: 33230297) with biallelic variants resulting in neurological regression in affected individuals, as well as CNS imaging consistent with hallmarks of Aicardi Goutieres syndrome. Variants were proposed to be loss of function. However,  all individuals had compound heterozygous variants, with authors proposing one severe and mild allele being causative of disease and homozygosity of a severe allele likely incompatible with life and homozygosity of a mild allele resulting in no disease.  
Evidence supporting this gene disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence (functional alteration in patient and non-patient cells). 12 variants from 20 probands from 15 families across 3 publications are included in this curation (PMID: 33230297, 35320431, 39748568). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical and functional alteration evidence (PMID: 33230297,35320431). It was demonstrated that loss of function of *RNU7-1* results in misprocessing of replication dependent histone RNA transcripts with alteration in expression including reduction of linker histone H1-4. It was subsequently shown that alterations in histone expression resulted in activation of interferon signalling via the cGAS/STING pathway. Analysis of interferon signalling gene expression in patient cells demonstrated a significant increase compared to controls. Lentivirus knockdown of H1-4 in a human monocytic cell line resulted in induction of interferon signalling gene expression (PMID: 33230297). 

This gene-disease relationship was limited on the basis of the calculated classification; however, it was upgraded to moderate by expert panel opinion weighing up all available evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date February 4, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*BICC1* was first reported in relation to incompletely penetrant autosomal-dominant CAKUT (congenital unilateral kidney dysplasia with contralateral renal hyperechogenicity) in 2012 (Kraus et al., PMID: 21922595). In OMIM, the following disease entity has been assigned: Susceptibility to renal dysplasia (OMIM:601331). In contrast to recessive Bicc1-mouse models (jcpk/bpk) and its association with several NPHPs (e.g. ANKS6), no cases of biallelic human *BICC1*-mutations with associated ciliopathies have been reported. Only three putative loss-of-function (LOF) variants (truncating, canonical splice site  and missense with potential splice effect) have been reported in three non-related probands (PMID: 21922595, PMID: 35005812); all of which were included in this curation. However, two of these variants did not segregate and were identified through single gene candidate screening (PMID: 21922595). The third variant, which was found to be de novo, was associated with bilateral renal aganesis (CAKUT) (PMID: 35005812). Another two monoallelic candidate missense variants could not be scored in this curation for lack of functional and genetic evidence (PMID: 28566479). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be LOF or de novo with dysinhibition of Wnt-signaling (PMID: 21922595). This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence (e.g. recessive animal models, expression studies, in vitro functional assays, etc.) (PMID: 12682776, PMID: 20215348, PMID: 29290488). 
In summary, due to the lack of genetic evidence, *BICC1* is only moderately associated with autosomal dominant CAKUT and cystic kidney disease with variable onset and expressivity. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 09/28/22 (SOP Version 8).

*ADAM22* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) in 2016 (Muona 2016, PMID: 27066583). Currently, at least 20 individuals have been reported with *ADAM22*-related DEE. All reported individuals have infantile-onset, treatment-resistant epilepsy (PMID: 35373813). Additional clinical features include moderate to profound global development/intellectual disability, hypotonia, delayed motor development, absent speech, spasticity, and brain MRI findings (PMID: 35373813). 

Six missense, two nonsense, one splicing, one frameshift, and one deletion of exons 3 and 4 that have been reported in thirteen probands in three publications (PMIDs: 27066583, 30237576, and 35373813) are included in this curation. Probands without phasing of the variants were not included in this curation. Functional studies were performed for all variants and supported a loss-of-function disease mechanism (PMIDs: 27066583 and 35373813). This is further supported by a knockout mouse model in which homozygous mice exhibit severe ataxia, convulsions, and die before weaning (PMID: 15876356). Additional evidence is available in the literature beyond what is referenced here; however, the maximum score for genetic and experimental evidence has been reached. 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *ADAM22* and autosomal recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 7, 2026 (SOP version 12).

The relationship between *SPG7* and autosomal recessive *SPG7*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 19, 2026. The *SPG7* gene encodes paraplegin, a mitochondrial inner membrane metalloproteinase that is a component of the m-AAA protease along with AFG3L2. The m-AAA protease is an ATP-dependent proteolytic complex of the mitochondrial inner membrane that degrades misfolded proteins and regulates ribosome assembly. 

The *SPG7* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *SPG7*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 1998 (PMID: 9635427). *SPG7* has been associated with one disease entity to date; spastic paraplegia 7, autosomal recessive [OMIM# 607259], however there have also been reports of an autosomal dominant *SPG7*-related disorder characterized by spasticity, ataxia, and/or optic atrophy (PMIDs: 11222789, 22571692, 39978794, 37983191).  Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, this Expert Panel found a difference in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability among these entities. Therefore, the autosomal recessive disease entity is considered distinct and is curated here. This has been renamed as autosomal recessive *SPG7*-related primary mitochondrial disease. The autosomal dominant disease entity has been split and curated separately. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 11 unique variants (four missense, two frameshift, one initiation codon, three nonsense, one intronic) identified in seven unrelated cases from six publications (PMIDs: 20186691, 24727571, 26260707, 31854126, 35243150, 39978794), although more affected individuals have been reported in the medical literature. Disease onset is typically in adulthood but can occur earlier in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include spasticity, ataxia, myopathy, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and optic atrophy. Multiple mitochondrial DNA deletions are seen in skeletal muscle.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a functional alteration in patient cells (PMIDs: 24466038, 9635427), cell culture model (PMID: 37766787), mouse model (PMIDs: 14722615, 16357941), and *Drosophila melanogaster* model (PMID: 29467464).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *SPG7* and autosomal recessive *SPG7*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 19, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *TBX3* gene is located on chromosome 12 at 12q24.21 and encodes T-box Transcription Factor 3 protein. *TBX3* is a transcription factor characterised by a T-box DNA-binding domain , a nuclear localization signal, two repression domains, and an activation domain. The *TBX3* transcription factor, either activator or repressor, plays a key role in the formation of structures such as the heart, limbs, mammary glands, and lungs during embryogenesis.

*TBX3* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant ulnar-mammary syndrome in 1997 (Bamshad et al 1997, PMID: 9207801). This condition is associated with posterior limb deficiencies or duplications, apocrine/mammary gland hypoplasia and/or dysfunction, abnormal dentition, delayed puberty in males, and genital anomalies. Bamshad et al. (1997) demonstrated variants in *TBX3* in 2 families with ulnar-mammary syndrome. Each variant (frameshift, splice donor site) was predicted to cause haploinsufficiency of *TBX3*, implying that critical levels of this transcription factor are required for morphogenesis of several organs. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level and experimental data. X (give number) heterozygous variants (nonsense, frameshift) in *TBX3* that have been identified in at least 8 unrelated patients with clinical features suggestive of autosomal dominant ulnar-mammary syndrome are included in this curation (Bamshad et al., 1997, PMID: 9207801; Sasaki et al., 2002, PMID: 12116211; Joss et al., 2011. PMID: 21199695; Tanteles et al., 2017, PMID:28145909; Galazzi et al., 2018, PMID:30550377; Wollnik et al., 2002, PMID: 12668170; Meneghini et al., 2005, PMID 16530712; Zhang et al., 2023, PMID: 36937985). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function, gene expression, non-human model systems (mouse) (Khan et al., 2020, PMID: 31669645; Chapman et al., 1996, PMID: 8853987; Gibson-Brown et al., 1996, PMID:8798150; Davenport et al., 2003, PMID: 12668638; Jerome-Majewska et al., 2005, PMID: 16222716; Frank et al., 2013, PMID: 23844108; Emechebe et al., 2016, PMID: 27046536).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *TBX3* and autosomal dominant ulnar-mammary syndrome (*TBX3*-related Ulnar-Mammary syndrome). This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date of April 22nd 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *TRMT1* gene encodes a tRNA methyltransferase involved in post-transcriptional RNA modification. *TRMT1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2011 (Najmabadi et al., PMID: 21937992). Clinical features include global developmental delay, intellectual disability, language deficits, and mild facial dysmorphism. Additional features in a subset of individuals can include behavioral abnormalities, seizures, microcephaly, short stature, gait abnormalities or poor coordination, and cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy. 
 
Eleven variants (4 frameshift, 4 splice site, 2 nonsense and 1 missense) that have been reported in 10 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 21937992, 26308914, 30289604, 31898845, 40245862) are included in this curation. Variants in *TRMT1* segregated with disease in 7 additional family members. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. 
 
This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including biochemical function, a zebrafish model and *in vitro* functional studies. Defects in multiple tRNA methyltransferases (*TRMT10A*, *WDR4*, *FTSJ1*, *ALKBH8*, *NSUN2*, and *NSUN6*) have been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders with overlapping clinical features (PMID: 30415557). *TRMT1* knockout zebrafish have reduced brain and body size, increased locomotor behavior and decreased neuronal cell proliferation (PMID: 40245862). Patient-derived fibroblasts and lymphoblastoid cell lines harbouring bi-allelic *TRMT1* variants demonstrate significantly reduced levels of N2,N2-dimethylguanosine (m2,2G) in tRNA (PMID: 40245862). 
 
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *TRMT1* and autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on March 4, 2026 (SOP version 12).

disease_title: palatal anomalies-widely spaced teeth-facial dysmorphism-developmental delay syndrome
disease_original_title: palatal anomalies-widely spaced teeth-facial dysmorphism-developmental delay syndrome
submitted_as_notes:
*KDM1A* is located on chromosome 1p36.12 and encodes lysine demethylase 1A protein. This protein is part of several histone deacetylase complexes, where it is involved in repressing expression of genes via histone demethylation. Variants in *KDM1A* have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: palatal anomalies-widely spaced teeth-facial dysmorphism-developmental delay syndrome (OMIM: 616728) and ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (OMIM: 620990). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found key differences in phenotype and a distinct molecular mechanism. Therefore, the two disease entities have been split. The split curation for autosomal dominant ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia will be curated separately. 

*KDM1A* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant palatal anomalies-widely spaced teeth-facial dysmorphism-developmental delay syndrome in 2014 (Tunovic et al., PMID: 24838796). This condition is associated with global developmental delay, brain anomalies (such as delayed myelination and thin corpus callosum), facial anomalies (including ptosis and posteriorly-rotated ears), digit anomalies, vision issues, and short stature. Thirteen variants (missense, nonsense) that have been reported in at least 13 probands in three publications (PMIDs: 24838796, 26656649, 40530541), and in ClinVar (SCV000803417.1, SCV002558982.1, SCV002304455.4, SCV002552609.2, SCV002526560.2, SCV000620108.2, SCV002003366.2, SCV005874571.1, SCV005439830.1) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse model, expression-level data, and biochemical functional evidence. Mouse model evidence demonstrates that *KDM1A* has a role in seizure susceptibility, status epilepticus, and fatality in response to pilocarpine treatment (PMID: 24735673). This gene is shown to be expressed in human neurons and control neuronal differentiation through H3K9 methylation (PMID: 25684206). Functional evidence indicates that knockdown of an isoform in neurons results in altered demethylation and inhibits neuronal differentiation. 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *KDM1A* and autosomal dominant palatal anomalies-widely spaced teeth-facial dysmorphism-developmental delay syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 10/28/2025 (SOP Version 11).

PAX5 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant PAX5-related leukemia predisposition in 2013 (Shah et al., PMID: 24013638). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, PAX5-related B lymphopenia and autism spectrum disorder, neurodevelopmental disorders/autism spectrum disorder and PAX5-related B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia predisposition. The split curation for autosomal recessive PAX5-related B lymphopenia and autism spectrum disorder has been curated separately by the antibody Deficiencies GCEP. The neurodevelopmental disorders/autism spectrum disorder assertion might be curated separately by another ClinGen GCEP. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. Nine variants (missense, frameshift, large deletion, splice variant) that have been reported in 30 probands in 10 publications (PMIDs: 24013638, 24287434, 35902733, 33036026, 26782422, 38571503, 37543654, 26115422, 39256601) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached (PMID: 29847298).  This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including animal models, expression studies and biochemical evidence studies (PMIDs: 30643249, 17851532, 17600970, 17658281). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between PAX5 and B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia predisposition. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date May 13, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection
disease_original_title: familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection
submitted_as_notes:
*MAT2A* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant familial thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (FTAAD) in 2015 (Guo DC *et al.*, 2015, PMID: 25557781).  Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. At least two missense variants have been reported in humans.This curation includes *MAT2A* variant c.1031A>C (p.Glu344Ala), which has been reported in a proband with thoracic aortic aneurysm and shown to segregate with disease in three additional family members (PMID: 25557781).

This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental data in the form of expression studies and in model systems. *MAT2A* expression in the aorta has been confirmed in humans and in two animal models (PMID: 23715323, 25557781, 39216871). Downregulation of *MAT2A* has been associated with aortic arch defects in zebrafish, increased aortic diameters in mice, reduced viability of vascular smooth muscle cells due to increased apoptosis (PMID: 25557781, 39216871).

This gene-disease pair was originally evaluated by the Heritable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection GCEP on July 3, 2016. It was reevaluated on December 5, 2025. As a result of this reevaluation, the classification did not change. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection subgroup of the Hereditary Cardiovascular Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date December 5, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

SCN3B encodes the sodium channel β-subunit 3 (known as Navβ3). SCN3B was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome in 2009 (Hu et al., PMID: 20031595). Navβ3 variants have been suggested to cause cardiac disease by modulating the trafficking of Nav1.5 to the cell membrane or by affecting the function of the Nav1.5 channel (PMID: 20031595, 23257389, 38450374, 20042427, 39761910).

Homozygous knockout mouse models implicate SCN3B in cardiac disease, with reports of electrophysiological abnormalities including shorter ventricular effective refractory periods and increased susceptibility to ventricular tachycardia following programmed electrical stimulation (PMID: 19351516). Evidence of perturbed atrial function with increased susceptibility to atrial tachycardia and fibrillation following atrial burst pacing has also been reported (PMID: 19796257). Immunoprecipitation experiments also show that Navβ3 interacts with Nav1.5 (PMID: 20042427, 39761910).

However, there is significant evidence suggesting that SCN3B variants are not a monogenic cause of autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome. This contradictory evidence includes evidence that some of the reported variants have high allele frequencies (PMID: 20031595, 23257389) and the fact that SCN3B also has very low mRNA expression in the heart (left ventricle TPM = ~0.5, GTEx), with SCN5A exhibiting much higher expression (left ventricle TPM = ~36, GTEx). Further, most of the functional work performed to assess SCN3B variants as having an impact on sodium current has been performed by co-expressing Navβ3 variants with Nav1.5 in cell models (PMIDs: 20031595, 23257389, 26179811, 39761910, 38450374, 21051419, 34867379). Given that SCN3B has low mRNA abundance within cardiac tissue, these models may overestimate the physiological effects of SCN3B variants on Nav1.5 function. SCN3B homozygous loss-of-function has also been reported in two consanguineous families with a neurodevelopmental disorder with no cardiovascular phenotype being reported in either heterozygous or homozygous carriers of truncating variants (PMID: 40879121). While homozygous knockout mouse models report evidence of perturbed electrophysiological function (PMIDs: 19351516, 19796257), these animal studies model a more severe genetic defect than the heterozygous missense variants reported in the literature. Finally, burden testing has failed to identify any statistically significant enrichment of SCN3B variants in patients with Brugada syndrome relative to controls (PMIDs: 25650408, 26220970).

The relationship between SCN3B and autosomal dominant Brugada syndrome was originally evaluated by the ClinGen Brugada Syndrome Gene Curation Expert Panel in 2017 and was classified as disputed. This gene-disease pair was re-evaluated by the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on 25 November, 2025. Following re-evaluation and the consideration of new evidence, the gene-disease classification was changed to refuted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disorders GCEP on 25 November, 2025 (in accordance with SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *SUCLA2* and *SUCLA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of June 17, 2024. The *SUCLA2* gene encodes succinate-CoA ligase ADP-forming subunit beta, an ATP-specific succinyl-CoA synthetase that functions in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle to catalyze the reversible synthesis of succinate and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). It is also thought to have a role in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance, possibly by stabilizing the nucleoside diphosphate kinase.

The *SUCLA2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *SUCLA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2005 (PMID: 10545952). *SUCLA2* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 5 (encephalomyopathic with or without methylmalonic aciduria) [OMIM# 612073]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *SUCLA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *SUCLA2* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on February 11, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Definitive. This current curation for the association with *SUCLA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 10 unique variants (seven missense, one complex rearrangement, one frameshift, and one splice site, c.534+1G>A, that is a founder variant in Faroe Islands, Denmark) identified in 10 unrelated cases from nine publications (PMIDs: 17301081, 23010432, 23759946, 27913098, 26475597, 25582465, 15877282, 26952923, 17287286). Disease onset is early in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, developmental delay and regression, encephalopathy, myopathy, choreoathetosis, dystonia, seizures, ptosis, sensorineural hearing loss, feeding difficulty, failure to thrive, and elevated lactate and methylmalonic acid.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 23385875), functional alteration in non-patient cells (PMID: 28769029), and non-human animal models (PMID: 24271779).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *SUCLA2* and autosomal recessive *SUCLA2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 17, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The relationship between *NDUFAF8* and *NDUFAF8*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 4, 2024. The *NDUFAF8* gene encodes NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) assembly factor 8.

The *NDUFAF8* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *NDUFAF8*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2020 (PMID: 31866046). *NDUFAF8* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 34 [OMIM# 618776]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *NDUFAF8*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *NDUFAF8* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on January 13, 2020 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Moderate. This current curation for the association with *NDUFAF8*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included four unique variants (one missense, one frameshift, one initiation codon, one intronic) identified in three unrelated cases from one publication (PMID: 31866046). Disease onset is early in life. Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, developmental delay and regression, seizures, feeding difficulty, optic atrophy, hypertensive crises, respiratory failure, intrauterine growth restriction, metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate. Complex I deficiency was noted in skeletal muscle and skin fibroblasts from affected individuals.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 31866046), functional alteration in patient cells (PMID: 31866046), functional alteration in non-patient cells (PMID: 27499296), rescue in patient cells (PMID: 31866046), and rescue in non-patient cells (PMID: 27499296). 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *NDUFAF8* and autosomal recessive *NDUFAF8*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 4, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *COX5A* and *COX5A*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 26, 2024. The *COX5A* gene encodes the cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) subunit 5A.

The *COX5A* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *COX5A*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2017 (PMID: 28247525). *COX5A* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 20 [OMIM# 619064]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *COX5A*-related primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two homozygous missense variants identified in two unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 28247525, 35246835). The first reported case had early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, developmental delay, failure to thrive, and isolated complex IV deficiency in skin fibroblasts. Dysmorphic features were also present (frontal bossing, synophrys, deep-set eyes, long eyelashes, short extremities, and short hands and feet).  There was a similarly affected sibling. The second case had failure to thrive, short stature, ovarian insufficiency, hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, metabolic acidosis, cortical atrophy, and complex IV deficiency in skin fibroblasts.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), mouse model (PMID: 37373547), and zebrafish model (PMID: 17761683).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *COX5A* and autosomal recessive *COX5A*-related primary mitochondrial disease. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 26, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

Spectrin repeat-containing nuclear envelope protein 1 (*SYNE1*:protein name nesprin) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive arthrogryposis multiplex congenita in 2009 (Attali et al., PMID: 19542096). Features of *SYNE1*-related arthrogryposis can include but are not limited to: decreased fetal movement, congenital contractures, hypotonia, kyphoscoliosis and or respiratory difficulty. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found a difference in the molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive 8 (OMIM: 610743) and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita 3, myogenic type (OMIM: 618484). This split is based on the observation that the arthrogryposis entity is entirely associated with biallelic loss of function variants that would affect the nesprin-1-alpha isoform. The split curation for autosomal recessive *SYNE1*-related spinocerebellar ataxia has been curated separately. 5 variants (3 nonsense and 2 truncating) that have been reported in 5 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 19542096, 24319099, 27782104, 35739559, 30626539) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model and an expression study showing expresion of the nesprin-1-alpha isoform is nearly entirely unique to skeletal muscle and cardiac tissue (PMIDs: 19008300, 24718612). No cerebellar features have been noted in the probands in the literature to date however the variants in this curation would also lead to loss of function in the large nesprin isoform which has been associated with the *SYNE1*-related spinocerebellar ataxia entity. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataxia GCEP on the meeting date December 10, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *ATP5MC3* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 9, 2026. The *ATP5MC3* gene encodes ATP synthase F(0) complex subunit C3, a component of ATP synthase (oxidative phosphorylation complex V).

The *ATP5MC3* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant primary mitochondrial disease in 2023 (PMID: 34636445), although the locus was first detected in a linkage study in 2009 (PMD: 19006192). *ATP5MC3* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; dystonia, early-onset, and/or spastic paraplegia [OMIM# 619681]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included three unique missense variants identified in four unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 34636445, 34954817). Clinical features in affected individuals include dystonia, spasticity, and developmental delay. Complex V activity was decreased in cultured skin fibroblasts.

The mechanism of disease is unclear. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and a *Drosophila melanogaster* model (PMID: 34636445).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel February 9, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The gene SLC6A5 was first implicated in autosomal recessive hyperekplexia 3 in 2006 (Rees et al., PMID: 16751771). SLC6A5 encodes the glycine transporter GlyT2, which is predominantly expressed in presynaptic axons within the brainstem, spinal cord, and, to a lesser extent, the cerebellum. GlyT2 plays an essential role in clearing glycine from the synaptic cleft, thereby terminating glycinergic neurotransmission. This process is critical for maintaining inhibitory signaling in the central nervous system.
Hyperekplexia 3 (OMIM #614618) is a rare neonatal-onset disorder characterized by exaggerated startle responses to unexpected sensory stimuli, muscle stiffness, hypertonia, cyanosis, and apnea, which can be life-threatening in early infancy. Symptoms may improve with age.
The gene–disease relationship is supported by genetic evidence from 23 unrelated probands reported across eight publications. This curation includes 28 SLC6A5 variants associated with autosomal recessive inheritance, including missense, nonsense, splicing, frameshift, and in‑frame deletion variants (PMIDs: 16751771, 22700964, 31370103, 16884688, 34266921, 31604777, 35841715, 40725001). Case‑level evidence strongly supports the association and exceeds the maximum score of 12 points.
Experimental data further substantiate the gene–disease relationship. Expression studies confirmed high GlyT2 expression in the brainstem and spinal cord, with lower expression in the cerebellum consistent with the clinical neurological features (PMID: 9845349). Biochemical studies established that GlyT2 is a sodium‑ and chloride‑dependent transporter required for regulating glycine levels at inhibitory synapses (PMIDs: 9845349, 14622583). SLC6A5-null mice reproduce key aspects of the human phenotype, including muscle stiffness, spasticity, rigid tone, and prolonged righting times, particularly after handling (PMIDs: 14622583, 22272310).In vitro studies of patient‑derived variants demonstrate reduced glycine transport activity due to impaired membrane localization and decreased protein expression, increased levels of immature protein and ubiquitination‑mediated degradation, and disrupted glycine or sodium binding that alters voltage-dependent responses (PMIDs: 16751771, 22700964, 31370103, 40725001).
Notably, the S510R variant has been reported in the heterozygous state without a second SLC6A5 variant in one proband and his reportedly affected parent. Functional studies suggested reduced glycine transporter activity mediated by a dominant-negative mechanism (PMID: 16751771). However, given the limited supporting evidence and the possibility of undetected 2nd variant, the association between SLC6A5 and autosomal dominant hyperekplexia 3 is not currently curated.
In summary, there is Definitive evidence supporting the association between SLC6A5 and autosomal recessive hyperekplexia 3, based on robust genetic and experimental findings that have been consistently replicated and upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP on February 27, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The Male Infertility GCEP’s preferred term for this curation is “macrozoospermia with multiflagellar polyploid spermatozoa,” which is an exact synonym for “spermatogenic failure 5" (MONDO:0009461). 

*AURKC* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive macrozoospermia with multiflagellar polyploid spermatozoa in 2007 (Dieterich et al., PMID: 17435757). Macrozoospermia is a severe male infertility disorder characterized by large-headed, often multiflagellated spermatozoa with abnormal chromosomal content. Over 100 affected individuals have been reported in the literature carrying biallelic *AURKC* variants. The majority of reported cases harbor a recurrent frameshift variant, NM_001015878.2(AURKC):c.145del (p.Leu49TrpfsTer23), particularly in individuals of North African origin. Three variants (e.g. frameshift, nonsense, and splice site) that have been reported in fifteen probands in three publications (PMIDs: 17435757, 25755131, 21733974) are included in this curation.  In all reported cases, affected men carry biallelic variants, while fertile parents are heterozygous carriers, consistent with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is believed to be biallelic loss of function. This gene disease relationship is also supported by expression and protein localization studies, in vitro functional assays, and a mouse knockout model demonstrating impaired spermatogenesis and abnormal sperm morphology (PMIDs: 38577799, 16386730, 17192404). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *AURKC* and autosomal recessive macrozoospermia with multiflagellar polyploid spermatozoa. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.
