This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on January 7, 2026 (SOP v11).

The relationship between *TARS2* and *TARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of December 16, 2024. The *TARS2* gene encodes mitochondrial threonyl-tRNA synthetase 2, one of the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which function in mitochondrial translation by catalyzing the attachment of amino acids to their cognate tRNAs. Defects in tRNA charging can result in impaired synthesis of protein subunits of oxidative phosphorylation complexes I, III, IV, and V. 

The *TARS2* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *TARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease in 2014 (PMID: 24827421). *TARS2* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 21 [OMIM# 615918]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and has been renamed as *TARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *TARS2* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on May 24, 2021 (SOP v7), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with *TARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included 11 unique variants (nine missense, one nonsense, one intronic) identified in seven unrelated cases from three publications (PMIDs: 24827421, 33153448, 34508595), although at least 24 probands have been reported to date (see PMID: 37454282 for report of a large cohort with literature review). Age of onset is typically in the first year of life and outcomes vary from death early in life to living in the third decade. The most common reported clinical features include severe developmental delay, regression, limb hypertonia, and seizures. More rare features include renal tubular acidosis, hearing loss, hepatic steatosis, and cardiomyopathy. Muscle biopsies show variable respiratory chain enzyme deficiencies. Brain imaging shows cerebellar atrophy and/or basal ganglia involvement. Blood lactate is elevated.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), functional alteration studies in patient cells (PMID: 24827421), and a zebrafish model (PMID: 37454282).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *TARS2* and autosomal recessive *TARS2*-related primary mitochondrial disease. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 16, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The *KCNJ13* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant cases of snowflake vitreoretinal degeneration in 2008 (Hejtmancik et al., PMID: 18179896). Affected individuals have a phenotypic spectrum that includes snowflake-like retinal deposits, focal retinal pigment epithelium degeneration, reduced macular function, reduced scotopic b-wave, corneal guttae, early onset cataracts, moderate myopia, dysmorphic optic discs, and/or increased risk of retinal detachment, with onset generally in the second decade of life or later. *KCNJ13* variants have separately been reported in relation to autosomal recessive Leber congenital amaurosis in 2011 (Sergouniotis et al., PMID: 21763485). Some features overlapped with the dominant cases, including early onset cataracts and moderate myopia, however, onset ranged from birth to early adulthood and distinguishing features included severely decreased electroretinogram responses from both rods and cones, severe decrease in central visual acuity and constriction of peripheral visual field, nyctalopia, nystagmus, fibrosis over the optic discs, and abnormalities of the retinal vasculature such as retinal arteriolar constriction, retinal neovascularization, and/or vitreous hemorrhage. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, cases of snowflake vitreoretinal degeneration were found to be distinguishable by both their molecular mechanism (a monoallelic missense variant p.Arg162Trp resulting in nonselective cation current causing cell depolarization) and mode of inheritance (autosomal dominant), in comparison to the biallelic loss-of-function mechanism of autosomal recessive Leber congenital amaurosis 16. While the two conditions share some overlapping phenotypic features, heterozygous carriers from recessive families have so far been found to be unaffected (PMID: 21763485, PMID: 35477418). Therefore, *KCNJ13*-related vitreoretinopathy and *KCNJ13*-related recessive retinopathy are considered two disease entities and curated separately.

This curation has scored one suspected disease-causing variant (the missense variant p.Arg162Trp), which was reported in three different probands in three publications (PMID: 18179896, PMID: 36440807, PMID: 35477418). All probands were heterozygous, with two known to have affected family members sharing the same genotype (PMID: 18179896, PMID: 35477418). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be dominant negative, with the missense variant resulting in nonselective cation current causing cell depolarization (PMID: 18179896, PMID: 23255580, PMID: 23977131, PMID: 33219695). Two publications contained families with multiple affected family members and were evaluated for segregation evidence (PMID: 18179896, PMID: 35477418).

This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence that *KCNJ13* is highly expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and to a lesser degree in retina and small intestine (PMID: 30239781). *KCNJ13* encodes a potassium channel (also known as Kir7.1) that localizes to long apical membrane extensions or microvilli of RPE cells (PMID: 28878288) and allows intracellular potassium ions to flow out into the subretinal space to maintain normal potassium levels during photoreception (PMID: 23255580). Functional studies exogenously expressing the p.Arg162Trp variant in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells, HEK293T cells,  or *Xenopus* oocytes have shown that the variant has localizes to the cell surface normally and interacts with the wild-type protein, but causes reduced channel activity, including when co-expressed with the wild-type protein (PMID: 23255580, PMID: 23977131, PMID: 33219695). The variant may disrupt part of a phosphoinositide binding site that is essential for stabilizing the open state of KCNJ13 (PMID: 33219695).

In summary, *KCNJ13* has Moderate evidence of association with *KCNJ13*-related vitreoretinopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, however, additional case-level evidence will be required to reach a more definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 3rd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*AIPL1* variants were first reported in relation to retinal disease in 2000 (Sohocki et al., PMID: 10873396). While *AIPL1* has been definitively associated with autosomal recessive retinopathy by the ClinGen Retinal Gene Curation Expert Panel, the single variant asserted to be associated with autosomal dominant inheritance was excluded from that curation. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the reported autosomal dominant cases were found to differ from the more established autosomal recessive cases in their mode of inheritance but to overlap in phenotype. The decision was made to split and curate them separately, with the recessive cases curated under AIPL1-related autosomal recessive retinopathy, and the asserted dominant cases evaluated in the present curation for inherited retinal dystrophy with autosomal dominant inheritance. 

The single variant that has been asserted to show autosomal dominant inheritance is an in-frame deletion, AIPL1:c.1053_1064del (p.Ala352_Pro355del). This variant is present at a frequency in gnomAD v4.1.0 that is inconsistent with a role as a primary cause of dominant disease, with over 1000 heterozygotes and 3 homozygotes. To date, *in vitro* functional studies have not supported a role for the in-frame deletion in subcellular localization or protein binding (PMID: 33067476). A transgenic mouse model expressing primate AIPL1 c.1053_1064del has been generated and the mice demonstrate retinal degeneration (PMID: 25274777). However, no additional evidence has been presented to support pathogenicity of heterozygous variants in AIPL1. While a number of other *AIPL1* variants have been identified in the heterozygous state in individuals with retinal disease, evidence for pathogenicity of these variants was not supportive of their role in disease (PMID: 3067476). In

In summary, preliminary evidence is sufficient to classify the association between *AIPL1* and autosomal dominant inherited retinal dystrophy as Disputed. Additional studies are needed either to support the association of heterozygous AIPL1 variants with retinal disease, or to refute the causality of these variants in the reported cases. This classification has been approved by the ClinGen Retina GCEP on April 3rd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *CEP89* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of July 29, 2024. The *CEP89* gene encodes centrosomal protein of 89 kDA. This protein is reported to be required for ciliogenesis, and also may play a role in mitochondrial metabolism modulating complex IV activity.

This gene has been reported in association with multisystem clinical features in the medical literature (PMID: 23575228). The proband had bilateral cataracts, hearing loss, feeding problems, developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, elevated serum lactate, and cystinuria. Complex IV deficiency was noted in muscle (22% of controls). The proband had a homozygous deletion that included two genes, *SLC7A9* (associated with cystinuria) and exons 15–19 of *CEP89*. The authors postulated that the *CEP89* deletion was causative of the features not explained by cystinuria. However, this Expert Panel elected not to include this case in this curation given the size of the deletion and because other genetic etiologies were not fully excluded.

Experimental evidence supporting the gene-disease relationship include expression data showing CEP89 is present in the mitochondrial intermembrane space (PMID: 23575228) and a *Drosophila melanogaster* model that showed growth defect when knocked down in the wing, lethality when knocked down in muscle, and disturbed structural integrity of the ommatidia when knocked down in the eye. Complex IV deficiency was noted in pupae from the strongest knockdown condition (PMID: 23575228).

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *CEP89* and primary mitochondrial disease has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role this gene plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 29, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

MASP1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive 3MC syndrome in 2010 (Sirmaci et al., PMID: 21035106). 3MC syndrome encompasses four rare disorders that were previously referred to as the Mingarelli, Malpuech, Michels, and Carnevale syndromes. The main features of these syndromes are facial dysmorphisms that include hypertelorism, blepharophimosis, blepharoptosis, and highly arched eyebrows. Cleft lip and palate, postnatal growth deficiency, cognitive impairment, and hearing loss are also consistently seen in patients with these syndromes. 13 variants (missense, nonsense, and splice site) that have been reported in 17 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 21035106, 21258343, 26419238, 26789649) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by an animal model that recapitulated phenotypes seen in humans with 3MC syndrome, and a protein interaction study describing the interaction between MASP1 and COLEC11 (PMIDs: 21258343, 21258343). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between MASP1 and autosomal recessive 3MC syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date January 15, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *IFT57* gene is located on chromosome 3 at 3.q13.12-q13.13 and encodes the Intraflagellar Transport Protein 57 (*IFT57*). This protein is essential for cilia assembly and function and plays a crucial role in intraflagellar transport. *IFT57* is part of a complex that connects IFTB to the motor protein kinesin 11. IFTB initiates the polymerisation process and IFTA then joins to complete the train. *IFT57* is also implicated in apoptosis and signalling pathways including the sonic hedgehog pathway. *IFT57* is expressed at high levels in the lung and testis, and at low levels in the kidney cortex and medulla, where it is found mainly in the proximal tubule.  

*IFT57* has only been reported associated with Orofaciodigital syndrome XVIII (OMIM:617927), which has autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance, and is considered an overlap of Orofaciodigital syndrome and Ellis-van Creveld syndrome. This disorder has variable if any kidney involvement but was included in this GCEP’s assessment because it is a ciliopathy.The GCEP-preferred disease name suggested for this disorder is ? Orofaciodigital syndrome XVIII (OMIM:617927) or Ciliopathy-*IFT57*. 

*IFT57* was first reported in relation to AR Orofaciodigital syndrome XVIII in 2016 (Thevenon et al, PMID: 27060890). The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported as Loss of Function. Clinical features include mainly facial, oral and digital anomalies. Short stature, limb shortening, congenital cardiac anomalies, retinal disease, midline high arched palate, cleft palate, cleft or lobulated tongue, cleft lip, dysplastic nails and teeth, oral frenulae, polydactyly and genu valgum may be present. Hearing, speech and intellect are normal. Kidney and urinary tract abnormalities are very variable, with urinary incontinence in one person, a short urethra in another person, increased urinary albuminuria (associated with diabetes)  and normal kidney imaging. 

At least three variants (a homozygous splicing variant in 2 offspring of a consanguineous Indian family; and a compound heterozygous variant in an Irish male with a missense and a frameshift change)  have been reported in three probands in two publications (PMID:27060890; PMID:40273360) that are included in this curation. Additional genetic evidence for the homozygous splicing variant was the functional impact of this variant on ciliary transport, with low *IFT57* staining mainly in the ciliary bases compared with controls; the same number of cilia but decreased ciliary tip staining; reduced anterograde transport in the subject’s fibroblasts; and reduced GLI1 transcription activation secondary to less sonic Hedgehog signalling pathway in patient fibroblasts compared with healthy controls. The compound heterozygous variants when expressed in fibroblasts had fewer ciliated cells and more abnormal cilia than controls.  A total of 4.6 points for genetic evidence was reached. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression (PMID:27060890), interaction with IFT172 (PMID:40273360) and functional alteration where an *IFT57* variant resulted in decreased ciliary anterograde transport in a patient-derived fibroblast cell line (PMID: 207060890). The cell culture system demonstrated that *IFT57* Val397Glu resulted in reduced binding of *IFT57*, *IFT172* and *IFT88* to the IFTB complex that impaired anterograde transport (PMID: 40273360). Partial rescue occurred with the administration of expression vectors with the ift57Val397Glu variant to a mouse ift57 gene knockout cell line (derived from mouse medullary collecting duct cells, PMID:40273360). This was in contrast with rescue with the ift57 wildtype (PMID:40273360). A total of 4 pts for experimental evidence was reached.

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *IFT57* and AROrofaciodigital syndrome. This has been demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy GCEP on the meeting date 11 August 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Variants in *BGN* have been reported in individuals with X-linked Meester-Loeys syndrome (MLS), X-linked familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (TAAD), and X-linked spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMDX). Given differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypes between TAAD/MLS and SEMDX, a split curation for SEMDX will be curated separately by the Skeletal Disorders GCEP in the future. Missense variants not affecting splicing have mainly been associated with SEMDX, whereas loss-of-function variants have been associated with TAAD/MLS. This current curation will be for the lumped disease entity of *BGN*-related syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection.

*BGN* was first reported in relation to aortic disease in mice in 2007 (PMID: 17502576) and in humans with X-linked syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections in 2017 (PMID: 27632686). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. Eight variants reported in eight probands from two publications are included in this curation (PMIDs: 27632686, 38531898). Variants included nonsense, frameshift, deletions, and splicing variants. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. In humans, Meester *et al.* (2017) described five families with loss-of-function variants in *BGN* who had an X-linked severe syndromic form of thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections, including features such as joint hypermobility, hypertelorism, malar hypoplasia, joint contractures, and reduced bone density (PMID: 27632686). Two male probands with very early onset aortic disease and mild skeletal dysplasia had *BGN* deletions spanning exons 2-8 that extended into the 5’ untranslated region of the *ATP2B3* gene, resulting in use of the *BGN* 5’-UTR to drive *ATP2B3* expression in skin fibroblasts (PMID: 38531898). *ATP2B3* has been associated with X-linked cerebellar ataxia and is not expressed in control skin fibroblasts. These two probands were not scored for this curation due to extragenic involvement.

In 2024, Meester *et al.* described an additional 13 probands and their relatives, and showed that *BGN* variants have reduced penetrance and variable expressivity. Some individuals had only subtle syndromic features or presented with aortic disease as late as 70 years old (PMID: 38531898). In addition to previous features described, some individuals also had peripheral or cerebral arterial aneurysms or dissections. In line with X-linked inheritance, disease was more penetrant in hemizygous males compared to heterozygous females. This study also showed loss of biglycan protein expression on western blot from skin fibroblasts of multiple individuals with the described *BGN* variants. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function, although one missense variant of uncertain significance was reported in a family with arterial aneurysms, joint hypermobility, and musculoskeletal injuries/pain (PMID: 41465473). 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and expression studies. Using immunohistochemistry and immunoelectron microscopy, Heegaard *et al.* (2007) showed that biglycan is detected in the aortic walls of wildtype mice, with the adventitia being the major site of biglycan deposition (PMID: 17502576). In *BGN*-knockout male mice, necrocopies following sudden death revealed major hemorrhage in the thoracic (82%) or abdominal (18%) cavity. Histology showed aortic rupture involving intimal and medial tears and dissection between media and adventitia (PMID: 17502576). In another study in *BGN*-knockout mice, radiographic, microradiographic, and histological analyses showed that the epiphyseal and metaphyseal trabecular structures in the femora, tibiae, and vertebrae of 6 month old mice were thinner, fewer, and poorly connected to each other compared to wild type. In addition, bone volume/total tissue volume was reduced to below 50% of wildtype. Total ash weight (mineral content) was also reduced in mutant long bones. These findings supported that disruption of *BGN* leads to an osteoporosis-like phenotype in mice (PMID: 9731537). 
Additionally, stained aortic tissue from two individuals with loss-of-function *BGN* variants showed increased phosphorylated SMAD2 positive nuclei (a specific marker of activated canonical TGF-β signaling) compared to controls, and was similar to aortic tissue from a proband with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (PMID: 27632686). Increased pSMAD2 and TGF-β signaling has also been observed in aortic tissue affected by thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, Marfan syndrome, and Loeys-Dietz syndrome (PMIDs: 18852674, 21493862, 29682117, 30037098).

This gene-disease pair was originally evaluated by the Heritable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 22, 2016. It was reevaluated on February 6, 2026. As a result of this reevaluation, the classification changed from Limited to Strong with the addition of new case-level and experimental evidence as described above. In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between *BGN* and X-linked syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Heritable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection subgroup of the Hereditary Cardiovascular Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date February 6, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *ATP5F1E* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of February 9, 2026. The *ATP5F1E* gene encodes the ATP synthase F(1) subunit epsilon, a subunit of oxidative phosphorylation complex V.

The *ATP5F1E* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease in 2010 (PMID: 20566710). *ATP5F1E* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency, nuclear type 3 [OMIM# 614053]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense variant identified in three unrelated cases from two publications (PMIDs: 20566710, 34954817). Affected individuals had neonatal lactic acidosis, myopathy, neuropathy, developmental delay, seizures, left ventricular hypertrophy, hearing loss, and cataracts. Complex V activity was decreased in fibroblasts.

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel February 9, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: SOX11-related complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies
disease_original_title: SOX11-related complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies
submitted_as_notes:
*SOX11* encodes a transcription factor that acts as a transcriptional activator. *SOX11* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant SOX11-related complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies in 2014 (Tsurusaki et al., PMID: 24886874). The disorder is characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, low body weight, and dysmorphic features. Patients may also have ocular malformations, ocular apraxia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, structural brain malformations, renal malformations, or autism. Although initially reported as a form of Coffin-Siris syndrome, individuals with *SOX11* syndrome exhibit a distinctive pattern of blood DNA methylation that differentiates it from other BAFopathies (PMID: 35341651).

Fourteen *de novo* variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) that have been reported in 14 probands in three publications (PMIDs: 24886874, 26543203, 35341651) are included in this curation. The majority of reported pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants are missense variants, located within or next to the high mobility group (HMG) box, a common motif in all SOX proteins that activate target genes via DNA binding. Therefore, the HMG box could be classified as a variant hotspot, further supported by several recurrent variants found in this domain. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function. Variants in multiple genes of the SRY-related (SOX) transcription factor family are associated with developmental disorders termed SOXopathies; examples of SOX genes involved in syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders include *SOX2*, *SOX3*, *SOX4*, *SOX5*, *SOX6*, and *SOX10*.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *SOX11* and autosomal dominant SOX11-related complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 20, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

POT1 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant familial melanoma in 2014 (Robles-Espinoza et al., PMID: 24686849). POT1 was also reported in relation to Coats plus (Takai et al., PMID: 27013236) and pulmonary fibrosis (Kelich et al., PMID: 35420632). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found a difference in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities: cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 3 (OMIM:620368), pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure syndrome, telomere-related, 8 (OMIM:620367), and tumor predisposition syndrome 3 (OMIM:615848). The split curations for autosomal recessive cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts and autosomal dominant pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure syndrome, telomere-related, have been curated separately. In total, 6 missense variants, 2 splicing variants, and 4 frameshift variants that have been reported in 21 probands in 7 publications (PMIDs: 38540414, 34769003, 32907878, 24686849, 38839987, 33050356, and 39156708) are included in this curation for POT1-related tumor predisposition syndrome (OMIM:615848). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a non-human model organism (PMID: 27869160) in which mice receiving a transplant of cells with POT1 variants develop DNA damage foci and dysplastic hematopoietic cells. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between POT1 and autosomal dominant POT1-related tumor predisposition syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Children, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date September 9, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *SALL1* gene is located on chromosome 16 at 16q12.1 and codes for the Spalt-Like 1 protein. *SALL1* includes 3 different DNA-binding zinc finger domains and alanine- and glutamine-rich regions that are frequently seen in transcription factors. The protein is a transcriptional repressor and is suspected to be a component of the NuRD histone deacetylase complex. 

*SALL1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Townes-Brocks Syndrome (TBS) in 1998 (Kohlhase et al., PMID: 9425907). The most common features of this condition include imperforate anus/anal stenosis, dysplastic ears, hearing loss, limb anomalies, digit anomalies, and renal features. The hearing loss is bilateral and mild-to-profound, and either conductive, sensorineural, or both. Auricular anomalies include overfolded helices and preauricular skin tags (9973281, 16088922, 17221874, 37644569, 38915054, 40348827). 13 variants (nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in at least 13 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 9973281, 16088922, 37644569, 39910415) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be either haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse models; expression-level evidence). Mouse models indicate that mutant mice have features including reduced body size, decreased kidney weight, other kidney anomalies, limb/digit anomalies, reduced cell proliferation, and exencephaly (PMIDs: 12915476, 26311113). Evidence in mice shows expression in the renal tubular epithelium (PMID: 26311113). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *SALL1* and autosomal dominant TBS. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date March 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*DPY19L2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive male infertility due to globozoospermia in 2011 (Koscinski et al., PMID: 21397063). Globozoospermia is characterized by round headed sperm lacking an acrosome, resulting in isolated male infertility without additional systemic or syndromic features. 

Eight variants (e.g. missense, deletion, nonsense, frameshift, splice site) that have been reported in twelve probands in four publications (PMIDs: 21397063, 21397064, 22653751, 33108537) are included in this curation. To date, more than 70 unrelated affected men have been reported with biallelic pathogenic variants in *DPY19L2* across multiple independent cohorts and populations (PMIDs: 21397063, 21397064, 22186015, 22653751, 33108537). Most cases (around 70-80%) carry a recurrent non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) mediated whole gene deletion, while remaining individuals have compound heterozygous or homozygous loss of function alleles, including nonsense, frameshift, splice site, exonic deletions, and rare pathogenic missense variants affecting conserved residues. No heterozygous carriers have been reported with infertility. Pathogenic variants are also absent or rare in gnomAD version 4.1.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function, supported by the variant spectrum, population constraint data, and consistent phenotypic presentation. Experimental evidence further supports this relationship, including testis specific expression and mouse knockout models demonstrating male infertility with acrosome and sperm head defects analogous to the human phenotype (Pierre et al., PMID: 23326625).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *DPY19L2* and autosomal recessive male infertility due to globozoospermia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on the meeting date January 7, 2026 (SOP v11).

disease_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies
disease_original_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies
submitted_as_notes:
*SPOP* is located on chromosome 17q21.33 and encodes Speckle-type BTB/POZ protein which forms homodimers and is involved in the ubiquitin proteasome pathway (Nabais Sa et al., 2020, PMID: 32109420). *SPOP* was first reported in relation to neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies, MONDO:0032942 and neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies, MONDO:0032943 in 2020 (PMID: 32109420) and has a previously well-established role in cancer. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working group, while there was no difference in inheritance patterns, there were differences in molecular mechanisms and slightly differing clinical presentations for each disorder. Variants resulting in neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies were found to cause disease through a gain of function mechanism and those that cause neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies, MONDO:0032943 cause disease through a dominant negative mechanism (PMID: 32109420). Therefore, the disease entities have been split into two. The curation for neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and dysmorphic facies has been curated separately.

Neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies, MONDO:0032943 is characterised by macrocephaly, poor growth/short stature, mild to moderate intellectual disability and consistent dysmorphic features including high/broad forehead, hypertelorism and pointed chin (PMID: 32109420). Other features such as congenital cardiac disease and endocrine abnormalities such as hypothyroidism are variably present.

7 variants (all missense) have been reported in 13 cases across 2 publications (PMID: 32109420, 36259278), Clinvar (SCV001432745.2, SCV003852901.1, SCV006071201.1, SCV005091493.1, SCV001987200.2) and GeneDx internal data are included in this curation. Functional data was applied at the variant level from an assay where variants from patients were introduced into a cell line and demonstrated that these variants acted through a dominant negative mechanism with reduced degradation of substrate below heterozygous wild type resulting in increased substrate amount in cells (PMID: 32109420, 28805821). The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be dominant negative (PMID: 32109420).

This gene-disease association is supported by experimental evidence (biochemical function and protein interaction) (PMID: 19818702, 32109420). Other genes involved in the ubiquitin proteasome pathway (*CUL3*, *CUL7*, *CUL4B*, *UBR1*, *UBE3B*) are strongly or definitively associated with neurodevelopmental or syndromic disorders. *SPOP* interacts on a protein level with *CUL3*. *SPOP* has a MATH domain which binds substrate to be tagged for degradation and binds *CUL3* via a BTB domain (PMID: 19818708, 14528312). 

In summary there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *SPOP* and autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with relative macrocephaly and with or without cardiac or endocrine anomalies, MONDO:0032943. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 4th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NOTCH3* and thrombocytopenia is supported by limited evidence. A single case report by Zhao and Li (2019; PMID: 31729093) described a family of Miao ethnicity with thrombocytopenia and a heterozygous *NOTCH3* missense variant R1694Q. The variant segregated with thrombocytopenia in the family, but the pedigree was small and no functional studies were performed. No other thrombocytopenia-associated genes were implicated. 

Experimental evidence directly linking *NOTCH3* to platelet biology is lacking. Indirect evidence suggests that Notch signaling plays a role in megakaryopoiesis and platelet activation (PMID: 26002683; PMID: 32277177), but these studies involve *NOTCH1* or *NOTCH2* rather than *NOTCH3.* Mouse and zebrafish models of *NOTCH3* loss-of-function show vascular defects and hemorrhage (PMID: 28293466; PMID: 24139282), but no platelet count abnormalities have been reported. Large CADASIL cohorts (PMID: 33712516; PMID: 35862191) and other *NOTCH3*-related phenotypes do not include thrombocytopenia as a feature and do not report the R1694Q variant in cases (MIM#s 615293, 125310, 621295, 130720, 608600 will be curated seperately).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.

*DDX23* encodes a member of the DEAD box protein family of ATP-dependent RNA helicases. *DDX23* is primarily involved in pre-mRNA splicing and spliceosome B complex formation. *DDX23* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2021 (Burns et al., PMID: 34050707). Phenotypic features reported in affected individuals include global developmental delay, muscular tone abnormalities, facial dysmorphic features, autism spectrum disorder or autistic features, and seizures (PMIDs: 34050707, 37596899). Other less common findings include gray matter heterotopia, and skeletal, renal, ocular and cardiac abnormalities. 

Eleven *de novo* missense variants that have been reported in 13 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 25363768, 34050707, 37596899, 38712318, 39039281) are included in this curation. Additionally, three missense variants with unknown inheritance that were reported in 3 probands in a large autism/intellectual disability study are also included in this curation (PMID: 33004838). All the missense variants reported by Burns et al. (PMID: 34050707) as pathogenic/likely pathogenic cluster within the N-terminal and C-terminal RecA-like domains. The mechanism of pathogenicity is unknown, since no functional studies have been performed; the clustering of missense variants suggests a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function and protein interaction.  Several genes of the DEAD box protein family of RNA helicases are associated with syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders, including *DDX3X*, *DDX6*, *DDX17*, and *DDX59*. *DDX23* interacts with SRSF1 (PMID: 38743621), a protein involved in pre-mRNA splicing that has also been implicated in a neurodevelopmental disorder. In engineered *E. coli* cells, mutant human *DDX23* abolishes spliceosomal intermediate products and interferes with spliceosome B complex assembly (PMID: 27377154). 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between *DDX23* and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. The classification was upgraded from limited to moderate based on the strength of evidence, particularly the variant clustering and their *de novo* nature. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on December 17, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

GRAP was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNB114) in 2019 (Li et al., PMID:30610177). One missense variant (c.311A>T, p.Gln104Leu) that has been reported in 4 individuals from 2 unrelated families in 1 publication is included in this curation (PMID:30610177). The mechanism of pathogenicity is unclear. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression data demonstrating that GRAP is localized in the spiral ganglion neuron fibers, inner and outer innervating auditory hair cells, and the utricular hair cells (PMID: 30610177). An animal model also suggests that this gene can cause functional and morphological abnormalities of the scolopidia and sensory neurons in compound heterozygous (drk6/drk14−7 and drk6/drke0A) and mosaic (eyFLP; drkΔ) Drosophila (PMID: 30610177). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.

Nonerythrocytic beta spectrin (SPTBN2) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia 14 in 2012 (Lise et al., PMID: 23236289). *SPTBN2* can involve but is not limited to: ataxia, developmental delay, cerebellar atrophy and intellectual disability. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found a difference in the molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities: spinocerebellar ataxia 5 (OMIM:600224), and spinocerebellar ataxia recessive 14 (OMIM:615386). The split curation for autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia 5 has been curated separately. Four variants (1 missense, 1 nonsense, 1 frameshift and 1 splice-site) that have been reported in four probands in four publications (PMIDs: 23236289, 23838597, 28636205, 31692161) are included in this curation. Case evidence includes segregation in a family with 7 genotyped affected homozygous carriers and 3 unaffected heterozygous carriers. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression data and a knockout mouse model (PMIDs: 20371805, 9826670). The mouse model showed features consistent with ataxia in mouse models and further supports the proposed loss of function mechanism by lack of phenotype in the heterozygous mice. In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *SPTBN2* and autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia 14. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.   This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataxia GCEP on the meeting date May 13, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*NFAT5* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant immunodeficiency disease in 2022 (PMID: 36238298). This condition is characterized by impaired adaptive and innate immune responses, including lymphopenia, abnormal B‑ and T‑cell function, poor antigen‑specific responses, and susceptibility to infections, particularly from Epstein-Barr virus. Two missense variants that have been reported in 2 probands in 1 publication (PMID: 36238298) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is presumed to involve haploinsufficiency of *NFAT5,* consistent with impaired osmoprotective gene induction and reduced lymphocyte survival under stress conditions (PMID: 10051678).

This gene–disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including biochemical function studies showing that *NFAT5* is required for tonicity‑responsive gene expression in lymphocytes (PMID: 10051678) and multiple mouse models demonstrating reduced thymic cellularity, peripheral lymphopenia, impaired lymphocyte proliferation, and diminished antigen‑specific immune responses in NFAT5‑deficient mice (PMIDs: 12421923, 15247420). These model systems together support a biological role for *NFAT5* in immune homeostasis, although they cannot model human‑specific phenotypes such as EBV susceptibility. 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene‑disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene‑disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date March 19, 2024 (SOP Version 9).

*LIPE* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive familial partial lipodystrophy in 2014 (Albert et al., PMID 24848981) in 4 siblings homozygous for the variant NM_005357.4:c.3203_3221del (p.Val1068GlyfsTer102) (reported as c.2300_2318 [p.Val767Glyfs
Ter102] to emphasize lack of translation of exon 1 in adipose tissue). We have curated the inheritance pattern for *LIPE*-related lipodystrophy as a recessive mode of inheritance as this has been consistently reported (Albert et al., PMID 24848981; Farhan et al., PMID: 25475467; Zotolov et al., PMID: 27862896; Sollier et al., PMID: 33112291; Zhou et al., PMID: 39113684). 

The phenotype is characterized by upper-body increased fat accumulation with lower-extremity lipoatrophy, together with hypertriglyceridemia, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, insulin resistance/diabetes, hepatic steatosis and myopathy and/or peripheral neuropathy (PMIDs: 24848981, 25475467, 27862896, 33112291, 39113684). Low serum adiponectin has been noted in two reports (PMIDs: 24848981, 33112291), and autofluorescent subretinal deposits have also been described (PMID: 33112291).
Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern or phenotypic variability. Therefore, the phenotypic presentations have been lumped into one disease entity, type 6 familial partial lipodystrophy (OMIM: 615980). Of note, p.V767GfsTer102/p.V1068GlyfsTer102 (see above) has been reported as enriched in an Amish cohort (~5% carrier frequency), and heterozygous carriers showed higher triglycerides, lower HDL-cholesterol, and increased diabetes/insulin resistance compared with controls (PMID 24848981); however, these heterozygous findings are nonspecific and were not curated as a distinct *LIPE*-haploinsufficiency disorder.

Nine nonsense or frameshift variants that have been reported in 7 probands in 5 publications are included in this curation (PMIDs 24848981, 25475467, 27862896, 33112291, 39113684). The aggregated score for case-level is 21 points. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is supported by expression studies, functional alteration in patient-derived cells and mouse models (PMIDs: 15961788, 11316346, 10639158, 33112291, 24848981). Total points for experimental evidence are 9, but the experimental evidence score is limited to a maximum of 6 points. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 18. 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *LIPE* and autosomal recessive type 6 familial partial lipodystrophy (OMIM:615980). This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on November 12, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

EFL1 is located on chromosome 15 (15q25.2) and encodes the elongation factor like GTPase 1. This gene directly interacts with SBDS to release eukaryotic translation initiation factor 6 (eIF6) from the 60S ribosomal subunit for 80S ribosomal assembly (PMID: 341158470). EFL1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive (AR) EFL1-related Shwachman-Diamond syndrome in 2017 (Stepensky et al. 2017 PMID: 28331068). This syndrome is characterized by exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, hematopoietic abnormalities, short stature, and metaphyseal dysplasia. 

Eleven variants reported in 11 probands across 5 publications are included in this curation (PMIDs: 29970384; 34237744; 39379149; 28331068; 34115847). However, three of these probands are not scored either due to absence of sufficient clinical description or presence of de novo variant in commonly tested Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) genes (PMIDs: 34115847;34237744). The mechanism of disease is loss-of-function where pathogenic variants in the EFL1 gene result in failure of elf6 release from the 60S subunit, thereby impairing 80S ribosomal assembly and reducing protein synthesis. Of note, the c.3205A>G p.Thr1069Ala variant is speculated to result in somatic uniparental disomy in bone marrow conferring an acquired selective advantage in the context of inherited compound heterozygosity (PMID: 34115847). However, even this less deleterious EFL1 variant  does not fully correct ribosome assembly and induces SDS features in cell line and animal models (PMID: 34115847).  

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by functional alteration in patient cells, non-human model organisms, biochemical evidence, and protein-protein interaction (PMIDs: 31151987; 34115847; 21536732; 24406167). Pathogenic EFL1 variants in patient cells are demonstrated to impede eIF6 release and attenuate translation (PMID: 31151987). The Efl1-K983R mouse line (Efl1K983R/K983R) exhibits impaired hematopoiesis, motor abnormalities, and cognitive deficits (PMID: 31151987). Furthermore, an orthologous model of compound heterozygosity recapitulates features of human disease with reduced hemoglobin, white blood cells, and platelets and impaired 80S ribosome assembly (PMID: 34115847). Zebrafish efl1 morphants model also recapitulates human SDS features, which are rescued by the human wild-type, but less by EFL1 p.Thr1069Ala mRNA (PMID: 34115847). SBDS and EFL1 are also shown to directly interact and catalyze the translational activation of ribosomes in eukaryotes (PMIDs: 24406167; 21536732). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between EFL1 and AR EFL1-related Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on 02/10/2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: neurodegeneration, childhood-onset, with cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline
disease_original_title: neurodegeneration, childhood-onset, with cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline
submitted_as_notes:
*CAPRIN1* encodes an mRNA-binding protein that regulates mRNA transport and translation, and plays a role in synaptic plasticity. CAPRIN1 is a component of stress granules and harbors a prion-like domain, like other RNA-binding proteins involved in neurodegenerative disorders. *CAPRIN1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant neurodegeneration, childhood-onset, with cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline in 2022 (Delle Vedove et al., PMID: 36136249) in two unrelated individuals with the same *de novo* missense variant, p.Pro512Leu. A third individual with the same variant and a similar phenotype was reported in 2025 (PMID: 39878554). The disorder is characterized by the onset of progressive gait and truncal ataxia during childhood (between the ages of 7 and 10), dysarthria, progressive muscle weakness and atrophy, sensorimotor axonal neuropathy, and cognitive decline with learning difficulties. Brain imaging shows cerebellar and cerebral atrophy. The variant exerts a gain-of-function effect by increasing the protein propensity to misfold and aggregate (PMID: 36136249).

Of note, *CAPRIN1* haploinsufficiency has been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment, autism, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (PMID: 35979925). This disease assertion was evaluated separately.

One recurrent missense variant (p.Pro512Leu) that has been reported in three probands in two publications (PMIDs: 36136249, 39878554) is included in this curation. The variant occurred *de novo* in two individuals, and was absent from the mother in the other one. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be gain of function (PMID: 36136249).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. The p.Pro512Leu variant forms insoluble ubiquitinated aggregates that sequester proteins associated with neurodegenerative disorders, including ATXN2, GEMIN5, and SNCA. iPSC-derived cortical neurons expressing the p.Pro512Leu variant exhibit reduced neuronal activity, reduced RNA affinity, and altered stress granule dynamics. CAPRIN1 is an interacting partner of ATXN2 and GEMIN5, associated with ataxia, and FMR1, associated with fragile X tremor/ataxia syndrome. 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. The classification was upgraded from limited to moderate due to the independent occurrence of a recurrent variant in three individuals with a similar phenotype and functional evidence showing a gain-of-function effect. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on February 18, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 2, autosomal dominant
disease_original_title: growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 2, autosomal dominant
submitted_as_notes:
*STAT5B* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 2 in 1998 (Iida K et al. PMID:9467570). GHISID2 is an autosomal dominant form of growth hormone insensitivity syndrome, a congenital disease characterized by short stature, growth hormone deficiency in the presence of normal to elevated circulating concentrations of growth hormone, resistance to exogeneous growth hormone therapy, and recurrent infections. Some patients may have features of mild immune dysregulation, such as eczema, increased serum IgE, asthma, or celiac disease.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, GHISID-2 (OMIM:618985), GHISID-1 (OMIM:245590). The split curation for autosomal dominant growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 2 has been curated separately.

Nine variants (missense, in-frame indel, nonsense) that have been reported in nine probands in five publications (PMIDs: 29844444, 20606392, 27234692, 29188236, 31902742) are included in this curation. Several functional studies of proband variants show non-stable expression and/or limited immunodetection. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be dominant negative. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and expression studies (PMIDs: 37162340, 22912632, 37162340, 9575217). Zebrafish models highlight growth defects (including cyclopia and pericardial edema), deficiency of IFG-I transcription in the liver, and defective postnatal skeletal muscle development (including bent spine). Biochemical function studies indicate that *STAT5B* is essential for IL-2–driven transcription of *IL2RA* (*CD25*) and *FOXP3*, crucial for Treg lineage specification. *STAT5B* deficiency leads to decreased Treg numbers and impaired function, promoting autoimmunity (e.g., eczema, autoimmune thyroiditis).

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *STAT5B* and autosomal dominant growth hormone insensitivity syndrome with immune dysregulation 2. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen PIRD GCEP on the meeting date January 20, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *NDUFB9* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of May 20, 2024. The *NDUFB9* gene encodes NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) subunit B9, which is essential for complex I activity and assembly. Defects of this protein lead to complex I deficiency.

The *NDUFB9* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease in 2012 (PMID: 22200994). *NDUFB9* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 24 [OMIM#618245]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 22200994; Patient 35838). This case was noted to have complex I deficiency in fibroblasts and a clinical presentation consistent with primary mitochondrial disease, however additional clinical details were not provided.  Of note, several cases were excluded from this curation due to the variant allele frequency in the general population (PMID: 38129218) and lack of segregation and no second variant identified (PMID: 22200994; Patient 33027). A case was also reported as part of a thesis (http://theses.ncl.ac.uk/jspui/handle/10443/5044) however this was excluded as the case was not published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416) and functional alteration studies in non-patient cells (PMID: 27626371).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 20, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

COL4A1 codes for the collagen IV alpha 1 chain. This forms a heterotrimer (alpha1alpha1alpha2) and network with the collagen alpha 2 chain. This network is the major protein found in basement membranes in development and, later, in blood vessels as well as other basement membranes. COL4A1 was first reported associated with brain small vessel disease in 2005 by Gould et al. (PMID:15905400); and with Nephropathy (Hereditary Angiopathy with Nephropathy, Aneurysms and Muscle Cramps, HANAC) by Plaisier in 2007 (PMID:18160688). These rare diseases mainly result in brain infarcts but are also associated with haematuria, proteinuria and kidney cysts. Common brain features seen in affected probands include porencephaly, ventriculomegaly, schizencephaly, and leukoencephalopathy. The brain malformation phenotypes are typically present in fetal or neonatal-onset cases (PMIDs: 16107487, 25719457, 32732225, 33846711, 37486637). A similar overlapping spectrum is seen in cases of autosomal dominant COL4A2 variants. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working group, we found no difference in the molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern between variants resulting in brain small vessel disease and HANAC or kidney cysts. Therefore both of these disease entities were lumped together into one. Many variants have been reported in COL4A1 but include mainly Gly missense substitutions in the intermediate collagenous domain as well as some truncating and splicing variants in many publications and databases. 

10 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splicing) that have been reported in at least 10 probands in 9 publications (PMIDs: 16107487, 18160688, 20733150, 20818663, 25719457, 27190376, 32515830, 36372235, 36922284) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence (biochemical function, protein interactions, expression studies, and non-human model organisms; PMIDs: 1635341, 18160688, 18219669, 26260163). Expression-level data indicates expression of the gene in the kidney blood vessels. Electron micrography shows that mutation of the COL4A1 gene leads to cerebral haemorrhage and kidney cysts. In a mouse model, COL4A1 homozygous mutants show lethality embryonically; both heterozygous and homozygous mutants have haemorrhages, retinal vessel tortuosity, albuminuria, haematuria, kidney cyts, as well as podocyte and glomerular basement membrane defects. 

In summary, COL4A1 is definitively associated with autosomal dominant COL4A1-related small vessel disease (and HANAC and kidney cysts). This has been reportedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glomerulopathy GCEP on the meeting date 02/12/2024 (SOP Version 10). On 02/24/2026, the Brain Malformations GCEP added a secondary contribution to the evidence summary regarding the brain-related phenotypes. The classification did not change and no new evidence was added, so there is no change to the date last evaluated or SOP version.

Variation in the *PITX2* gene was first reported in relation to Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome in 1996 (Semina et al., PMID: 8944018]). Affected patients exhibit ocular features that are localized to the anterior segment, and frequently include iris hypoplasia, corectopia, polycoria, posterior embryotoxon, and predisposition to the development of glaucoma. A subset of patients exhibits additional extraocular features, including redundant periumbilical skin or umbilical hernia, and dental abnormalities such as hypodontia and/or microdontia. Patients with ocular presentation only may be diagnosed with anterior segment dysgenesis, which was first reported in relation to *PITX2* in 1998 (PMID: 9437321, PMID: 9618168). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the molecular mechanism (monoallelic loss of function) and mode of inheritance (autosomal dominant) were found to be consistent among patients with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome 1 and anterior segment dysgenesis 4, while the phenotypic variability between them appeared to represent a spectrum of disease rather than separate disease entities. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *PITX2* variants have been lumped into a single disease entity, referred to as *PITX2*-related anterior segment dysgenesis syndrome.

This curation has scored sixteen suspected disease-causing variants (one nonsense, six frameshift, two predicted to disrupt splicing, five missense affecting the homeobox domain of the encoded protein, and two additional missense variants). These variants have been collectively reported in sixteen probands in five publications (PMID: 8944018, PMID: 9437321, PMID: 12381896, PMID: 28513611, PMID: 35882526). Three of the probands were associated with large families in which the variant co-segregated with the affected status of family members (PMID: 8944018, PMID: 9437321). More case-level evidence is available in the literature (PMID: 19513095), but its inclusion in this curation was not necessary to reach the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be monoallelic loss of function, characterized in some cases by truncation of the majority of the protein product and in other cases by missense variants within the homeobox domain that cause defects in transactivation (PMID: 19218601).

This gene-disease association is supported by biochemical evidence that PITX2 functions as a transcription factor to coordinate normal tissue development (PMID: 23975681). *PITX2* is highly expressed in ocular tissues, particularly the cornea, retinal pigment epithelium and trabecular meshwork (PMID: 30239781). PITX2 physically interacts with and colocalizes with FOXC1, another transcription factor associated with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome through an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance (PMID: 16449236). Phenotypes of affected human patients are recapitulated by various model organisms with *PITX2* loss-of-function, including defective anterior segment development and dental abnormalities in mice that are consistent with the proposed role of PITX2 in the genesis of these tissues (PMID: 10498698, PMID: 16203745).

In summary, *PITX2* has a Definitive association with *PITX2*-related anterior segment dysgenesis syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Glaucoma and Neuro-Ophthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 17th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*NRXN2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2011 (Gauthier et al., PMID: 21424692). Since the initial report of a frameshift variant in an individual with autism that was shown to lead to loss of function *in vitro* (PMID: 21424692), only five other truncating variants have been reported in individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders. The phenotype information is very limited. Five variants were identified in cohort sequencing studies of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and no clinical information was provided (PMIDs: 21424692, 30392784, 31398340, 31981491). Another variant was identified in a child with global developmental delay and syndromic features, including microcephaly and congenital heart defect (PMID: 37120078).

Six frameshift variants that have been reported in six probands in five publications (PMIDs: 21424692, 30392784, 31398340, 31981491, 37120078) are included in this curation. Two occurred *de novo*, two were paternally inherited, and two were of unknown inheritance. In one family, the heterozygous father had a history of severe language delay (PMID: 21424692). In another family, the paternally inherited variant was present in two brothers with ASD but not in their sister, who was also diagnosed with ASD (PMID: 31398340). *NRXN2* truncating variants have also been reported in a control subject in an autism exome study (PMID: 31981491), an unaffected parent of a child with autism (PMID: 35982159), and in 10 schizophrenia cases and 9 controls (PMID: 35396579). In addition, *de novo* missense variants in *NRXN2* have been observed in individuals with developmental disorders (PMID: 33057194) and ASD (PMIDs: 35982159, 36368308). However, because there is no experimental evidence of gene impact for any of these variants, they were not scored. *NRXN2* is highly constrained for truncating variants (pLI = 1, LOEUF = 0.32, gnomAD v4.1.0) and also exhibits constraint for missense variants (Z score = 3.1). Of note, no single gene deletions affecting *NRXN2* were identified. Deletions involving other genes in addition to *NRXN2* were not counted as evidence because the contribution of the other genes cannot be ruled out. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, based on the few reported variants, but no functional studies have been performed.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including biochemical function, protein interactions, and mouse models. Neurexins are presynaptic cell adhesion molecules that bind to postsynaptic ligands, such as neuroligins. They mediate signaling across the synapse and shape the properties of neural circuits by specifying synaptic functions. There are three *NRXN* genes (*NRXN1*, *NRXN2*, and *NRXN3*) that each produce longer α-NRXN and shorter β-NRXN isoforms. Heterozygous deletions in *NRXN1* cause complex neurodevelopmental disorder with reduced penetrance and variable expressivity, and are also enriched in schizophrenia and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder.

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 15, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

AARS1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 29 (DEE29) in 2015 (OMIM: 616339, PMID: 25817015) and later in association with autosomal recessive trichothiodystrophy 8, non-photosensitive (TTD8) in 2021 (OMIM: 619691, PMID: 33909043). Additionally, AARS1 variants have been associated with autosomal dominant conditions, namely Charcot Marie Tooth type 2N (OMIM: 613287) and leukoencephalopathy, hereditary diffuse, with spheroids (HDLS2) (OMIM: 619661). These dominant disorders have been curated separately. AARS1 encodes a cytoplasmic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and plays a key role in the first step of protein translation through the charging of tRNA molecules with alanine (PMID: 34446925).  

DEE29 was initially characterized clinically as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, deficient cerebral myelination, and peripheral neuropathy with or without congenital vertical talus (PMID: 25817015). Since that time, it has been recognized as a spectrum of infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy with deficient myelination and late-onset disease with posterior predominant leukoencephalopathy, with the early-onset form typically presenting within the first year of life and the late-onset form presenting at variable ages >1 year (PMID: 34446925). Most affected individuals demonstrate developmental delay, seizures, truncal hypotonia, microcephaly, and develop spastic tetraparesis over time. Ophthalmologic dysfunction can also occur. 

Two cases of individuals presenting with autosomal recessive, nonphotosensitive trichothiodystrophy have been reported in association with bi-allelic variants in AARS1. Both patients were found to have developmental delay and neurologic regression, in addition to sulfur-deficient brittle hair and nails with ichthyosis. One patient demonstrated delayed myelination on brain MRI and both cases demonstrated impact of functional evidence of AARS1 variant on rate of tRNA charging. 

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in molecular mechanisms, inheritance pattern, and phenotypic variability from other disease entities associated with AARS1 variants. Therefore, the following disease entities were split and curated separately: autosomal dominant AARS1-related leukoencephalopathy (Limited) and autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie Tooth type 2N (Definitive). Regarding the autosomal recessive conditions DEE29 and TTD8, we found that the phenotypes likely represent a clinical spectrum, and that there is no difference in molecular mechanism. Therefore, the DEE29 and TTD8 disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, autosomal recessive AARS1-related leukoencephalopathy.  

This curation includes 20 unique variants that have been reported in the biallelic state in 16 probands across 5 publications (PMIDs: 25817015, 34446925, 33909043, 28493438, 33294374). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a naturally-occurring mouse model as well as a yeast model. Similar to humans, the mouse model presents with ataxia and follicular dystrophy and is predicted to affect tRNA charging (PMID: 16906134). The yeast complementation model demonstrated viability through introduction of a wild-type ALA1 (yeast ortholog of AARS1) vector in haploid yeast strain with endogenous ALA deleted  (PMID: 25817015).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between AARS1 and the disease entity now known as AARS1-related leukoencephalopathy (MONDO:0014593). This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. 

This classification was approved by the Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy Working Group GCEP on September 3, 2025  [SOP Version 11].

CADM3: autosomal dominant axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease

Evidence Summary: Cell adhesion molecule 3, CADM3, was initially shown to segregate with clinical features of autosomal dominant, axonal type Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) in three unrelated families, including one confirmed de novo case, (Rebelo et al., PMID: 33889941). Clinical features of CMT axonal type include distal muscle weakness and atrophy with significant upper limb involvement, sensory loss, and foot and hand deformities, (Yalcouye et al., PMID: 38074074, Rebelo et al., PMID: 33889941). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. Two missense variants have been reported in 6 families.  CADM3, expressed in axons, interacts with CADM4, expressed by myelinating Schwann cells, to mediate  the structural organization of myelinated fibers. Stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy imaging revealed decreased co-localization of the mutant CADM3 with CADM4 at intercellular contact sites (PMID: 33889941). Mice carrying the corresponding human mutation (Cadm3Y170C) showed reduced expression of the mutant protein in axons. Cadm3Y170C mice showed abnormal axonal organization.  In summary, there is MODERATE evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.  This classification was approved by the ClinGen Charcot-Marie-Tooth Expert Panel on 02-05-26 (SOP Version 11).

Gene-Disease Validity Standard Operating Procedures, (SOP)-SOP 11

*TNNI1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital myopathy in 2024 (Donkervoort *et al.* PMID: 38569017). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability for *TNNI1* variant carriers. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split and curated separately: 1) autosomal recessive congenital myopathy expressed as a hypocontractile phenotype with early-onset; and 2) autosomal dominant congenital myopathy expressed as a hypercontractile phenotype with childhood and adult onset. 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship include case-level, experimental, and expression data. The initial cohort study by Donkervoort *et al.* identified one missense variant and one in-frame deletion variant in two probands with nemaline myopathy with clinical presentations of mainly muscle cramping, myalgias, stiffness, reduced exercise endurance, fatigue, difficulty swallowing, and presence of nemaline bodies in patient muscle tissue (PMID: 38569017). The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain of function. In addition, Nishimori *et al.* reported a *TNNI1* nonsense variant in a family with proximal arthrogryposis, joint contractures, serum high creatinine kinase levels, abnormal muscle pathology, and without muscle weakness (PMID: 34934811). Disease segregation within the families reported by Donkervoort “et al.” and Nishimori *et al.* was limited to two generations. 

The gene-disease association is supported by expression data (Uhlen *et al.* PMID: 25613900, Li *et al.* PMID: 36520026) and functional alteration in patient myofiber biopsy (Donkervoort *et al.* PMID: 38569017) which supports a hypercontractile phenotype consistent with a potential gain-of-function mechanism, however, direct functional evidence and investigation is still required. 

In summary, there is LIMITED evidence to support the association between *TNNI1* and autosomal dominant congenital myopathy. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease association. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Myopathy Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date November 24, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*OPN1MW* was first reported in relation to X-linked cases of blue cone monochromacy in 1989 (Nathans et al, PMID: 2788922), which was caused by a combined disruption of the red/green visual pigment gene array (later named *OPN1LW* and *OPN1MW*, respectively). Affected males had markedly impaired color vision, with or without reduced visual acuity, photophobia, and nystagmus. Electroretinogram showed normal rod and S cone function, but absent responses attributable to L and M cones. Subsequent publications starting in 1992 (Winderickx et al, PMID: 1302020) have described a more limited phenotype associated with monogenic disruption of the *OPN1MW* gene alone, characterized as deuteranomaly and/or deuteranopia.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting guidelines, this curation has focused on cases in which the cause of disease is monogenic *OPN1MW* loss-of-function, with the disease entity referred to as *OPN1MW*-related cone dysfunction. However, it is important to note the higher frequency and clinical importance of blue cone monochromacy resulting from digenic *OPN1LW* and *OPN1MW* loss-of-function variants.

Three missense variants have been reported in 5 probands, and one variant located in the promoter region of the *OPN1MW* gene has been reported in 32 probands, across 4 publications (PMIDs: 1302020, 11772996, 12051694, 12626747). All of the probands scored in this curation were males who harbored the variant allele in the hemizygous state. Large families with co-segregation of the genotype with affected status were not found, so segregation evidence did not contribute to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship.

Reports describing a strictly monogenic phenotype for *OPN1MW* remain limited, underscoring the greater clinical relevance of the digenic form involving both *OPN1MW* and **OPN1LW*. The curated evidence for the monogenic form reached a Moderate level of scoring and did not independently meet criteria for a Definitive classification. Therefore, the association was manually classified as Definitive in the broader clinical context. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.
