This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence indicating that *OPN1MW* encodes a medium-wave-sensitive opsin that enables photoperception of green-range wavelengths, consistent with patients’ lack of spectral sensitivity for green light when the gene is disrupted (PMID: 12051694). Functional assays in non-patient cells expressing the disease-associated variant p.Cys203Arg demonstrated protein misfolding, instability, and loss of normal opsin activity, including failure to absorb light at the appropriate wavelength and inability to activate transducin (PMID: 9152227). *OPN1MW* is highly specifically expressed in the human retina (PMID: 30239781). Although *OPN1MW* is a primate-specific gene, subretinal delivery of cone opsins in a mouse model of blue cone monochromacy restored cone outer segment structure and cone-mediated ERG responses, supporting the biological plausibility of therapeutic rescue (PMID: 28751656). The neighboring gene *OPN1LW* shares a similar function (encoding a long-wave-sensitive opsin that enables photoperception of red-range wavelengths), and its disruption similarly results in color vision defects (PMID: 9579484, PMID: 10191338, PMID: 15148406).

In summary, *OPN1MW* is Definitively associated with *OPN1MW*-related cone dysfunction. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on September 4th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *OXA1L* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of August 26, 2024. The *OXA1L* gene encodes a mitochondrial membrane insertase that mediates the cotranslational insertion of integral membrane proteins into the mitochondrial inner membrane, and functions in the assembly of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes IV and V.

The first and only report of *OXA1L* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2018 (PMID: 30201738). *OXA1L* has been associated with a single disease entity to date; severe, childhood‐onset mitochondrial encephalopathy and combined respiratory chain deficiency (PMID: 30201738). This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included two variants (one frameshift variant and one missense variant that leads to exon skipping and loss of function) identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 30201738). Clinical features in the single reported case include neonatal onset of hypotonia and developmental delay; he then developed a febrile illness at 5 years old and experienced rapid deterioration and onset of seizures and encephalopathy prior to cardiorespiratory arrest. Brain imaging showed dysgenesis of the corpus callosum.

The mechanism of disease is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416), rescue in patient cells (PMID: 30201738), *OXA1L* knockout *Drosophila melanogaster* model (PMID: 30201738), and *OXA1L* knockout in HEK293T cells (PMID: 30201738).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on August 26, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

SLC35C1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II in 2001 (Lühn et al., PMID 11326279; Lübke et al. PMID 11326280). At least nine variants (missense, frameshift, nonsense, in-frame deletions) that have been reported in 8 probands in 7 publications (PMIDs 11326279, 11326280, 24403049, 16455955, 35338746, 30630937, 12406889) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached. Patients have a range of symptoms, including developmental delay, growth delay, dysmorphic features, recurrent infections, hypotonia, and impaired neutrophil motility. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. This gene-disease relationship is supported by in vitro and in vivo assays showing a defect in fucosylation (PMIDs 11326279, 24403049, 16455955) as well as a mouse model (PMID 17276979). In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between SLC35C1 and autosomal recessive leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date November 3, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*FOXH1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital heart disease (CHD) in 2010 (De Luca et al., PMID: 19933292). *FOXH1* has also been implicated in holoprosencephaly, however, the relationship between *FOXH1* and congenital heart disease was evaluated separately from holoprosencephaly due to differences in clinical presentation.
At least seven unique missense variants were reported in ten individuals with CHD (PMID: 32003456). Experimental evidence supporting this gene disease relationship included expression in the outflow tract, common atrium, and ventricle of human embryos, protein interaction data with MEF2C and NKX2-5, a zebrafish rescue model which demonstrated dosage-dependent differences in rescue potential, and a mouse null model that failed to form the outflow tract and right ventricle (PMIDs: 15363409, 18538293, 32003456). In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *FOXH1* and autosomal dominant congenital heart disease. Although more human genetic evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date December 3rd, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

FLT3 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant leukemia predisposition in 2016 (de Smith et al., PMID: 27683039). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found insufficient evidence of difference in molecular mechanisms, inheritance patterns, or phenotypic variability, although in the small number of reported patients the majority presented with myeloid-related disease. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: predisposition to B-ALL, aplastic anaemia, MDS and AML. Seven missense variants that have been reported in 8 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 27683039, 33283233, 38212634, 39080258, 39773519) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be gain of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, expression studies and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 7630197, 10698507, 11756186, 12796379). FLT3 is expressed in hematopoietic cells and leads to AKT and MAPK pathway activation (PMID: 7630197, 12796379). Activating alterations in FLT3 result in cell proliferation and viability, with constitutive activation of STAT and MAPK pathways (PMID: 10698507). Activating FLT3 alterations in a murine BMT model can induce myeloproliferative disease (PMID: 11756186), however an activating FLT3 alteration alone in a murine model is not sufficient to cause leukemogenesis (PMID: 25873173). In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between FLT3 and autosomal dominant leukemia predisposition. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date 18th November 2025 (SOP Version 11].

The relationship between *PET117* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 4, 2024. The *PET11*7 gene encodes a cytochrome *c* oxidase chaperone important for complex IV biogenesis and assembly.

The first and only report of *PET117* in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2017 (PMID: 28386624). *PET117* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 19 [OMIM# 619063]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease.   Of note, *PET117* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on May 13, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous variant identified in one case from one publication (PMID: 28386624), in a child with LSS.

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 27977873) and functional alteration in non-patient cells (PMID: 37247699).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on November 4, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

The relationship between *UQCRQ* and primary mitochondrial disease was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of October 7, 2024. The *UQCRQ* gene encodes ubiquinol-cytochrome *c* reductase (mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III) subunit 7, a small core-associated protein.

The first and only report of the *UQCRQ* gene in relation to autosomal recessive primary mitochondrial disease was in 2008 (PMID: 18439546). *UQCRQ* has been associated with one disease entity to date; mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 4 [OMIM# 615159]. This is one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework, and is considered a primary mitochondrial disease. Of note, *UQCRQ* was first curated by this Expert Panel for its association with Leigh syndrome spectrum (LSS) on October 14, 2019 (SOP v6), with a final classification of Limited. This current curation for the association with primary mitochondrial disease includes cases with LSS.

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. This curation included one homozygous missense variant identified in affected individuals from one kindred in one publication (PMID: 18439546). Affected individuals had LSS, profound global developmental delay, dystonic posturing, athetoid movements, and ataxia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed in five affected individuals showed bilateral symmetric abnormal findings in the basal ganglia. Muscle biopsies appeared normal. Plasma lactate ranged from slightly to significantly increased.

The mechanism of disease is suspected to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a biochemical function shared with other genes associated with primary mitochondrial disease (PMID: 33340416).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the NICHD/NINDS U24 ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 7, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

The *MYCN* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Feingold syndrome type 1 in 2005 (van Bokhoven et al., 2005, PMID: 15821734). This syndrome is characterized by digital anomalies (including brachymesophalangy and syndactyly), microcephaly, gastrointestinal atresias (esophageal and/or duodenal), and variable neurodevelopmental differences. Several unique and recurrent heterozygous loss-of-function variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, or whole-gene deletions) have been reported in unrelated individuals with consistent phenotypes.

Evidence supporting this gene–disease relationship includes both case-level and experimental data. Pathogenic variants have been described in more than ten affected probands across several publications and are included in this curation (van Bokhoven et al., 2005 PMID: 15821734; Marcelis et al., 2008 PMID: 18470948; Cogent et al., 2011 PMID: 21224895; Tedesco et al., 2021 PMID: 33442900), with most reported variants occurring de novo or showing autosomal dominant segregation in multiple affected family members. Additional clinical evidence exists in the literature.The mechanism of disease is monoallelic loss of function, supported by truncating variants and whole-gene deletions.

*MYCN* is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor critical for embryonic development, including in the limb mesenchyme, neural tissues, and enteric epithelium. Expression studies in human embryos show strong developmental expression in these relevant tissues. Western blot confirms *MYCN* protein isoforms are expressed in the fetal brain. In vivo experiments in mice and zebrafish further support the role of *MYCN* in embryogenesis. Conditional knockout of *Mycn* in mouse limb mesenchyme causes shortened limbs and downregulation of miR-17~92, a known *MYCN* target. Zebrafish *mycn* morphants exhibit microcephaly and craniofacial hypoplasia, which are rescued by co-injection of wild-type zebrafish *mycn* mRNA  (Li et al., 2022 PMID: 36318514). Single-cell RNA-seq revealed a *Mycn*-sensitive epithelial subpopulation with reduced proliferation. Ribosomal profiling and Northern blot analyses demonstrated defective rRNA processing and reduced 40S, 60S, and 80S ribosomes, impairing translation. Suppressed mTOR signaling contributed to the phenotype, which was mimicked by rapamycin and partially rescued by L-leucine or Rheb supplementation, highlighting *MYCN*’s role in ribosome biogenesis and intestinal development.

In summary, *MYCN* is definitively associated with autosomal dominant Feingold syndrome type 1. This classification is supported by multiple de novo and segregating loss-of-function variants in affected individuals, functional data from patient cells and animal models, and rescue experiments. This has
been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date July 2nd, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

**TMEM163 Hypomyelinating Leukodystrophy 25, autosomal dominant**
Preferred name: TMEM163-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy

TMEM163 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 25 in 2022 (Yan et al., PMID: 35455965). Affected individuals present with nystagmus, visual deficits, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, ataxia, hypomyelination, and abnormalities of the corpus callosum. Onset occurs in infancy. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found a consistent phenotype and no difference in molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern; therefore, the single disease entity of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 25 has been maintained. 

The *TMEM163* gene encodes for transmembrane protein which is shown to be involved in zinc efflux (PMID: 31697912). Four missense variants have been reported in 6 probands across 2 publications (PMIDs: 35455965, 35953447) and are included in this curation. All variants occurred de novo in the affected individuals, except one case in which the variant was inherited from a mosaic parent. All variants had supporting functional data, yielding a total of 6 points of genetic evidence. The mechanism of pathogenicity has not been definitively determined although a dominant-negative mechanism has been suggested (PMID: 35455965, 35953447). 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (4.5 points). A zebrafish model demonstrated dysplasia of the larvae, locomotor disability as well as myelination defects as a result of reduced number of oligodendrocytes, recapitulating the human phenotype (PMID: 35455965). Rescue studies show that tmem163 knockdown zebrafish embryos injected with an in vitro synthesized mRNA encoding the human wild-type TMEM163 result in partial rescue, with 50% of embryos having no phenotype while embryos injected with mRNA harboring human TMEM163 variants resulted in embryos with a more severe phenotype (PMID: 35455965). A mouse oligodendrocyte cell line (‘oli-neu’) expressing the TMEM163 p.L76P mutant construct demonstrated significant reduction in cellular processes compared to wild type (PMID: 35953447). Given that these processes’ native role is to wrap around axons, thereby forming the myelin sheath, reduction of these processes is considered a cellular recapitulation of a hypomyelination phenotype. 

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *TMEM163* and autosomal dominant hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 25, also known as TMEM163-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy GCEP on the meeting date April 15, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

PDE1C was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNA74) in 2018 (Wang et al. 2018, PMID: 29860631). This gene encodes phosphodiesterase 1C, a member of the cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase 1 family (PMID: 1326532). Four missense variants have been reported in association with hearing loss; however, two of the individuals reported had additional variants in hearing loss-associated genes and were not included in the scoring of this gene-disease validity scoring (PMID: 38400873, 34556655). One large family with autosomal dominant, postlingual, and progressive hearing loss was reported to have a missense variant in PDE1C identified via whole exome sequencing and segregated with disease (PMID: 29860631). Of note, this variant was also found to be present in gnomAD at a frequency of 0.022% (14/44830) in East Asian chromosomes. An in vitro phosphodiesterase functional assay was performed and the mutant was found to affect  both cAMP and cGMP hydrolysis (PMID: 29860631). A second missense variant was identified in a cohort of individuals with hearing loss, though specific phenotypic information was not reported (PMID: 36597107). PDE1C is expressed in outer (OHC) and inner (IHC) hair cells in mouse cochlea (PMID: 29860631). It is also expressed in the human inner ear, with the highest expression in glial and chondrocytes (https://umgear.org/). In summary, there is limited evidence supporting this gene disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hearing Loss Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 15, 2026. Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) version 12.

The *SNORA31* gene is located on chromosome 13 at 13q14.13 and encodes Small Nucleolar RNA, H/ACA Box 31, a noncoding RNA gene. The gene is predicted to be a guide RNA responsible for pseudouridylation of 18S ribosomal RNA and small nuclear RNA (Kiss *et al*., 2004, PMID: 15199136). 

*SNORA31* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant susceptibility to herpes simplex encephalitis in 2019 (Lafaille *et al*., 2019 PMID: 31806906). Authors identified five individuals in a cohort with herpes simplex encephalitis that carried rare variants in *SNORA31*. Two variants across three of these probands are included in this curation. Both variants have supporting functional evidence indicating that these variants reduce transcript expression, suggesting a loss-of-function mechanism. Because *SNORA31* is located within the fifth intron of *TPT1*, associated variants are currently listed under the *TPT1* transcript. The appropriate HGVS nomenclature for these entries is undergoing internal review. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (functional alteration and model systems), specifically in vitro functional assays showing that patient cells and cell culture models have an increased susceptibility to HSV-1 (PMID: 31806906). 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date March 4, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

SH2B3 was first reported in relation to AR myeloproliferation and autoimmunity in 2013 (Perez-Garcia et al. PMID: 23908464). SH2B3 functions as a negative regulator of multiple cytokine and growth factor receptor signaling pathways. The SH2B3 protein directly binds JAK via its SH2 domain and plays a relevant role in hematopoiesis. Both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant modes of inheritance were described, presenting a semidominant pattern. The disease onset typically occurs in the neonatal period or within the first few months of life. Clinical manifestations are characterized by a myeloproliferative disorder, with variable features including hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, monocytosis, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, and autoimmune disease. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two: SH2B3-related myeloproliferation and autoimmunity and Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) predisposition.The split curation for autosomal recessive JMML predisposition is curated separately. Sixteen variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) have been reported in 16 probands in five publications (PMIDs: 38152053, 37981895, 37206266, 40481232, 23908464) and are included in this curation. In the context of a semidominant mode of inheritance, probands have been identified harboring homozygous (n = 10) and heterozygous variants (n = 6). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, gene expression analysis, and biochemical studies (PMIDs: 23908464 and 37206266). Experiments have been conducted to evaluate gene expression in patient-derived cells, altered biochemical function, phenotype rescue in patient derived cells, and the effects of zebrafish sh2b3 knockdown showing a disease‑related phenotype. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between SH2B3 and semidominant SH2B3-related immune system disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date August 12th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*TBC1D32* (TBC1 Domain Family Member 32) is located on 6q22.31. It encodes TBC1 domain family member 32,  a TBC-domain containing ciliary protein which plays a crucial role in ciliary function and development, particularly in the retina and brain.  The encoded protein is involved in sonic hedgehog signaling (shh), which stabilizes cell cycle-related kinase Ccrk. Together with CDK20, it controls the structure of the primary cilium by coordinating assembly of the ciliary membrane and axoneme, allowing GLI2 to be properly activated in response to Shh signaling. Ciliopathies describe a heterogeneous group of disorders resulting from abnormal ciliary function or structure. *TBC1D32* was first reported in association with autosomal recessive Oral-Facial-Digital Syndrome Type IX in 2020 (PMID: 32573025), Oral-Facial-Digital Syndrome Type IX is characterized by a severe ciliopathy phenotype with clinical features of midline cleft, microcephaly, and colobomatous microphthalmia/anophthalmia with variable presence of polydactyly, absent pituitary and congenital heart disease. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level and experimental data. 11 variants (including missense, nonsense, splice site and frameshift) reported in 10 probands from 4 publications have been included in this curation (PMID:24285566, 32573025, 32060556, 36826837). Additional clinical evidence can be found in the literature (PMID:37768732; doi.org/10.5734/JGM.2021.18.1.64). These variants are reported in homozygous and compound heterozygous states with loss of function as the mechanism of disease. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. Knock-out mouse model (bromi) demonstrates that lack of the *TBC1D32* protein leads to grossly abnormal cilia in which large empty spaces are formed on one side of the axoneme in a pattern that suggests abnormal coordination of axoneme and ciliary membrane growth. *bromi* (Broad-Minded) is an ENU-mutagenesis derived mouse line that is characterized by abnormal brain development, severe microphthalmia and polydactyly (PMID: 20159594, 32060556). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *TBC1D32* related Ciliopathy. This classification is approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 18, 2025.

SCO2 was first linked to Mitochondrial Complex IV Deficiency, Nuclear Type 2 in 1999. Children with these mutations presented with fatal cardioencephalomyopathy often before 2 years of age. However, in 2016 Rebelo et al. identified patients from 2 families with compound heterozygous mutations in SCO2 that associated with early-onset axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth Type 2 (CMT2) associated with copper deficiency. Rebelo et al presented functional evidence that SCO2 and COXII expression was decreased, copper was reduced in patient fibroblasts, and complex IV activity was decreased. Barcia et al. (2019) found a family with two siblings presenting with cerebellar ataxia and progressive peripheral axonal neuropathy. Spectrophotometric analysis of respiratory chain enzymes on skeletal muscle homogenate showed isolated COX deficiency. Gangfu et al (2022) corroborated these findings in a family with two affected brothers presenting with early-onset CMT2 and a novel homozygous missense variant in SCO2. Gangfu et al. showed functional evidence that there was decreased COX activity and proteomic data displaying altered COX subunits. In total, 6 variants from 3 families were scored totaling 4.5 points of genetic evidence. In a mouse model by Yang et al (2010), decreased COX activity was observed in a SCO2 knock in and knock out mouse model. This gave only one point of evidence as the nerve was not examined. Furthermore, Rebelo et al (2016) and Jaksch et al. (2001) show that copper deficiency is a common alteration in SCO2 patients (+0.5 points). Lastly, the SCO2 gene product completes a biochemical function shared with other known CMT2 genes. ATP7A is another CMT2 gene in which recessive variants cause copper dysfunction (+0.5 points). In total, we find 8 points of evidence (5 points from genetic evidence and 3 points from functional evidence) giving SCO2 a moderate classification.

*PTCRA* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Combined Immunodeficiency due to autosomal recessive pre-TCR alpha deficiency (previously IMD26) in 2024 (Materna et al., PMID: 38422122). Combined Immunodeficiency due to autosomal recessive pre-TCR alpha deficiency presents with a highly variable phenotype. Patients have increased susceptibility to recurrent infections, which may be mild or severe and can occur at any age, but often in 20s or 30s, a small or absent thymus, newborn screening positive for decreased TRECs (though may not develop clinical features), and T-cell abnormalities with impaired development of alpha/beta T cells. 7 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, large deletion) that have been reported in 7 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 38422122, 39805825) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 38422122, 10570293, 9208843). Knockout of *Ptcra* in mice result in decreased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. This can be rescued with the expression of *Ptcra* lacking its cytoplasmic tail. Additionally, CD34+ patient cells with loss of function variants do not differentiate into alpha beta T cells at the same rate as control cells do. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *PTCRA* and AR Combined Immunodeficiency due to autosomal recessive pre-TCR alpha deficiency. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP on the meeting date December 18th 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *MYCN* gene is located on chromosome 2 at 2p24.3 and encodes *MYCN*, a basic helix–loop–helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) transcription factor belonging to the MYC family. *MYCN* plays a critical role during embryonic development, particularly in the developing nervous system, where it regulates neural progenitor proliferation, cell-cycle progression, ribosome biogenesis, metabolism, and neuronal migration. *MYCN* was initially associated with Feingold syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by *MYCN* loss-of-function variants, characterised by microcephaly, digital anomalies, gastrointestinal atresia, and intellectual disability. More recently, gain-of-function (GoF) variants in *MYCN* have been identified as the cause of a distinct megalencephaly–polydactyly syndrome, which represents a mirror phenotype to Feingold syndrome. This condition is characterised by megalencephaly or macrocephaly, postaxial polydactyly, cortical thickening, abnormal neuronal migration, developmental delay, and congenital anomalies.

Nishio et al. (2023, PMID: 37710961) and Kato et al. (2019, PMID: 30573562) independently reported affected individuals with heterozygous *MYCN* missense variants clustering within the N-terminal phosphodegron region, including c.173C>T (p.Thr58Met) and c.179C>T (p.Pro60Leu). Five missense variants that have been reported in 5 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 37710961, 30573562) and ClinVar (SCV006277950.1, SCV005391319.1) are included in this curation.
*MYCN* protein levels are tightly controlled through phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, primarily mediated by sequential phosphorylation at Ser62 and Thr58 and recognition by the SCF-FBW7 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Functional studies in non-patient cells demonstrated significantly reduced Thr58 phosphorylation and increased *MYCN* stability for both p.Thr58Met and p.Pro60Leu compared with wild-type *MYCN*, while transcriptional activation of canonical *MYCN* targets such as CCND1 and CCND2 was preserved or enhanced. These findings support a gain-of-function disease mechanism driven by prolonged *MYCN* activity rather than increased intrinsic transcriptional potency. Additional clinical support comes from individuals with nearby missense variants affecting the same regulatory region, including p.Pro44Thr and p.Pro60Ser, reported in ClinVar and diagnostic laboratories, with overlapping phenotypes of macrocephaly, developmental delay, and craniofacial anomalies. Although functional data are limited for these variants, their clustering within the degradation-regulatory domain supports a shared pathogenic mechanism. Experimental evidence further supports this gene–disease relationship including biochemical function, expression, animal model, and functional alterations in non-patient cells (PMIDs: 28969385, 24705253,  30573562, 37710961) 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this  gene–disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date January 7th 2026 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: congenital heart disease with heterotaxy syndrome
disease_original_title: congenital heart disease with heterotaxy syndrome
submitted_as_notes: *ZIC3* was first reported in relation to X-linked recessive congenital heart disease with heterotaxy in 2004 (Ware et al., PMID: 14681828). In addition to congenital heart disease, this condition is associated with situs ambiguus (such as impacting the spleen, lungs, and liver). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in inheritance pattern or phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: Congenital heart defects, nonsyndromic, multiple types, 1, X-linked (OMIM: 306955); Heterotaxy, visceral, 1, X-linked (OMIM: 306955); and VACTERL association, X-linked (OMIM: 314390). Fourteen variants (missense, small in-frame insertions, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in at least 14 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 14681828, 23427188, 24123890, 30622330, 36567274) are included in this curation. The maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (2 mouse models; PMIDs: 11959836, 16496285, 23999067). Null mutant mice show embryonic lethality, complex congenital heart disease, and heterotaxy. Hypomorphic mutant mice show complex congenital heart disease, heterotaxy, and minimal embryonic lethality. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ZIC3* and X-linked recessive congenital heart disease with heterotaxy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date 10/7/2025 (SOP Version 11).

*PIP5K1C* encodes phosphatidylinositol phosphate kinase type 1 gamma (PIP5KIγ), which phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) to produce phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), a membrane lipid that plays essential roles in multiple cellular processes in the brain. *PIP5K1C* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant PIP5K1C-related neurodevelopmental disorder in 2023 (Morleo et al., PMID: 37451268). Affected individuals present with developmental delay, intellectual disability, acquired microcephaly, seizures, visual abnormalities, dysmorphic features, and brain MRI abnormalities.

Three *de novo* missense variants that have been reported in 9 probands in one publication (PMID: 37451268) are included in this curation. One variant, p.Tyr221Cys, was identified in 6 unrelated individuals. The three reported variants are located in the catalytic domain of the PIP5KIγ protein kinase. Additional *de novo* missense variants have been reported in individuals with developmental disorders (PMID: 33057194), but they were not included in this curation because there is no functional evidence supporting their pathogenicity. The  mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain of function, resulting in increased PI(4,5)P2 levels. Consistent with this mechanism, increased PI(4,5)P2 levels due to pathogenic mutations in phosphatases that dephosphorylate PI(4,5)P2 have been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including Lowe (*OCRL*) and Joubert (*INPP5E*) syndromes and congenital muscular dystrophy with cataracts and intellectual disability (*INPP5K*) (PMID: 37451268).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including functional alteration in patient cells, shared biochemical function with established disease genes, and zebrafish models expressing patient variants that recapitulate aspects of the human phenotype (PMID: 37451268).

Of note, biallelic variants in *PIP5K1C* leading to loss of function have been reported in relation to autosomal recessive lethal congenital contractural syndrome 3 (PMIDs: 17701898, 38491417). This assertion will be assessed separately.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *PIP5K1C* and autosomal dominant PIP5K1C-related neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This gene-disease pair was originally evaluated by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 7, 2025. It was reevaluated on October 14, 2026 (SOP Version 12). As a result of this reevaluation, no new cases were found but the classification increased from Strong to Definitive because no contradictory evidence has emerged in the three years since the first publication.

*CBFB* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant CBFB-related cleidocranial dysplasia in 2022 (Beyltjens et al., PMID: 36241386). This condition has features of clavicular anomalies (varying from unilateral ‘clavicle bipartita’ to bilateral clavicular aplasia); dental anomalies (including delayed or lack of deciduous teeth eruption and supernumerary teeth); skull abnormalities (such as maxillary hypoplasia); and additional bone anomalies (including delayed bone age and pseudoepiphyses of the metacarpals/metatarsals). Six variants (nonsense, frameshift, splicing, large deletion, and complex rearrangement) that have been reported in at least six probands in two publications (PMIDs: 36241386, 39894570) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse models, biochemical functional evidence; PMIDs: 12434152, 12434156, 25262822). Mouse models show that mutants have delayed bone formation; lack of clavicles; poor bone calcification; cranial defects; and severely inhibited osteoblast differentiation and chondrocyte maturation. Biochemical functional evidence shows that the gene is key in RUNX protein family stability and osteoblast/chondrocyte differentiation. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CBFB* and autosomal dominant CBFB-related cleidocranial dysplasia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 2/19/2026 (SOP Version 12).

*GIGYF1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2015 (Krumm et al, PMID: 25961944). Individuals with variants in *GIGYF1* have been reported with neurodevelopmental delays and/or autism spectrum disorder; however, individuals with similar variants have also been observed in the general population or in reportedly unaffected parents of affected individuals. Deep phenotyping of parents in these studies is often unavailable. Twenty six de novo variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in 26 affected probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 33057194, 36924980, 31452935, 31981491, 25961944, 28135719) are included in this curation. In view of an uncertain disease mechanism, a tolerance to heterozygous loss-of-function in population databases, and lack of detail on phenotypic features in the large cohort papers referenced, all loss-of-function variants were downgraded from 1.5 points to 0.5 points.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models (PMIDs: 35917186 and 36924980). Heterozygous mouse models showed anxiety and impaired social behaviors, suggestive of autistic behaviors (PMIDs: 35917186 and 36924980). Knockout zebrafish models showed behaviors of anxiety and impaired social interactions, also consistent with autistic behaviors (PMID: 36924980).

While the relationship between *GIGYF1* and complex neurodevelopmental disorder has been replicated over time resulting in a Definitive classification, the extent of reduced penetrance and variable expressivity is currently unknown (PMID: 35917186). This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism GCEP on the meeting date September 14, 2023 (SOP Version 10).

MBD4 (Methyl-CpG Binding Domain 4) was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant uveal melanoma in 2020 (Repo et al., PMID: 32421892). MBD4 is located on chromosome 3q21.3 and has an MBD region at the N-terminus that attaches to methylated DNA and plays a part in protein interactions. It also has a C-terminal mismatch-specific glycosylase region that plays a role in DNA repair. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities, uveal melanoma (OMIM: 606660) and tumor predisposition syndrome 2 (OMIM: 619975). The split curation for autosomal recessive tumor predisposition syndrome 2 has been curated separately. 12 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splicing) that have been reported in at least 10 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 32421892, 38060262) are included in this curation. Additional variants in two case-control studies were included (PMIDs: 32239153, 32421892). One study showed enrichment of loss-of-function variants in affected patients compared to controls (PMID: 32239153), while the other showed no such enrichment of this variant type (PMID: 32421892). Thus, only the former study was scored. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse model, functional alteration, biochemical function, interaction evidence; PMIDs: 17285135, 27086921, 32239153, 37957685). Experimental evidence shows that the gene plays a role in mismatch repair, tumor prevention, and protection from tissue injury. The MBD4 protein is shown to form a complex with MLH1 and PMS2, both of which are definitively associated with autosomal recessive Mismatch Repair Cancer Syndrome and autosomal dominant Lynch Syndrome. This complex is key in DNA mismatch repair (PMID: 37957685). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively. This classification was kept at moderate due to a study with conflicting case-control data (PMID: 32421892). This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cancer GCEP on the meeting date 02/27/2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ATN1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) in 1994 (Koide R *et al.* PMID:8136840 and Burke JR *et al.* PMID: 7951323). Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder caused expanded CAG repeats in the ATN1 gene, with affected individuals commonly reported to have 48 or more repeat units (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK583218/). In 2019, *ATN1* was reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital hypotonia, epilepsy, developmental delay, digit abnormalities (CHEDDA) (Palmer E. *et al.* PMID: 30827498). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into separate disease entities: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (MIM 125370) and Congenital Hypotonia, Epilepsy, Developmental delay, and digital anomalies (MIM 618494). This curation is to assess the relationship between *ATN1* and DRPLA. The split curation for *ATN1*-related CHEDDA will be assessed separately.
 
Although *ATN1*-related DRPLA is most prevalent in the Japanese population (PMID: 36809552), affected individuals from other ethnic populations outside of Japan have been reported (PMIDs: 7951323, 9251070, 12925365, 34022586, 37243799 and doi:10.1016/j.jns.2019.10.1486). Individuals affected by DRPLA with homozygous *ATN1* CAG repeats and family history of consanguinity have been reported separately by Sato *et. al.* in 1995 and by Kurohara *et al.* in 1997 (PMIDs: 7477999 and 9109905), however, they were not included in this curation as there not been any recent reports of autosomal recessive cases of *ATN1*-related DRPLA and the majority of DRPLA patients reported in the literature showed heterozygous pathogenic expanded CAG repeats in *ATN1*, indicative of autosomal dominant inheritance. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be dominant negative mechanism as the expansion of polyglutamine residues in atrophin-1 impacts caspase cleavage of ATN1 and subsequent separation of N-terminal and C-terminal, resulting in C-terminal fragment mislocalization and pathogenic accumulation in the cytoplasm, ultimately leading to increased cellular toxicity in neurons (PMIDs: 21577324, 23933208). Seventeen *ATN1* expanded CAG variants with allele sizes over 48 repeats that have been reported in seventeen probands in nine publications (PMIDs: 7951323, 8136840, 9251070, 12925365, 28432641, 34022586, 37243799, 39181274, 40552560) are included in this curation. In addition, pathogenic expanded CAG repeats in *ATN1* have been reported to segregate with DRPLA in families (PMIDs: 7951323 and 39181274). 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal and rescue models, tissue expression and in vitro studies (PMIDs: 22342974, 23715323, 34968706, 39921111). Transgenic mice and drosophila models displayed ataxia and reduction in mobility similar to human DRPLA patients (PMIDs: 22342974 and 39921111). Rescue experiments involving intracerebroventricular infusion of a CAG-specific small molecule, naphthyridine–azaquinolone, induced CAG repeat contraction in the striatum, diminished mutant ATN1 aggregation, reduced body weight loss, and improved motor coordination and balance in transgenic Q113 ATN1 mice (PMID: 34968706). Bulk tissue gene expression data from the GTEx Portal indicates *ATN1* is highly expressed in the brain among other tissues (PMID: 23715323, dbGaP Accession phs000424.v10.p2). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ATN1* and autosomal dominant DRPLA. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataxia GCEP on the meeting date May 13, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

ELP1 was first reported in relation to Autosomal Recessive Familial Dysautonomia (FD) in 2001 (Anderson et al, PMID: 11179021; Slaugenhaupt, PMID: 11179008). At least 2 missense variants and 1 splice region variant have been reported in humans. The splice region variant, c.2204+6T>C, is a founder variant in the Ashkenazi Jewish (AJ) population, found in >99.5% of patients with the disease. A common ancestral haplotype (FD major haplotype) is shared among all these individuals. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level and experimental data. 

Variants in this gene have been reported in more than 32 probands in 3 publications (PMID: 11179021, 11179008, 12687659). All individuals except one were of AJ extraction. The one other individual had one parent who was AJ and had the splice region variant.
   
The mechanism for disease is expected to be haploinsufficiency. Individuals with FD have the defective ELP1 protein, but also express the wild-type. There is tissue-specific expression of variant ELP1 in neuronal tissues, where the amount of wild-type ELP1 is lesser than the threshold for normal cell function and development. 
  
This gene-disease association is supported by functional evidence from expression in non-patient cells, animal models, rescue evidence in animal models and humans. The development of a mouse model for FD was a result of several attempts. Knock-out of Elp1 in mice was embryonic lethal. Introducing the splice region variant in the mouse genome did not cause a disruption in Elp1, perhaps due to better splicing efficiency in mice. Introducing the human FD transgene reproduced the splicing defect in mice; however, no FD phenotype was observed due to the expression of endogenous mouse Elp1. The FD phenotype was recapitulated when the human FD transgene was introduced in Elp1-Δ20/flox mice (PMID: 26769677, 22922231). The plant cytokinin, Kinetin, is shown to mitigate the splicing defect and increase the expression of wild-type ELP1 mRNA in humans and mouse models. Human wild-type ELP1 was also shown to rescue embryonic lethality in Elp1-knockout mice. Additionally, a transcriptomic analysis (PMID: 38698036) of neuronal tissues in a relevant ELP1 mouse model found significantly more differentially expressed genes in the peripheral nervous system involved in peptidergic nociceptors and myelinated sensory neurons. Both relevant in the disease mechanism of familial dysautonomia.

In summary, this gene-disease relationship is classified moderate; however, since most of the affected individuals have the same founder variant, scoring them additively will result in this gene-disease relationship being definitive.  While more evidence regarding this gene-disease relationship will strengthen the classification, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.

*NKACP1*L was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive immunodeficiency 72 with autoinflammation in 2020 simultaneously by three separate authors (PMIDs: 32646852, 32647003, 32766723). Patients reported with this disorder can have recurrent bacterial infections, antibody abnormalities, lymphoproliferation, atopy, autoimmune disease and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. Seven missense variants have been reported in nine probands in three publications are included in this curation. The heterozygous parents all appear unaffected. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. NKACP1L encodes for HEM-1, a haematopoietic linage-restricted protein. A review on the function of HEM-1 can be found in PMID: 3902667. Experimental data includes functional studies (PMIDs: 32646852, 32647003, 32766723), mouse model (PMID: 32646852) and rescue in cultured cell lines (PMIDs: 32646852, 32647003). More experimental evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence experimental evidence (6 pts.) has been reached. 
In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.
This classification was approved by the ClinGen PIRD GCEP on the meeting date 9th of June 2026 (SOP Version 12).
In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.
This classification was approved by the ClinGen PIRD GCEP on the meeting date 9th of June 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: congenital heart disease with heterotaxy syndrome
disease_original_title: congenital heart disease with heterotaxy syndrome
submitted_as_notes: *NODAL* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital heart disease with heterotaxy syndrome in 1997 (Gebbia et al., PMID: 9354794). This gene has been associated with isolated congenital heart disease and heterotaxy, visceral, 5, autosomal. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanisms, inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the two entities have been lumped into one disease entity. At least 12 unique variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site) have been reported in 14 probands in seven publications (PMID: 19064609, 19553149, 19933292, 30293987, 34328347, 34666056, 38605286). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. Some variants were inherited from healthy parents showing approximately 50% penetrance (PMID: 38605286). This gene-disease relationship is supported by biochemical function data showing that NODAL is a crucial signaling molecule belonging to the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily, and animal models recapitulating the disease phenotype (PMID: 17287255, 12231623, 30446628). In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between the *NODAL* gene and autosomal dominant congenital heart disease with heterotaxy syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date August 5th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*GLI3* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant GLI3-related Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Spectrum in 1997 (Kang et al., PMID: 9054938; Radhakrishna et al., PMID: 9354785; and Wild et al., 1997, PMID: 9302279). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no differences in phenotypic variability or inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome (GCPS; OMIM: 175700) and Acrocallosal Syndrome (ACS). Also, there were no differences in phenotypic variability or inheritance pattern. Thus, the following disease assertions were lumped: Pallister-Hall Syndrome (PHS; OMIM: 146510) and Oral-Facial Digital Syndrome (OFDS). However, GCPS/ACS disease entity was split from the PHS/OFDS disease entity due to differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability. The split curation for PHS/OFDS will be curated separately. 8 variants (missense, frameshift, splicing) that have been reported in at least 6 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 22903559, 25606469, 32495660, 34424959) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function (PMID: 22903559). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse models; PMIDs: 1289066, 1322743, 8387379). Mutant mice display anomalies like preaxial and post axial polydactyly; interfrontal skull bone; and reduced GLI3 expression. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *GLI3* and autosomal dominant GLI3-related Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Spectrum. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 3/19/2026 (SOP Version 12).

*GCK* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant (AD) monogenic diabetes in 1992 (Froguel et al., PMID: 1545870). This disease entity is often referred to as maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) 2 (MODY2) and *GCK*-MODY, as well as *GCK*-associated hyperglycemia. *GCK* encodes the glucokinase protein, which acts as a glucose sensor that regulates insulin secretion in response to rising blood glucose levels. *GCK*-related hyperglycemia is characterized by lifelong, stable, mild fasting hyperglycemia that falls in the impaired fasting glucose to low diabetic range (HbA1c: 5.6-7.6% and fasting glucose: 100-144 mg/dL) and generally neither responds to nor requires treatment. Furthermore, individuals exhibit a normal response to a glucose load, and generally have a much lower prevalence of the vascular complications that are often associated with diabetes (PMID: 24430320). 

We have curated the inheritance pattern for *GCK*-related monogenic diabetes as semidominant because hyperglycemia due to GCK deficiency follows a dosage-dependent pattern. Individuals harboring a heterozygous pathogenic loss of function variant display the mild fasting hyperglycemia phenotype described above, whereas the presence of biallelic pathogenic loss of function variants results in permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM). PNDM is a more severe presentation characterized by insulin-requiring hyperglycemia with onset occurring within the first six months of life and is often associated with intrauterine growth restriction and low birth weight. It is often found in families of individuals with PNDM, that upon closer evaluation, the parents of the affected individual are found to have mild fasting hyperglycemia, consistent with *GCK*-related hyperglycemia.  As such, a semidominant mode of inheritance was selected for this curation, and evidence from families displaying both autosomal dominant and recessive forms of inheritance were included. The mechanism for both *GCK*-related hyperglycemia and PNDM is loss-of-function. Of note, there are also some reports of individuals harboring biallelic *GCK* variants that are diagnosed with diabetes outside the neonatal period (PMID: 24001579, 25015100, 31197960). 

Numerous variants in *GCK* have been reported in association with *GCK*-related hyperglycemia and PNDM, including missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splicing. Evidence supporting the association of *GCK* with monogenic diabetes includes case level data, segregation data, and experimental data. The aggregated score for genetic evidence, including case-level and segregation data is 12 points. For the purposes of this summary, 25 variants in GCK in 24 probands from 16 publications have been curated: 11 with AD GCK-related hyperglycemia,10 with AR PNDM, and 3 with AR non-neonatal diabetes (PMIDs: 1570017, 11372010, 14578306, 15644838, 18571549, 21104275, 21518409, 23085272, 24001579, 25015100, 25555642, 25850297, 26587058, 27269892, 27289208, 31197960). Additionally, literature describing *GCK* segregation data within families was evaluated (PMIDs: 1545870, 1570017, 11372010, 14578306, 18571549, 21104275, 21518409, 23085272, 26587058, 27269892). More evidence is available to support the gene-disease association in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached, this literature has not been curated exhaustively. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (total 6 points), including expression studies, animal models, and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 7665557, 1354782, 1557365, 17353190, 23715323, 24309898). 

In summary, *GCK* is definitively associated with semidominant monogenic diabetes, including AD *GCK*-related hyperglycemia and AR PNDM. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting working group, we found differences in molecular mechanisms, inheritance patterns, and phenotypic variability underlying the *GCK*-related disease entities. autosomal dominant maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) 2 (MIM:125851) and autosomal recessive permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (MIM:606176) have been lumped together into the current curation because of the overlapping underlying molecular mechanism (loss-of-function *GCK* variants. Familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, type 3 (MIM:602485) has been split into a separate curation due to the difference in underlying molecular mechanism (heterozygous activating *GCK* variants) and phenotype. Type 2 diabetes (polygenic; MIM:125853) will not be curated since the contribution of *GCK* in these instances is the result of common variants with a small effect.

*DENND5B*  encodes a DENN domain-containing guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for Rab proteins, which are key regulators of intracellular vesicular trafficking. *DENND5B* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2024 (Scala et al., PMID: 38387458) in 5 individuals with *de novo* missense variants. Clinical features were variable and included developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, facial dysmorphism, abnormal behavior (including autism spectrum disorder), early-onset epilepsy, white matter abnormalities, and cortical gyration defects.

Seven  variants (6 missense and 1 splice region) that have been reported in 7 probands in 1 publication (PMID: 38387458) are included in this curation. Five of the variants occurred *de novo* and two were of unknown inheritance. All the *de novo* variants are within or in close proximity to the DENN and RUN1 domains. Only three missense variants with functional evidence of pathogenicity were scored at full points.  The three variants in the RUN1 domain showed decreased protein levels (possibly due to disrupted protein folding), and defective intracellular vesicle trafficking, with impaired lipid uptake and distribution (PMID: 38387458). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function. Another member of the DENN domain Rab family of GDP-GTP exchange factors, *DENND5A*, is involved in a neurodevelopmental disorder with overlapping phenotype.

In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *DENND5B* and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.  This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel  on May 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to CDKN1C mutation
disease_original_title: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to CDKN1C mutation
submitted_as_notes:
CDKN1C (cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 1C), also known as p57Kip2, was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) with parent‑of‑origin effects in 1996 (PMID: 8841187). CDKN1C is located at chromosome 11p15.5 and encodes a cyclin‑dependent kinase inhibitor that plays a key role in regulating cell‑cycle progression and cellular proliferation. CDKN1C is a maternally expressed imprinted gene, with the paternal allele normally silenced. Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome is a congenital overgrowth disorder characterized by prenatal and/or postnatal macrosomia, macroglossia, abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, umbilical hernia), visceromegaly, neonatal hypoglycemia, and ear creases or pits. Individuals with Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome are also at increased risk for embryonal tumors in childhood. Per ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group criteria, disorders associated with CDKN1C were split into separate disease entities. Loss‑of‑function or silencing of the maternally inherited allele causes Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome(OMIM:130650), whereas gain‑of‑function variants,typically affecting the PCNA‑binding domain,cause growth‑restriction phenotypes such as IMAGe syndrome(OMIM:614732) or, more rarely, Silver‑Russell syndrome (OMIM:180860). These conditions differ with respect to molecular mechanism, inheritance, and phenotypic presentation and are therefore curated separately.
13  pathogenic variants in CDKN1C have been reported in individuals with Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome across independent publications (PMIDs:39502854, 20503313, 11106355, 34065128, and 8841187). The variant spectrum includes nonsense, frameshift, splice‑altering, and deleterious missense variants, consistent with loss of gene function. Pathogenic variants are associated with disease only when maternally inherited, consistent with the imprinted expression of CDKN1C. Segregation of maternally inherited CDKN1C variants with Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome has been demonstrated in multiple families, while paternal inheritance does not result in phenotype(PMID: 19550435). More genetic evidence supporting this relationship is available in the literature; however, the maximum score for genetic evidence has been reached. The mechanism of disease is loss of function of the maternally expressed CDKN1C allele, leading to reduced or absent p57Kip2 activity and subsequent dysregulation of cell‑cycle control during development(PMID: 19550435). This can occur through coding loss‑of‑function variants as well as through epigenetic silencing of CDKN1C, most commonly in the context of imprinting defects at the IC2/KvDMR1 region. This gene disease relationship is further supported by extensive experimental evidence. CDKN1C expression is reduced or absent in patient‑derived cells from individuals with Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome, including cases without identifiable coding variants, and chromatin immunoprecipitation studies demonstrate enrichment of repressive chromatin marks at the CDKN1C promoter in patient cells (PMIDs: 16061564, 14627666, and 26077438). In vitro functional studies show loss of protein function and abnormal cellular localization for Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome–associated variants(PMIDs: 26077438,10323243 and 11106355). Mouse models with targeted disruption of the maternally inherited CDKN1C allele exhibit prenatal overgrowth, organomegaly, skeletal abnormalities, and perinatal lethality, whereas disruption of the paternal allele alone does not result in abnormal phenotype, reflecting the parent‑of‑origin effects observed in humans (PMIDs: 9136926, 17517131, and 8646780). Additional experimental evidence exists in the literature, but the maximum score for experimental evidence has been reached.
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CDKN1C and autosomal dominant Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.
This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hereditary Cancer Gene Curation Expert Panel on [04/24/2026] (SOP Version 12).

CHRNA1 Related Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome is a clinically variable syndrome resulting from functional abnormalities of the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction.  The CHRNA1 gene encodes the alpha subunit of the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR), a membrane spanning protein channel that controls signaling between nerve and muscle cells.   Both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant patterns of inheritance are observed. The autosomal recessive disease is due to absence or severely reduced protein expression which in turn reduces the number of nACh receptors, or functional alterations that limit channel opening time. The autosomal dominant disease is the result of prolonged opening and activity of the channel.  The autosomal dominant disease is curated separately. 
 
Clinical features of autosomal recessive disease vary from mild to severe.  Null variants or missense variants that result in severely reduced expression cause more severe features often with prenatal onset that can include fetal akinesia deformation sequence with joint contractures and pterygia, growth restriction, polyhydramnios, and fetal hydrops. Neonates have profound hypotonia and respiratory distress, requiring respiratory support and gavage feeding. Those with residual protein or variants that reduce channel opening time have a broader range of clinical symptoms that include muscle weakness, increased fatigability, facial diplegia, weakess of the ocular muscles, and ptosis.  
 
We have curated 16 variants in CHRNA1 (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice variants, deletion) across 8 publications (PMIDs: 36092864, 33756069, 24121633, 18806275, 18252226, 12588888, 10195214, 22728938). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. The gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence showing reduced CHRNA1 expression and activity in patient cells, reduced CHRNA1 activity in NEK cells transfected with specific CHRNA1 variants, animal models including homozygous null variants which are lethal in mice and two separate zebrafish models (PMIDs: 18252226, 9475746, 34077687, 18806275, 24121633, 12588888). In summary, the CHRNA1 gene is definitively associated with autosomal recessive CHRNA1 Related Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome.  This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Prenatal GCEP on the meeting date May 15, 2024 (SOP Version 10).

*NR5A1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant NR5A1-related sex development disorder in 1999 (Achermann et al., PMID: 10369247). Pathogenic variants in *NR5A1* (encoding Steroidogenic Factor 1, SF-1) cause a wide clinical spectrum of reproductive and endocrine dysfunction. In 46,XY individuals, this ranges from complete sex reversal with female external genitalia and Müllerian structures to milder forms of under-virilization such as hypospadias or isolated infertility. In 46,XX individuals, the most frequent manifestation is primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) (PMID: 21078366). Although SF-1 is essential for adrenal development, clinical adrenal insufficiency is observed in only a minority of cases. The condition is characterized by autosomal dominant inheritance with notable phenotypic variability and incomplete penetrance.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: 46XX sex reversal 4 (OMIM:617480), 46XY sex reversal 3 (OMIM:612965), premature ovarian failure 7/adrenocortical insufficiency (OMIM:612964), spermatogenic failure 8 (OMIM:613957). 

Nineteen variants (including missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in 27 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 27378692, 20887963, 23299922, 40882352, 37409232, 29027299) are included in this curation. The genetic evidence for *NR5A1* includes variants that are distributed across critical functional domains of the protein, specifically the Zinc-finger DNA-binding domain (DBD) and the Ligand-binding domain (LBD). Multiple de novo occurrences have been documented in individuals with severe 46,XY differences of sex development (DSD) and adrenal insufficiency, providing strong evidence for pathogenicity. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. 

Segregation of *NR5A1* variants with disease have been demonstrated in multiple families, with affected individuals showing variable expressivity ranging from complete 46,XY sex reversal and adrenal insufficiency to milder phenotypes such as hypospadias, infertility, or isolated primary ovarian insufficiency in 46,XX individuals. Reduced and incomplete penetrance has also been observed (PMID: 33296094), consistent with prior reports and known biological roles of SF-1 in gonadal and adrenal development. Notably, the same heterozygous variant may result in 46,XY sex reversal in a proband while being present in a fertile, phenotypically 'normal' father (PMID: 27378692). Despite this variability, the enrichment of rare, damaging variants in affected cohorts compared to population databases (e.g., gnomAD) strongly supports the association.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including animal models, expression studies, and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 9774680, 11124111, 26269506, 22419830, 18703422, 8187173, 37494420).  *NR5A1* encodes steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1), a nuclear receptor that regulates adrenal and gonadal development and steroidogenic function (PMID: 20595937). Consistent with this role, Nr5a1 knockout in mice causes complete adrenal and gonadal agenesis, leading to 46,XY sex reversal with female external genitalia and presence of Müllerian structures (PMID: 18987494). At the molecular level, SF-1 cooperates with SRY-related factor SOX9 to activate Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) transcription in Sertoli cells (PMID: 9774680), a crucial step for Müllerian duct regression during male differentiation. 

SF-1 function is dosage-sensitive, as demonstrated by hypomorphic mouse models. Nr5a1 mutant male mice with partial SF-1 expression show signs of androgen insufficiency – including cryptorchidism, impaired spermatogenesis, and undervirilized genitalia – due to disrupted Leydig cell development (PMID: 26269506). In females, SF-1 is essential for ovarian function: granulosa cell-specific SF-1 knockout mice have hypoplastic ovaries with reduced follicle number, absent corpora lutea, and infertility (PMID: 18703422), and prenatal ovarian depletion of SF-1 dramatically reduces the primordial follicle reserve by increasing oocyte loss (PMID: 37494420). These findings establish SF-1’s critical role in forming the ovarian reserve and correlate with 46,XX primary ovarian insufficiency observed in *NR5A1*-haploinsufficient women. Finally, functional assays of patient-derived *NR5A1* variants support their loss-of-function impact: several missense mutations identified in 46,XY DSD or idiopathic male infertility significantly impair SF-1’s transcriptional activity on target promoters in vitro (PMID: 20887963). Together, this experimental evidence solidifies the role of *NR5A1* in adrenal and gonadal development and links its dysfunction to disorders of sex development, adrenal insufficiency, ovarian failure, and infertility.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *NR5A1* and NR5A1-related sex development disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on January 21, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

UFM1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy in 2017 (Hamilton et al., PMID: 28931644). The authors described the disorder as a recessive variant of hypomyelination with atrophy of the basal ganglia and cerebellum (H-ABC), and the entity was catalogued in OMIM as hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 14. The UFM1 gene encodes for the ubiquitin-like protein Ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1). UFM1 has been reported to be involved in processes such as managing ER function, including selective autophagy of the ER, and the maintenance of p53 stability (Komatsu et al. 2024, PMID: 38141606). Affected individuals have global developmental delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly, growth impairments including short stature, drug resistant seizures, cerebellar hypoplasia, delayed CNS myelination and/or hypomyelination, and basal ganglia anomalies (PMID: 35189806). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. 

Two unique variants, 1 promoter region deletion variant and 1 missense variant, have been reported in the homozygous state in 30 probands across 6 publications and are included in this curation (PMID: 28931644, 29868776, 34573312, 35189806, 36082649, 33807868). Both variants have supporting functional data. The recurrent promoter region deletion variant NM_001286704.1: c.-273_-271delTCA has been reported to be a founder variant in the Roma population. Variants in this gene have segregated with disease across multiple relatives across multiple families (PMID: 28931644, 29868776). The mechanism of pathogenicity is still being researched, but these variants have been reported to cause disease through a hypomorphic effect (PMID: 28931644, 29868776).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including protein interaction evidence, a mouse model, and a drosophila model (28931644, 29868776, 27545674, 31914610). Hamilton et al. used a luciferase activity assay to show that the founder mutation significantly reduced promoter and transcriptional activity in neuronal cell lines (SY5Y neuroblastoma and U373 astroglioma), but not in HeLa and HOG-F2 oligodendroglioma cell lines (PMID: 28931644). Nahorski et al. performed various assays that illustrated a hypomorphic effect of the founder mutation on the ability of UFM1 to interact with its conjugates, including its E1 enzyme (UBA5) and E2 enzyme (UFC1)  (PMID: 29868776). Muona et al. generated CNS-specific Ufm1 knockout mice to show that impaired UFM1 function results in similar effects of conjugate formation disruption, as well as neonatal death, microcephaly, and apoptosis in specific neurons (PMID: 27545674). Yu et al. used RNA interference of UFM1 as well as other proteins in the UFM1 cascade to discover that dysfunction of the cascade in Drosophila results in overall decreased brain volume, a reduced number of neuroblasts, disruption of cell cycle progression/processes (PMID: 31914610).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between UFM1 variants and leukodystrophy, hypomyelinating, 14 (MONDO:0033486), also known as UFM1-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy gene curation expert panel on the meeting date 3/22/2026 (SOP Version 12).

Biallelic SPINK5 germline loss-of-function variants were first identified in families with Netherton syndrome (NS) in 2000 (PMID: 10835624). SPINK5 deficiency is associated with a classic clinical triad of congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, trichorrhexis invaginata (bamboo hair), and severe atopic manifestations. Clinical defects are multisystemic and frequently include life-threatening hypernatremic dehydration in the neonatal period, failure to thrive, severe skin inflammation, enteropathy, and markedly elevated serum IgE levels accompanied by hypereosinophilia and severe allergies. Most curated pathogenic variants are nonsense, frameshift, or splice-site variants predicted to result in loss of function.
