Multiple unique variants from individuals across multiple publications have been curated (PMID: 11511292, 37102386, 41611084, 24577329). Heterozygous carriers of pathogenic SPINK5 loss-of-function variants do not develop Netherton syndrome. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence has been reached (12 pts).
	Studies examining SPINK5 function utilize patient-derived cells and skin biopsy tissues to support this gene-disease relationship. SPINK5 encodes the lympho-epithelial Kazal-type-related inhibitor (LEKTI), a multidomain serine protease inhibitor primarily expressed in the outer granular layer of stratified epithelial tissues. In healthy skin, LEKTI inhibits the activity of epidermal serine proteases, such as kallikreins KLK5, KLK7, and KLK14, which are essential for physiological desquamation and epidermal remodeling (PMID: 17596512). LEKTI has been shown to be expressed in healthy human epidermis but is absent in patients harboring bi-allelic pathogenic SPINK5 variants (PMID:12915442). In vitro functional data demonstrates that this deficiency causes increased epidermal protease hyperactivity, which leads to the premature cleavage of desmosomes, specifically via the rapid degradation of desmoglein (PMID:17989726, 16628198). Mouse models of SPINK5 deficiency replicate the key clinical features of human Netherton syndrome. These animals exhibit altered desquamation, impaired keratinization, hair malformations, severe skin barrier defects, and high postnatal mortality due to dehydration and skin-barrier failure (PMID: 15619623, 38316920). In summary, SPINK5 is definitively associated with autosomal recessive Netherton syndrome. This association is supported by extensive human genetic evidence, functional studies in patient-derived tissues and cells, biochemical data demonstrating LEKTI-dependent inhibition of epidermal kallikreins, and mouse models recapitulating key features of the human disease. This association has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.

This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID Working Group  on 5/21/2026 (SOP Version 11).

*SYCE1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive SYCE1-related gametogenic failure in 2014 (de Vries et al., PMID: 25062452). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: premature ovarian failure (OMIM: 616947) and spermatogenic failure (OMIM:616950). 

Five variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in five probands in three publications (PMIDs: 25899990, 25062452, 40936058) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is believed to be biallelic loss of function (PMID: 25062452). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, expression studies, and in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 32917591, 19247432, 33508233, 32402064, 32402064).  

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *SYCE1* and SYCE1-related gametogenic failure. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on April 15, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*CYP26B1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive lethal occipital encephalocele-skeletal dysplasia syndrome in 2011 (Laue et al., PMID: 22019272). This condition is often associated with intrauterine fetal demise, stillbirth, or neonatal death. However, probands may survive into adolescence or adulthood. Features of this condition include craniosynostosis (such as coronal, lambdoid, or sagittal); facial anomalies (like midface retrusion, frontal bossing, brachycephaly, and small ears); delayed ossification; digit anomalies (like oligodactyly or long/slender fingers and toes); narrow thorax; radiohumeral fusions; hearing loss; and respiratory issues. Nine variants (missense, splicing) that have been reported in at least seven probands in four publications (PMIDs: 22019272, 27410456, 34160123, 37755482) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function (PMID: 22019272). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse and zebrafish models; PMIDs: 15030763, 22019272). Mouse and zebrafish models show that CYP26B1 deficiency leads to skeletal anomalies like short limbs and inappropriate joint fusion; improper skeletal patterning during development; reduced body size; and craniosynostosis. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date 2/19/2026 (SOP Version 12).

*DDX59* encodes a putative RNA helicase and it was first reported in relation to ciliopathy-*DDX59* in 2013 (Shamseldin et al., PMID: 23972372). This disorder is characterized by abnormalities of the face, oral cavity, and digits, in addition to intellectual disability and various organ abnormalities including heart, kidney, and gastrointestinal tract (PMIDs: 23972372, 28711741, 29127725). While the exact biological function of *DDX59* remains unknown, a recent study provided strong biochemical evidence suggesting that *DDX59* is a bona fide ATP-dependent helicase (Ekumi, K.M., 2020, Master’s Thesis, Univ. of Saskatchewan).

Four variants (two missense, one frameshift, and one stop loss) reported in five probands across three publications were included in this curation. Experimental evidence consisting of expression data and functional alteration data from patient and non-patient cells were scored toward case-level evidence. The scored expression data include the detection of *Ddx59* in the developing palate, lips, and limb buds of mouse embryos by in-situ hybridization, and detection by immunoblotting of decreased steady-state levels of *DDX59* protein from patient derived fibroblasts harboring a homozygous missense variant (PMID: 23972372). The scored functional alteration data include partially defective Sonic hedgehog signaling as evidenced by a decrease in GLI transcriptional activation in patient derived fibroblasts (PMID: 23972372) and cilia formation defects in cell lines harboring a *DDX59* missense variant introduced by CRISPR- genome editing (Ekumi, K.M., 2020, Master’s Thesis, Univ. of Saskatchewan). Other data that were reviewed but not scored include the biochemical characterization of *DDX59*, which also demonstrated that both missense variants previously identified by Shamsheldin et al. (2013) are essential for *DDX59* helicase activity (Ekumi, K.M., 2020). These biochemical data were not scored because they are intrinsic to the protein function and do not provide direct evidence to support this gene-disease association. 

In summary, there is Limited evidence supporting the relationship between *DDX59* and ciliopathy-*DDX59*. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 06/28/2023 (SOP Version 9).

*KCNJ11*, which encodes the Kir6.2 subunit of the β‐cell ATP‐sensitive potassium channel, was first reported in relation to familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia 2 (OMIM: 601820) in 1996 (Thomas et al., PMID: 8923010). Both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritances have been described in congenital hyperinsulinism for *KCNJ11* variants; in keeping with ClinGen curation practice, these inheritance patterns are evaluated separately. Of note, a subset of cases are caused by paternally inherited heterozygous variants that are usually implicated in recessively inherited congenital hyperinsulinism but in these cases lead to focal disease due to somatic loss-of-heterozygosity within an area of the pancreas, resulting in expression of this AR condition in a histologically focal manner; this has been curated with the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

Individuals with pathogenic *KCNJ11* variants typically present with hypoglycemia due to dysregulated insulin secretion. Autosomal dominant cases, which include missense and other in-frame alterations, typically cause gating defects in channels but do not disrupt the channels’ ability to reach the cell surface, whereas autosomal recessive variants typically cause trafficking defects or severe loss of function where the channels are absent or non-functional (PMIDs: 16332676, 37056678). 

Evidence supporting relationship of this gene with hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia includes case-level data and experimental data. A limited number of confirmed autosomal dominant cases have been identified. For this curation we have scored 10 probands from 5 publications (PMIDs: 31464105, 18596924, 23275527, 31997554, 16332676). While there are additional cases in the literature that may be examples of autosomal dominant inheritance, given the possibility of focal disease we have restricted this curation to cases where the disease is confirmed to be diffuse, and, when variants were paternally inherited, required either functional data consistent with a dominant mechanism (for example, a gating defect in a channel that traffics normally) or informative parental phenotyping. The aggregated score for case and segregation-level data is 5 points. 

This gene–disease relationship is further supported by experimental data. *KCNJ11* is highly expressed in pancreatic β cells, and Kir6.2 has been shown to coimmunoprecipitate and physically associate with SUR1 (encoded by ABCC8), forming the hetero‐octameric channel complex (PMIDs: 8549751, 9488482). Functional studies in cells expressing patient variants have also demonstrated that variants result in reduced intrinsic open probability or other gating abnormalities in channels that reach the plasma membrane, consistent with a dominant loss‐of‐function mechanism (PMIDs: 31464105, 16332676). Total points for experimental evidence are 1. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 6.
Taken together, the available genetic and experimental data support a limited level of evidence for the association of *KCNJ11* with autosomal dominant hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia under the ClinGen gene–disease validity framework. The association of KCNJ11 with autosomal recessive hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and autosomal dominant monogenic diabetes have been split and curated separately. This classification was approved by the Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on April 1st, 2026. Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) - SOP12.

disease_title: polyglucosan body myopathy 1 with or without immunodeficiency
disease_original_title: polyglucosan body myopathy 1 with or without immunodeficiency
submitted_as_notes: *RBCK1* (HOIL-1) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive polyglucosan body myopathy 1 (PGBM1) with or without immunodeficiency in 2012 (Boisson et al., PMID: 23104095). RBCK1 is a part of the LUBAC complex and therefore has a role in NF-kappaB signaling. It is also important in myogenesis, as it is enriched in fast-twitch glycolytic muscle fibers. PGBM1 is characterized by a variable phenotype spectrum, with onset often during childhood though it can be much later in life. The majority of patients present with progressive proximal muscle weakness, resulting in difficulties in ambulation. Many patients develop progressive dilated cardiomyopathy, and a subset present with severe immunodeficiency. 7 unique variants (6 frameshifts leading to early stop, 1 stop-gain) that have been reported in 7 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 29260357, 38588043, 23104095, 38922716, 32187699) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function (PMIDs: 29260357, 38588043, 23104095, 38922716, 32187699).  This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and in vitro functional assays. (PMIDs: 25599590, 23104095, ). Specifically, knockout mouse models with abrogated *Rbck1* expression presented with features of human disease, including increased susceptibility to certain infections and increased PAS-positive deposits (PMID: 25599590). Immortalized patient cells with early stop variants demonstrated impaired NF-kappaB-dependent responses to TNFR families, which aligns with the susceptibility of these patients to invasive pyogenic bacterial disease (PMID: 23104095). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *RBCK1* and autosomal recessive polyglucosan body myopathy 1 (PGBM1) with or without immunodeficiency. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP on the meeting date May 21st, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 2
disease_original_title: cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 2
submitted_as_notes:
STN1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Coats plus syndrome in 2016 (Simon et al., PMID 27432940), which has also been called cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 2 (CRMCC2). Both conditions are characterized by retinal telangiectasia and exudates (Coats disease), leukodystrophy and brain cysts, osteopenia with a tendency to fractures and poor bone healing, and a high risk of life-limiting gastrointestinal bleeding caused by vasculature ectasias in the stomach, small intestine and liver (PMID: 22267198). The STN1 gene encodes STN1 subunit of CST Complex, which functions in a telomere-associated complex with CTC1 and TEN1. The CST complex appears to protect telomeres by inhibiting telomerase activity (PMID 2276344). Coats plus has also been associated with biallelic variants in CTC1 (PMIDs: 22387016, 22267198, 22532422, 30891747). Variants in STN1 have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: Coats plus syndrome, Cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts 2 (CRMCC2). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in molecular mechanisms or inheritance pattern; furthermore we found that the spectrum of phenotypic variability could exist between the described disease entities. Therefore, Coats Plus and CRMCC2 have been lumped into one disease entity, CRMCC2 (MONDO:0015026), also known as STN1-related telomere biology disorder. 
Six variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in at least four probands in three publications are included in this curation (27432940, 34110109, 32627942). The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function (Simon et al., 27432940). This gene-disease relationship is supported by animal models, biochemical function, protein interaction, functional alteration of patient cells (PMIDs 27432940, 19854130, 22964711). A zebrafish STN1-knockdown model demonstrated a similar phenotype to humans with biallelic STN1 variants, with the zebrafish exhibiting telangiectasias and anemia (27432940). Patient fibroblasts when compared to control fibroblasts demonstrated significantly decreased population doublings, however when introduced to exogenous WT STN1 the patient fibroblasts were able to increase population doublings (27432940). STN1 is known to coimmunoprecipitate with CTC1, which has already been implicated in Coats plus (19854130). Finally, it is known that STN1 shares a similar role to CTC1 in that it protects telomeres; when STN1 was knocked down in HeLa cells, there was an increase in telomere breakage, which has also been demonstrated in cells with CTC1 knockdown (22964711, 22531781).
In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date 4/27/26 (SOP Version 12).

BLTP1 (historically KIAA1109) is a non-vesicular lipid transport protein involved in transfer of phospholipids between organelle membranes, with critical roles in synaptic vesicle recycling at the neuromuscular junction [PMID:19640479, 40973493].  Biallelic pathogenic variants in BLTP1 are associated with autosomal recessive Alkuraya-Kucinskas syndrome (MIM#617822; MONDO:0060631), first reported in a neonate with hydrocephalus, pleural effusions, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, micrognathia and neonatal death by Alazami, 2015 [PMID:25558065].  Since its initial report more than 20 probands with biallelic variants in BLTP1 have been reported, some of which segregated with disease in affected individuals [PMID:25558065, 29290337, 30221345, 30906834, 32657846, 38278647, 40206966], with reported variants including missense, nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice, and multi-exon deletions reported, and maximum points for genetic evidence (12pts) has been reached for this curation.  The mechanism of BLTP1-assocaited disorder is proposed to be loss of function, and while there is not a definitive genotype-phenotype correlation both the age of lethality and phenotypic severity are loosely associated to variant severity, with biallelic loss of function (nonsense, frameshift) most often associated with fetal demise or neonatal lethality.  Phenotypes in individuals with Alkuraya-Kucinskas syndrome include prenatal findings of arthrogryposis and variable brain malformations including hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, vermian atrophy, reduced white matter, neuronal migration or gyral defects, anomalies of the pons, cerebellum and brainstem, and agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. Other prenatal findings reported in a subset of affected individuals include cystic hygroma, micrognathia, pleural effusion, and hydrops fetalis.  Neonatal respiratory insufficiency and neonatal death are common in severely affected individuals with developmental delay, intellectual disability, progressive development of contractures with age, seizures, and hypotonia observed in those surviving the neonatal period [PMID:25558065, 29290337, 30221345, 30906834, 32657846, 38278647, 40206966].  Functional evidence including multiple non-animal model organisms support the role of loss of BLTP1 in association with Alkuraya-Kucinskas syndrome (MIM#617822; MONDO: 0060631), and have been scored for an additional 2.5 points.  Given this and its replication in literature over time, the association with BLTP1 (formerly KIAA1109) with Alkuraya-Kucinskas syndrome is curated as Definitive by the Prenatal Gene Curation Expert Panel (Gene-Disease Validity SOPv11) on January 21, 2026.

*TAB2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital heart disease in 2010
(Thienpoint et al, PMID 20493459). At least 14 rare variants (2 missense, 12 loss-of-function) have been reported in humans. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. *TAB2* has been noted to be associated with the following disease entities: atrial septal defect, bicuspid aortic valve, valvular dysplasia, valvular stenosis, and ventricular septal defect (OMIM 160710). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, these disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, *TAB2*-related syndromic congenital heart disease. Variants in this gene have been reported in at least 14 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs 20493459, 27452334, 28386937, 34741306, 34456334, 34995729), using an allele frequency threshold of 1x10-5. This gene-disease relationship is supported by expression studies, animal models, and cellular models. Expression studies confirmed that TAB2 is expressed during zebrafish embryogenesis and human development (PMID 20493459). Zebrafish depletion of tab2 by morpholino led to early cardiac dysfunction and disrupted development (PMID 20493459). Human induced pluripotent stem cell models of cardiac development demonstrated disorganized sarcomeric structure in *TAB2*-deficient cells (PMID 39905300). In summary, *TAB2* is definitively associated with autosomal dominant **TAB2*-related syndromic congenital heart disease. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date January 5th, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *CEP120* gene is located on chromosome 5 at q23.2 and encodes a protein that functions in the microtubule-dependent coupling of the nucleus and the centrosome, which is required for centriole elongation from a procentriole. It expresses in a variety of tissues and organs, including the kidney. Multiple disease entities have been reported in association with this gene. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was no evidence of differences in their molecular mechanism and/or inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity. 

*CEP120* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive ciliopathies in 2015 (Shaheen et al., PMID: 25361962). Clinical presentations include developmental delay, hypotonia, abnormal breathing and eye movements, truncal ataxia, auditory pathway abnormalities, molar tooth sign with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly, and callosal hypoplasia, craniofacial dysmorphism, skeletal anomalies, and renal involvement such as pyelocalyceal dilation, hydronephrosis, or cystic kidneys. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. 

Fifteen variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) have been reported in 14 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 25361962, 37547106, 27208211, 38050708, 37272176, 34930662) and are included in this curation. The maximum genetic evidence was reached, considering case-level data, and functional data. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by non-patient cells, and non-human models. *CEP120* deficiency induces ciliopathies in mice and zebrafish (PMIDs: 37982452, 38177914, 29847808, 25361962). A total of 5/6 points for experimental evidence was reached. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CEP120* and ciliopathy-*CEP120*. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on the meeting date June 25th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

INPPL1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive opsismodysplasia in 2013 (Huber et al., PMID: 23273569; Below et al, PMID: 23273567). Opsismodysplasia is a type of spondylodysplastic skeletal dysplasia that is characterized by pre- and postnatal micromelia with extremely short hands and feet and specific radiological features such as severe platyspondyly, squared metacarpals, delayed skeletal ossification, and metaphyseal cupping. Individuals often have dysmorphic facial features including hypertelorism, frontal bossing, short nose with anteverted nostrils, and a long philtrum. Prenatal findings often include short limbs/long bones, short hands and feet, narrow/bell-shaped thorax, and decreased mineralization. Increased nuchal translucency, cystic hygroma, hydrops, and poly/oligohydramnios have also been reported. Outcomes are variable and range from perinatal lethality to survival into adulthood. The perinatally lethal form is often associated with a narrow/bell-shaped chest with subsequent pulmonary hypoplasia. Twenty-four variants (missense, in-frame indel, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and duplication) that have been reported in 12 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 23273569, 28869677, 34094554) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including in vitro functional assays and rescue models (PMID: 28869677). These studies showed that fibroblasts from OPS patients demonstrate a lack of SHIP2 expression and decreased cell migration. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between INPPL1 and autosomal recessive opsismodysplasia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Prenatal GCEP on the meeting date March 24, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*METTL23* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive intellectual disability in 2014 (PMIDs: 24501276, 24626631). Clinical features consistently reported in affected individuals include intellectual disability, global developmental delay, and various dysmorphic facial features such as a depressed nasal bridge and thin vermilion border (PMID: 39026940).

Six variants (including splicing, frameshift, and a single missense variant) reported in 6 probands across 5 publications (PMIDs: 39026940, 32878022, 32439618, 24501276, 24626631) are included in this curation. The homozygous missense variant lacks functional evidence of pathogenicity and was assigned only 0.2 points. Within three of the families, the variants were found to segregate with disease across 11 individuals (PMIDs: 24626631, 24501276, 32878022).  The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function (PMIDs: 39026940, 24626631). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including protein interactions and functional studies (PMID: 24501276). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *METTL23* and autosomal recessive intellectual disability. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism GCEP on February 17, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The *EVC* gene is located on chromosome 4 at 4p16.2 and encodes the EvC ciliary complex subunit 1. The protein encodes a 992-amino acid protein with a transmembrane domain, 3 nuclear localization signals, and a leucine zipper motif. This protein creates a complex with *EVC2* and is located at the base of the primary cilia to regulate Hedgehog signaling. This *EVC-EVC2* complex is involved in endochondral growth and skeletal development. *EVC* has been shown to be expressed in human embryonic tissue within the developing bone, heart, kidney, and lung (Ruiz-Perez et al., PMID: 10700184). 

Multiple disease entities have been reported in association with this gene, including autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld syndrome  and autosomal dominant Weyers acrofacial dysostosis (WAD). Patients with biallelic *EVC* gene variants have been reported to have features involving short stature and limbs, postaxial polydactyly, dysplastic nails, congenital heart defects, atrial septation, and genitourinary anomalies. Affected individuals may have dental anomalies similar to acrofacial dysostosis.  One case reported by Ruiz-Perez et al. (2000) noted that a child with compound heterozygous variants in *EVC* and features of Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, had one parent clinically described as having features of WAD with a heterozygous *EVC* variant. There are no additional cases describing an individual with a heterozygous *EVC* variant being affected. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was no evidence of differences in the molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, or phenotypic spectrum. Therefore, these disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld syndrome: MONDO:0009162.

The *EVC* gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld syndrome in 1964 (McKusick et al., PMID: 14217223). At least 30 variants (nonsense, frameshift, missense, splice site) have been reported in 28 probands across 3 publications (PMIDs: 10700184, 23220543, 34930662). The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function. A maximum score of 12 points for genetic evidence was reached, considering case-level data and segregation data. The literature contains additional case reports. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression studies and animal models. The scored expression data include the detection of cloned *EVC* in human embryonic bone, heart, kidney, and lung in human embryonic tissue at Carnegie stages 19 and 21 (Ruiz et al., PMID: 10700184). In addition, another expression study noted cloned mouse *EVC* being expressed strongest in the secondary heart field (Sund et al., PMID: 19251731). A mouse model for Ellis-van Creveld syndrome was created and *EVC* knockout mice were observed to develop shortened ribs, shortened limbs, and dental abnormalities (Ruiz-Perez et al., PMID: 17660199). This study also demonstrated that with the loss of *EVC* the downstream Ptch1 and Gli1 genes had reduced expression and caused Hedgehog signaling defects. Another mouse model created by Nakatomi et al. (PMID: 23315474) found that the absence of *EVC* caused varying defects in molar tooth development. Finally, a mouse model created by Caparros-Martin et al. (PMID: 23026747) investigated *EVC* knockout and *EVC2* knockout mice (single and double homozygous mutants). The skeletal phenotypes between these mouse models were indistinguishable. This study also noted that the *EVC* and *EVC2* complex are mutually required for expression in the cilium and promote Hedgehog signaling that is necessary for normal endochondral bone formation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for experimental evidence (6 points) has been reached.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *EVC* and autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on the meeting date September 24th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

submitted_as_notes: *BLOC1S1* (Biogenesis of Lysosome-Related Organelles Complex 1 Subunit 1) is located at chromosome 12 at 12q13.2 and encodes a protein that is part of the BORC and BLOC-1 complexes. *BLOC1S1* localizes to the surface of lysosomes and is necessary for endosomal sorting, vesicular trafficking, and keeping lysosomes properly positioned. Affected patients primarily present with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with epileptic encephalopathy, spasticity, hypotonia, optic atrophy, and hypopigmentation. These variants impair normal lysosomal and autophagic functions in the brain. Six variants (five missense, one splice site) across three publications have been included in this curation (PMIDs: 33875846, 36070637; 41887224). The mechanism of disease is loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including a mouse model, Drosophila model, and biochemical function evidence (PMIDs: 25898163, 25183008, 20015953). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic disease GCEP on the meeting date April 1, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The *FAM149B1* (Family with sequence similarity 149 member B1) gene is located at chromosome 10 at 10q22.2. The encoded protein is involved in the localization of proteins to the cilium and cilium assembly, and is required for normal SHH/smoothened signaling and proper development. *FAM149B1* was first reported in connection with autosomal recessive Joubert syndrome 36 in 2019 (Shaheen et al., 2019 PMID:30905400). Patients typically present with partial or complete agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, molar tooth sign, global developmental delay, ocular movement abnormalities, and mesoaxial polydactyly. Three variants (2 frameshift, 1 nonsense) reported in three probands across two publications were included in this curation (PMIDs: 34828254, 30905400). The mechanism of disease is predicted to be loss of function. This gene-disease pair is also supported by experimental evidence including protein interaction and functional alteration in patient cells (PMIDs: 30905400,35609210). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification is approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 18, 2025 (SOP v11).

The relationship between *TTN* and autosomal dominant *TTN*-related myopathy, dominant-negative TTNsv was first reported in 2024 (PMID: 37935568). It is due specifically to monoallelic, multi‑exon in‑frame deletions/CNVs that escape NMD and produce an expressed, internally deleted titin and is supported by multiple independent probands with consistent phenotypes as well as by experimental data from patient muscle. Nine probands were curated from Perrin et al., 2024 (PMID: 37935568) and Gohlke et al., 2024 (PMID: 39277846). In five Perrin families (A, B, F, G, H), affected individuals carry large in‑frame A‑, I‑, or A/M‑band deletions with muscle RNA‑seq demonstrating 50% mutant allele expression and in‑frame exon–exon junctions, confirming NMD escape and supporting expression of a shortened titin isoform. Clinical features across these families include congenital, childhood‑onset, or adult‑onset proximal and/or distal muscle weakness, contractures, variable respiratory involvement, and in some cases cardiomyopathy. Families with out‑of‑frame deletions (D, E) or in‑frame deletions without RNA confirmation (C) were not included as evidence for this mechanism. Gohlke et al. Case 5 (same pedigree originally described in Roggenbuck 2019) provides mechanistic confirmation of the exons 346–362 deletion as in‑frame, with allelic balance ~0.46, co‑expression of full‑length and shortened titin (loss of M‑band domains M8–M9), Z‑disk and M‑line disruption on electron microscopy, and increased titin‑dependent passive tension in slow fibers with preserved active contractility. Together, these patient‑derived data demonstrate a dominant‑negative structural mechanism caused by incorporation of an internally deleted titin molecule into sarcomeres. Experimental evidence (2.5 points) includes *TTN* expression in striated muscle (PMID: 16949617), relevant biochemical function (PMID: 20551232), muscle RNA‑seq demonstrating mutant transcript stability (PMID: 37935568), and patient‑tissue functional alteration including altered force mechanics and structural disruption (PMID: 39277846). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged.

Of note, across the Congenital Myopathies GCEP’s *TTN* curations, disorders were separated based on distinct molecular mechanisms, variant classes, inheritance patterns, and phenotype clusters. Autosomal dominant Tibial muscular dystrophy (TMD), caused by last‑exon variants producing a late‑onset distal myopathy, and HMERF, caused by exon 344 missense variants, are mechanistically and clinically distinct from both recessive congenital titinopathies (biallelic LOF; lumped all recessive presentations—including LGMD2J, centronuclear‑like myopathy, Salih myopathy, Emery‑Dreifuss‑like myopathy, titinopathy with congenital contractures, minicore myopathy, and distal titinopathy) and the present entity involving multi‑exon in‑frame CNVs that escape NMD and produce an internally deleted titin. Therefore, each disorder is curated separately.

*PTCH1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant holoprosencephaly in 2002 (Ming et al., PMID: 11941477). Disease-causing variants in the *PTCH1* gene have been found to cause a disorder characterized by holoprosencephaly, developmental delay, neurodevelopmental delay, seizures, and craniofacial anomalies. Most of the disease-causing variants are missense variants. 

Four variants (missense) that have been reported in five probands across two publications (PMIDs: 17001668, 37880672) are included in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model (PMID: 10395791). In this study, overexpression of Ptch in the mouse neural tube resulted in suppression of Gli1 and Ptch1 expression, indicating impaired Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling. A subset of mice with increased Ptch activity exhibited fusion of the lateral ventricles, consistent with holoprosencephaly. This phenotype parallels that observed in Shh null mice, which develop holoprosencephaly and cyclopia, supporting the conclusion that elevated PTCH activity functionally inhibits SHH pathway signaling during forebrain development. 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism GCEP on July 9th, 2025 (SOP Version 10).

*SLC40A1* (a.k.a FPN1, MTP1, and IREG1) was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant hemochromatosis type 4 in 2001 (Njajou et al., PMID:11431687). Hemochromatosis type 4 is an iron overload disorder where patients present with a clinical manifestation classified into one of groups: (1) an early onset rise in ferritin levels with low to normal transferrin saturation and iron accumulations, particularly in macrophages; (2) high ferritin levels with high transferrin saturation and prominent parenchymal iron loading (OMIM:#606069).  

25 variants (24 missense, 1 in frame deletion) that have been reported in 21 probands in nine publications (PMIDs: 12857562, 12730114, 38886778, 16111902, 11518736, 25744502, 33385755, 24714983, 11431687, 29237594) are included in this curation. No predicted or proven null variants are included in this curation, but functional evidence showing a loss of protein function and a mislocalization of the gene product has been demonstrated for several variants (PMIDs: 24714983, 33385755, 29237594). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached.

The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, with some variants contributing a hypothesized gain-of-function effect (PMID: 24714983). 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, model rescues, expression studies, protein interaction, and biochemical function (PMIDs: 10747949, 38508867, 38508867, 10693807, 16054062). The human phenotype has been recapitulated in a mouse model with targeted mutagenesis (PMID: 16054062). A hypochromic phenotype has been rescued in deficient zebrafish with treatment with a plasmid expressing the gene (PMID: 10693807). This gene’s protein product binds to HAMP as a part of its regulation, which has been curated by this group to have a definitive relationship with a hemochromatosis phenotype (PMID: 38508867). 
This protein is expressed in the relevant tissues to the disease (PMID: 38508867). The biochemical function, cellular iron export, is consistent with the disease phenotype, iron accumulation in cells (PMID:10747949). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *SLC40A1* and autosomal dominant hemochromatosis type 4. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen General Inborn Errors of Metabolism GCEP on the meeting date March 27, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*Monoallelic* pathogenic variants in *INSR*, which encodes the insulin receptor protein, were first reported in association with type A insulin resistance syndrome described by C. Ronald Kahn et al. in 1976. In the current curation, we have curated the inheritance pattern for autosomal dominant monoallelic cases causing type A insulin resistance. Autosomal recessive *INSR*-related severe insulin resistance syndromes, known historically as Donohue syndrome and Rabson–Mendenhall syndrome, are curated separately.

INSR protein is a heterotetrameric glycoprotein composed of two extracellular α-subunits and two transmembrane β-subunits (α₂β₂), linked by disulfide bonds. The α-subunits are responsible for binding insulin, while the β-subunits span the membrane and contain an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain. When insulin binds to the receptor, it induces a conformational change that activates the kinase domain, leading to autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues and initiation of downstream signaling pathways such as the PI3K–AKT pathway and MAPK pathway. These signaling cascades mediate key biological effects of insulin, including glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipid metabolism, protein synthesis, and cell growth (PMIDs: 1327927, 3009519; Taylor et al., 1992 review).

Individuals with autosomal dominant (monoallelic) *INSR* variants typically present with type A insulin resistance syndrome, representing the mildest end of the clinical spectrum. Affected individuals usually develop insulin resistance in adolescence or early adulthood, characterized by marked hyperinsulinemia, acanthosis nigricans, and, in females, hyperandrogenism with features such as oligomenorrhea or polycystic ovarian syndrome (PMIDs:15232309,29877041,33995269). In contrast to the severe recessive forms, these individuals generally lack significant growth abnormalities, dysmorphic features, or early-life metabolic decompensation. Most monoallelic variants are heterozygous missense changes affecting the tyrosine kinase domain of the receptor, leading to impaired insulin signaling through a dominant mechanism while preserving partial receptor function (PMIDs: 1327927, 20339196). This residual activity accounts for the milder clinical presentation and later onset compared to biallelic *INSR*-related disorders. Rare cases show that homozygous or compound heterozygous *INSR* variants can also cause a milder phenotype similar to type A insulin resistance, likely due to partial preservation of receptor function (PMID: 32018348,12970295,10733238), highlighting that *INSR*-related disorders exist on a clinical spectrum with variable genotype–phenotype correlation.  Several kindreds with dominantly inherited insulin resistance segregating with simple loss of function of one allele have been reported (PMIDs: 9356044, 2687060, 8530617, 20339196, 9356044, 8175972), but the expressivity/penetrance of insulin resistance related to simple heterozygous deficiency is yet to be fully defined.

Per the criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we identified differences in inheritance patterns and phenotypic variability among variants associated with biallelic and monoallelic *INSR*-related insulin resistance syndromes. Therefore, the curation of *INSR* has been split into (1) autosomal recessive Donohue and/or Rabson–Mendenhall syndrome and (2) autosomal dominant type A insulin resistance syndrome.
Evidence supporting the relationship of this gene with autosomal dominant type A insulin resistance includes case-level data and experimental data. Variants in this gene have been curated in at least 22 probands in 18 publications (PMIDs; 41360184, 35634501, 38289143,1890161, 2168397, 35661079,8390949, 8096518, 8243830, 33728347, 9356044, 39619220, 7989492, 29877041, 28181734,8082780,10733238,16127220) with clinical and phenotypic features consistent with type A insulin resistance syndrome. More evidence is available to support the gene-disease association in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached, this has not been curated exhaustively.

This gene–disease relationship is supported by in vitro functional assays, protein interactions, expression studies, and mouse models (PMIDs:28181734, 23715323, 7935368, 15713666, 9038347)., and mouse models. Total points for the experimental evidence are 6. Total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 18.

In summary, *INSR* is definitively associated with autosomal dominant type A insulin resistance syndrome, with most cases presenting in adolescence or early adulthood. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on May 13, 2026. Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) - SOP12.

The *B2M* gene is located on chromosome 15 at 15q21.1 and encodes beta-2-microglobulin, a serum protein found in association with the major histocompatibility complex class I heavy chain on the surface of nearly all nucleated cells. The protein has a predominantly beta-pleated sheet structure that can form amyloid fibrils in some pathological conditions. *B2M* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant hereditary systemic amyloidosis 6 in 2012 (Valleix et al., PMID: 22693999). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities: hypercatabolic hypoproteinemia (OMIM:241600) and hereditary systemic amyloidosis 6 (OMIM:620659). The split curation for autosomal recessive hypercatabolic hypoproteinemia has been curated separately. Two missense variants that have been reported in two probands in two publications (PMIDs: 22693999, 35575118) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be gain of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by variant-level evidence showing that  D76N *B2M* results in increased abundance compared to wild type of an intermediate of the *B2M* folding pathway that plays a role in priming the amyloid transition (PMID:24014031). No experimental evidence was scored. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date May 6, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The CHSY1 gene was first reported to be causative of autosomal recessive Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome (TPBS, OMIM #605282) in 2010 (Li et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129728; Tian et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129727). TPBS is a rare skeletal development disorder characterized by short stature, bilateral, symmetric preaxial brachydactyly and hyperphalangism of digits, facial dysmorphism, dental anomalies, sensorineural hearing loss, delayed motor and mental development, intellectual disability, and macrophthalmia accompanied by bilateral blue sclera in some patients (Temtamy et al. 1998. PubMed ID: 9823490; Race et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 19952732; Li et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129728; Tian et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129727; Sher and Naeem. 2014. PubMed ID: 24269551). In addition, one missense variant in this gene has been reported in the heterozygous state in a patient with neuropathy which may indicate a dominant negative effect mechanism, however a larger number of patients are needed for further study (Izumikawa et al. 2013. PubMed ID: 23811343). Based on the different phenotype and inheritance pattern, this gene-disease relationship will be assessed separately.

The CHSY1 gene is located on chromosome 15q26.3 and encodes chondroitin sulfate synthase 1 (CHSY1), which is a dual glycosyltransferase, transferring glucuronic acid (GlcA) and N-acetyl-galactosamine (GalNAc) residues from UDP-GlcA and UDP-GalNAc, respectively, to the non-reducing end of the elongating chondroitin polymer to form the repeating disaccharide of chondroitin sulfate (CS). CHSY1 is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues and localizes to Golgi apparatus, or secreted. Depletion of CS is observed in a skin section from a patient versus that in control skin (Tian et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129727). Moreover, the upregulation of JAG1 and HES1 expression with CHSY1 deficiency were observed. This could be reversed with a wild-type but not a Fringe catalytically dead CHSY1 construct indicating CHSY1 is a secreted FRINGE enzyme required for adjustment of NOTCH signaling throughout human and fish embryogenesis and particularly during limb patterning. In Chsy1-deficient mice, a decrease in 4-O-sulfation and increase in 6-O-sulfation as well as nonsulfated GalNAc residues were detected (Wilson et al. 2012. PubMed ID: 22280990). Furthermore, in embryonic fibroblast cultures from Chsy1-deficient mice, Gli1, the transcriptional target of Hedgehog, is elevated which may indicate that CS and Hedgehog protein may coordinately modulate bone development.

To date, 14 variants in CHSY1 (OMIM #608183) including five missense, three nonsense, five deletion, and one splicing variant have been reported or submitted to ClinVar as pathogenic or likely pathogenic as causative for TPBS. This curation includes seven variants (two missense, one nonsense, three deletion, and one splicing variant) in the homozygous state in seven probands from seven consanguineous families in three publications (Li et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129728; Tian et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129727; Sher and Naeem. 2014. PubMed ID: 24269551). The score for genetic evidence has reached the maximum of 12 pts. The inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. This includes the non-human animal models of zebrafish and mouse with CHSY1 deficiency, which recapitulate the clinical and histopathological features of the disease in humans (Li et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129728; Tian et al. 2010. PubMed ID: 21129727; Wilson et al. 2012. PubMed ID: 22280990; Macke et al. 2020. PubMed ID: 31754016). (Experimental evidence – 4 points).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CHSY1 and autosomal recessive TPBS/CHSY1-CDG. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on June 15, 2026 (SOP Version v12).

The *FTL* gene codes for the ferritin light chain. The *FTL* subunit of the ferritin enhances iron nucleation. It also protects the heteropolymer against aggregation and precipitation that may occur while incubating with Fe (II) during iron incorporation. Variants in *FTL* have been reported in individuals with Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 3; NBIA3/Hereditary Neuroferritinopathy (NF)/Adult-onset basal ganglia disease (MIM# 606159). The disease displays autosomal dominant inheritance. Linkage analysis and Haplotype analysis was conducted in one publication (PMID: 11438811) led to sequencing of the FTL gene. and published LOD score included in the scoring.  Summary of case-based evidence: 10 variants, with 9 duplications (frameshift variants) and one substitution have been documented. The frameshift variants in exon 4, affect the C-terminal sequence. This causes disordered four-fold pores allowing iron leakage and enhanced formation of toxic, improperly coordinated iron. (PMIDs: 16116125, 15099026, 19514068, 18854324, 11438811, 22818529, 15835264, 19117339, 24825732, 18413574, 24907184, 25809671). Summary of experimental evidence: This gene-disease association is supported by experimental evidence from the study on apoferritin when subjected to high iron increments, heteropolymers of ferritin with L:H ratios are highly efficient in incorporating iron (PMID: 8182740). The studies in the transgenic FVB-mouse model expressing the pathogenic human FTL mutant c.498InsTC under the PGK promoter, confirmed the presence of ferritin/iron bodies in most tissues, principally in the brain: the main hallmark of the neuroferritinopathy patients and of the reported neuroferritinopathy mouse model (PMID: 25689865, 25447222). Further, in a second  transgenic mouse model study (PMID: 19519778),  homozygous FTL-Tg mice (FTL-Tg 4) expressing the variant (c.498-499InsTC) showed the presence of ferritin nuclear inclusions in the brain. Functional studies (PMID: 18755684): Analysis of recombinant WT- and MT-FTL (mutant p.Phe167SerfsX26) polypeptides expressed in E. coli suggest that, since the C terminus is exposed external to the protein shell in the MT-FTL, these homopolymers have a diminished ability to sequester iron and show enhanced aggregation compared to wild type homopolymers, as iron levels are increased. Expression study (PMID: 20159981), where analysis of mutant ferritins (L148fs, L154fs, L167fs) expressed in transfected E. coli cells was studied for iron incorporation as both homopolymers and heteropolymers along with H-ferritin. It was observed that the mutant ferritin incorporated little iron when supplied in ferrous or ferric forms. In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between variants in the *FTL* gene and Neuroferritinopathy. Further, biochemical studies (PMID: 21029774), demonstrated that the *in vitro* functional problems characterized in mutant-containing ferritin heteropolymers in the study, support a connection to demonstrated cellular abnormalities in patients with HF and in an animal model consistent with both a loss of normal function and a gain of toxic function of ferritin. In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between variants in the *FTL* gene and Hereditary neuroferritinopathy. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP on June 12th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features
disease_original_title: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features
submitted_as_notes:
*ELP2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features in 2011 (Najmabadi et al., PMID: 21937992). Affected individuals demonstrate a range of phenotypic severity included but not limited to intellectual disability, developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder, as well as motor features including spastic diplegia, choreoathetosis, and ataxia.  

Eight variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice site) that have been reported in 7 probands within 6 publications (PMIDs: 25847581, 28726809, 33393008, 33510603, 34653680, 33976153) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function (PMID:33976153).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by *in vitro* functional assays for commonly reported missense variants as well as two mouse models (PMID: 33976153). Affinity, enzymatic activity, and *in vitro* analyses of purified human and murine *ELP2* proteins show that commonly identified single amino acid substitutions impair the activity and function of the *ELP2* complex in tRNA modification during translation. Two mouse models, a homozygous p.His206Arg and compound heterozygous p.His206Arg/p.Arg462Gln, modified using CRISPR-Cas9 editing exhibited physical manifestations of developmental delay and severe motor defects including stereotypic behavior in the form of repetitive self grooming and abnormal hind-limb clasping, features commonly identified in ID/ASD mouse models. Neuroimaging of the homozygous p.His206Arg mice revealed loss of axonal tract integrity among major cortical white matter in the brain (PMID:33976153). Lastly, morphologic abnormalities were identified in the cortical neurons of the mutant mice and impairment of neurogenesis was seen by analysis of the brain tissue at the peak of neurogenesis (PMID:33976153). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ELP2* and autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder with motor features. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability/Autism GCEP on the meeting date June 23, 2025 (SOP Version 10).

*IFT43* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive short-rib thoracic dysplasia and cranioectodermal dysplasia in 2011 (Arts et al., PMID: 21378380). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, Short-rib thoracic dysplasia 18 with polydactyly (OMIM:617866) and Cranioectodermal dysplasia 3 (OMIM:614099). Four variants (missense, start loss) have been reported in 5 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 28400947, 21378380, 29896747, 26489029) and are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (e.g. animal models, expression studies, in vitro functional assays, etc.; PMIDs: 28207750; doi:10.64898/2026.01.14.699321). This knockout mouse study demonstrated it causes a skeletal phenotype. Other experimental evidence reported (IP assays and rescue experiments) supported the ciliopathy. In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *IFT43* and autosomal recessive short-rib thoracic dysplasia and cranioectodermal dysplasia. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Skeletal Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 22, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

The *PPP2R5C* gene encodes the B56δ regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), an intracellular serine/threonine phosphatase. *PPP2R5C* was first described in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder as a candidate gene in 2015 (Loveday et al., PMID: 25972378), and reported as a disease gene in 2025 (Verbinnen et al., PMID: 39978342). The disorder is characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, delayed walking, variably impaired intellectual development, behavioral abnormalities (including autism spectrum disorder), and poor or absent speech. Most affected individuals have a large head circumference or macrocephaly, and about half have dysmorphic facial features. About half of patients have seizures. 

Twelve *de novo* variants (missense and in-frame deletions) reported in 12 probands in two publications (PMIDs: 25533962, 39978342) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature (PMID: 39696819), but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. Several variants are recurrent, including p.Gly122Lys reported in four unrelated individuals. Most reported *PPP2R5C* variants cluster within a highly conserved acidic loop of the B56γ regulatory subunit that interfaces with the PP2A A (scaffolding) and C (catalytic) subunits. Functional studies demonstrate that the majority of variants impair A- and/or C-subunit binding, frequently accompanied by reduced substrate binding and phosphatase activity, consistent with disruption of PP2A-B56γ–mediated substrate dephosphorylation (PMID: 39978342). While five cases of heterozygous loss-of-function *PPP2R5C* variants have been reported (PMID: 39978342), they were not included in the curation because the role of loss-of-function variants as a disease mechanism is unclear at this time. Indeed, loss-of-function variants have been observed in apparently unaffected individuals, and may be inherited from an unaffected parent. These observations argue against haploinsufficiency and suggest a dominant-negative disease mechanism for missense and in-frame variants (PMID: 39978342).

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including protein interaction and biochemical function. Pathogenic variants in other members of the protein phosphatase 2A gene family, *PPP2R1A*, *PPP2CA* and *PPP2R5D*, also cause neurodevelopmental disorders with overlapping phenotypes.

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *PPP2R5C* and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 16, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*IQSEC1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2019 (PMID: 31607425). The core phenotype observed in all reported cases includes severe intellectual disability, short stature, speech impairment, facial dysmorphia, and behavioral problems. 

Four variants (three missense and one frameshift) that have been reported in three probands in two publications (PMIDs: 31607425, 41738068) are included in this curation. Of note, two unrelated probands reported in 2019 with two novel missense variants curated here (PMID: 31607425) are from consanguineous families with affected siblings that have the same clinical phenotype and homozygous *IQSEC1* variants that were identified by exome sequencing. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss- or partial loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence, including a mouse model with a conditional *Iqsec1* deletion in neurons that displayed increased dendritic spine density and immature morphology (PMID: 31607425). 

In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *IQSEC1* and complex neurodevelopmental disorder. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism GCEP on the meeting date April 21, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: autoinflammation, panniculitis, and dermatosis syndrome, autosomal recessive
disease_original_title: autoinflammation, panniculitis, and dermatosis syndrome, autosomal recessive
submitted_as_notes:
OTULIN was first reported in relation to autoinflammation, panniculitis, and dermatosis syndrome, autosomal recessive (also known as OTULIN-related autoinflammatory syndrome, ORAS/AIPDS) in 2016. OTULIN encodes a linear/Met1-linked deubiquitinase that negatively regulates linear ubiquitin signaling and downstream inflammatory signaling, including TNF/NF-kB-associated pathways. This curation was performed for the autosomal recessive phenotype only.

The gene–disease relationship is supported by multiple unrelated probands/families with biallelic OTULIN variants reported across independent publications. Initial evidence came from Damgaard et al. 2016 (PMID: 27523608), which described three affected members of a consanguineous Pakistani family with a homozygous missense variant. Zhou et al. 2016 (PMID: 27559085) reported additional independent families, including one Pakistani family overlapping the original report and two Turkish families with homozygous missense and frameshift variants. Additional independent autosomal recessive cases were reported by Damgaard et al. 2019 (PMID: 30804083), describing a new patient with homozygous p.Gly281Arg; Nabavi et al. 2019 (PMID: 30796585), describing a canonical splice-site variant; and Zinngrebe et al. 2022 (PMID: 35170849), describing an atypical late-onset compound heterozygous case. Overall, the curated evidence includes both predicted/proven null and other variant types, with a total genetic evidence score of 10 points.

Experimental evidence supports the mechanism that loss of OTULIN function causes dysregulated linear ubiquitin signaling and autoinflammation. Curated evidence includes biochemical function and functional alteration in patient cells, for a total experimental evidence score of 2.5 points. Across the cited studies, patient-derived cells showed abnormal linear ubiquitination and dysregulated inflammatory/TNF signaling, and variant-specific functional studies supported deleterious effects on OTULIN stability, binding, catalytic activity, or splicing.

disease_title: retinitis pigmentosa-hearing loss-premature aging-short stature-facial dysmorphism syndrome
disease_original_title: retinitis pigmentosa-hearing loss-premature aging-short stature-facial dysmorphism syndrome
submitted_as_notes: The *EXOSC2* gene (exocyst complex component 2) is located on chromosome 9 at 9q34.12 and encodes a protein that is part of exosome complex, a multi-protein complex capable of degrading various types of RNA molecules. *EXOSC2* was first reported in relation to retinitis pigmentosa-hearing loss-premature aging-short stature-facial dysmorphism syndrome in 2016 (PMID:26843489: Di Donato et al. 2016). Six variants (5 missense, 1 splice-site) reported in four probands across three publications have been included in this curation (PMIDs: 26843489, 36344539, 36069504). The mechanism of disease is predicted to be loss of function. This gene-disease pair is also supported by experimental evidence, namely a zebrafish KO model (PMID: 33333712). In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *EXOSC2* and retinitis pigmentosa-hearing loss-premature aging-short stature-facial dysmorphism syndrome. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date March 21st, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: retinal dystrophy, optic nerve edema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and migraine headache syndrome
disease_original_title: retinal dystrophy, optic nerve edema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and migraine headache syndrome
submitted_as_notes:
ALPK1 was first implicated in autosomal dominant monogenic disease in a report of 5 families all with retinal dystrophy, optic nerve edema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and migraine headaches in 2019 (Williams et al, PMID:30967659). The same heterozygous variant in ALPK1 (c.710C>T, [p.Thr237Met]) was identified in all 5 families. This report was extended to 13 families, one with a second deleterious variant p.Tyr254Cys in a second report, highlighting more of the inflammatory features of the disease in 2022 (Kozycki et al, PMID: 35868845). Individuals with ROSAH syndrome have been found to have a variety of symptoms including ocular findings (optic disk elevation, uveitis, retinal vasculitis and retinal degeneration), inflammatory arthritis, splenomegaly, gastrointestinal inflammation, cytopenias, headaches, malaise, dental anomalies (carries and enamel defects) – potentially driven by hyposalivation, anhidrosis, and inability to lactate (Kozycki et al, PMID: 35868845).

Variants in this gene have been reported in at least 15 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 35868845, 30967659, 36543582). Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 17 additional family members, which have been included in this curation. 

The gene disease relationship is supported by experimental evidence. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain of function.  Studies in primary samples and in vitro assays with mutated ALPK1 constructs lead to increased NF-κB signalling, STAT1 phosphorylation and interferon gene expression signature. Knock-in mice with the Alpk1 T237M mutation exhibited subclinical inflammation and have elevated serum levels of CXCL1, CXCL10 and CCL2 (Kozycki et al, PMID: 35868845). 

In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between ALPK1 and autosomal dominant ROSAH. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Autoinflammatory GCEP on the meeting date 01/09/2024 (SOP Version 10).

disease_title: vertebral anomalies and variable endocrine and T-cell dysfunction
disease_original_title: vertebral anomalies and variable endocrine and T-cell dysfunction
submitted_as_notes: The *TBX2* gene is located on chromosome 17 at 17q23.2 and encodes the T-Box transcription factor 2 protein, which acts as a transcriptional repressor. *TBX2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant vertebral anomalies and variable endocrine and T-cell dysfunction (VETD) in 2018 (Liu et al., PMID: 29726930). VETD is characterized by cardiac anomalies, skeletal malformations, immune deficiency, endocrine abnormalities, developmental delay, behavioral problems, and facial dysmorphism. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental evidence. Three missense variants and 1 nonsense variant that have been reported in six patients in three publications are included in this curation (PMIDs: 29726930, 35311234, 36733940). An additional case was published in PMID: 39843441 (2025) but insufficient phenotypic details were available to include the case in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental data including biochemical function, protein interaction, expression, and model organism data. For biochemical function, *Tbx2* and *Tbx3* share 90% amino acid similarity within the T-box domain and function predominantly as transcriptional repressors (PMID: 29726930). TBX3 is definitively associated with ulna-mammary syndrome. An electromobility shift assay (EMSA) conducted by Habets et al. (2002) demonstrated that Nkx2.5 and *Tbx2* form a large ternary complex (protein interaction), which represses ANF promoter activity (PMID: 12023302). Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments (ChIP) demonstrated that *Tbx2* binds to Grem1 limb regulatory element (PMID: 23633963):; however, this finding was not scored, as GREM1 is not listed as disease-associated in OMIM. Immunofluorescence staining using a mouse monoclonal antibody against *TBX2*, as performed by Sizarov et al. (2011) demonstrated *TBX2* expression in the human heart (PMID: 21403123). Harrelson et al. (2004) reported that homozygous mouse embryos are embryonically lethal due to cardiovascular insufficiency; however the score was downgraded as heterozygous mice appear normal and fertile (PMID: 15459098). In summary, there is limited evidence to support the relationship between *TBX2* and autosomal dominant VETD. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification is approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 22, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*SLC7A14* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive “retinitis pigmentosa 68” in 2014 (Jin et al, 2014, PMID: 24670872). Seven individuals have been reported with bi-allelic variants in this gene. All of these individuals are Chinese with onset of symptoms in childhood, and all are either homozygous for c.988G>A (p.Gly330Arg) or c.1391G>T (p.Cys464Phe), or compound heterozygous for one of those variants and another missense variant (Jin et al, 2014, PMID: 24670872; Guo et al, 2019, PMID: 30924391). Evidence suggests that the p.Gly330Arg variant affects protein localization (Jin et al, 2014, PMID: 24670872; Giffen et al, 2022, PMID: 35394837). In gnomAD v4.1.0, c.988G>A (p.Gly330Arg) and c.1391G>T (p.Cys464Phe) have minor allele frequencies (MAFs) in the East Asian population of 0.02079 (933/44,880 alleles, 11 homozygotes) and 0.01146 (514/44,856 alleles, 3 homozygotes), respectively. The ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel considers these MAFs to be too high for these variants to be disease-causing. Additional studies have been conducted in Chinese and Japanese cohorts with retinopathy and no individuals with rare biallelic variants in SLC7A14 were identified (Sugahara et al, 2017, PMID: 27028480; Dan et al, 2020, PMID: 31960602). Individuals with heterozygous missense variants in these genes have been reported, but the clinical significance is unknown.

Regarding experimental evidence, in mice, *SLC7A14* is mainly expressed in the brain, spinal cord and retina (inner nuclear layer and photoreceptor layer) (Jin et al, 2014, PMID: 24670872). The gene has a similar expression pattern in zebrafish. Knock-out mice, and knock in mice with the p.Gly330Arg variant exhibit abnormal ERGs and thinning of the retina, in addition to progressive hearing loss, recapitulating the disease phenotype in humans (Jin et al, 2014, PMID: 24670872; Giffen et al, 2022, PMID: 35394837). Zebrafish in which Slc7a14 expression has been knocked down using a morpholino approach tended to have small eyes and had an abnormal response to light-dark transitions (Jin et al, 2014, PMID: 24670872, Zhuang et al, 2019, PMID: 31921845).

In summary, based on the high minor allele frequencies for the c.988G>A (p.Gly330Arg) and c.1391G>T (p.Cys464Phe) variants, the evidence supporting the relationship between *SLC7A14* and autosomal recessive “retinitis pigmentosa 68” has been disputed by the ClinGen Retina GCEP. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role that *SLC7A14* plays in this disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina GCEP on July 8, 2026 (SOP v12).

disease_title: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to XIAP deficiency
disease_original_title: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to XIAP deficiency
submitted_as_notes:
*XIAP*, also known as *BIRC4*, was first reported in relation to X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to *XIAP* deficiency in 2006 (Rigaud S, et al., 2006, PMID: 17080092). X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to XIAP deficiency is a variable immune dysregulation disorder that often presents with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, splenomegaly, hypogammaglobulinemia, inflammatory bowel disease, cytopenia, and recurrent and/or complicated infections (PMID: 34222142). Nine variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, and intragenic deletion) that have been reported in 9 probands in 3 publications (PMIDs: 17080092, 23973892, 40296086) are included in this curation. Segregation of a *XIAP* variant with this disorder in a single family was included as evidence (PMID: 17080092). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss of function (PMIDs: 17080092, 18055022, 18769721, 23973892, 24611904, 40296086, 42039706).  

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, expression studies, and in vitro functional (PMIDs: 17080092, 18055022, 18769721, 24611904, 42039706). *XIAP*-/- mice recapitulate aspects of human disease (PMID: 18769721, 42039706). Patient-derived T- cells display increased susceptibility to apoptosis following stimulation that can be rescued by expression of WT XIAP (PMID: 17080092).

Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant is currently the only curative option for patients with X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to *XIAP* deficiency (PMIDs: 23131490, 23766462 , 24084330, 24942029, 25412586, 27815752).  

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *XIAP* and X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to XIAP deficiency. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time (need to change to other wording if not definitive, according to the ClinGen template). This classification was approved by the ClinGen Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders GCEP on the meeting date July 21, 2026 (SOP Version 12)].

*EOGT* was first reported in relation to Adams-Oliver syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder, in 2013 (Shaheen et al, PMID: 23522784). Adams-Oliver syndrome is characterized by aplasia cutis congenita (ACC), typically affecting the vertex of the scalp, with underlying skull defects in more severe cases; transverse terminal limb defects; cutaneous vascular abnormalities such as cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita; and, in some cases, congenital heart defects, vascular anomalies, growth impairment, and, less commonly, developmental delay or neurological abnormalities.  
*EOGT* encodes EGF domain-specific O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase which, in the ER, catalyzes the addition of a single O-GlcNAc residue to specific serine or threonine residues EGF-like repeats of secreted and cell-surface proteins such as NOTCH1 and other Notch receptors. Variants in EOGT have been implicated in only one condition, Adamas-Oliver syndrome 4.
Ten variants (5 missense, 3 splice site, 2 frameshift) that have been reported in ten probands in six publications (Shaheen et al, 2013, PMID: 23522784; Cohen et al, 2014; PMID: 23860037; Meester et al, 2018, PMID: 29924900; Schröder et al, 2019, PMID: 31368252; Dudoignon et al, 2020, PMID: 31654484; He et al, 2026, PMID: 41959640) are included in this curation. Segregation evidence from three distantly-related families in the Bedouin population, which led to the identification of a founder frameshift variant, c.1074delA (p.Gly359AspfsTer28), was included (Cohen et al, 2014; PMID: 23860037). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function.
This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. *EOGT* was first identified as a novel OGT in Drosophila that O-GlcNAcylated the EGF repeats of Notch and Dumpy (Matsuura et al, 2008, PMID: 18948267, Sakaidani et al, 2011, PMID: 2215843). The gene was later cloned in mice and shown to rescue a posterior wing blistering phenotype resulting from RNAi knockdown of the Drosophila gene (Sakaidani et al, 2012, PMID: 22310717). O-GlcNAcylation of Notch1 enhances the binding of DLL1 and DLL4 to NOTCH1, thereby promoting downstream transcription of Notch target genes (Ogawa et al, 2015, PMID: 25488668). As the Notch signaling pathway is important in vascular development and angiogenesis, the role of EOGT is consistent with the features observed in patients with Adams-Oliver syndrome. Furthermore, the Eogt null mouse was shown to have vascular defects in the retina (Sawaguchi et al, 2017, PMID: 28395734).
