Of note, four of the six genes implicated in Adams-Oliver syndrome are in the Notch signaling pathway (RBPJ, NOTCH1, DLL4, EOGT (Tișa et al, 2025, PMID: 41516051). 
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *EOGT* and Adams-Oliver syndrome 4, and autosomal recessive condition. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on July 6, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome
disease_original_title: agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome
submitted_as_notes:
The *CDH2* gene is located on chromosome 18 at 18q12.1, and encodes cadherin-2, a calcium-dependent cell adhesion protein that mediates cell-cell adhesion. *CDH2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome (ACOGS) in 2019 (Accogli et al., 2019, PMID: 31585109). Features associated with ACOGS most commonly include developmental delay and/or intellectual disability, callosal malformations, cardiac abnormalities, ocular abnormalities (often Peters anomaly), genital anomalies in males, and facial dysmorphism. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in phenotypic presentation. Therefore the following disease entities have been split,  arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia (OMIM:618920) and dilated cardiomyopathy (MONDO:0005021) have been curated separately. 

This curation includes 16 patients from six different publications harbouring 15 different *CDH2* variants - ten missense, two frameshift, one canonical splice-site and two stop-gain variants. The variants were confirmed to arise de novo in 14 cases (PMID: 31585109; Reis et al., Nov 2019, PMID: 31650526; Meng & Gong, 2021, PMID: 34711036; Kanjee et al., 2022, PMID: 35708058; Westenius et al., 2024, PMID: 38268232, Abdul Rahman et al., 2025, PMID: 40293216). The maximum points (12 pts) were reached for genetic evidence. 

This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental data including biochemical function and model organism data. The curation includes two mouse models supportive of disease association. Mice with a conditional inactivation of N-cadherin in the cerebral cortex display cortical disorganization and lack a corpus callosum (Kadowaki et al., 2007, PMID:17222817). Conditional cdh2 knockout (Lens-Cre+,Cdh2flox/neo) mouse embryos presented with a small eye phenotype with severe lens deterioration and hyperplastic iris development. In addition, two zebrafish models were curated but not scored due to lack of controls needed for inclusion here. A cdh2 knockout zebrafish model showed early lethality, as well as several anomalies such as absence of somites, microphthalmia, malformations throughout the body and head, and cardiac deformity (Ferreira et al., 2023, PMID: 37166408). A CRISPR knockdown of cdh2 in zebrafish resulted in head and brain malformations and developmental delay (Fernandes et al., 2024, PMID: 39449741). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the gene-disease relationship between *CDH2* and autosomal dominant agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in literature, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic disease GCEP on the meeting date March 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

B4GALT1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation in 2002 (Hansske et al. PMID:11901181). Five variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in 5 probands in 5 publications (PMIDs: 11901181, 30653653, 32157688, 21920538, 33258288) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached. B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation is characterized by severe psychomotor and developmental delay, as well as blood coagulation abnormalities. The disease mechanism appears to be biallelic loss of function. Heterozygous carriers are reportedly unaffected. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by in vitro and in vivo assays showing a defect in glycosylation (PMIDs 11901181, 31800099) as well as animal models (PMIDs 11463354, 9155011).  In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between B4GALT1 and autosomal recessive B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date May 18, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*NAA20* encodes the catalytic subunit of N-acetyltransferase complex B (NatB), which catalyzes acetylation of specific N-terminal methionine residues on proteins. *NAA20* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive syndromic intellectual disability in 2021 (PMID: 34230638). Affected individuals present with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, impaired speech, and microcephaly. Additional features observed in some individuals include facial dysmorphisms, brain malformations (such as corpus callosum dysgenesis, malformations of cortical development, and cerebellar dysplasia), ataxic gait, congenital heart defects, and epilepsy (PMIDs: 34230638, 37191084). To date, the phenotypic spectrum has been described based on a limited number of affected individuals (n=7) from 3 unrelated families (PMIDs: 34230638, 37191084). Therefore, identification and characterization of additional families will be important to further delineate the full clinical spectrum of this condition.
Four variants (3 missense, 1 frameshift) that have been reported in 3 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 34230638, 37191084) are included in this curation. Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 4 additional family members. Functional studies of the reported missense variants demonstrate impaired acetylation activity and/or disruption of NatB complex formation (PMIDs: 34230638,  37191084). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function (PMIDs: 34230638,  37191084), but additional studies are needed to better understand the pathogenesis of different *NAA20* variants.
This gene–disease relationship is further supported by biochemical evidence. Other subunits of the N-alpha-terminal acetyltransferase family have been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders with overlapping phenotypes, including *NAA10* and *NAA15*.
In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *NAA20* and autosomal recessive syndromic intellectual disability. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. The classification was upgraded from limited to moderate due to phenotypic overlap among affected individuals and functional studies showing reduced NAA20 catalytic activity. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 1, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures
disease_original_title: developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures
submitted_as_notes:
*ARFGEF1* (ADP-Ribosylation Factor Guanine Nucleotide-Exchange Factor 1) is located at chromosome 8 at 8q13.2 and encodes a brefeldin A-sensitive guanine nucleotide exchange factor that activates ARF1 and ARF3 to promote vesicular trafficking and maintain Golgi structure. *ARFGEF1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures in 2020 (Teoh et al., PMID: 31678406).

Ten variants including 1 missense, 5 nonsense, 2 frameshift, and 2 essential splice site variants that have been reported in ten probands from three publications (PMIDs: 31678406, 34113008, 35782386) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental evidence including a heterozygous knockout mouse model which recapitulates the developmental delay and increased susceptibility to seizures observed in affected individuals (PMID: 31678406). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ARFGEF1* and autosomal dominant developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic disease GCEP on the meeting date November 21, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*DMRT1* was initially implicated in human disorders of sex development through reports of individuals with large terminal deletions of chromosome 9p24 who presented with 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis or sex reversal. These deletions encompass several genes including *DMRT1*, suggesting a dosage-sensitive role of this region in sex determination. In 2010, Ledig et al. reported the first individual with 46,XY differences of sex development (DSD) carrying a smaller heterozygous deletion affecting *DMRT1* itself, providing more direct evidence that haploinsufficiency of *DMRT1* disrupts normal testicular development and establishing *DMRT1* as an autosomal dominant cause of 46,XY DSD (PMID:20685758).

*DMRT1*-related 46,XY DSD is characterized by impaired or incomplete testicular differentiation in individuals with a 46,XY karyotype. Affected individuals may present with gonadal dysgenesis, ovotesticular DSD, ambiguous genitalia, or complete sex reversal with female external genitalia despite the presence of a Y chromosome (PMIDs: 31745530, 28295047, 26005864, 27711951, 20685758, 33057194, 22573722). Histological findings may include dysgenetic testes, mixed gonadal tissue containing both ovarian and testicular elements, or underdeveloped seminiferous tubules. *DMRT1* encodes a highly conserved transcription factor containing the characteristic DM DNA-binding domain and plays a critical role in sex determination and the differentiation and maintenance of male gonadal cell fate (PMIDs: 9490411, 17459496). Disruption of DMRT1 function interferes with the transcriptional regulation of genes required for testis development and maintenance of male gonadal identity.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities: spermatogenic failure (MONDO: 0004983) and 46,XY differences of sex development (MONDO:0020040). The split curation for autosomal dominant spermatogenic failure has been curated separately.

Seven missense variants and two deletions (involving only *DMRT1*) in nine probands across seven publications are included in this curation (PMIDs :31745530, 28295047, 26005864, 27711951,  36110220, 20685758, 22573722). Several variants occur within or near the conserved DM DNA-binding domain, suggesting disruption of transcriptional regulation as a pathogenic mechanism. In addition, heterozygous deletions in *DMRT1* have been reported in individuals with gonadal dysgenesis or ovotesticular DSD, further supporting haploinsufficiency as a disease mechanism. Both point mutations and CNVs support haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative effects as mechanisms (PMID: 26005864). The enrichment of rare, damaging variants in affected cohorts compared to population databases (e.g. gnomAD) strongly supports the relationship.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (biochemical function, animal model systems, expression; PMIDs: 26005864, 40169148, 21775990, 25683803, 25725066, 27940159, 32001440, 34096593, 17567962, 10704857). Expression studies demonstrate that *DMRT1* is expressed in a sex-specific manner in embryonic gonadal tissue, including the human genital ridge during the critical period of sex determination (PMID: 10704857) and in mouse gonads during embryonic development, with expression in Sertoli cells of the testis and in somatic cells of the ovary (PMID: 17567962). Structural and biochemical studies demonstrate that *DMRT1* binds DNA through the conserved DM domain and functions as a sequence-specific transcription factor regulating genes required for testis differentiation; variants affecting DNA-contact residues disrupt binding and are consistent with the transcriptional regulatory role of *DMRT1* in sex determination (PMID: 26005864). Mechanistically, *DMRT1* cooperates with *SOX9* to regulate sex-biased chromatin regions and maintain Sertoli cell identity, while loss of *DMRT1* disrupts *SOX9* binding and promotes transdifferentiation of Sertoli cells toward graulosa-like cells (PMID: 34096593). Animal models further support a conserved role for *DMRT1* in male gonadal development. Heterozygous *DMRT1* knockout rabbits (DMRT1+/−) show impaired testicular development, hypoplastic testes, and germ cell abnormalities consistent with gonadal dysgenesis observed in human 46,XY DSD (PMID: 40169148). In mouse models, loss of Dmrt1 in Sertoli cells results in transdifferentiation toward granulosa-like cells, activation of female pathway genes such as *FOXL2*, repression of male pathway genes including *SOX9*, and feminization of the XY gonad, demonstrating that *DMRT1* is essential for maintaining male gonadal identity (PMID: 21775990). Conversely, ectopic expression of Dmrt1 in XX mouse ovaries reprograms granulosa cells toward a Sertoli-like fate and induces testis-like structures, demonstrating that *DMRT1* is sufficient to direct male somatic cell fate in the gonad (PMIDs: 25683803, 25725066). Additional evidence from zebrafish models shows that loss-of-function mutations in dmrt1 lead to failure of male differentiation, female-biased sex ratios, and intersex gonadal structures, recapitulating key aspects of human gonadal dysgenesis (PMIDs: 27940159, 32001440). Together, these findings demonstrate that *DMRT1* is a key regulator of testicular differentiation and maintenance of male gonadal identity, and that disruption of its function leads to gonadal dysgenesis and disorders of sex development.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *DMRT1* and 46,XY differences of sex development. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on the meeting date March 18, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*CIDEC*, also known as *FSP27*, was first reported in association with autosomal recessive *CIDEC*-related familial partial lipodystrophy in 2009 (Rubio-Cabezas et al., PMID: 20049731). The affected individual was an Ecuadorean female with adolescent-onset lipodystrophy who was homozygous for the nonsense variant NM_001321142.2:c.556G>T (p.Glu186Ter). The inheritance pattern was curated as autosomal recessive, consistent with the homozygous loss-of-function variant identified in the affected individual. 

The reported patient had partial lipodystrophy affecting the limbs, femorogluteal region, and abdominal subcutaneous fat, accompanied by severe insulin-resistant diabetes mellitus, hypertriglyceridemia, hepatic steatosis, and reduced circulating adiponectin (PMID: 20049731). Another patient was reported to have partial lipodystrophy, acanthosis nigricans, and marked insulin resistance and was found to be homozygous for the rare *CIDEC* missense variant NM_001199623.2:c.224G>T (p.Ser75Ile) (PMID: 41596298). However, she also carried a novel homozygous *WRN* missense variant, NM_000553.4:c.1856T>G (p.Leu619Arg), and both variants were classified as variants of uncertain significance. Because *WRN*-associated disease may also present with partial lipodystrophy phenotype and insulin resistance (PMID: 23849162) and both variants were novel missense variants, the specific contributions of both the *CIDEC* and *WRN *variants to this patient’s phenotype remain uncertain. Therefore, this case does not provide unequivocal independent evidence for *CIDEC*-related disease. Per the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, the available evidence supports evaluation under a single disease entity: autosomal recessive CIDEC-related familial partial lipodystrophy.

One homozygous variant reported in one proband was included in this curation (PMID: 20049731). The case-level evidence received 3 points. This gene-disease relationship is further supported by expression studies, biochemical function, protein interaction, functional alteration, and mouse model data (PMIDs: 17884815, 20049731, 22144693, 23399566, 24627478, 18654663, 18682832, 25565658, 34508658, 35963433, 36800289). Total points for experimental evidence are 5, and the combined genetic and experimental evidence totals 8 points. 

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between *CIDEC* and autosomal recessive *CIDEC*-related familial partial lipodystrophy. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on the meeting date July 15, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

GNAI3 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant auriculocondylar syndrome in 2012 (Rieder et al., PMID: 22560091). This condition is characterized by distinctive auricular malformations, most notably “question mark ear,” defined as a spectrum of congenital auricular clefting in which there is partial to complete separation between the ascending helix and the lobule, resulting in a configuration resembling a question mark. Individuals can also have ear hypoplasia, severe micrognathia/mandibular hypoplasia; other mandibular anomalies; and facial dysmorphisms (such as round face, cleft palate, and facial asymmetry). 9 variants (all missense) that have been reported in 19 probands in 9 publications (PMIDs: 22560091, 23315542, 25026904, 33723370, 34789173, 35170830, 36797717, 38177409, 39014351) and in ClinVar (Athena Diagnostics (SCV002817290.1); GeneDx (SCV005325112.1, SCV000618754.3); LabCorp Genetics (SCV004434179.3); and Medicover Genetics (SCV005387608.1) internal data) are included in this curation. Variants cluster between residues 40-48. Some variants, such as p.Gly40Arg, p.Gly40Val, and p.Ser47Asn, have been recurrently found in affected probands. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be dominant negative (PMID: 25026904). Experimental evidence (a mouse model) was evaluated (PMID: 23236180) but not scored since it lacked a specific craniofacial phenotype. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial GCEP on the meeting date 5/21/2026 (SOP Version 12).

*MEIS1* was first reported in relation to congenital thrombocytopenia in 2022 (Steinberg-Shemer et al., 2022 PMID: 35130804). *MEIS1* is a homeobox gene that acts as a transcriptional regulator of genes involved in embryonic development, cell differentiation, hematopoiesis, and neural development. To date, there has been one report of a de novo heterozygous variant in *MEIS1* causing severe congenital thrombocytopenia. Additionally, MEIS1 overexpression is common in leukemias (specifically MLL-fusion-induced leukemia) and is caused by upstream activation of oncogenes interacting with MEIS1, not specific variants in the MEIS1 gene, and is not included in this curation. Evidence supporting this gene-disease curation includes case level data and experimental data.

Summary of Case Level Data (1 point): One de novo heterozygous splicing variant (c. 432+5G>C) that has been shown to lead exon skipping and a premature stop codon.  This variant as been reported in a single proband.

Summary of Experimental Evidence (2.5 points): This gene disease relationship is supported by mouse model systems (Azcoitia et al., 2005 PMID: 15882575; Hisa et al., 2004 PMID: 14713950; Miller et al., 2016 PMID: 26986211), a zebrafish model (Cvejic et al., 2011 PMID: 21048033) and functional alteration in non-patient cells (Wang et al., 2018 PMID: 29358086).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. 

This gene-disease relationship was curated by the ClinGen Hemostasis and Thrombosis (H/T) Gene Curation Expert Panel using Gene Clinical Validity Standard Operating Procedures (SOP), Version 11.

Activating variants in the *GCK* gene, which encodes glucokinase, a hexokinase expressed in pancreatic β-cells, were first reported in association with familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (HH) in 1998 (Glaser et al., PMID: 9435328). These variants typically follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.  Gain-of-function variants in *GCK* lead to increased glucokinase activity, resulting in a lowered glucose threshold for insulin secretion. Consequently, pancreatic β-cells inappropriately secrete insulin at low blood glucose concentrations, causing hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (PMIDs:37725835,34680961). Heterozygous activating variants are associated with autosomal dominant hyperinsulinism and demonstrate marked phenotypic variability. Clinical presentation ranges from severe neonatal-onset hypoglycemia to milder forms presenting later in childhood or adulthood. While some individuals exhibit persistent hypoglycemia requiring treatment, others may have intermittent or relatively mild symptoms. Rarely, atypical presentations have been reported in individuals with activating variants in *GCK*, including mild or asymptomatic hypoglycemia, variable severity, hypoglycemia unawareness, and diagnosis later in life. Considerable variability can also be observed within families.  

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern as well as molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability underlying the *GCK*-related disease entities. Therefore, we have split curations for these disease entities. The present curation includes autosomal dominant *GCK*- related hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia caused by activating (GOF) variants only.   Autosomal dominant forms of monogenic hyperglycemia caused by heterozygous inactivating (LOF) variants (MONDO:0015967) and permanent neonatal diabetes caused by bi-allelic inactivating variants are curated separately as semi-dominant *GCK*-related monogenic diabetes.  

The clinical presentation of individuals with activating variants in *GCK* is characterized by hyperinsulinism, typically presenting as persistent or intermittent hypoglycemia during the neonatal or infantile period, although later-presenting cases have also been reported. Activating variants lower the glucose threshold for insulin secretion by increasing glucokinase activity, resulting in inappropriate insulin release at low blood glucose concentrations. Affected individuals can activate ketogenesis after prolonged fasting, a distinguishing feature from other forms of hyperinsulinism.  Many affected individuals have a partial response to medical therapy, particularly diazoxide, although treatment response is variable. These variants predominantly cluster in the allosteric activator site within the small domain near the hinge region, where they stabilize the active conformation of the enzyme and increase glucose affinity. However, additional activating variants have been identified in the hinge and distal large-domain regions, demonstrating that multiple structural domains contribute to glucokinase activation through distinct mechanisms (PMIDs: 14517946, 18450771,19790256,15277402, 29425029). Classification of HI as *GCK*-related HI is established by identification of a pathogenic activating GCK variant. In some cases, pancreatic histology may demonstrate enlarged or hyperplastic islets, which can be seen in other HI etiologies. 

Dominantly acting gain-of-function variants in *GCK* gene have been curated in at least 17 probands across 11 publications (PMIDs: 3468096, 9435328, 21454522, 15277402, 24890200, 37725835,18450771,19884385,11916951,17976205,31094068,) with clinical presentations consistent with GCK- related hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Additional evidence supporting this gene-disease association is available in the literature, but as the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached this has not been exhaustively curated.  

The gene–disease relationship is strongly supported by gain-of-function mechanism, with evidence from functional studies demonstrating increased glucokinase activity, expression data, and animal models. The total points for the experimental evidence are 5, and the combined total points for genetic and experimental evidence together are 17.  

In summary, *GCK* is definitively associated with autosomal dominant hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia due to activating variants. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time.

This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Diabetes GCEP on the meeting date June 3, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, epilepsy, and absent speech
disease_original_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, epilepsy, and absent speech
submitted_as_notes: The *UNC13A* gene is located on chromosome 19 at 19p13.11 and encodes unc-13 homolog A, or Munc13-1, which is one of four genes in the UNC13 homolog gene family. *UNC13A* was first reported in association with an autosomal recessive congenital nervous system disorder by Engel et al. (2016), who described a proband with a homozygous stop-gained variant presenting with microcephaly, cortical hyperexcitability, and myasthenia (PMID 27648472). Probands with this condition exhibit a neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by profound global developmental delay and early-onset seizures. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. 12 variants (4 missense, 1 nonsense, 2 frameshift, and 5 splice region) that have been reported in ten probands were included in this curation  (PMIDs: 27648472, 28771251, 36447687, 39039281, 41125872). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease association is supported by animal models, expression studies, and in vitro functional assays. Munc13-1 is highly expressed in the brain and at the neuromuscular junction, where it localizes to presynaptic terminals and plays a critical role in synaptic transmission by regulating release site assembly, synaptic vesicle priming, activity-dependent replenishment of the releasable vesicle pool, calcium channel proximity, and short-term synaptic plasticity (PMIDs: 17167095, 30690332). In vivo and in vitro experiments have demonstrated that loss of *UNC13A* can alter various properties of neuronal and neuromuscular synaptic transmission and lead to muscle weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and perinatal lethality (PMIDs: 10440375, 27648472, 33771998, 37243591, 39634123). Gene editing studies have demonstrated that *UNC13A* recessive variants reduce gene expression, fail to localize to the synapse, and alter synaptic plasticity in neuronal cell models (PMID: 41125872). In summary, there is definitive evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 17, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with speech delay, movement abnormalities, and seizures
disease_original_title: neurodevelopmental disorder with speech delay, movement abnormalities, and seizures
submitted_as_notes: The *UNC13A* gene is located on chromosome 19 at 19p13.11 and encodes unc-13 homolog A, or Munc13-1, which is one of four genes in the UNC13 homolog gene family. *UNC13A* was first reported in association with an autosomal dominant congenital nervous system disorder by Lipstein et al. (2017), who described a proband with a de novo missense variant, p.(Pro814Leu), presenting with developmental delay, dyskinetic movement disorder and tremors (PMID: 28192369). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. The p.(Pro814Leu) variant has since been demonstrated to be a common recurrent de novo disease-causing variant in multiple publications (PMID: 33057194, 39634123, 41125872). Eight variants (7 missense, and 1 two amino acid in frame substitution) have since been reported in association with developmental delay (especially speech delay), ataxia, tremor or dyskinetic movements in 18 unrelated probands are included in this curation (PMID: 31130284, 39634123, 41125872). Asadollahi et al. (2025) also reported a familial missense variant, p.(Cys587Phe), and proposed a subtype of *UNC13A*-related autosomal dominant disease characterized by mild-to-moderate intellectual disability and seizures (PMID: 41125872) (not scored). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be gain of function. This gene-disease association is supported by animal models, expression studies, and in vitro functional assays. Munc13-1 is highly expressed in the brain and at the neuromuscular junction, where it localizes to presynaptic terminals and plays a critical role in synaptic transmission by regulating release site assembly, synaptic vesicle priming, activity-dependent refilling of the releasable vesicle pool, calcium channel proximity, and short-term synaptic plasticity (PMIDs: 17167095, 30690332). Overexpression of patient variants in cell culture has demonstrated increased calcium signaling, and gene editing of both mouse hippocampal neurons and C. elegans has shown a gain-of-function phenotype with respect to synaptic vesicle release, vesicle depletion, and neuromuscular paralysis (PMID: 39634123, 41125872). In summary, there is definitive evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date April 17, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The KLHL3 gene is located on chromosome 5 at q31.2 and encodes kelch-like protein 3. KLHL3 is a substrate-specific adapter in the BCR E3 ubiquitination ligase complex which regulates ion transport in the distal nephron (Louis-Dit-Picard et al., PMID:22406640). The BCR complex mediates the ubiquitination of WNK4 and WNK1, activators of the OSR1/SPAK-NCC pathway which causes hypertension when overexpressed (Wakabayashi et al., PMID: 23453970). Pathogenic variation in KLHL3 impairs the ability of KLHL3 to bind to CUL3 and/or WNK4/1, leading to the misregulation of renal salt, K+, and H+ which ultimately causes PHAIID (Boyden et al., PMID: 22266938). KLHL3 was first reported in relation to semidominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type II D (PHAIID) in 2006 (Boyden et al., PMID: 22266938). 27 variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) that have been reported in 24 probands in one publication (PMIDs: 22266938) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence (animal models, expression studies, and in vitro functional assays; PMIDs: 22406640, 23387299, 23453970, 24821705, 28052936, 30148674). KLHL3 is expressed in the distal convoluting tubule and connecting tubule of the kidney, and is shown to interact with CUL3 and WNK4 which are both implicated in PHAII. The variant, R528H, along with multiple other variants (Ohta et al., PMID: 23387299) have extensive evidence of functional alteration in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, multiple mouse models show pathogenic variation in KLHL3 and KO in both heterozygous and homozygous mouse models phenocopying PHAIID and mirroring the reported molecular mechanism. In summary, KLHL3 is definitively associated with semidominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type II D. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Tubulopathy GCEP on the meeting date 01/20/2022 (SOP Version 8).

The *KCTD1* (potassium channel tetramerization domain containing 1) gene is located on chromosome 18 at 18q11.2 and encodes a protein containing a BTB (Broad-complex, tramtrack and bric a brac) protein-protein interaction domain. This protein negatively regulates the AP-2 family of transcription factors and the Wnt signaling pathway. Variants in this gene are associated with Scalp-Ear-Nipple (SEN) syndrome, a rare genetic disorder characterized by defects in the scalp, malformed ears, and absent/hypoplastic nipples. *KCTD1* was first reported in connection with SEN syndrome in 2013 (Marneros et al., 2013, PMID: 23541344). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. 

Thirteen variants (12 missense, 1 inframe insertion) reported in 13 probands across five publications have been included in this curation (PMIDs: 8042668; 23541344; 39424163; 33883917; 34456244). The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including biochemical function, protein interaction, and model organism data). GST pull-down assays demonstrated *KCTD1* and transcription factor AP-2α interact directly in vitro (PMID: 191153150). Variants in TFAP2A cause Branchio-Oculo-Facial syndrome, which presents with clinical characteristics that overlap with those found in individuals with *KCTD1* variants. *KCTD1* and AP-2α overexpression is shown to decrease β-catenin expression levels (PMID:33000225). The canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway is one of the downstream regulated pathways of *KCTD1*, and it serves a crucial role in ectoderm patterning and craniofacial development. KCDT1 WT is also required for cell cell viability of keratinocytes (PMID: 38113115). Inactivation of Kctd1 in the kidney (Six2Cre+Kctd1fl/fl mice) results in a terminal differentiation defect in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) that impairs renal function and leads to a severe interstitial renal fibrosis in the adult with aging, similarly as seen in SEN syndrome patients (PMID: 38113115). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *KCTD1* and autosomal dominant SEN syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date June 4, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *RNU12* gene is located on chromosome 22 at 22q13.2 and encodes a snRNA (U12), part of the U12-dependent minor spliceosome complex involved in recognition and splicing of minor introns. *RNU12* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *RNU12*-related minor spliceopathy disorder in 2017 (Elsaid et al., PMID: 27863452). The features associated with *RNU12*-related disorder are highly variable. Compound heterozygotes with the n.*3C>T variant and a second rare variant in *RNU12* have been described with multiple malformations including clavicular hypoplasia, craniosynostosis, delayed closure of fontanelles, genitourinary malformations, developmental delay, and skin findings such as porokeratosis (Xing et al., PMID: 34085356). Individuals with biallelic variants that do not include the n.*3C>T variant present with cerebellar atrophy, hypotonia, seizure, and global developmental delay (PMID: 27863452). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity, CDAGS syndrome (OMIM:603116) and spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 33 (OMIM:620208). 

Nine variants in a non-protein-coding gene that have been reported in ten probands in two publications (PMID: 34085356, 27863452) are included in this curation. Variants in this gene segregated with disease in thirteen additional family members (PMID: 27863452). RNA sequencing analysis on blood from affected individuals revealed significant retention of minor introns in multiple genes, consistent with a dysfunction of *RNU12*, which is involved in minor intron splicing (PMID: 27863452). This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental data including biochemical function and protein interaction (PMID: 38484052, 27863452).

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. Although the total score is 6.3, the Syndromic Disorders GCEP opted to upgrade the classification from Limited to Moderate due to the number of reported cases at this time, as well as convincing functional evidence of minor intron splice impacts. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic disease GCEP on the meeting date February 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*GUF1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) in 2016 (Alfaiz et al., PMID: 26486472). The study reported a homozygous missense variant (c.1825G>T, p.Ala609Ser) in three siblings with infantile spasms, refractory seizures, hypsarrhythmia, hypotonia, and global developmental delays. This variant is supported by a functional study in a yeast model described by Alfaiz et al. (PMID: 26486472). To date, the p.Ala609Ser variant is the only pathogenic variant in *GUF1* reported in ClinVar, with additional benign and/or unknown significance (VUS) missense, nonsense, and frameshift variants reported. A termination and splice site variant have also been reported (PMIDs: 37820178 & 32487729), however these individuals were scored at zero due to high allele frequency and high homozygote counts in gnomAD v4.1. 

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date April 7, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*CST3* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Acys amyloidosis in 1987 (Jensson O et al., PMID:3673496). Acys amyloidosis is reported in Icelandic families who have amyloid deposition in cerebral and spinal arteries and arterioles that leads to recurrent hemorrhagic strokes, brain damage, and fatality. Only one missense variant has been reported in humans. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data, segregation data, and experimental data. 

Variants in *CST3 *have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: autosomal dominant, adult onset leukodystrophy without amyloid angiopathy and ACys. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found distinct differences in molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability between the disease assertions for *CST3*. One single missense variant is reported in Acys amyloidosis and only truncating variants are reported with adult-onset leukodystrophy. Neuropathologic studies do not show cerebral amyloid angiopathy or amyloid deposition in the adult-onset leukodystrophy cases. This is a defining feature of the Acys amyloidosis. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split: leukodystrophy, adult-onset, autosomal dominant, without amyloid angiopathy (MONDO:0979226) and Acys amyloidosis (MONDO:0005620). The split curation for autosomal dominant leukodystrophy without amyloid angiopathy (MONDO:0979226) has been curated separately.

Variants in this gene have been reported in at least 2 probands in 2 publications (PMID:1352269, 7482672). There is functional evidence that supports an upscoring of this variant (PMID:6886625, 8108423). Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 46 additional family members.

This gene-disease relationship is supported by expression studies showing the protein expressed highly in the brain and a cell culture model showing the same variant protein aggregation seen in patients (PMID: 24309898, 10193512).

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.

This classification was approved by the ClinGen Neurovascular Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date June 24, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ADGRL1* encodes an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor, also known as latrophilin 1, which has been implicated in synaptic development, maturation, and activity. *ADGRL1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2022 (Vitobello et al., PMID: 35907405). Clinical features observed in affected individuals include developmental delay, variable intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, hypotonia, sleep disturbances, and mild facial dysmorphism. Less common findings include macrocephaly, overweight, joint hypermobility, and seizures.

Thirteen variants (missense, nonsense, and frameshift) that have been reported in 8 probands in 1 publication (PMID: 35907405) and in 5 clinical laboratory submissions to ClinVar are included in this curation. In cases where parental testing was performed, the variants occurred *de novo*, except for 1 nonsense variant present in 2 affected siblings and inherited from the father with intellectual disability. *ADGRL1* is highly constrained for loss-of-function variants (pLI = 1, LOEUF = 0.28, gnomAD v4.1.1) and missense variants (Z score = 5.05). The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function (PMID: 35907405). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experiments in cultured neurons showing that Adgrl1 is essential for the assembly of inhibitory synapses (PMID: 38684366).

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *ADGRL1* and autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel on April 15, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*KCNT2* was first reported in relation to complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2017 (Gururaj, et.al. PMID: 29069600). This condition is characterized by early-onset seizures, global developmental delays, dysmorphic features, short stature, and neurological features such as hypotonia, spasticity, and poor visual attention.  

Included in this curation are 17 total variants (1 small deletion and 16 missense variants). They have been reported in 22 probands in 8 publications (PMIDs: 38510274, 37062836, 29740868, 34061450, 34276763, 29069600, 32773162, 32931186). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is attributed to an alteration of channel electrophysiology, including some studies that suggest a gain-of-function mechanism (PMID: 29069600). There are published functional studies showing a decrease in channel activity for certain variants (PMID: 37062836) and two truncating variants have been published in the literature (PMID: 32038177), however they have not been included in this curation and haploinsufficiency as a mechanism for this disease association is unclear at this time.  

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *KCNT2* and complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date June 16, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*GNB2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 2020 (Fukuda et al., PMID: 31698099). Clinical features observed in affected individuals include intellectual disability, developmental delay, hypotonia, dysmorphism, and autism. Less common findings include epilepsy and cardiac malformation. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities: sick sinus syndrome 4 (OMIM:619464) and neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and dysmorphic facies (OMIM:619503). 

At least 7 missense variants have been reported in humans. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, caused by perturbations in the interaction surface of the alpha and beta subunits of the GPCR protein, leading to attenuated expression of the beta subunit bound to and activating downstream effectors (PMID: 34183358). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by delayed neuronal migration and morphogenesis in Gβ2 knockdown mice (PMID: 28334111). 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism GCEP on the meeting date March 26th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ME2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive epilepsy in 2005 (Greenberg et al., PMID: 15532013). A homozygous haplotype containing rs608781 (ClinVar ID: 1676763) was associated with susceptibility to adolescent-onset idiopathic generalized epilepsy via family-based and case-control evidence. 

Evidence refuting this gene-disease relationship is population frequency data from gnomAD v4.1.1 that indicates this variant is too common to cause epilepsy, with a filtering allele frequency of 0.92. Additionally, no significant association was found between *ME2* and epilepsy in a GWAS meta-analysis of over 29,000 cases and 52,000 controls (International League Against Epilepsy Consortium on Complex Epilepsies 2023, PMID: 37653029). Of note, this gene has also been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and autism. These assertions will be assessed separately. 

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *ME2* and epilepsy has been refuted and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date May 19, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

SLC46A1 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive hereditary folate malabsorption (HFM) in 2006 (Qiu et al., PMID: 17129779). HFM is characterized by impaired intestinal folate absorption and reduced transport of folate into the central nervous system, resulting in systemic and cerebrospinal fluid folate deficiency. Clinical manifestations include megaloblastic anemia, recurrent infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, failure to thrive, and neurologic impairment. Findings are usually reversible with parenteral folate administration. The immunologic phenotype is thought to result from impairment of DNA synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation. Heterozygous carriers do not manifest clinical symptoms.
Seventeen unique variants (8 missense, 9 null) identified in fifteen probands from nine publications (PMIDs: 17129779, 17446347, 20005757, 20795774, 21333572, 23816405, 24534056, 29390264, 33146883) were included in this curation. Additional supporting cases have been reported in the literature, including segregation data (PMID: 20005757); however, the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached.
The disease mechanism is loss of function of the proton-coupled folate transporter (PCFT), resulting in impaired folate absorption and transport. Multiple patient-derived variants have been shown experimentally to abolish or markedly reduce folate transport activity (PMIDs: 17129779, 21602279, 17446347). Additional experimental evidence supports this gene–disease relationship. SLC46A1 knockout mice develop severe pancytopenia with macrocytic anemia and impaired erythroid maturation due to systemic folate deficiency, recapitulating key features of human disease (PMID: 21346251). Qiu et al. demonstrated that PCFT is highly active at acidic pH, localizes to the plasma membrane, and is highly expressed in the duodenum, consistent with folate absorption in the proximal small intestine. They also show that patient-derived mutant proteins exhibit markedly reduced or absent folate transport activity compared with wild-type PCFT (PMID: 17129779).
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between SLC46A1 and autosomal recessive hereditary folate malabsorption. This relationship has been replicated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been consistently upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP on July 16, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The *FEM1C* gene is located on chromosome 5 at 5q22.3, and codes for the FEM1 homolog C protein. This protein facilitates ubiquitin-resembling ligase-substrate adaptor function, and is key in ubiquitin-contingent protein catabolic processes through the C-end degron rule pathway. *FEM1C* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder in 2023 (Dubey et al., 2023 PMID: 36336956). Probands with this condition exhibit global developmental delay, moderate intellectual disability, pyramidal signs, ataxia, hypotonia, spasticity, ocular anomalies(including nystagmus and strabismus), and facial dysmorphisms (such as wide nasal bridge, malar hypoplasia, and posteriorly rotated ears). Two variants (both missense) that have been reported in two probands in one publication and a ClinVar submission are included in this curation (PMID: 36336956; and GeneDx/Illumina Laboratory internal data (ClinVar: SCV003802834)). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function (PMID: 36336956). No scorable experimental evidence was found. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 5/15/2026 (SOP Version 12).

The P2RX1 gene was first associated with platelet dysfunction in 2000 by Oury et al. (PMID: 10816552), who reported a somatic heterozygous 3-bp deletion (p.Leu351del) in a child with severe mucocutaneous bleeding and selective impairment of ADP-induced platelet aggregation; this variant was later shown to be incompatible with P2X1 biology as an ATP-gated ion channel rather than an ADP receptor, leading to its reclassification as a VUS by OMIM. A second case was shared via internal ClinGen Hemostasis/Thrombosis GCEP communication by Dr. Marie-Christine Kopp in April 2026, describing a patient with non-syndromic inherited platelet function disorder carrying a heterozygous nonsense variant (c.100C>T; p.Arg34Ter), normal platelet count and size, and selective aggregation defects to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine. Despite these two reports, genetic evidence remains limited and biologically inconsistent with known P2X1 function, while experimental data from mouse models support a role in high-shear thrombosis but not in a matching human bleeding phenotype. In summary, there is disputed evidence to support a gene-disease relationship between P2RX1 and platelet dysfunction, and this classification was determined following review by the ClinGen Hemostasis/Thrombosis GCEP.

*CD27* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive *CD27*-related lymphoproliferative and immune disorder in 1998 (Schmitter et al., PMID: 10444164). *CD27* is a member of the TNF receptor superfamily. It is required for regeneration and long term maintenance of T-cell immunity. It binds with CD70 ligand and serves a key role in regulating survival, function, and differentiation of T, B, NK and plasma cells. *CD27*-related lymphoproliferative and immune disorder is described as having disease onset within the first few months or years of life. This condition has a highly variable phenotype which can range from asymptomatic, to borderline hypogammaglobulinemia, to fully symptomatic with life-threatening EBV-related complications, as well as hematologic malignancies. Two null variants and five missense variants reported in 12 individuals in 5 publications (PMIDs: 22197273, 22801960, 25843314, 32041749, 28011863) are included in this curation. These variants are supportive of the gene-disease relationship with case-level data, segregation data, and functional data. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and expression studies (PMIDs: 11062504, 10444164, 33827115). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CD27* and autosomal recessive lymphoproliferative and immune disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date December 9th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal dominant, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy, type 1
disease_original_title: cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal dominant, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy, type 1
submitted_as_notes: NOTCH receptor 3 (*NOTCH3*) was first reported in relation to cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal dominant, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) in 1997 (Joutel et al., PMID 9388399). CADASIL often presents initially with migraines usually with aura and progresses to recurrent cerebral ischemic events, and cognitive decline (PMID 28231783). The disease is most commonly associated with cysteine altering variants (cysteine sparing variants have also been observed) in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFr) domain consisting of 34 repeats (exons 2-24) with variable severity based on where in the domain the variant occurs (PMID 41018180). Accumulation of granular osmiophilic material, which consists of the *NOTCH3*-extracellular domain, is considered a hallmark of the disease though there are examples of patients where this finding was absent (PMID 32231578). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found a difference in the molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities: Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal dominant, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM:125310), Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM:621295), Lateral meningocele syndrome (OMIM:130720), and Lipodystrophy, familial partial, type 1 (OMIM:608600). There are several cases with CADASIL features that carry biallelic *NOTCH3* variants however whether those cases are more severe than monoallelic cases is still a topic of debate so this curation will focus on autosomal dominant inheritance (PMID 32457593). The split curations for Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM:621295), Lateral meningocele syndrome (OMIM:130720), and Lipodystrophy, familial partial, type 1 (OMIM:608600) will be curated separately. To date, over 280 *NOTCH3* variants have been reported in CADASIL cases but this curation will focus on a total of 12 variants (10 missense, and 2 short, in-frame deletions) that have been reported in 12 probands in 12 publications (PMIDs 10716263, 11706120, 11486103, 18273901, 23572112, 25604251, 15304596, 21217157, 16717210, 25959358, 35523050) are included in this curation. Case-control evidence from a cohort of dementia and stroke patients with a well-matched control cohort showed a significant enrichment of rare, EGFr domain variants in the cases vs controls (PMID 34404235). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to involve aggregates of NOTCH3 extracellular domain in vessel walls but there is also evidence that altered interactions with ligands like JAG1 are part of the mechanism (PMID 32231578). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, expression data, cell culture models and functional alteration studies (PMIDs 42002114, 38592587, 23715323, 39759869, 41806331, 21217517). Two mouse models are able to recapitulate either the aggregate formation alone or aggregate formation and cognitive decline while the cell culture models provide further evidence of aggregate formation and vessel wall changes. Lastly, functional alteration evidence shows that in some cases there may be a dominant negative effect with aggregate formation and that receptor-ligand interactions can be altered leading to downstream effects on transcriptional regulation. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *NOTCH3* and cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.This classification was approved by the ClinGen Neurovascular Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date June 24, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: HMGB1-related brachyphalangy, polydactyly and tibial aplasia syndrome
disease_original_title: HMGB1-related brachyphalangy, polydactyly and tibial aplasia syndrome
submitted_as_notes:
*HMGB1* (High Mobility Group Box 1) is located at chromosome 13 at 13q12.3 and encodes a high mobility group box protein that functions as a DNA chaperone and prototypical damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP). *HMGB1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant *HMGB1*-related brachyphalangy, polydactyly and tibial aplasia syndrome in 2023 (Mensah et al., PMID: 36755093). The disorder is characterized by a distinct skeletal phenotype which includes brachydactyly, brachyphalangy of fingers, tibia aplasia or hypoplasia, polydactyly, and contractures of large joints. Additionally, most affected individuals present with developmental delay, hearing impairment and genitourinary abnormalities, and more variably, microcephaly, malformed ears, and blepharophimosis.

*HMGB1* has also been associated with autosomal dominant *HMGB1*-related neurodevelopmental disorder. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in the molecular mechanism and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities, autosomal dominant *HMGB1*-related brachyphalangy, polydactyly and tibial aplasia syndrome (MONDO: 0700354), and *HMGB1*-related neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID: 34164801). The split curation for autosomal dominant *HMGB1*-related neurodevelopmental disorder will be curated separately.

Two frameshift variants, both located in intrinsically disordered acidic C-terminal tail region of *HMGB1* that have been reported in at least six probands from two publications and a ClinVar entry (PMIDs: 36755093, 20661588; ClinVar ID 1810206) are included in this curation. Both frameshift variants lead to protein extension and the addition of arginine residues which cause the acidic C-terminal to become basic. In vitro studies using recombinant protein and overexpression in continuous cell lines demonstrate mutant protein is associated with altered nuclear localization and a suspected gain of function mechanism of pathogenicity (PMID: 36755093). This gene-disease relationship is supported by experimental data, namely expression. Expression data showing differential spatial and temporal expression of Hgmb1 protein in the developing mouse limb (PMID: 17548469). A *Hmgb1* homozygous targeted knock out mouse model also supports a role for *Hmgb1* protein in bone development during embryogenesis but the model was not scored because of difference in zygosity and variant type (PMID: 17548469).

In summary, there is moderate evidence supporting the relationship between HMBG1 and autosomal dominant brachyphalangy, polydactyly and tibial aplasia syndrome. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Syndromic disease GCEP on the meeting date February 24, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

VMA21 was first reported in relation to a congenital disorder of glycosylation in 2020 (PMID: 32145091). This gene is an assembly chaperone of the vacuolar ATPase mapped to chromosome X28 (PMID: 32145091). In addition to CDG, VMA21 has been associated with X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy (XMEA) and follicular lymphoma (PMIDs: 37756622, 40033998) To date, three male patients with VMA21 mutations have been diagnosed with CDG syndrome (PMIDs: 32145091, 37756622, 40033998). Their clinical features range from liver cholestasis and steatosis to mild hypercholesterolemia. These symptoms were associated with increased levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at early ages, followed by hypercholesterolemia in two of these patients (PMIDs: 32145091, 40033998). The hemizygous mutations identified are single nucleotide substitutions resulting in missense mutations and premature stop codons (PMID: 32145091). While no animal model currently exists for this CDG, there are animal models for XMEA (PMID: 40033998). This may provide a platform for future studies. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on July 6, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*MUSK* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive congenital myasthenic syndrome in 2004 (PMID: 15496425) and fetal akinesia deformation sequence in 2015 (PMID: 25612909). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity termed *MUSK*-related myasthenic syndrome: Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome 9 (MONDO:0014587) and Fetal akinesia deformation sequence 1 (MONDO:0100101). Seventeen variants (11 missense, 4 nonsense, 2 frameshift) that have been reported in twelve probands in nine publications (PMIDs: 15496425, 19949040, 20371544, 25537362, 25612909, 29704306, 30719842, 37091828, 37721175) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function via biallelic pathogenic variants that lead to deficient postsynaptic structure at the neuromuscular junction, defective acetylcholine receptor clustering and, ultimately, impairment of the signaling pathway (PMID: 38566418). 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, expression studies, in vitro functional assays (PMIDs: 8653786, 18718936, 20371544, 23715323). Bulk tissue gene expression data from the GTEx Portal indicates *MUSK* is highly expressed in skeletal muscle (PMID: 23715323, dbGaP Accession phs000424.v10.p2). *MUSK* interacts with *DOK7*, a gene determined to be definitively associated with congenital myasthenic syndrome by ClinGen (PMID: 20371544). Transgenic knockout mice demonstrated immobility at birth with high mortality recapitulating the reduced intrauterine movement and fetal death in human cases of *MUSK*-related Fetal akinesia deformation sequence fetal FADS (PMID: 8653786). Futhermore, a transgenic mouse model of the murine p.V790M variant (human equivalent of *MUSK*:p.V789M) recapitulated the human congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS) phenotype when the p.V790M variant was heterozygous with a loss-of-function allele (PMID: 18718936). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *MUSK* and autosomal recessive *MUSK*-related congenital myasthenic syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Myopathies and Myasthenic Syndromes Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date April, 27th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

GPR161 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant GPR161-related medulloblastoma predisposition in 2019 (Begemann et al., PMID: 31609649). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found differences in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities: GPR161-related medulloblastoma predisposition, Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome, Spina bifida. Five variants (missense, in-frame indel, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in seven probands in two publications (PMIDs: 31609649, 39184053) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including animal and cell culture models, expression studies and biochemical assays (PMIDs: 29386106, 23332756, 38326651). In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between GPR161 and autosomal dominant GPR161-related medulloblastoma predisposition. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition GCEP on the meeting date January 13, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

SHH Evidence Summary: 
The Brain Malformations GCEP concludes that there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between SHH and autosomal dominant holoprosencephaly 3 (HPE3) as of June 23, 2026. Variants in sonic hedgehog (SHH; OMIM: 600725) were first reported in relation to autosomal dominant HPE3 (OMIM: 142945) in 1996 (Roessler et al., PMID: 8896572). Holoprosencephaly is a severe congenital brain malformation defined by failure of the embryonic forebrain to cleave into two distinct hemispheres. The clinical spectrum ranges from alobar HPE (complete non-cleavage with a single fused ventricle and absent interhemispheric fissure) to semilobar and lobar forms. It extends to microforms including single median maxillary central incisor (SMMCI) and hypotelorism. Facial features including cleft lip and palate and ocular hypotelorism are common and typically correlate with the severity of the brain malformation. SHH encodes a secreted morphogen critical for spatial patterning of the central nervous system and facial midline. The active N-terminal signaling domain (SHH-N) binds the PTCH1 receptor complex, assisted by co-receptors GAS1, CDO, and BOC, to drive downstream GLI-mediated transcription essential for forebrain midline induction. Cases of HPE3 have been reported as de novo, maternally inherited, or paternally inherited, consistent with autosomal dominant transmission. Reduced penetrance and variable expressivity are documented features of this gene-disease relationship. Obligate carriers of SHH variants may present with microforms such as SMMCI or hypotelorism rather than overt HPE, and some carriers remain clinically unaffected, as demonstrated by a paternally inherited variant (p.Leu382Pro) in a family with fetal HPE reported in Paulussen et al. 2010.

Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: holoprosencephaly 3 (OMIM:142945), microphthalmia/coloboma 5 (OMIM:611638), and single median maxillary central incisor (OMIM:147250). 
  	
At least 15 unique variants, including nonsense, frameshift, in-frame deletion, and missense variants distributed throughout the SHH-N signaling domain, have been reported in scored probands across four publications (Nanni et al. 1999, PMID: 10556296; Paulussen et al. 2010, PMID: 20531442; Gekas et al. 2012, PMID: 23181171; Savastano et al. 2014, PMID: 24764759). Additional family segregation evidence was contributed by candidate-gene sequencing across four kindreds. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached.
  	
The mechanism of pathogenicity is haploinsufficiency: heterozygous loss-of-function variants reduce the effective dose of SHH signaling in the developing forebrain, thereby failing midline induction and leading to HPE (PMIDs: 15888442, 19060208, 31685615). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence across five independent categories, including biochemical function, protein interaction, expression, functional alteration, and model systems, achieving a maximum experimental score of 6.0 points (PMIDs: 15888442, 19060208, 19478089, 31685615). 
  	
In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between SHH and autosomal dominant holoprosencephaly 3 (HPE3). This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Brain Malformations Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 23, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

SPNS2 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss in 2019 (Ingham et al., PMID: 30973865). Onset of this hearing loss is in infancy/early childhood and has been observed as downsloping and high-frequency. Four variants (missense, inframe deletion, frameshift, nonsense) that have been reported in two probands in two publications are included in this curation (PMIDs: 30973865, 36494063). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function (30973865). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse models, rescue evidence, expression level data; PMIDs: 25356849, 37552762). Homozygous knockout mice have progressive hearing loss, reduced endocochlear potential, and ocular anomalies (such as corneal opacity). The hearing phenotype was rescued in mice that received a recombinase allele and tamoxifen injection. Expression-level data shows strong expression of the gene in the cochlea (specifically the lateral wall and Organ of Corti) in wild-type mice, but significantly reduced expression in mutants. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hearing Loss GCEP on the meeting date 7/15/2026 (SOP Version 12).

Pathogenic variants in OTOF are associated with auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder (ANSD), a form of hearing loss characterized by defective synaptic transmission between Inner Hair Cells (IHCs) and auditory nerve fibers (PMID: 20301429).  OTOF (NM_001287489.2) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive sensorineural hearing loss (DFNB9) in 1999 (PMID: 10192385). Of note, there is another OTOF transcript, NM_194248.3, which is expressed in the brain and is not relevant to hearing. Therefore, the hearing loss evidence should be evaluated in the context of the cochlear transcript NM_001287489.2. Five variants (nonsense, missense, splice site) that have been reported in four probands in four publications (PMIDs: 10192385, 11483641, 12127154, 24135434) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function, as a lack of OTOF results in abolished depolarization-induced exocytosis of Ca2+ ions in IHCs (PMID: 17055430). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by an expression study showing OTOF expression in cochlear hair cells during embryonic development and postnatally (PMID: 17055430). Protein interaction studies have also indicated that OTOF interacts with MYO6, a gene that is implicated in hearing loss and controls targeting of intracellular proteins to the membrane of inner hair cells (PMID: 19417007). OTOF also interacts with syntaxin1 and SNAP25 (which are involved in synaptic vesicle exocytosis) in a Ca2+-dependent manner (PMID: 17055430). Additionally, Otof -/- mice were shown to have a decreased number of ribbon synapses in the IHCs at 15 days old and had profound hearing loss (PMID: 17055430). Another study using a pachanga mouse model demonstrated that mice with a homozygous missense variant had profound deafness (PMID: 20562868). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between OTOF and autosomal recessive sensorineural hearing loss. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.
OTOF gene therapy has demonstrated efficacy and safety across preclinical and clinical studies, culminating in a recent regulatory approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Initial clinical trials using DB-OTO (dual Adeno-Associated Virus 1 gene therapy) showed substantial functional improvement in children with OTOF-related hearing loss (PMID: 41085057). These findings were reinforced by multiple subsequent early-phase trials, which consistently demonstrated improvement in auditory thresholds and speech perception across treated participants (PMIDs: 38839897, 38280389, 40690227). Subsequently, a single-arm, multicentre trial expanded these findings to a larger and more diverse population, including a broader age range and a longer follow-up duration, further supporting the safety and sustained efficacy of AAV1-hOTOF (PMID: 42020731). Based on robust evidence, this therapy was approved by the U.S. FDA, marking a significant milestone as one of the first gene therapies for genetic hearing loss.

*ATP2A2* was evaluated by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP in June 2026 due to its presence on at least 8 multi-gene testing panels for epilepsy per data from the Genetic Testing Registry at the time of review. Disease assertions available for this gene were reviewed in accordance with the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Criteria. Variants in *ATP2A2* have primarily been reported in individuals in the literature with autosomal dominant Darier disease, a primarily dermatological condition. Additionally, variants in *ATP2A2* have been reported in individuals with autosomal dominant acrokeratosis verruciformis (AKV), autosomal dominant susceptibility to rhabdomyolysis, and in one family with autosomal recessive progressive proximal myopathy. As discussed below, while some individuals with variants in this gene and these other clinical presentations have also been reported to have epilepsy (PMIDs: 10441325, 11168576, 30345710, and 28498512), *ATP2A2* does not appear to be a primary cause of epilepsy; therefore, the Epilepsy GCEP is splitting this disease assertion from the others to refute. The other diseases are not being evaluated as part of this curation.

*ATP2A2* was first reported in three individuals with epilepsy and Darier disease in 1999 (PMID: 10441325). At least six individuals with variants in *ATP2A2* (four missense, a frameshift, and a canonical splice) amongst over 200 other individuals with molecularly confirmed Darier disease have been reported to have epilepsy (PMIDs: 10441325, 11168576, 30345710). One individual with AKV and a recurrent missense variant has been reported to have short recurrent seizures not related to fevers (PMID: 28498512). Due to clinical suspicion of Darier disease, genetic testing for the seven probands described with seizures was limited to sequencing of only the *ATP2A2* gene; other potential genetic etiologies for their epilepsy were not ruled out. The frequency of epilepsy amongst individuals with *ATP2A2*-related Darier disease is similar to that of the general population frequency of epilepsy. Epidemiologic studies of individuals with clinically diagnosed Darier Disease show a slightly elevated risk for epilepsy; however, this risk is still relatively low, indicating that *ATP2A2* is not a primary epilepsy gene (PMID: 38820685, 38531956, 20456342).

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *ATP2A2* and autosomal dominant epilepsy has been refuted, and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on June 16, 2026 (SOP version 12).

MINAR2 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNB120) in 2022 (Bademci et al., PMID: 35727972). Four variants (frameshift, nonsense, missense) that have been reported in four probands in two publications (PMIDs: 35727972, 41130944) are included in this curation. One family was reported with six segregations. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, as a loss of function mouse model resulted in elevated ABR and DPOAE thresholds (PMID: 35727972). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a loss of function mouse model that recapitulates the human phenotype, expression data showing that MINAR2 is highly expressed in the cochlea (PMID: 35727972), and a study showing that loss of MINAR2 reduces reduces cholesterol localization to the inner ear hair bundles in zebrafish (PMID: 36317962). In summary, there is strong evidence to support the relationship between MINAR2 and autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted.
