*TNK2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive epilepsy in 2013 (Hitomi et al., PMID: 23686771). Four years later, Mao et al. (PMID: 27977884) reported four variants (missense or nonsense) in two families with autosomal recessive infantile spasms. However, the authors of the original report (PMID: 23686771) responded with a retraction of their publication after it became clear that the variant was too frequent in the general population to be the cause of the disease (2,790/1,601,154 alleles and 25 homozygotes in gnomAD v4.1). No further credible genetic evidence for the association of *TNK2* with epilepsy has been reported. In addition, *TNK2* is relatively tolerant to both missense and loss of function variants according to gnomADv4.1. 

In summary, the evidence supporting the relationship between *TNK2* and autosomal recessive epilepsy has been refuted and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Epilepsy GCEP on the meeting date July 21, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

CSF1R was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive brain abnormalities, neurodegeneration, and dysosteosclerosis (BANDDOS) in 2019 (PMID: 30982608, 30982609). The condition is characterized by early disease onset (<18 years old), developmental delay and/or cognitive decline, spasticity with abnormal reflexes and other pyramidal signs, parkinsonism, dysphagia, seizures, and speech disturbances. On radiographic imaging, patients typically present with diffuse osteosclerosis of the craniofacial bones (most prominent in the skull base), platyspondyly and sclerosis of the vertebral bodies, sclerotic pelvic bones, and tubular bones. MRI findings include progressive bilateral white matter lesions, calcifications, cerebral atrophy, ventriculomegaly, agenesis/thinning of the corpus callosum, Dandy-Walker malformation, and malformation of cortical development (PMID: 30982608, 30982609, 37349768). The CSF1R gene encodes the colony stimulating factor-1 receptor, which is a class III tyrosine kinase, and acts as a cell-surface receptor for CSF1 and IL-34 (PMID: 18467591). CSF1R is mainly expressed in the myeloid cells. The survival, proliferation, and differentiation of cells belonging to this lineage is maintained by CSF1R signaling (PMID: 24742461). Variants in CSF1R have also been reported individuals with the following disease entity: autosomal dominant hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids [HDLS; also known as adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP)], which is characterised as an adult-onset disorder and includes behavioral, cognitive, and personality changes with  progressive motor impairment +/- seizures or ataxia.  Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern, phenotypic variability, and potentially molecular mechanism for the gene CSF1R. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities: autosomal recessive CSF1R-related disorder (aka BANDDOS, OMIM: 164770) and autosomal dominant CSF1R-related disorders (aka HDLS/ALSP, OMIM: 221820). The split curation for autosomal dominant CSF1R-related disorder has been curated separately. This curation includes 9 probands with 9 distinct variants (missense, nonsense, insertion, in-frame deletion, frameshift, and splicing) across 6 publications (PMID: 30982609, 30282608, 33749994, 32464672, 37349768, 38934054). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has been reached. The disease mechanism is believed to be loss of function. The gene-disease relationship is also supported by an animal model (PMID: 22046273) involving mice homozygous for a null mutation in the CSF1R gene, which recapitulated the microglial depletion and enlarged ventricles seen in affected individuals along with compressed parenchyma. A second knock-out mouse model (PMID: 11756160) was shown to recapitulate the skeletal phenotype, specifically osteopetrosis, seen in patients with biallelic CSF1R variants. Additional experimental evidence exists, but was not included in this curation as definitive status had been reached. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CSF1R and autosomal recessive CSF1R-related disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated over time in both the research and clinical diagnostics settings, and has been upheld over time. 

This classification was approved by the Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy Working Group on April 21, 2026 (SOP Version #11).

*MCM9* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive MCM9-related gametogenic failure in 2014 (Wood-Trageser et al., PMID: 25480036). Variants in *MCM9* have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: premature ovarian insufficiency (PMID: 25480036), non-obstructive azoospermia (PMID: 36769638), ovarian dysgenesis 4 (OMIM: 616185). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, or phenotypic variability. Therefore, all of these disease entities have been lumped into one, MCM9-related gametogenic failure (http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/MONDO_1060226). 

Nine different predicted nonsense variants that have been reported in twenty probands in nine publications (PMIDs: 31042289, 24580036, 36769638, 30406445, 26771056, 32613604, 26806154, 35690514, 40593474) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is supported by animal models and in vitro functional assays. *MCM9* binds to *MCM8* and *HROB*, both being involved in gametogenesis (PMIDs: 37535404, 22771115, 38678026). Absence of *MCM9* causes defects in homologous recombination repair mechanism (PMID: 22771115). Additionally, *MCM9* knockout mice show non-obstructive azoospermia or oligozoospermia in male mice and premature ovarian insufficiency in female mice (PMIDs: 22771120, 21987787). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence to support the relationship between *MCM9* and autosomal recessive MCM9-related gametogenic failure. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on the meeting date April 1, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: inflammatory skin and bowel disease, neonatal, 1
disease_original_title: inflammatory skin and bowel disease, neonatal, 1
submitted_as_notes:
*ADAM17* (also known as TACE, TNF-α converting enzyme) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive inflammatory skin and bowel disease, neonatal, 1 in 2011 by Blaydon et al. (PMID: 22010916). NISBD1 is a severe multisystem disorder characterized by neonatal- or infantile-onset inflammatory skin disease, including erythroderma, pustular dermatitis, perioral and perianal erythema, together with chronic diarrhea/enteropathy, recurrent cutaneous and systemic infections, failure to thrive, and variable abnormalities of hair, nails, and immune function. *ADAM17* encodes a membrane-bound metalloprotease that mediates ectodomain shedding of numerous cell-surface proteins, including TNF-α, IL-6 receptor, and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) ligands, thereby regulating epithelial barrier homeostasis, tissue repair, and inflammatory signaling.

At least nine unique *ADAM17* variants have been reported in seven probands across seven publications (PMIDs: 22010916, 25804906, 32447396, 33953303, 34993966, 40968583, 42015567). The reported variant spectrum includes frameshift variants, a multi-exon deletion, a canonical splice-site variant, a synonymous splice-disrupting variant, and multiple missense variants. Several variants have direct functional evidence demonstrating impaired *ADAM17* activity, which abolish ectodomain shedding activity in cell-based assays. No clinical manifestations have been reported in heterozygous carriers from families with NISBD1-associated *ADAM17* variants.

This gene-disease relationship is further supported by experimental evidence including biochemical function studies, expression analyses, functional alteration studies, and animal models. *ADAM17* expression is demonstrated in disease-relevant tissues including skin and intestine, and affected patient tissues show markedly reduced or absent *ADAM17* protein expression (PMID: 22010916). Patient-derived peripheral blood mononuclear cells exhibit defective TNF-α release despite preserved or increased production of other inflammatory cytokines, consistent with loss of *ADAM17* sheddase activity (PMID: 22010916). Mouse models with reduced or absent adam17 function recapitulate major components of the human phenotype, including epithelial abnormalities, hair defects, impaired intestinal homeostasis, defective epithelial regeneration, and increased susceptibility to colitis (PMIDs: 22236242, 26283731, 9812885, 20603312).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ADAM17* and autosomal recessive inflammatory skin and bowel disease, neonatal, 1. This relationship has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel (SOP Version 12).

Of note, a single family with autosomal dominant hypotrichosis associated with a heterozygous *ADAM17* variant has been reported (PMID: 38771644); however, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether this represents a distinct disease entity or a milder allelic manifestation of *ADAM17* deficiency, and therefore this assertion was not included in the present curation.

LZTR1 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Schwannomatosis (SWN) in 2014 (Piotrowski et al. 2014, PMID: 24362817). SWN is a rare, inherited tumor syndrome that leads to an increased risk for Schwannoma development. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found other disease entities associated with this gene (Noonan Syndrome 10 - AD [MONDO:0014693] and Noonan Syndrome 2 – AR [OMIM:605275]) that were split from this curation. Nine variants (nonsense, splice site, frameshift, and missense) that have been reported in 9 probands described in 2 publications (PMIDs: 24362817 and 25008767) and one case-control study (PMID: 35391499) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be heterozygous LOF. Pathogenic loss-of-function variants are not uncommon in the general population, and the expected penetrance of SWN is extremely low in individuals with no family history (<1%)(PMID:  35361920
). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (expression studies) (PMIDs: 25335493). Heterozygous loss of LZTR1 alone is not sufficient to trigger the development of schwannomas. Development of  LZTR1-related schwannomatosis is dependent on additional somatic mutational events known as the 3-step/4-hit model that causes biallelic loss of function of both LZTR1 and NF2.PMID: 24362817). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between LZTR1 and autosomal dominant Schwannomatosis. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This gene-disease pair was curated on 08/21/2025 by the Hereditary Cancer GCEP (SOP Version 11).

disease_title: ectodermal dysplasia 10B, hypohidrotic/hair/tooth type, autosomal recessive
disease_original_title: ectodermal dysplasia 10B, hypohidrotic/hair/tooth type, autosomal recessive
submitted_as_notes: *EDAR* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia in 1999 (Monreal et al., PMID: 10431241). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in inheritance pattern and molecular mechanism. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, autosomal dominant hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (OMIM:129490), autosomal recessive hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (OMIM:224900), and nonsyndromic tooth agenesis. The split curations for autosomal dominant hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia and nonsyndromic tooth agenesis will be curated separately. 19 variants (missense, splice site, frameshift, small deletion) that have been reported in 15 probands in seven publications (PMIDs: 10431241, 16435307, 18816645, 16029325, 15373768, 17501952, 20979233) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model of reduced cusp number and tooth size in mice with loss-of-function variants in EDAR (PMID:19340299). An expression study showed that EDAR was expressed in the outer and inner root sheaths and secondary hair germ, and EDAR signaling was shown to be involved in hair cycle control (PMID:17148670). Additionally, the expression pattern of EDAR-null mice during tooth morphogenesis was restricted to ectodermal tissue (PMID:11203701). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *EDAR* and autosomal recessive hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Craniofacial Malformations GCEP on the meeting date July 16, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ZBTB11* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder in 1995 (Stromme et al., PMID: 7586637). The condition is regressive, with phenotypes usually presenting around three to five years of age and increasing in severity through life. Intellectual disability (ranging from mild to profound), along with other features, such as contractures, coordination problems, cataracts, and combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA) are common phenotypes across affected individuals.

Nineteen variants (14 missense, 1 nonsense, and 4 small deletion/duplications leading to frameshift) that have been reported in 13 probands in four publications (PMIDs: 29893856, 31130284, 35104841, 38899514) are included in this curation. All de novo and unknown inheritance variants are within the C2H2 zinc finger domain. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function due to reduced binding to transcriptional targets (PMIDs: 35104841, 38355937). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. 

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and functional expression studies (PMID: 29893856). Other members of the ZBTB gene family (*ZBTB18, ZBTB20*) have previously been associated with intellectual disability and similar syndromic disorders (PMIDs: 24193349, 25017102), however intellectual disability and/or autism in these genes are associated with autosomal dominant inheritance.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ZBTB11* and autosomal recessive syndromic complex neurodevelopmental disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Intellectual Disability and Autism GCEP on the meeting date June 2, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_original_title: cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1
submitted_as_notes: Notch Receptor 3 (*NOTCH3*) was first reported in relation to cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 in 2015 (Pipucci et al., PMID 25870235). Biallelic null variation in *NOTCH3* is associated with, but not limited to the following features: early onset leukoencephalopathy, seizure, early onset stroke, global developmental delay and spasticity. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in the molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into two disease entities, Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal dominant, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM: 125310), Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM: 621295). Myofibromatosis, infantile 2 (OMIM: 615293), Lateral meningocele syndrome (OMIM: 130720), and Lipodystrophy, familial partial, type 1 (OMIM: 608600) which have also been associated with *NOTCH3* variation are not curated here as they represent different disease entities characterized by specific variant localization or a lack of case data to clearly determine their relationship with the current curation. The split curation for Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal dominant, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM: 125310) has been curated separately. 8 variants (1 missense, 2 nonsense, and 5 frameshift) that have been reported in 7 probands in 6 publications (PMIDs: 25870235, 35026854, 38824264, 37688971, 32980981, 41196431) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function (PMID 39191170). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by mouse model and expression data (PMIDs 23715323, 18347334, 25477343). Knock-out mouse models show a more severe reaction to induced ischemic injury than WT mice, an effect which was rescued by WT human *NOTCH3*; and damage to vascular smooth muscle tissue similar to that found in patients. Additionally, *NOTCH3* is heavily expressed in vascular tissue which is relevant to the disease features in cases. In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *NOTCH3* and autosomal recessive *NOTCH3*-related autosomal recessive cerebral arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Neurovascular GCEP on the meeting date August 26, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection
disease_original_title: familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection
submitted_as_notes:
*FOXE3* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissections in 2016 by Kuang *et al* (PMID: 26854927) who described eight heterozygous variants in *FOXE3* suspected to cause disease in individuals with acute aortic dissection inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. In contrast, biallelic variants in *FOXE3* are associated with a spectrum of ocular anomalies such as autosomal recessive anterior segment dysgenesis, congenital cataract, primary aphakia, sclerocornea and microphthalmia (PMIDs: 11159941, 16826526). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Work Group, we found differences in molecular mechanisms and inheritance patterns and we did not identify overlap or segregation data in favor of merging these clinical entities. Therefore, familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (FTAAD), cataract 34 multiple types (MIM# 612968), and anterior segment dysgenesis 2 (also known as congenital primary aphakia) (MIM# 610256) have been split into multiple disease entities. The gene-disease relationships between *FOXE3*, congenital cataract, and anterior segment dysgenesis were curated separately by the ClinGen Glaucoma / Neuro-Opthalmology Gene Curation Expert Panel. This curation is for the gene-disease relationship between *FOXE3* and autosomal dominant familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection (FTAAD) (MONDO:0019625). 

Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship between *FOXE3* and FTAAD includes case-level, segregation and experimental data. Four variants (three missense and one frameshift) that have been reported in four probands in two publications (PMIDs: 26854927 and 39226896) are included in this curation. Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 5 additional family members. Kuang *et al.* (PMID: 26854927) described a large family of European descent (TAA337) with 8 cases of acute aortic dissection and a combined LOD score of 3. Ascending aorta pathological studies from an affected individual in this family revealed loss of smooth muscle cells between elastin fibers. The disease penetrance in family TAA337 was specific to males only as female carriers, despite being in their sixth and seventh decades of life at time of report, did not show symptoms of aortopathy. Therefore, only five affected individuals were applied to the segregation score. A second family (MS300) was also reported to be affected by aortic root dilatation and had three members with the variant FOXE3*:p.Gly137Asp, however, there were not enough segregations in this family to qualify as scorable evidence as per the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity Standard Operating Procedures (version 12).

This gene-disease relationship is further supported by experimental data in the form of tissue expression, zebrafish and mouse models. While bulk tissue gene expression data from the GTEx Portal indicates *FOXE3* to be expressed in the aorta, the value of this evidence was reduced as the level of gene expression in the aorta (0.097 TPM) was not high compared to other tissue types (PMID: 23715323, dbGaP Accession phs000424.v10.p2). Kuang *et al* knocked down Foxe3 using morpholinos in Zebrafish and showed that it disrupts aortic arch development while knockdown of p53, a key regulator of SMC apoptosis, rescued this phenotype (PMID: 26854927). Kuang *et al* also showed transverse aortic constriction (TAC) led to altered aortic remodeling and increased rupture in Foxe3 knockout mice and that inhibition of p53 rescued aortic developmental defects and aberrant aortic remodeling in the Foxe3 knockout mice that underwent TAC (PMID: 26854927). A loss of function disease mechanism for *FOXE3*-related FTAAD is uncertain as other spontaneous and targeted mouse models of homozygous Foxe3 disruption recapitulated human patient ocular features anomalies without cardiac abnormalities or aortopathy (PMIDs: 10652278, 16199865).

The number of published cases of *FOXE3*-related FTAAD post 2016 is very limited. A missense variant *FOXE3*:p.R90L was mentioned in a cohort of thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection patients (Bulat A. Ziganshin, PHD thesis 2024, https://doi.org/10.7916/7xzc-gg92), however, it was not included in the curation as it is not rare in the population (GrpMax AF >0.0001) and it was also reported in patients presenting with autosomal recessive primary aphakia and autosomal dominant Peters’ anomaly, both without FTAAD (PMID: 25504734 and AJ Churchill *et al.* Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science 2002). Queries to submitters of several *FOXE3* variants in ClinVar tagged with the condition “cardiac phenotype” did not result in any phenotypic association to FTAAD (Clinvar IDs: SCV006556805.1 (VCV001998828.5), SCV005025916.1 (VCV001009731.10), SCV003758557.3 (VCV000427852.14), SCV005584152.1 (VCV000861248.9), SCV005025950.1 (VCV003226204.1)). Finally, an extensive literature search did not reveal evidence of increased burden of rare variants in *FOXE3* within relevant FTAAD/aortopathy patient cohorts or biobank studies (PMIDs: 37426142, 38256594). 

This gene-disease pair was originally evaluated by the Heritable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 15th, 2016. It was reevaluated on June 19th, 2026. As a result of this reevaluation, the classification was downgraded from MODERATE to LIMITED, based on limited case-level evidence as well as the lack of new genetic and experimental evidence clearly attributing *FOXE3* with FTAAD. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Heritable Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection subgroup of the Hereditary Cardiovascular Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel on June 19th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

Lysosome-associated membrane protein 3 (*LAMP3*) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive interstitial lung disease in 2025 (Louvrier et al., PMID: 40023045). The first report of *LAMP3* autosomal recessive inherited interstitial lung disease in an animal model was in 2020 (Dillard et al., PMID: 32150563). *LAMP3*-related disease can include but is not limited to: neonatal respiratory distress, oxygen dependency, ground-glass opacification, and dyspnea. The age of onset is not clearly described in all of the curated cases but appears to be in childhood for the cases in this curation.

7 variants (4 missense, 2 frame-shift, and 1 canonical splice-site) that have been reported in 5 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 40023045, 41653023) are included in this curation. 2 missense variants (Gly388Arg and Thr268Met) showed abnormal glycosylation and reduced protein expression. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models and expression studies (PMIDs: 25613900, 34161347, 32150563, 40023045). The Human Protein Atlas shows *LAMP3* protein expression in Lung, Lymph node, and Tonsil tissues only. *LAMP3* encodes a lysosomal membrane glycoprotein that localizes to lamellar bodies (LB) in alveolar type II (AT2) cells, the specialized epithelial cells responsible for surfactant production and secretion. Both humans and mice show LAMP3 dysfunction resulting in conspicuous LBs within AT2 cells. LAMP3 dysfunction was inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern in a pedigree of Airedale Terrier and recapitulated human phenotypes like: failure to thrive, poor suck, and neonatal respiratory distress which presented as a refusal to suckle and lethargic at birth in Airedale Terriers. *LAMP3* is involved in surfactant protein metabolism, through at least the interaction with SP-B and SP-C, and that *LAMP3* abnormalities may be associated with an alteration in surfactant protein homoeostasis. Additionally, SFTPC and SFTPB are curated definitive by the ILD GCEP for SFTPC-related interstitial lung disease and surfactant metabolism dysfunction, pulmonary, 1 respectively.

In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between *LAMP3* and autosomal recessive *LAMP3*-related interstitial lung disease. Three years must elapse from the first proposal of the assertion to reach a definitive classification without any valid contradictory evidence. We will re-evaluate this gene-disease relationship at that time to determine if an upgraded classification of definitive is warranted. This classification was approved by the ClinGen ILD GCEP on the meeting date August 18 2026 (SOP Version 12).

Eukaryotic translation elongation factor 2 (*EEF2*) was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia 26 (SCA26) in 2012 (Hekman et al., PMID 23001565). The first report of a de novo neurodevelopmental disease was from Nabais Sá in 2021 (PMID: 33355653). Disease related to variation in *EEF2* can include but is not limited to: progressive ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria, cerebellar atrophy, developmental delay, abnormal cerebral morphology, and dysmorphic features. Age of onset for *EEF2* related disease has been reported in adults for the SCA26 entity with an earlier onset in childhood for the de novo neurodevelopmental disease. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group there were no differences in the allelic requirement or genetic mechanism between spinocerebellar ataxia 26 (OMIM:609306) and a disease entity characterized by de novo variants and referred to as *EEF2*-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder in at least one 2024 report (PMID 39359947). No cases have been described with both early onset neurodevelopmental disorder features and late onset progressive ataxia at the time of this curation. It is possible however that the cases with de novo *EEF2* variants were too young for late onset ataxia features to develop. 9 variants (8 missense, and 1 nonsense) that have been reported in 9 probands/families in 6 publications and 1 ClinVar submission (PMIDs 23001565, 39812846; SCV002549140.2) are included in this curation. The initial family in PMID 23001565 included segregation data with haplotype data for three generations and a total of 24 affected with the p.Pro596His variant and 28 unaffected without the variant. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function that involves altering protein translation at the ribosome by affecting -1 programmed ribosomal frameshifting and termination codon recognition. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a mouse model, yeast model, and in vitro functional data of a reduction in GTP hydrolysis (PMIDs 35993189, 23001565, 36470424). The heterozygous, homologous *EEF2* knockout mouse model did not show any features of ataxia but did show an impact to social behavior and similar dysfunctional protein synthesis found in a yeast model expressing the same variant. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataxia GCEP on the meeting date September 9, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*PDYN* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia in 2004 (Verbeck et al., PMID: 15306549). Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level data and experimental data. *PDYN* variants were reported in as low as 0.1% of ataxia cohorts (PMIDs: 15306549, 21035104, 22287014, 23108490, 23471613, 25595316, 32587707). For the purposes of this gene disease validity curation, the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataxia Gene Curation Expert Panel estimates the expected frequency of *PDYN* variants in ataxia to be less than 1 in 100,000 (0.00001) based on the available literature on *PDYN* as well as prevalence studies in undiagnosed ataxia cohorts (PMIDs: 25133958, 25497598, 29482223, 29915382, 31692161, 34234304). Twelve variants reported in fourteen probands with autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia are included in this curation, however, most of them had minor allele frequencies above this threshold (PMIDs: 21035104, 22287014, 22985506, 23108490, 23471613, 27190015, 29915382, 32587707, 42008026). Therefore, evidentiary values of the variants in this curation were adjusted accordingly. For example, the recurrent variant *PDYN*:p.R138S has been reported in three unrelated probands (PMIDs: 21035104, 22287014, 42008026), was shown to segregate with disease in nine additional family members of a large Dutch pedigree (PMID: 15306549) and exhibited reduced dynorphin B and Leu-enkephalin processing via *in vitro* functional assay (PMID: 21035104). However, this variant’s evidentiary score was reduced as its minor allele frequency is above 0.00001 with observations in 84 of 1614078 alleles in gnomADv4.
This gene-disease relationship is supported by expression studies, a mouse model and *in vitro* functional assays. Bulk tissue gene expression data from the GTEx Portal indicates *PDYN* is highly expressed in the brain but with very low expression in the cerebellum (PMID: 23715323, dbGaP Accession phs000424.v10.p2). Transgenic mice with the *PDYN*:p.R212W variant displayed elevated mutant dynorphin A, resulting in Purkinje cell loss and motor dysfunction and recapitulation of clinical features in human cases of spinocerebellar ataxia (PMID: 26169942). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Cerebellar Ataxia Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date August 12th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The SEMA3E gene was first associated with autosomal dominant CHARGE syndrome in 2004 (PMID: 15235037), but the associated, presumed de novo variant p.Ser703Leu was later reclassified as a variant of unknown significance (PMID: 32441320, Hamosh (2022)). A subsequent report further links another SEMA3E variant to a fetus from terminated pregnancy with ultrasound consistent with the CHARGE syndrome (PMID: 31691538). Heterozygous SEMA3E variants exhibit a broad phenotypic spectrum, including intellectual disability and Kallmann syndrome characterized by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (PMID: 25985275, 38593951, 35628442). Although immunodeficiency is a recognized feature in other genetic causes of CHARGE syndrome (driven by abnormal thymic development and T-cell lymphopenia), clinical manifestations of immunodeficiency were only linked to a presumed de novo SEMA3E variant in one genetic screening study of an IEI cohort report describing twins with an inborn error of immunity phenotype but none of the typical CHARGE syndrome features, and detailed immunophenotyping was not performed (PMID: 32441320). Mechanistically, zebrafish knockdown studies demonstrate typical CHARGE-like non-immunological phenotypes that can be rescued by SEMA3E overexpression (PMID: 31464029). 
In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. 
 
This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID Working Group on 8/20/2026  (SOP Version 12).

Integral membrane protein 2B (*ITM2B*) was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant familial British dementia in 1999 (Vidal et al., PMID: 10391242). Features of *ITM2B* related disease can include but are not limited to: cerebral amyloid angiopathy, early onset dementia, ataxia, and in some families visual impairment has been reported. The age of onset is variable but can be as early as the third decade. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in the molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, or phenotypic variability; therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entities, familial British dementia (OMIM: 176500), and familial Danish dementia (OMIM: 117300). An isolated *ITM2B* - related ocular disease entity was first asserted in 2014 by Audo et. al; PMID: 24026677. At this time the isolated ocular disease entity (Retinal dystrophy with inner retinal dysfunction and ganglion cell abnormalities; OMIM: 616079) is not being curated as there are too few cases to determine if it represents a truly distinct disease entity. 

4 variants (3 stop-loss, and 1 insertion leading to a frame-shift that causes an extension of the protein) that have been reported in 4 probands in 4 publications (PMIDs: 10391242, 10781099, 39625954, 37038821) are included in this curation. Genetic evidence also includes segregation in 3 kindreds (PMIDs: 39625954, 10781099, 10391242). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to involve the formation of amyloid deposits (PMIDs: 37280119). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a rat model carrying a knock-in of the variant identified in the Danish kindred and recapitulates the major features of disease as well as expression data and co-immunoprecipitation data showing physical interaction with APP (PMIDs: 15983050, 41354963, 10391242). In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Neurovascular GCEP on the meeting date September 23, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ERCC6L2* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive bone marrow failure syndrome in 2014 (Tummala et al., PMID: 24507776). Affected individuals have features of bone marrow failure, myelodysplastic syndrome, or acute myeloid leukemia. Microcephaly and developmental delay have been described in some individuals. Heterozygote carriers have not been described to have a clinical phenotype. Although *ERCC6L2* is ubiquitously expressed, including across hematopoietic cell lineages, there is a surprising lack of immune phenotype involving T and B-cells in existing literature. Eleven variants (including frameshift, truncating, exon deletion) that have been reported in fourteen probands in nine publications (PMIDs: 24507776, 27185855, 42415356, 41710027, 36952636, 39906419, 37696499, 29633571, 29987015) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (including in vitro functional assays) (PMIDs: 24507776, 27185855, 32355287, 36156210). Experimental evidence from a study using human A549 cells demonstrates that *ERCC6L2*-knockdown reduced cell survival upon exposure to DNA-damaging agents and also demonstrated that the *ERCC6L2* gene is involved in the DNA-damage response pathway (Tummala et al., PMID: 24507776). In another study, evaluation of patient cells showed DNA repair deficiency due to loss of a DNA repair factor caused by a homozygous nonsense mutation in *ERCC6L2* (Zhang et al., PMID: 27185855). Another experiment found *ERCC6L2*‐deficient cells have decreased colony development of hematopoietic stem progenitor cells and delayed generation of red blood cells, demonstrating a similar phenotype seen in patient cells (Armes et al., PMID: 36156210). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ERCC6L2* and autosomal recessive bone marrow failure syndrome. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP on the meeting date August, 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: combined immunodeficiency due to POLE2 deficiency
disease_original_title: combined immunodeficiency due to POLE2 deficiency
submitted_as_notes:
*POLE2* was first reported in relation to combined immunodeficiency due to *POLE2* deficiency in 2016 (Frugoni et al., PMID: 26365386). *POLE2* deficiency is characterized by combined immunodeficiency, recurrent respiratory infections, agammaglobulinemia, absent NK cells, T cell lymphopenia and neutropenia, absent circulating B cells, increased effector memory T cells, undetectable TRECs, severe dyspnea with hypoxia, hepatomegaly, and hypothyroidism. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be homozygous loss of function.

The curation of *POLE2* related to *POLE2* deficiency includes both case-level and experimental evidence. One variant, a canonical splice site variant has been reported in a single individual (PMID: 26365386). Heterozygous carriers from this single family were reportedly not identified to have any clinical features associated with *POLE2* deficiency. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. Cell cycle proliferation studies on the patient’s peripheral blood leukocytes and fibroblasts showed abnormal cell cycle activity. This was partially rescued when cultured fibroblasts from the patient was transfected with wild type *POLE2*-containing vector (PMID: 26365386). It is unclear if abnormal cell cycle activity as a result of loss of *POLE2* is a mechanism for immunodeficiency.

In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship.

This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID/CID Gene Curation Expert Panel on the meeting date 05/16/2024 (SOP Version 9).

disease_title: intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal recessive 80, with variant lissencephaly
disease_original_title: intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal recessive 80, with variant lissencephaly
submitted_as_notes:
*CASP2* was first reported in relation to Intellectual Developmental Disorder, Autosomal Recessive 80, with Variant Lissencephaly, in 2024 (Uctepe et al., PMID: 37880421). 5 variants (2 nonsense, 2 frameshift, and 1 canonical splice site variant) that have been reported in 8 probands in 2 publications (PMIDs: 37880421, 39672921) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function. No variant functional evidence or experimental evidence exists to support this gene-disease association. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the gene-disease 
relationship between *CASP2* and Intellectual Developmental Disorder, Autosomal Recessive 80, with Variant Lissencephaly. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Brain Malformations GCEP on the meeting date September 21, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*IFNAR2* was first reported in relation to **autosomal recessive (AR) IFNAR2-related immunodeficiency (previously referred to as immunodeficiency 45)** in 2015 (Duncan et al., PMID: 26424569). *IFNAR2* encodes one of the two chains of the receptor of type I interferons. IFNAR2-related immunodeficiency is characterized by patients who present with severe adverse reactions (e.g. meningoencephalitis, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) to live attenuated viral vaccines and life-threatening respiratory infections with COVID-19 or influenza. Laboratory studies have shown affected individuals have an impaired response to alpha-interferon, impaired type I interferon signatures after stimulation, and heightened vulnerability to multiple viruses *in vitro*. Of note, this gene has also been implicated in susceptibility to Hepatitis B virus (OMIM:610424). This will be assessed separately as it appears that *IFNAR2* variants associated with susceptibility to HBV are gain of function.

**6 variants** (1 missense, 1 nonsense, 1 splice donor, and 3 indel leading to a premature stopgain, 4 of which were found in homozygous state, remaining 2 were in compound heterozygous state) that have been reported in **5 probands in 5 publications** (PMIDs: 33544838, 39436454, 35442417, 33193576, 26424569) are included in this curation. None of the parents or siblings who were heterozygous carriers showed any clinical phenotype. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (**12 pts.**) has been reached.

The mechanism of pathogenicity **is reported to be loss of function**. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by **rescue of patient cells, *in vitro* functional assays, and mouse models** (PMIDs: 35442417, 26424569, 26424569, 26424569, 30473701). A null mouse model recapitulates disease with increased morbidity and mortality in response to influenza A infection (PMID: 30473701).

Additionally, patient dermal fibroblasts were unable to develop an antiviral state in response to exogenous IFN-α with no expression of antiviral gene products. These cells also showed complete failure of tyrosine phosphorylation of JAK1, TYK2, or STAT1/2 in patient cells exposed to IFN-α or IFN-β, a finding recapitulated in another paper with whole blood cells from the patient (PMIDs: 26424569, 33193576). Rescue of patient fibroblasts with *IFNAR2* restored STAT1 phosphorylation in response to IFNβ stimulation (PMID: 35442417).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *IFNAR2* and **autosomal recessive IFNAR2-related immunodeficiency**. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time.

This classification was approved by the **ClinGen SCID-CID GCEP** on the meeting date **March 19, 2026 (SOP Version 12)**.

*WNK4* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHAII) in 2001 (Wilson et al., PMID: 11498583). Features of affected probands are hypertension, hyperkalemia, hyperchloremia, and metabolic acidosis. 12 variants (all missense) that have been reported in at least 13 probands in 10 publications (PMIDs: 11498583, 15292344, 15998707, 19016006, 21196779, 21764813, 26920127, 30773290, 31044551, 34622103) are included in this curation. Mutations causative of disease cluster in exons 7 and 17. The genetic mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be gain-of-function (PMID: 11498583). This results in gain of NCC (NaCl cotransporter) function through loss of degradation (PMID: 12515852) and loss of inhibitory regulation of ROMK (renal outer medullary potassium channel).

Features caused by WNK4 variants in PHAII are the reverse phenotype of those caused by loss-of-function variants in NCC associated with Gitelman Syndrome. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence (mouse models, interaction evidence, expression-level evidence; PMIDs: 16964266, 17488636, 33491560). Mouse models expressing disease-causing WNK4 variants recapitulate the human phenotype of hypertension, hyperkalemia, and hypercalciuria. Mouse models also show that OSR1/SPAK kinase-NCC phosphorylation is activated by mutated WNK4, leading to disease.

WNK4 is strongly expressed in the human kidney, based on Northern blot and Humphrey's lab data. WNK4 protein concentrations are controlled by the function of the cullin 3 (CUL3)-Kelch-like family member 3 (KLHL3) E3 ligase complex. CUL3 and KLHL3 are both definitively associated with pseudohypoaldosteronism.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between WNK4 and autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Tubulopathy GCEP on the meeting date 7/21/2026 (SOP Version 12).

The Tectonic Family, Member 1 (TCTN1) gene is located on chromosome 12 at 12q24.11, spans 13 exons, and consists of 592 amino acids. It encodes encodes a protein involved in ciliogenesis and Hedgehog signaling. TCTN1 is a component of the ciliary transition zone complex, interacting with other ciliopathy-related proteins such as TCTN2, TCTN3, MKS1, TMEM67, and CEP290. It plays a critical role in regulating ciliary membrane composition and signaling pathways, particularly the Hedgehog (Hh) pathway, which is essential for embryonic development.

Multiple disease entities have been reported in association with this gene. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was no evidence of differences in their molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern, and phenotypic variability was associated with a spectrum, rather than isolated disease entities. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: Joubert Syndrome 13 (JBTS13), Meckel-Gruber Syndrome (MKS), and Varadi syndrome (Orofaciodigital syndrome type VI). The lumped disease entity is autosomal recessive ciliopathy. 
	
Joubert Syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, “Molar tooth sign” on MRI, hypotonia, ataxia, developmental delay, variable involvement of the kidney (nephronophthisis), liver, and retina. The first case of Joubert Syndrome 13, in association with TCTN1, was first reported in 2011 (Garcia-Gonzalo et al., PMID 21725307). Meckel–Gruber Syndrome is a severe, often lethal ciliopathy with occipital encephalocele, polycystic kidneys, polydactyly. Additional features include liver fibrosis, cardiac anomalies, and pulmonary hypoplasia. Varadi Syndrome is a subtype of orofaciodigital syndrome with craniofacial abnormalities, polydactyly and cerebellar malformations (overlapping with Joubert syndrome).

A total of 16 variants, (splice acceptor, slice donor, missense, frameshift, nonsense, inframe deletion, intron variant) have been reported in over 12 probands in 12 publications (PMIDs: 21725307, 22693042, 26123494, 26477546, 26489806, 28593008, 28631893, 31302911, 32139166, 34980503, 39097279, 39731278) were included in this curation. The first publication is from 2011, while the most recent one is from 2025. The maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached, considering case-level data and segregation data.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental studies (including a mouse model, rescue evidence, biochemical functional data, expression-level evidence, and interaction evidence; PMIDs: 12723291, 16357211, 21725307). Mouse and human TCTN1 were first identified in the 2006. TCTN1 (also known as tectonic) is first expressed during gastrulation stages in the ventral node in in the gut endoderm, limb buds, notochord, somites, neural tube, and floorplate. Tectonic was shown to be required for Hh-mediated patterning of the ventral neural tube. Tectonic mutants lacking a histologically distinct floorplate and died, displaying holoprosencephaly, a defect associated with reduced Hh signaling. Tectonic acts in neural patterning by positively regulating the Hh pathway and also acts downstream of Ptch and Rab23, negatively regulating the Hedgehog signaling pathway, and its function is required for their effects to be seen. 

TCTN1 was later identified as a novel disease gene in ciliopathies in 2011 through comprehensive genetic, structural, and functional analyses. At the molecular level, TCTN1 forms part of a ciliopathy-associated protein complex and interacts with multiple transition zone proteins, including TCTN2, TCTN3, B9D1, MKS1, TMEM67, TMEM216, CEP290, and CC2D2A, with strong evidence that TCTN1, TCTN2, and TCTN3 function together within the same complex. Localization studies demonstrate that TCTN1 and its interactors are enriched at the ciliary transition zone, where they regulate the composition and organization of ciliary proteins. Functional experiments further show that loss of TCTN1 disrupts the localization of key transition zone components, such as MKS1 and TMEM67, indicating a role in maintaining transition zone integrity. Together, these findings support that TCTN1 is an essential structural and functional component of the ciliary transition zone complex, required for proper ciliogenesis and ciliary signaling.

Another previous study investigated the physiological role of TCTN1 in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, showing that full-length TCTN1 could rescue the tctn1 cell line, which is a TCTN1-null mutant.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between TCTN1 and autosomal recessive ciliopathy. This has been demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel GCEP on the meeting date Febbruary 25th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

CFAP20DC was first reported in association with autosomal-recessive primary ciliary dyskinesia in 2025 in a Saudi pediatric patient homozygous for the nonsense variant NM_198463.2:c.508C>T, p.(Arg170Ter), corresponding to NM_001394063.1:c.883C>T, p.(Arg295Ter). A subsequent multicenter study by Gerard et al., 2026 identified 24 affected individuals from 16 families and seven countries with eight distinct biallelic CFAP20DC variants, including nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-site, multiexon deletion, in-frame deletion alleles, and recurrent p.(Arg295Ter) cases. Affected individuals suffered from chronic and severe airway disease marked by early-age onset of bronchiectasis, predominantly in the middle and lower lungs, and absence of ciliary ultrastructural defects. 
Case-level evidence reaches the ClinGen maximum of 12 genetic evidence points. 
Experimental evidence includes enrichment of CFAP20DC expression in deuterosomal cells and functional abnormalities in patient-derived respiratory epithelial cells. Affected cells showed cytoplasmic mislocalization and abnormal orientation of basal bodies, reduced generation of multiple motile cilia, abnormal localization of the basal-foot marker CNTRL, and markedly impaired ciliary particle transport. No convincing contradictory evidence was identified.
The combined evidence score is 14.5 points, comprising 12 genetic and 2.5 experimental evidence points.

disease_title: vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 3
disease_original_title: vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 3
submitted_as_notes:
The *NADSYN1* was first reported in association with autosomal recessive congenital NAD deficiency disorder (CNDD) in 2019 - Szot JO et al., PMID:  PMID: 31883644. Since the initial report, multiple affected individuals from unrelated families with biallelic *NADSYN1* variants have been described. Affected individuals demonstrate a highly variable multisystem phenotype that includes vertebral, cardiac, limb, renal, and craniofacial abnormalities, among other developmental defects. Nine variants variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) that have been reported in seven probands in four publications (PMID: 35491967, PMID: 36649848, PMID: 38357931, PMID: 31883644) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss-of-function. Although heterozygous *NADSYN1* variants have also been reported in at least nine individuals with congenital vertebral malformations and multisystem abnormalities, unaffected heterozygous relatives reported in subsequent studies and the potential influence of environmental factors on NAD levels leave the clinical significance and penetrance of heterozygous variants uncertain (PMID: 36649848, PMID: 37300479).
Functional characterization of disease-associated missense variants demonstrated significantly reduced *NADSYN1*-dependent NAD synthetase activity, with several variants exhibiting near-complete or complete loss of enzymatic activity (PMID: 38357931). Consistent with these findings, disruption of *NADSYN1* in human cell lines results in impaired maintenance of intracellular NAD levels under conditions of limited nicotinamide availability and broad alterations in cellular metabolism (PMID: 38132878). Additionally, Nadsyn1 knockout mice develop embryonic lethality and multisystem congenital malformations under conditions of limited maternal NAD precursor availability, including abnormalities of the kidneys, eyes, lungs, heart, vertebrae, palate, abdominal wall, and neural tube, recapitulating major features of the human disorder. Supplementation with NAD precursors capable of bypassing the *NADSYN1*-dependent metabolic block, including nicotinamide (NAM) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), prevented or reduced adverse developmental outcomes, further supporting NAD deficiency as the underlying disease mechanism (PMID: 38357931).
In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *NADSYN1* and autosomal recessive congenital NAD deficiency disorder. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP at the meeting on September 25, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*PLAGL1* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital heart disease in 2012 (Xuan et al. PMID: 22784302). A synonymous variant and an intronic variant were reported in two individuals with congenital heart disease but were not scored due to a lack of predicted or proven damaging impact for the synonymous variant and high population frequency without proven functional impact for the deep intronic variant (PMID: 22784302, 39402625). This gene-disease relationship is supported by expression studies in the developing murine heart, protein interaction studies between Zac1 and Nkx2-5, and a *Plagl1*-null mouse model with cardiac malformations (PMID: 20167925). In summary, due to the lack of convincing human genetic evidence, the relationship between *PLAGL1* and autosomal dominant congenital heart disease has been disputed and no valid evidence remains to support the claim. More evidence is needed to either support or entirely refute the role of *PLAGL1* in this disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date on August 4, 2026. (SOP Version 12).

*SLC25A32*, which encodes the mitochondrial flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) transporter, was first implicated in autosomal recessive riboflavin-responsive exercise intolerance in 2016 (Schiff et al., PMID: 26933868). The initial patient presented with recurrent exercise intolerance and was found to carry compound heterozygous c.425G>A (p.W142X) and c.440G>A (p.R147H) variants. One year later, a patient carrying a homozygous c.-264_31delinsCTCACAAATGCTCA variant was reported with a severe neuromuscular phenotype of early-onset ataxia, myoclonus, dysarthria, muscle weakness, and exercise intolerance (PMID: 28443623). Subsequently, two additional patients homozygous for the c.272G>T (p.G91V) variants were reported to experience hypoglycemia and vomiting triggered by febrile illness without muscle weakness or exercise intolerance (PMID: 34764427). Recently, a female patient carrying compound heterozygous c.521A>G (p.Y174C) and c.704A>G (p.K235R) variants was reported with a broad phenotype that included muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, dyspnea, fatigue, growth retardation, motor dysfunction, borderline intellectual disability, enlarged lateral ventricle by brain imaging, fibular hypoplasia and progressive club feet (PMID: 35727412). Biochemical abnormalities across the affected individuals included elevated acylcarnitine profiles, resembling those observed in multiple acyl-CoA carnitine dehydrogenase deficiency (MADD), elevated lactic acid and urinary organic acids. Riboflavin supplement improved clinical and biochemical phenotypes in all reported cases (PMID: 26933868, 34764427, 35727412). Therefore, five variants (four missense and one nonsense) in four probands with highly variable manifestations and severity were included in this curation.

This gene-disease relationship was supported by experimental evidence. *In vitro* studies demonstrated that the p.R147H variant failed to rescue yeast growth on glycerol and was associated with reduced mitochondrial complex II/III activity, indicating impaired mitochondrial respiratory chain function (PMID: 26933868). A knock-in (KI) mouse model carrying the K235R/Y174C variants demonstrated motor dysfunction, mildly disrupted acylcarnitine profile in skeletal and brain tissues, accumulation of glutaric acid and decreased formate levels. Although riboflavin supplementation didn’t rescue the motor functions in the KI mice, the model partially recapitulated the patient phenotype (PMID: 35727412). Further studies revealed that *SLC25A32* mutant disrupted folate homeostasis by blocking FAD transport from cytosol into mitochondrial, resulting in inhibition of mitochondrial flavoenzyme activity, impairment of electron chain function, and damage of muscle and brain (PMID: 35727412).

Of note, the *SLC25A32* knockout (KO) mice were embryonic lethal. Mutant embryos are presented with variable neural tube closure (NTC) defects that can be rescued by formate supplement. These embryos demonstrated glycine cleavage defect secondary to dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLDH) deficiency (PMID: 35727412). In humans, one fetus with anencephaly was reported to be compound heterozygous for c.267_268dup and c.391G>T (p.G131X) variants. Experimental studies showed these variants failed to rescue glyB auxotrophic phenotype (PMID: 29666258). Additionally, four heterozygous missense variants (p.T71A, p.A128T, p.G55V, p.S260N) were also reported in fetuses with NTC defects. However, segregation analysis and functional evidence were not provided. Because NTC defects are not currently recognized as an OMIM disease entry associated with *SLC25A32*, and the inheritance patterns reported in these cases are inconsistent with recessive disease mechanism reported in KO mice model, this association was excluded from the present curation. 

In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *SLC25A32* and autosomal recessive riboflavin responsive exercise intolerance. This classification was approved by the ClinGen General Inborn Errors of Metabolism Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 10, 2026 (SOP v12).

SCD5 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss in 2020 (Lu X et al., PMID:31972369). Two missense variants c.626G>C (p.Trp209Ser), c.452T>G (p.Phe151Cys) have been reported in two probands in two publications (PMID: 31972369, 40121402). One family was reported with eight segregations. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be dominant negative. The age of onset of HL varied from 20 to 65 years old and the audiometric profiles were highly asymmetric (PMID: 31972369). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence. SCD5 is primarily expressed in the human fetal and adult brain (GTEx Portal), and protein expression was also observed within the inner ear of guinea pig cochlea and human fetal cochlea (IHC based expression data, PMID: 31972369). Guinea pig cochlea was used as mice lack a true SCD5 orthologue due to rodent-specific gene loss, limiting their suitability as models for human SCD5-associated disease. In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship and more evidence is needed to support a causal role. Simultaneously, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Hearing Loss GCEP on the meeting date 8/19/2026 (SOP Version 12).

The *SCLT1* gene is located in chromosome 4q28.2 and encodes the Sodium Channel And Clathrin Linker 1 protein. The protein is required for ciliogenesis and ciliary vesicle formation. It is ubiquitously expressed at varying levels in all tissues.

Although no disease assertion has been made in the OMIM datase, variants in *SCLT1* have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: Oral-facial-digital syndrome IX, retinitis pigmentosa, Senior-Loken syndrome, and Bardet-Biedl syndrome. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no differences in phenotypic variability. Therefore, these disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity. The preferred disease name suggested for this disorder is autosomal recessive ciliopathy-*SCLT1*.

*SCLT1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive ciliopathy in 2014 (Adly et al., PMID: 24285566). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss-of-function. Patients with biallelic *SCLT1* variants presented with cystic kidney disease, nephronophthisis, orofacial cleft, genital anomalies, neurodevelopmental delay, intellectual disability, retinitis pigmentosa, and hepatic dysfunction. At least seven variants (canonical splice site, missense, splice site, indel) reported in five probands in five publications (PMID: 24285566, 30425282, 32253632, 37246745, 38924217) are included in this curation. There was functional evidence supporting the effect of the missense and splice site variants (PMID: 24285566, 30425282, 32253632, 37246745, 38924217). A total of 6.5 pts. for genetic evidence was reached.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by biochemical function, expression studies, functional alteration in  non-patient cells, and animal models (PMID: 23348840, 36407107, 30425282, 39696441, 28486600). SCLT1 protein expression was observed in the tubule cells of the adult mouse kidney and the SCLT1 signal is observed at the basal part of the photoreceptor ciliary axoneme and the distal part of the basal body (PMID: 30425282). It was found that another ciliopathy gene, *CEP164*, depends on *SCLT1* for centriolar localization; disruption of Sclt1 in mesenchymal cells prevents the recruitment of CEP164 to the basal body (PMID: 23348840, 36407107). Depletion of *SCLT1* in RPE1 cells completely blocked cilia formation; similarly, NIH3T3 cells depleted of SCLT1 showed reduced anchoring of the cilium to the plasma membrane, indicating disrupted early ciliogenesis (PMID: 23348840, 39696441). Additionally, SCLT1 deficiency in knockout mouse embryos and mice results in a classic ciliopathy phenotype characterized by polydactyly, cleft palate, cystic kidneys, and shortened intestines (PMID: 28486600, 36407107). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for experimental evidence (6 pts.) was reached.

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship for *SCLT1* that we are terming autosomal recessive ciliopathy-*SCLT1*. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders Expert Panel GCEP on the meeting date December 8, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

*PYCR2* was first reported in association with autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 10 in 2015 (Nakayama T et al., PMID: 25865492). The characteristic clinical presentation of affected individuals includes failure to thrive, microcephaly, craniofacial dysmorphism, progressive psychomotor disability, hyperkinetic movements, and axial hypotonia with variable appendicular spasticity. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated global brain atrophy and white matter T2 hyperintensities (PMID: 34037307; PMID: 3714174). More recent reports have asserted that variants in the *PYCR2* gene may also be associated with a late childhood to adult-onset hereditary spastic paraplegia (PMID 32920934 ; PMID: 37141741) phenotype. The individuals reported presented primarily with lower limb spasticity and gait difficulty. While brain imaging appreciated some changes and atrophy, there was no clear hypomyelination observed. However, there appears to be enough phenotypic overlap to consider a possible spectrum of presentation, with HSP being on the milder end. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in molecular mechanism, inheritance pattern, or phenotypic variability. Therefore, the single disease entity has been maintained: hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 10 (OMIM: 616420). 
Multiple pathogenic variants, including missense, splice-site, and nonsense variants, have been reported in numerous probands across several publications (PMID: 27130255; PMID: 32330411; PMID: 27860360; PMID: 33771508) and are included in this curation. Although additional evidence exists in the literature, the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 points) has already been reached. The proposed disease mechanism is loss of function, with functionally tested missense variants demonstrating reduced enzymatic activity relative to the wild-type protein. While these variants were reported in patients with HLD10, the seven cases of HSP were found to harbor two unique homozygous missense variants (M195T and V128A). These late childhood to adult-onset hereditary spastic paraplegia cases were not included in the overall genetic evidence scoring, as the maximum score had already been reached and functional studies were not available for these variants, despite their location amongst other variants reported in patients with HLD10. Notably, the M195T and V128A variants have not been reported in individuals with HLD10 to date. 

Functional studies further support the gene–disease relationship. *Pycr2 *knockout mouse models phenocopied the human disorder, including microcephaly and hypomyelination. Neurochemical studies demonstrated elevated cerebral glycine levels in both mutant mice and affected individuals (PMID: 33734376). Five of the seven individuals reported with the HSP phenotype also exhibited cerebral glycine peaks on MRS (PMID: 3714174). Additional mechanistic studies linked *PYCR2* deficiency to upregulation of SHMT2, resulting in increased glycine levels that may contribute to neurotoxicity and the leukodystrophy phenotype. SHMT2 knockdown partially rescued neurite defects and axonal beading in *Pycr2* knockout neurons (PMID: 32330411). Furthermore, morpholino-based knockdown of the zebrafish *PYCR2* ortholog, *pycr1b*, recapitulated the human microcephaly phenotype. This phenotype was rescued by wild-type human PYCR2 mRNA, but not by mutant mRNAs, further supporting the pathogenicity of the identified variants (PMID: 25865492).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *PYCR2 *and autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 10, also known as *PYCR2*-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, and potentially a broader phenotypic spectrum including a hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotype. This association has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been consistently upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP at the meeting on May 22, 2026. The Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalpathy GCEP also contributed to this curation. (SOP Version 12).

The *MT-TF* gene (mitochondrially encoded tRNA phenylalanine) encodes tRNA-Phe, which is essential for mitochondrial protein synthesis. *MT-TF* was first reported in connection with 
familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy in 2001 (Tzen et al., 2001, PMID: 11231339). Four unique variants (m.608A>G, m.616T>C, m.643A>G, m.591C>T) from fourteen probands across seven publications have been identified (PMIDs: 11231339, 20142618, 28267784, 31722346, 34514217, 34607911, 36100708). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression and functional alteration assays (PMIDs: 34607911, 28267784). In summary, there is Moderate evidence supporting the relationship between MT-TF and familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on February 12th, 2024 (SOP Version 11).

*PRKACA* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant cardioacrofacial dysplasia (MIM: 619142) in 2020 (Palencia-Campos et al., PMID: 33058759). This condition is characterized by short stature; facial anomalies (like midface hypoplasia and micrognathia); dental anomalies (such as diastema and hypodontia); nail dysplasia; cardiac features (including atrioventricular septal defect); long/narrow thorax; digit anomalies (like post axial polysyndactyly and brachydactyly); short long bones; and genu valgum. One recurrent missense variant, p.Gly137Arg, that has been reported in at least eight probands in four publications (PMIDs: 33058759, 33875766, 38357848, 39706863) and from one clinical lab (GeneDx; ClinVar SCV002818851) is included in this curation. One proband with an in-frame deletion and skeletal features such as low bone density, genu valgum, and patellar dislocation, as well as cardiac and muscular anomalies, was reported (PMID: 42157491). However, this proband was not scored due to lacking the digital, limb, and rib features seen in probands with the p.Gly137Arg variant. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be partial loss-of-function (PMID: 33058759). This gene-disease relationship is supported by just half a point of experimental evidence (expression-level data from Human Protein Atlas). Experimental data indicates that this protein is expressed in bone marrow. No scorable animal models were reported in the literature. In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Skeletal Disorders GCEP on the meeting date 9/2/2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ZFPM2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital diaphragmatic hernia in 2005 (Ackerman et al., PMID: 16103912). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, congenital heart disease (OMIM:187500), diaphragmatic hernia 3 (OMIM:610187), and 46,XY sex reversal 9 (OMIM:616067). The split curation for autosomal dominant congenital heart disease has been curated separately. Eleven variants (nonsense, missense, deletion, and frameshift) that have been reported in 11 probands in five publications (PMIDs: 16103912, 17568391, 24702427, 21525063, 29966037) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is currently unclear. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by an animal model showing that mice with a truncated Zfpm2 protein had pulmonary hypoplasia and abnormal diaphragmatic development (PMID:16103912). ZFPM2 is also expressed in the early amuscular diaphragm and muscularized diaphragm and is required for the induction of HGF in the developing diaphragm (PMID:16103912). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *ZFPM2* and autosomal dominant congenital diaphragmatic hernia. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date August 4, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

PCK2 encodes the mitochondrial phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK-M), a mitochondrial matrix enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. In contrast to the cytosolic isoform (PCK1), PCK2 primarily functions in cataplerosis, linking the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle to glycolysis and multiple biosynthetic pathways rather than serving as the principal gluconeogenic enzyme. Although the mechanisms regulating PCK2 transcription remain incompletely understood, PCK2 has been shown to play an important role in cellular adaptation to metabolic stress, particularly in cancer cells, where it promotes survival during amino acid starvation and endoplasmic reticulum stress (PMID: 34020084).
PCK deficiency was first described in 1974 by Fiser et al. (https://doi.org/10.1203/00006450-197404000-00552 PMID: unavailable), based on the clinical phenotype and markedly reduced hepatic phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase activity measured in liver biopsy specimens . A subsequent report by Hommes et al. (PMID: 176867) described a similar biochemical phenotype. However, these historical reports predated molecular genetic testing and therefore could not establish a relationship between *PCK2* and disease.
A later publication reported a single individual with compound heterozygous variants in *PCK2*; however, both variants were classified as variants of uncertain significance, had benign in silico predictions, and lacked sufficient functional or segregation evidence to support pathogenicity. In addition, the clinical information was limited, and this case was not scored.
More recently, two individuals with biallelic *PCK2 *variants were reported with peripheral neuropathy (Sondheimer et al., PMID: 36845668). Although *Pck2 *knockout mice demonstrated reduced sural nerve conduction velocities, occasional temporal dispersion, and increased variability in axon and myelin sheath diameters, consistent with a mild demyelinating peripheral neuropathy, the reported human evidence remains limited and has not been independently replicated. Consequently, this evidence was not scored for the present curation.
Experimental studies have also implicated *PCK2* in skeletal development. Li et al. generated *Pck2* knockout mice that developed skeletal dysplasia and demonstrated partial rescue of the skeletal phenotype following metformin treatment (Li et al., PMID: 36376627). Because these studies were performed independently of the human genetic evidence supporting the disease association curated here, they were not scored.

In summary, there is limited evidence supporting the relationship between *PCK2* and autosomal recessive PEPCK deficiency, mitochondrial. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP at the meeting on June 26, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*PC* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive pyruvate carboxylase deficiency in 1987 (Yoshida Y et al., PMID: 5358431). Pyruvate carboxylase (PC) deficiency is a metabolic disorder typically presenting with poor growth, developmental delay, epilepsy, and metabolic acidosis, and is classified into three clinical forms of varying severity. Type A (infantile form) involves early-onset lactic acidosis, motor delay, intellectual disability, growth failure, and neurologic features such as hypotonia, ataxia, and seizures, with death often occurring in early childhood. Type B (severe neonatal form) is the most severe, presenting in the neonatal period with hypothermia, respiratory failure, profound lactic acidosis, hyperammonemia, and neurologic impairment, usually leading to death within the first eight months of life. Type C (intermittent/attenuated form) is milder, characterized by relatively normal or mildly delayed development, episodic metabolic acidosis, movement abnormalities, and rare seizures, with some individuals surviving into adulthood. Several variants (e.g., missense, splice site, frameshift) have been reported in multiple probands in three publications (PMID: 37207470, PMID: 24114256, PMID: 35782291) and are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be loss of function. Disease severity in pyruvate carboxylase deficiency shows a loose genotype–phenotype correlation: missense and intronic variants are more commonly associated with the milder types A and C, while truncating or nonsense variants are typically linked to the more severe type B. However, it remains unclear whether additional disease-modifying factors influence outcomes for specific variants (Lasio MLD et al., PMID: 20301764). Of note, one specific variant has been identified as a founder mutation (c.1828G>A; p.A610T) in North American Indigenous populations (Ojibwa and Cree), where it is associated with type A pyruvate carboxylase deficiency characterized by infantile onset, profound developmental delay, and early childhood mortality (Lasio MLD et al., PMID: 20301764; Mhanni AA et al., PMID: 34485016). Functional studies of PC demonstrate its essential role in mitochondrial metabolism. In non-patient renal tubular epithelial cells (CL:0005010), loss of PC resulted in impaired mitochondrial function and an altered cellular metabolic state, consistent with disruption of its canonical enzymatic activity as a pyruvate carboxylase (GO:0004736) (Huang H et al., PMID: 39836535). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *PC* and autosomal recessive pyruvate carboxylase deficiency.
