This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen IEM GCEP at the meeting on April 10, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*ZFPM2* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant congenital heart disease in 2003 (Pizzuti et al., PMID: 14517948). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, congenital heart disease (OMIM:187500), diaphragmatic hernia 3 (OMIM:610187), and 46,XY sex reversal 9 (OMIM:616067). The split curation for autosomal dominant diaphragmatic hernia 3 will be curated separately. 13 missense variants that have been reported in 15 probands in five publications (PMIDs: 24469719, 28372585, 31028076, 29018978, 21919901) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity is unclear. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by a *Zfpm2*-null mouse model (PMID:10888889), rescue in cardiomyocytes of *Zfpm2*-null mouse embryos (PMID:10892744), and biochemical function data showing that ZFPM2 interacts with the adenovirus-associated protein p300 and competes with GATA4 for binding p300 (PMID:15220332). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Heart Disease GCEP on the meeting date on July 7, 2026. (SOP Version 12).

The *CILK1* gene is located on chromosome 6 at 6p12.1 and encodes a ciliogenesis-associated kinase 1 that is important for regulating primary cilia formation, length, and intraflagellar transport. Multiple disease entities have been reported in association with this gene: Epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic susceptibility to 10 (MIM:617924); Cranioectodermal dysplasia 6 (MIM: 621337); and Endocrine-cerebroosteodysplasia (MIM:612651). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, there was evidence of differences in molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern between Epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic susceptibility to 10 and the other assertions. Therefore, the following disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity: Cranioectodermal dysplasia 6, and Endocrine-cerebroosteodysplasia. The Epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic susceptibility to 10 assertion has been split and will be curated by the Epilepsy GCEP. Ciliopathy-*CILK1* was first reported in 2009 (Lahiry et al., 2009, PMID: 19185282). Four unique variants (three missense, one frameshift) from five probands across three publications have been identified (PMID: 19185282, 27069622, 40615527). The mechanism of disease is loss-of-function. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by animal models, rescue, functional alteration, and biochemical evidence (PMIDs: 19185282, 27069622, 27466187, 40615527).

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *CILK1* and autosomal recessive ciliopathy-*CILK1*. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on November 26th, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *CEP83* gene is located on chromosome 12 at 12q22 and encodes centrosomal Protein 83, a critical protein found at the centriolar distal appendages that acts as a scaffold for primary cilium assembly. *CEP83* was first reported in connection with ciliopathy in 2014 (Failler et al., 2014, PMID: 24882706). Fourteen unique variants (six nonsense, four missense, three deletions, one frameshift) from ten probands across three publications have been identified (PMIDs: 24882706, 32173348, 33938610). The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss-of-function whereby its dysfunction leads to ciliopathies by impairing ciliary membrane docking and initial axoneme formation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by protein interaction, expression, and functional alteration studies (PMIDs: 31455668, 32173348, 24882706). In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between CEP83 and ciliopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Kidney Cystic and Ciliopathy Disorders GCEP on September 22nd, 2021 (SOP Version 8).

The *RNU4-2* gene was first reported in relation to human disease in two 2024 publications reporting patients with a multi-system neurodevelopmental disorder referred to as ReNU syndrome (PMID: 38821540, PMID: 38991538). Affected patients harbored variants in the heterozygous state, predominantly as *de novo* occurrences on the maternally inherited allele. Clinical features included global developmental delay, intellectual disability, expressive language deficits, hypotonia, facial dysmorphism, short stature, and/or abnormalities in brain morphology such as ventriculomegaly. Visual dysfunction was also reported in the majority of patients, accompanied by features such as strabismus, nystagmus, and/or optic nerve hypoplasia (PMID: 38991538). The disease spectrum associated with *RNU4-2* variants subsequently expanded to include later-onset cases described as non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa (PMID: 41513982). These cases were distinguishable based on their later ages of onset, germline inheritance on either paternal or maternal alleles within families with multiple affected members, and association with variants located in the vicinity of stem-I, stem-II, and the U4 5′ stem-loop rather than in Stem III or the adjacent T-loop associated with ReNU syndrome. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, cases diagnosed as non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa vs. ReNU syndrome are similar in their autosomal dominant patterns of inheritance, but differ in molecular mechanism (predominantly inherited variants extending the 5’ internal loop vs. *de novo* variants in the stem-III or the adjacent T-loop region). They also appear to be distinguishable in their clinical features (isolated retinal phenotypes vs. syndromic features affected multiple systems). Therefore, cases caused by monoallelic variants in *RNU4-2* have been split into two separate disease entities. The present curation has focused on the isolated retinal phenotype, referred to as *RNU4-2*-related retinopathy, while the Syndromic Disorders GCEP has separately evaluated *RNU4-2* in relation to neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, brain anomalies, distinctive facies, and absent language (MONDO:0971172).

Two suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (one base pair substitution and one single-base pair insertion). Together, these variants have been reported in fifteen total probands in one publication (PMID: 41513982). Future functional studies will be required to determine their mechanism of pathogenicity, however, both variants are predicted to alter an internal loop within *RNU4-2* that may impact the stability of the U4/U6 duplex within the spliceosome. At least one patient harbored the variant as a *de novo* occurrence, indicating the tendency of the same variant to recur in multiple unrelated but similarly affected individuals. Four families with co-segregation of the variant with affected status contributed to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship (PMID: 41513982).

This gene-disease association is also supported by biochemical evidence that the *RNU4-2* gene produces a non-coding RNA component (U4) of the U2-dependent spliceosome. Some of the genes that produce the U6 RNA component of the spliceosome (*RNU6-1*, *RNU6-2*, *RNU6-8* and *RNU6-9*) similarly harbor variants reported in relation to retinitis pigmentosa (PMID: 41513982). The U4 and U6 components base-pair together in the context of the spliceosome (PMID: 28781166). *RNU4-2* is highly expressed in a subset of ocular tissues from the retina, retinal pigment epithelium, cornea, conjunctiva, and optic nerve (PMID: 30239781).

In summary, *RNU4-2* has a Strong association with *RNU4-2*-related retinopathy. Additional evidence from the research and diagnostic settings will be needed to meet the requirement for replication over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on October 1st, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

The *CRB1* gene was first reported in relation to ocular disease in 1999, in affected members from a family with autosomal recessive inheritance who were diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa 12 (PMID: 10373321). The spectrum of disease with autosomal recessive inheritance subsequently expanded to include cases diagnosed as Leber congenital amaurosis 8 or Coats-like exudative vasculopathy (PMID: 11389483). Cases with autosomal dominant inheritance also emerged in 2005 with the publication of a family with members diagnosed with pigmented paravenous retinochoroidal atrophy (McKay et al., PMID: 15623792). Family members with pigmented paravenous retinochoroidal atrophy exhibited variable expressivity of clinical features including paravenous chorioretinal atrophy, bone spicule pigmentation, optic disc drusen, loss of visual acuity after age 30 years, and/or decreased rod electroretinogram amplitudes. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the pigmented paravenous retinochoroidal atrophy cases were distinguishable from autosomal recessive cases by their mode of inheritance, the scarcity of additional affected families following the initial report, and the absence of evidence of affected status among heterozygous carriers from the autosomal recessive pedigrees. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *CRB1* variants have been split into two separate disease entities, with the present curation focusing on autosomal dominant cases.

Two suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (both missense), which have been reported in two total families (PMID: 15623792, PMID: 40623937). The variants both show high frequencies among control individuals in the gnomAD database, and functional characterization of their potential mechanism of pathogenicity has not been performed. At least one reported family had multiple affected individuals who were heterozygous for the suspected disease-causing variant, but they were not sufficient in number to contribute to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship through segregation evidence (PMID: 15623792).

This gene-disease association is supported by evidence that *CRB1* is highly specifically expressed in the human retina and to a lesser extent in the retinal pigment epithelium, the optic nerve, and the brain (PMID: 30239781). CRB1 protein localizes to the subapical cell surfaces of rod, cone, and Müller glial cells in order to maintain adherens junctions, regulate apical-basal polarity, and modulate apical membrane size in collaboration with the cadherin-catenin complex (PMID: 760678,7 PMID: 28424578, PMID: 32817065). Animal models of biallelic *CRB1* loss-of-function show ocular or photoreceptor dysfunction, but their relevance to autosomal dominant human disease is unclear (PMID: 28306104, PMID: 39965731, PMID: 32817065, PMID: 12915475).

In summary, *CRB1* has a Disputed association with autosomal dominant pigmented paravenous retinochoroidal atrophy. This assertion has been found in at least 2 publications but has very limited segregation and proband evidence accumulated over the past 20 years since the initial report, as well as questions about the potential for the variants to be disease-causing. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on July 2nd, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: male infertility due to acephalic spermatozoa
disease_original_title: male infertility due to acephalic spermatozoa
submitted_as_notes:
*PMFBP1* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive male infertility due to acephalic spermatozoa in 2018 (*Zhu et al.*, PMID: 30032984). This condition is characterized by male infertility due to oligozoospermia with a high proportion (greater than 90%) of acephalic sperm. Nine variants (e.g. nonsense, frameshift, splice site mutation) that have been reported in eight probands in four publications (PMIDs: 30032984, 30298696, 35860846, 41462896) are included in this curation. More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. 

The mechanism of pathogenicity is believed to be biallelic loss of function, as mutations of *PMFBP1* tend to cause failure in sperm head-tail coupling apparatus assembly (PMID:30032984). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by mouse models. (PMIDs:30032984, 30298696). *Pmfbp1 -/-* mouse models phenocopied acephalic spermatozoa syndrome in human patients, showing male infertility (PMID: 30032984, 30298696). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *PMFBP1* and autosomal recessive male infertility due to acephalic spermatozoa. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Male Infertility GCEP on the meeting date April 1, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*RPL27* was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant Diamond-Blackfan anemia 16 (DBA16) in 2015 (Wang et al., PMID: 25424902). DBA16 is a rare bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, erythroid hypoplasia, and pure red cell aplasia. Three variants (2 missense and 1 splicing) that have been reported in four probands in four publications (PMIDs: 25424902, 30503522, 38988374, 10.1016/j.exphem.2023.06.208) are included in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by functional alteration data, and rescue experiment in a morpholino zebrafish model (PMIDs: 25424902). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen GCEP on the meeting date September 8, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

SMARCAL1 was first linked to autosomal recessive Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia (SIOD) in 2002 (Boerkoel et al., PMID: 11799392). SMARCAL1 has been more recently reported in association with autosomal dominant SMARCAL1-related tumor predisposition in 2020 (Akhavanfard et al., PMID: 32371905). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in molecular mechanism, but a difference in inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability was found. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia (SIOD) (OMIM: 606622) and SMARCAL1-related tumor predisposition. The split curation autosomal recessive Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia (SIOD) was previously curated separately.
 
Two case-control studies with 2,349 individuals with osteosarcoma are included in this curation (PMIDs: 41066719, 40996338). Oak et al., an aggregate variant analysis, showed an odds ratio of 6.3, 95% CI = 2.5 to 13.6, p<0.0001 for osteosarcoma compared to non-cancer controls (PMID: 41066719). Rafati et al., an aggregate variant analysis, showed an odds ratio of 5.4, 95% CI = 2.5 to 11.5, p<0.0001 for osteosarcoma compared to cancer-free individuals in the European subset of data (PMID: 40996338). In addition to case-control studies, 12 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site) that have been reported in 15 probands (8 with osteosarcoma and 7 with other cancers including sarcoma, glioma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) and malignancies of the nervous system) in 2 publications (PMIDs: 32371905, 36656928) and in ClinVar (ClinVar IDs: 645077 (Accession: SCV007596980.1), 577921(Accession: SCV007596982.1), 4851566 (Accession: SCV007596981.1)) are included in this curation. No experimental evidence that supports this gene-disease relationship was found, and therefore none was included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of function, but it is unclear due to the lack of experimental evidence.
 
In summary, there is strong evidence supporting the relationship between SMARCAL1 and autosomal dominant SMARCAL1-related tumor predisposition. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in clinical genetic data, and but has not been upheld over time since both case-control studies were published in 2025. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Predisposition (CAYA) GCEP on the meeting date June 10, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*RPGRIP1* was first reported in relation to *RPGRIP1*-related retinopathy in patients described as having Leber Congenital Amaurosis, in 2001 (Dryja et al, PMID: 11283794; Gerber et al, PMID: 11528500). Variants in *RPGRIP1* have been reported in individuals with a clinical diagnosis of Leber Congenital Amaurosis 6 (MIM# 613826), cone-rod dystrophy 13 (MIM# 608194) and achromatopsia. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found no difference in the molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern for these conditions. Therefore, those disease entities have been lumped into one disease entity for the purpose of this curation. In addition, an Indian patient who was compound heterozygous for variants in *RPGRIP1* and *SLC4A4* has been reported with "juvenile-onset open-angle glaucoma phenotype with concomitant corneal dystrophy" (Gupta et al, 2026, PMID: 41581050). Due to the different phenotype and inheritance pattern, this gene-disease relationship may be classified separately by another ClinGen GCEP.

Eleven variants (7 frameshift, 3 nonsense, 1 single-exon deletion) that have been reported in 8 probands in four publications (Dryja et al, 2001, PMID: 11283794; Gerber et al, 2001, PMID: 11528500; Suga et al, 2024, PMID: 39669618; Tareen et al, 2025, PMID: 40737315) are included in this curation. One variant (NM_020366.4:c.2710+374_2895+78del), which results in deletion of exon 18, is a founder variant in the Japanese population that is consistently associated with symptoms of achromatopsia when found in homozygosity (Suga et al, 2024, PMID: 39669618; Mizobuchi et al, 2026, PMID: 42102949). More evidence is available in the literature, but the maximum score for genetic evidence (12 pts.) has been reached. The mechanism of pathogenicity is loss of function.

This gene-disease relationship is also supported by experimental evidence including the localization to, and function of, the protein in the connecting cilium of photoreceptor cells (Hong et al, 2001, PMID: 11104772; Loi et al, 2025, PMID: 41270749), specific expression of the gene in photoreceptors and localization to the connecting cilium on those cells, physical interaction with the products of other genes known to be involved in retinopathy, including *CEP290* (Gerber et al, 2010, PMID: 20200501) and *RPGR* (Ropeman et al, 2000, PMID: 10958648; Boylan et al, 2000, PMID: 10958647). Animal models have also been reported including a naturally occurring variant in dogs with progressive retinal atrophy (Mellersh et al, 2006, PMID: 16806805), and a knock-out mouse with a retinal phenotype that recapitulates the human condition (Zhao et al, 2003, PMID: 12651948). 

In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between *RPGRIP1* and *RPGRIP1*-related retinopathy, an autosomal recessive condition. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in research and clinical diagnostic settings and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina GCEP on July 2nd, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

GINS4 was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive combined immunodeficiency due to GINS4 deficiency by Conte et al in 2022 (PMID: 36345943). This condition is characterized by neutropenia, viral and bacterial infections, and NK cell deficiency with impaired maturation. The T and B cell counts along with immunoglobulin levels were within normal ranges for all patients. Half of the patients presented with either dental abscesses or gingivitis. Evidence supporting this gene-disease relationship includes case-level and experimental data. Of the 5 reported cases, one individual presented at birth with intrauterine growth restriction, growth delay, tonsillar hypertrophy, cryptorchidism, and developed seizures with intracranial calcification, suggestive of CMV infection because these features were not reported present in any of the other probands. By 3 years of age the patient experienced multiple infections including varicella, recurrent otitis media, necrotizing nasolabial ulcers, gastrointestinal sepsis, and pneumonia. The patient and sister were compound heterozygous (missense and non-sense); however the sister had a milder case including varicella and recurrent herpes labialis, which was also observed mother (non-sense mutation carrier) (PMID: 36345943). Functional studies using cells derived from this original family demonstrated variable NK cell maturation across the affected siblings despite the same genotype, thus supporting the variable expressivity within this family (PMID:40768335). A single missense variant, p.V171M was found homozygous in three reportedly unrelated families from the same region of Africa, Comoros, suggesting this may be a founder mutation (PMID:340510848). Both parents of each proband were reportedly healthy heterozygotes for a single variant, suggesting necessity of biallelic variants to cause disease. However, those with LOF variants may exhibit mild features.

This gene-disease relationship is supported by biochemical function, expression studies, functional assays, and protein interactions  (PMIDs: 36345943, 40768335). Briefly, the GINS4 protein was demonstrated to be a part of the GINS complex which is important for DNA replication, specifically it acts as a helicase to unwind DNA. Other genes within this complex have been demonstrated to lead to NK cell abnormalities when disrupted (eg; GINS1 deficiency). Conte et al (2022) demonstrated that the alterations identified in the original family impacts GINS4 stability and the stability of other GINS complex proteins. Furthermore, they showed that these variants are associated with mild delays in cell cycle progression, but does not impact DNA replication fork speed and symmetry but does impair mitotic exit and entry into S phase. With regards to its role in NK cell maturation, the same group demonstrated that GINS4 is essential for NK cell differentiation through study of affected individuals cells (PMID: 36345943 and 40768335). 

In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Whilst more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen SCID/CID GCEP on the meeting date November 20th 2025 (SOP Version 11).

Variants in the *CABP4* gene were first reported in relation to cases of night blindness with autosomal recessive inheritance in the year 2006 (Zeitz et al., PMID: 16960802). The spectrum of disease has subsequently expanded to include affected patients described with congenital cone-rod synaptic disorder (PMID: 19074807), Leber congenital amaurosis (PMID: 20157620), incomplete congenital stationary night blindness similar to Åland eye disease (PMID: 28002560), photoreceptor-bipolar cell transmission disorder (PMID: 29525873), or congenital stationary synaptic dysfunction (PMID: 28559085). These affected patients exhibit reduced visual acuity, often with onset in early childhood, that may remain stable for some time following diagnosis. Additional features can include nystagmus, photophobia, strabismus, color vision defects, night blindness, and/or electroretinogram responses showing an electronegative waveform or reduced amplitudes from cones and/or rods. A recent publication has also shown co-segregation of a *CABP4* variant with affected status in a family with autosomal dominant inheritance of nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy (PMID: 29108277). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the cases with a recessive mode of inheritance shared a biallelic loss-of-function mechanism, with overlapping phenotypes that were consistent with a single spectrum of disease. On the other hand, the autosomal dominant family was distinguished by the epilepsy phenotype that had not previously been noted among heterozygous carriers from the autosomal recessive pedigrees. Therefore, cases caused by inherited *CABP4* variants have been split into two separate disease entities, with the present curation focusing on autosomal recessive cases referred to as *CABP4*-related retinopathy.

Eight suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (three nonsense, two frameshift, two missense, and one disrupting a canonical splice site), which have been collectively reported in seven probands in six publications (PMID: 16960802  PMID: 19074807  PMID: 20157620  PMID: 28002560  PMID: 29525873  PMID: 28559085 ). All probands were homozygous or compound heterozygous for their respective variants, and none were reported to have consanguineous parents. One family had evidence of the variant segregating with affected status, but did not have a sufficient number of affected members to contribute to the scoring (PMID: 20157620). The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be biallelic loss-of-function, characterized in some cases by frameshift, nonsense, or canonical splice site variants predicted to result in nonsense-mediated decay.

This gene-disease association is also supported by experimental evidence that *CABP4* exhibits its highest expression levels in retina tissue (PMID: 30239781). *CABP4* encodes a calcium-binding protein that localizes to the presynaptic region and interacts with the Cav1.4 channel (encoded by the *CACNA1F* gene) to modulate its voltage activation (PMID: 15452577). A mouse model harboring a homozygous deletion of exons 1 and 2 recapitulates one of the features of the human patients by exhibiting reduced light-adapted and dark-adapted ERG responses, as well as reduced current responses from rod outer segments and reduced voltage-clamp flash measurements from rod bipolar cells (PMID: 15452577). Underlying these functional defects are histological abnormalities including thinning of the outer plexiform layer, fewer photoreceptor terminals in the outer plexiform layer, flat rod spherules and cone pedicles, and abnormal localization of presynaptic cytomatrix markers (PMID: 15452577). 

In summary, *CABP4* is definitively associated with *CABP4*-related retinopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence, leading to a Definitive classification. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina GCEP on September 3rd, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*CHST11* was first reported in relation to congenital disorder of glycosylation (also known as osteochondrodysplasia, brachydactyly, and overlapping malformed digits) in 2015 (Chopra et al., PMID: 26436107). Two variants (gross deletion, inframe deletion) that have been reported in two probands in two publications are included in this curation. This gene-disease relationship is also supported by segregation evidence (Shabbir et al., PMID: 29514872), biochemical function studies (Hiraoka, et al., PMID: 10781601), and a mouse model (Klüppel et al., PMID: 16079159). In summary, there is limited evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. Although more evidence is needed to support a causal role, no convincing evidence has emerged that contradicts the gene-disease relationship. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation GCEP on the meeting date October 5, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_original_title: severe early-onset pulmonary alveolar proteinosis due to MARS deficiency
submitted_as_notes: Methionyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (*MARS1*) was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive interstitial lung and liver disease in 2013 (van Meetl et al., PMID: 24103465). Features of disease can include but are not limited to: liver disease, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, anemia, and developmental delay. Age of onset for all cases in this curation were in either infancy or early childhood. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group, we found differences in the inheritance pattern and phenotypic variability. Therefore, the following disease entities have been split into multiple disease entities, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2U (OMIM: 616280) and Interstitial lung and liver disease (OMIM: 615486). The Spastic paraplegia 70, autosomal recessive (OMIM: 620323) and Trichothiodystrophy 9, nonphotosensitive (OMIM: 619692) entities were not curated due to limited case evidence avialable at the time of curation. The split curation for autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2U (OMIM: 616280) has been curated separately by the Charcot-Marie Tooth GCEP. 16 variants (14 missense, 1single amino acid insertion, and 1 nonsense) that have been reported in 11 probands in 10 publications (PMIDs: 24103465, 25913036, 37936900, 29655802, 30271085, 28148924, 34585293, 32833345, 34496286, 30723866) are included in this curation. The mechanism of pathogenicity appears to be loss of methionyl-tRNA synthetase activity and decreased methionine incorporation (PMIDs 24103465, 25913036). This gene-disease relationship is also supported by expression and biochemical function evidence where in vitro enzyme kinetics show a decrease in funciton for variant protein (PMIDs: 29775242, 23715323).  In summary, there is moderate evidence to support this gene-disease relationship. While more evidence is needed to establish this relationship definitively, no convincing contradictory evidence has emerged. This classification was approved by the ClinGen ILD GCEP on the meeting date October 20, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

disease_title: renal tubular acidosis, distal, 4, with hemolytic anemia
disease_original_title: renal tubular acidosis, distal, 4, with hemolytic anemia
submitted_as_notes:
The *SLC4A1* gene is located on chromosome 17 at cytoband q21.31. The gene encodes ​​both the erythroid (eAE1, band 3) and the kidney (kAE1) isoforms of the AE1 protein. There are two versions of this protein that differ in size: the 93kDa version in erythrocytes, and the 43kDa version in the alpha-intercalated cells in the kidney. The longer (93kDa) version of AE1, found in erythrocytes, has two regions: a 43kDa transmembrane chloride/bicarbonate exchanger protein and a 50kDa domain. In erythrocytes, the 43kDa transmembrane chloride/bicarbonate exchanger protein acts in facilitating carbon dioxide exchange between the erythrocytes and the tissues. In the kidney, the 43kDa transmembrane chloride/bicarbonate exchanger protein is found in the alpha-intercalated cells and is involved in release of acid into the urine (via Cl/HCO3- exchange). Importantly, this 43kDa transmembrane domain is fully functional on its own, including in the kidney. In addition to exchanging ions via the 43kDa transmembrane region, the longer AE1 protein (found in erythrocytes) has a 50kDa domain that anchors the membrane cytoskeleton to the membrane through an ankyrin-binding site (band 2.1) and also contains binding sites for hemoglobin and several glycolytic enzymes. Thus, SLC4A1 is a pleiotropic gene, with variation associated with both hematologic conditions (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis and ovalocytosis) and the renal disease entity of distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA).

Distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA), also often referred to as type 1 RTA, is caused by a decreased capacity of the α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct to excrete protons. This process is mediated by two proteins: the H+-ATPase (expressed at apical/luminal membrane) and Cl−/HCO3− exchanger AE1 (basolateral membrane).
Biochemically, this disorder is characterized by a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with normal plasma anion gap, hypokalaemia and hypercalciuria with hypocitraturia causing nephrocalcinosis. Due to disruption of urine acidification, urinary pH is >5.5. Common features of dRTA include: vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, failure to thrive and/or rickets. Patients may also present with muscle weakness or paralysis, which occurs secondary to severe hypokalemia, and/or polyuria, which may result from electrolyte imbalances. To date, multiple genes have been associated with dRTA: these include ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4, genes encoding subunits of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, which are associated with an autosomal recessive form of dRTA, and SLC4A1, which has been associated with both autosomal dominant distal renal tubular acidosis (AD-dRTA; MONDO:0008368; OMIM MIM #179800) and autosomal recessive renal tubular acidosis, distal, 4, with hemolytic anemia (AR-dRTA; MONDO:0012700; OMIM MIM #611590). 

*SLC4A1* has also been associated with autosomal dominant distal renal tubular acidosis (AD-dRTA; MONDO:0008368; OMIM MIM #179800). As autosomal dominant SLC4A1-dRTA and autosomal recessive SLC4A1-dRTA have different modes of inheritance and molecular mechanisms of disease (as reviewed in PMID: 19565014), they were split and curated separately per the guidelines outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Working Group and as approved by the ClinGen Tubulopathy Gene Curation Expert Panel. 

At least ten variants in *SLC4A1* have been associated with AR-dRTA with hemolytic anemia, including missense variants altering conserved amino acid residues in the transmembrane regions of the AE1 protein (e.g., p.G701D (PMID: 9854053) and p.S773P (PMID: 15211439) in transmembrane segments 9 and 10), as well as in-frame deletions (e.g., p.Val850del, PMID: 10926824) and protein-truncating variants (e.g., p.Q203*, PMID: 31933135). These variants have been identified in multiple cases, including homozygotes and compound heterozygotes, with familial segregation and supporting functional data (e.g., PMID: 9854053, PMID:22126643, PMID: 33068675, PMID: 20151848, PMID: 15211439, PMID: 15252044, PMID: 10942416, PMID: 17215882, PMID: 31933135, PMID: 10926824, PMID: 18266205, PMID: 20028337, PMID: 27718309) supporting the pathogenicity of these SLC4A1 variants for AR-dRTA with hemolytic anemia. 

The gene-disease association is further supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence, including biochemical function (PMID: 16239253), expression (PMID: 3618786), and rescue data (PMID: 21455273). There is also non-human model organism evidence: SLC4A1 knockout mouse models showed dRTA and nephrocalcinosis accompanied by hypercalciuria, hyperphosphaturia, and hypocitraturia (PMID: 17409310). In summary, the *SLC4A1* gene is Definitively associated with AR-dRTA with hemolytic anemia. The gene-disease association has been repeatedly demonstrated in both the research and clinical diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Tubulopathy GCEP on the meeting date 4/6/2022 (SOP Version 8).

disease_title: systemic lupus erythematosus related to C4A
disease_original_title: systemic lupus erythematosus related to C4A
submitted_as_notes:
The *C4A* gene encodes the acidic isoform of complement factor 4, part of the classical pathway. C4 protein deficiency was first reported in relation to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in the 1970’s, with specific C4A deficiency first reported in the 1980’s. Since then, many studies have investigated the evidence relating lower *C4A* copy number to increased risk of developing SLE.

Genetic evidence includes case reports of homozygous loss of *C4A* or absence of C4A protein (often called C4AQ0), which were not curated due to the lack of information on and thus potential variability of the deletion boundaries and absence of genetic information, respectively. A recent report of an SLE patient with a homozygous predicted loss of function variant in *C4A* and confirmed location of the variant in the *C4A* gene (PMID 40788338) has been given the maximum score (3 points).

A number of case-control studies of various cohort sizes and ancestries, as well as two meta-analyses (PMIDs 28205620, 32691186) have been published. Older case-control studies used allotyping/C4A protein detection and were therefore not scored. Nine case-control studies (PMIDs 7481564, 10529130, 12480675, 19287147, 23335107, 26800705, 29050534, 31387635, 35315244) show a statistically significant relationship between lower *C4A* copy number and increased risk of SLE. Six additional case-control studies (PMIDs 21904924, 22387014, 26814708, 29080553, 38594415) provide statistically significant support for the relationship between *C4A* and SLE, but lack gender matching between the case and control cohorts. Two large case-control studies (PMIDs 32499649, 40617727) used imputation to infer the copy number of *C4A* and also support the relationship. We awarded points to only a small number of these studies due to substantial uncertainty regarding the deletion boundaries. Three case-control studies (PMIDs 21695597, 34580371, 39800843) showed a lack of statistical significance. 

Experimental evidence includes a lupus mouse model where expression of the human *C4A* isotypic region leads to a reduction in autoimmunity relative to C4B-expressing mice (PMID 33147456).

In summary, there is **moderate** evidence supporting the relationship between *C4A* and autosomal recessive systemic lupus erythematosus. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Systemic and Incomplete Lupus Erythematosus GCEP on the meeting date December 10, 2025 (SOP Version 11).

The *RBP3* gene was first reported in relation to retinal disease in 2009, in affected members from a family with autosomal recessive inheritance who were diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa as adults (den Hollander et al., PMID: 19074801). Subsequent studies expanded the spectrum of disease to include individuals diagnosed with high myopia and retina dystrophy in childhood (PMID: 25766589). Affected individuals generally exhibit progressive loss of visual acuity, high myopia, tessellated fundus, night blindness, peripheral visual field constriction, reduced electroretinogram amplitudes from rods and/or cones, optical coherence tomography showing retinal thinning, pigmentary retinopathy with attenuation of retinal blood vessels, and/or cataracts. Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping & Splitting Working Group, the diverse cases shared similarities in their retinal features, mode of inheritance (autosomal recessive), and underlying molecular mechanism (biallelic loss-of-function). Therefore, cases caused by inherited RBP3 variants have been lumped into a single gene curation focusing on a disease entity referred to as *RBP3*-related retinopathy.

Nine suspected disease-causing variants were scored as part of this curation (one missense, seven nonsense, and one frameshift). These variants have been collectively reported in eight probands in four publications (PMID: 19074801, PMID: 25766589, PMID: 37806543, PMID: 40895869). The variant types and functional studies of disease-causing missense variants (PMID: 23486466) indicate that the mechanism of pathogenicity is biallelic loss-of-function. The reported families had relatively small numbers of affected individuals, so segregation evidence did not contribute to the scoring of the gene-disease relationship.

This gene-disease association is also supported by biochemical evidence that *RBP3* encodes an interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein that facilitates the transfer of retinoids in the visual cycle, helps to transport lipids between the RPE and photoreceptors, and has a thiol-dependent antioxidant activity that maintains the balance between reduction and oxidation in the retina (PMID: 33328889). *RBP3* shows highly specific expression in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (PMID: 30239781). Mice with homozygous knockout of the *Irbp* exon 1 and promoter show slowly progressive loss of photoreceptor nuclei and changes in the structural integrity of the receptor outer segments on histological exam (PMID: 10508404, PMID: 10750831) accompanied by histological confirmation of apoptosis (PMID: 21642628) and loss of rod and cone electroretinogram amplitude relative to wild-type and heterozygous controls (PMID: 9614228, PMID: 10750831). Partial coherence interferometry and photorefraction studies showed the mice increasingly become myopic (PMID: 21642628), despite minor defects in visual cycle kinetics including recovery of 11-cis-retinal and regeneration of rhodopsin (PMID: 10508404, PMID: 10750831).

In summary, *RBP3* has a Definitive association with *RBP3*-related retinopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina Gene Curation Expert Panel on May 20th, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*CTNNA1* was first reported in association with autosomal dominant maculopathy in 2016 (Saksens et al., PMID: 26691986). The retinal phenotype is characterized by adult-onset patterned pigmentary changes involving the macula and retinal pigment epithelium, initially described as butterfly-shaped pattern dystrophy. The disease is generally slowly progressive, although macular atrophy and choroidal neovascularization have also been reported.

The *CTNAA1*-related maculopathy phenotype was previously split from *CTNNA1*-related cancer predisposition by the Hereditary Cancer GCEP. The two conditions show distinct phenotypes and variant spectra: cancer is predominantly associated with loss-of-function variants, whereas the retinal phenotype is associated with heterozygous missense variants. No families with both phenotypes have been reported 

Seven unique missense variants have been reported in individuals with *CTNNA1*-related maculopathy (p.Glu307Lys, p.Leu318Ser, p.Ser322Leu, p.Thr325Ala, p.Ile431Met, p.Glu432Lys, and p.Ser439Phe, PMIDs: 26691986, 33137351, 38573304, 40455352). Several of these variants cluster within two regions of α-catenin, involving residues Leu318–Thr325 and Ile431–Glu432. The recurrent p.Leu318Ser variant segregated with the retinal phenotype in two families, with a combined estimated LOD score of 3.0.

The disease mechanism is not fully established. The reported missense variants cluster in regions of α-catenin involved in mechanosensing and adherens junction regulation. Experimental evidence includes *CTNNA1* expression in human retinal pigment epithelium, functional alteration in non-patient cells, and a *Ctnna1* mouse model (PMIDs: 23487591, 39786338, 26691986). The mouse model carries the missense variant p.Leu436Pro, which has not been reported in humans but is located close to disease-associated human variants. Heterozygous mice showed progressive retinal pigment mottling and structural and functional RPE abnormalities. *Ctnna1* knockout models were not scored, as loss of function does not appear to be the disease mechanism and these models mainly showed developmental eye abnormalities that did not closely resemble the human phenotype.

*CTNNA1* variants have also been reported in familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) (PMID: 33497368). This evidence was not included because the phenotype and proposed mechanism differ from *CTNNA1*-related patterned maculopathy and may represent a separate gene-disease relationship.

In summary, *CTNNA1* has a Definitive association with *CTNAA1*-related maculopathy. This has been repeatedly demonstrated in both research and diagnostic settings, and has been upheld over time without the emergence of contradictory evidence. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Retina GCEP on September 3rd, 2026 (SOP Version 12).

*C4B* was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) in 1984 (Voigtländer et al., PMID: 6084933). Early proband reports used allotyping (a protein-based assay) to report *C4B* copy number and can therefore not be used as evidence (PMIDs: 6084933, 3265961, 7814456). The relationship between *C4B* copy number variation and SLE has been assessed in a number of case-control studies with various cohort sizes and ancestries. The genotyping techniques used in these case-control studies generally did not support the detection and evaluation of precise deletion/duplication boundaries. Overall, 14 case-control studies found no statistically significant difference in *C4B* copy number between cases and controls (PMIDs: 12480675, 17503323, 19287147, 21904924, 23335107, 26814708, 27274095, 29050534, 29080553, 34580371, 35315244, 38594415, 39800843, 40617727). Five case-control studies found a significantly lower (PMIDs: 9777334, 22387014, 26800705, 31387635, 32499649), while one cohort/study found a significantly higher *C4B* copy number in cases compared to controls (PMIDs: 22387014). Two meta-analyses found no effect of *C4B* copy number on SLE risk (PMIDs: 28205620, 32691186). 

In summary, there is **limited** evidence supporting the relationship between *C4B* and autosomal recessive systemic lupus erythematosus. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Systemic and Incomplete Lupus Erythematosus GCEP on the meeting date March 11, 2026 (SOP Version 11).

OTUD1 is a deubiquitinase that was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant autoimmune disease in 2018 (Lu et al., PMID: 30100102). 

Variants in *OTUD1* have been reported in individuals with the following disease entities: systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ulcerative colitis (UC) (Lu et al., PMID: 30100102). Per criteria outlined by the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting guidelines, we found no difference in the potential molecular mechanism or inheritance pattern. Therefore, SLE, RA and UC were lumped into one disease entity, autoimmune disease.

Genetic evidence included in this curation consists of 7 heterozygous missense variants that have been reported in 10 individuals in two publications (PMIDs: 30100102, 41930824).

Experimental evidence showed an effect of 4 of the variants on the deubiquitinase activity of OTUD1 (PMID: 30100102). An *OTUD1* homozygous null mouse model showed increased susceptibility to dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis (PMID: 34876703).

In summary, there is **limited** evidence supporting the relationship between *OTUD1* and autosomal dominant autoimmune disease. This classification was approved by the ClinGen Monogenic Systemic and Incomplete Lupus Erythematosus GCEP on the meeting date August 12, 2026 (SOP Version 12).
